                                                 Preface
   TC 3-97.61 is the Army’s doctrinal publication for military mountaineering. It provides doctrinal guidance
   and direction for how U.S. forces train military mountaineers to operate in complex and mountainous terrain.
   This training circular is designed to work in conjunction with and complement ATP 3-21.50 and
   ATP 3-90.97. This manual enables leaders and Soldiers to understand mountain and cold-weather
   environments; their effects on personnel, operations, and equipment; and most importantly, how units train
   Soldiers to prepare to deploy in complex mountain environments.
   The principle audience for this publication is all members of the profession of arms. Commanders and staffs
   at all levels, including Army headquarters serving as joint task force or multinational headquarters, should
   also refer to applicable joint or multinational doctrine concerning military mountaineering techniques and
   procedures. Trainers and educators throughout the Army will use this publication to tailor their curriculum
   to the demands of military mountaineering.
   This publication provides the conceptual framework for conventional forces to train Soldiers in military
   mountaineering and serves as a foundation for more demanding collective mountain warfare training. It
   addresses training for mountain and cold weather at the tactical level. (See ATP 3-21.50 for higher-level
   collective information.)
   Commanders, staffs, and subordinates ensure that their decisions and actions comply with applicable United
   States, international, and, in some cases, host-nation laws and regulations. Commanders at all levels ensure
   that their Service members operate in accordance with the law of armed conflict and the rules of engagement.
   (See FM 6-27 for legal compliance.)
   The use of a trade or brand name does not constitute endorsement of the product or website.
   TC 3-97.61 uses joint terms where applicable. Selected joint and Army terms and definitions appear in both
   the glossary and the text. Terms for which TC 3-97.61 is the proponent publication (the authority) are marked
   with an asterisk (*) in the glossary. When first defined in the text, terms for which TC 3-97.61 is the proponent
   publication are boldfaced and italicized, and definitions are boldfaced. When first defining other proponent
   definitions in the text, the term is italicized with the proponent designator and number at the of the definition.
   Following uses of the term are not italicized.
   TC 3-97.61 applies to the Active Army, Army National Guard/Army National Guard of the United States,
   and United States Army Reserve unless otherwise stated.
   The proponent for this publication is the United States Army Maneuver Center of Excellence. The preparing
   agency is the United States Army Maneuver Center of Excellence, Department of Tactics, Training, and
   Doctrine. Send comments and recommendations on DA Form 2028 (Recommended Changes to Publications
   and Blank Forms) to Commander, U.S. Army Mountain Warfare School, ATTN: MWS-Z, 08 Mountain
   School Road, Jericho, Vermont 05465; by email to: ng.vt.vtarng.list.amwsinfo@army.mil; or submit an
   electronic DA Form 2028.




26 November 2025                                   TC 3-97.61                                                     xv
This page intentionally left blank.
                                             Introduction
   Operating in a mountainous environment is a continual exercise in problem solving and critical thinking.
   This document presents proven, utilitarian techniques for approaching the mountain and cold-weather
   problem issues. This training circular should not be interpreted as prescriptive in nature but rather a starting
   place and solid reference for best practices and risk mitigation. There is no substitute for experience and
   practice when dealing with mountainous environments. As the old adage goes, “There are bold climbers and
   there are old climbers. There are no bold old climbers.”
   TC 3-97.61 incorporates changes to terminology, concepts, constructs and proven tactics, techniques, and
   procedures (TTP) developed during the past decade in military mountaineering.
   The following summarizes each chapter and appendix in TC 3-97.61:
       • Chapter 1 establishes a working definition and classification of mountainous terrain. While some of
            this content is self-explanatory, it is imperative for leaders, especially in the light Infantry
            community, to be intimately familiar with the dismounted mobility classification tool and its
            implications on movement and maneuver.
       • Chapter 2 contains important changes to the qualification levels of military mountaineers and basic
            guidance on unit-level training programs. While operating in mountainous terrain is an
            environmental variable and not a mission, leaders must understand that they will often be forced to
            fight both the enemy and the environment. A unit that can successfully fight in the mountains can
            rapidly adapt to fighting in other conditions; in contrast, a unit untrained in mountain operations will
            not be able to rapidly transition.
       • Chapter 3 contains information on the multitude of environmental injuries common to operating in
            the mountains. Diagnosing and treating these injuries should be a training priority for medical
            personnel preparing to move into a cold weather or high-altitude environment.
       • Chapter 4 touches on the requirement for a base high level of physical fitness due to the exertion
            needed to exist and move in mountainous terrain. Soldiers require additional caloric intake to
            maintain peak performance in these conditions. While it may seem counterintuitive, dehydration is
            a common problem experienced by Soldiers operating in the cold. Critical to the success of any unit
            operating in these conditions is not only having the proper clothing and equipment but also
            understanding its proper wear and application. Knowing how to function and being “comfortably
            cool” are acquired skills.
       • Chapter 5 focuses on identifying and mitigating the avalanche threat. Snow science is a discipline
            in itself, but by following these basic tenets, units can intelligently navigate the risks of operating in
            avalanche terrain and respond to avalanches when they occur.
       • Chapter 6 provides details on movement techniques unique to the mountain environment and
            introduces basic climbing equipment and principles. This chapter also provides information on
            over-snow mobility including the use of alpine ski techniques, snowshoeing, the wear and
            application of crampons, and ice climbing.
       • Chapter 7 elaborates on many of the principles found in TC 3-25.26. Specifically, it focuses on the
            nuance of orientation and navigating and route finding under conditions where the most direct route
            is often undesirable due to limitations imposed by technical terrain features.
       • Chapter 8 provides step-by-step guides to the knots military mountaineers will require during system
            construction and navigating terrain problems. A thorough understanding and working knowledge of
            these knots and principles are required before attempting any of the tasks detailed in the remainder
            of this training circular. All unit members operating in mountainous terrain need to be proficient in
            the contents of this chapter. As this knowledge is extremely perishable, refresher training on these
            topics should be a recurring part of any training schedule.
       • Chapter 9 details the general principles of anchor construction and provides step-by-step instructions
            for constructing tree, rock, earth, snow, and ice anchors. As most mountaineering accidents occur




26 November 2025                                    TC 3-97.61                                                   xvii
Introduction



               at the anchor, increased focus should be given to gaining Soldier experience in anchor site selection
               and construction.
        •      Chapter 10 covers under what conditions it is appropriate to move on and off rope. Specifically
               addressed are top rope climbing, lead climbing, alpine belay techniques, and three-man climbing
               techniques. Top rope climbing is the preferred method to familiarize untrained personnel and level 1
               mountaineers with the principles of climbing. In an operational environment, leaders must balance
               the need for speed and security with the inherent fall hazards associated with climbing outside of a
               training environment.
        •      Chapter 11 discusses fixed ropes. Moving along a fixed rope is a terrific way to reduce fall hazards
               and increase control of the element while moving through technical terrain. In a limited amount of
               time, inexperienced personnel can be taught to navigate difficult terrain successfully and safely
               along fixed ropes. Also discussed in this chapter are principles of rappelling and more advanced
               methods of ascending and descending while hanging from a fixed rope.
        •      Chapter 12 is an overview on how operating in a mountainous environment often requires moving
               Soldiers, weapon systems, and equipment up, over, down, and around steep rugged terrain. This
               chapter also delivers instructions on the principles of mechanical advantage for lifting and creating
               friction in lowering.
        •      Chapter 13 covers the advantages, disadvantages, and applicability of individual, team, and belayed
               crossing techniques. Seasonal snowmelt will frequently create water obstacles of varying width,
               depth, and current. Ideally, any personnel who may be required to perform stream crossings are
               competent swimmers. Risk management during any water crossing should include personnel serving
               in a lifeguard/safety role and medics prepared to treat hypothermia.
        •      Chapter 14 discusses the fundamentals of glacier travel and crevasse rescue. Glaciers cover
               10 percent of the earth’s land. Climate change has increased the trafficability of the Arctic
               Northwest Passage and technological gains have made it possible to access natural resources in
               several inhospitable climates where it was previously infeasible. The Army’s ability to maneuver
               and fight on glaciers will become increasingly relevant in the coming years.
        •      Chapter 15 elaborates on the requirements for units operating in these environments to prepare for
               prolonged field care and practice high- and low-angle rescue scenarios.
        •      Chapter 16 outlines techniques for establishing tensioned rope systems used to move equipment and
               casualties over linear-vertical terrain obstacles. These techniques can save time and reduce the risk
               associated with crossing such obstacles. Mountain streams and ravines present a significant hazard
               and barrier to dismounted troop and equipment movement.
        •      Appendix A describes prominent classification systems for general dismounted movement in
               terrain, as well as various types of rock climbing and ice climbing routes. Military mountaineers
               require a common language for classifying routes so that difficulties associated with navigating
               them can be clearly communicated during operations.
        •      Appendix B discusses the use of nonmilitary route planning resources, such as online collections of
               climbing routes and guidebooks. Open-source route planning tools complement doctrinal techniques
               and military resources. Given that few suitable mountaineering sites exist on military installations,
               off-post sites need to be considered for training.
        •      Appendix C covers general standards for mountaineering equipment and identifies the contents and
               implications of various Army mountaineering kits. Throughout this publication, military
               mountaineering equipment is presented and discussed along with the techniques to employ it as
               applicable. However, certain general aspects of military mountaineering equipment do not fit into
               the flow of any of this training circular’s primary chapters.




xviii                                               TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                 Chapter 1
                                  Mountain Environment
   Around the world, mountain ranges form natural borders and boundaries. Historically, they
   have formed the edge of human settlement and wilderness; today, mountains still define many
   national borders and conflict regions. Mountain environments are demanding and tough, with
   conditions that interfere with all warfighting functions. To fight in the complex terrain of
   mountainous regions, military mountaineers must become familiar with the significant
   challenges that this environment presents. This rugged terrain will prove to be an overwhelming
   challenge to the untrained and inexperienced Soldier. Military mountaineers must understand
   how mountain environment characteristics affect them, the mission, their equipment, and the
   enemy during military operations. Rough terrain slows movements and canalizes troops into
   narrow corridors. Steep slopes make vehicle traffic possible only on roads that require
   extensive engineering and are vulnerable to attack and natural hazards, such as rockslides and
   avalanches. Harsh weather limits air resupply and close air support. Radio communications can
   only be maintained by securing exposed ridge tops. Key terrain often requires significant effort
   to secure and an even larger commitment to sustain. To succeed in this environment, Soldiers
   must be prepared mentally and physically.

SECTION I – MOUNTAIN TERRAIN
   1-1. Mountains exist all over the world and their character is defined by their climate and geology. Regardless
   of their differences, a common feature of all mountains is rugged terrain. This rugged, broken environment
   presents additional challenges to movement and survival to those experienced in most combat environments.
   Operations in the mountains require Soldiers to be physically fit and leaders to be experienced in this terrain.
   (See figure 1-1, page 2.) Problems arise in moving men and transporting loads up and down steep and varied
   terrain. Operational success is contingent on our ability to understand the environment, recognize hazards,
   and anticipate problems.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                  1
Chapter 1




            Figure 1-1. Soldiers in mountainous terrain



2                           TC 3-97.61                    26 November 2025
                                                                                                 Mountain Environment



DEFINITION: TYPES AND FORMATIONS OF MOUNTAINS
   1-2. Mountains are landforms that rise more than 500 meters above the surrounding plain and are
   characterized by steep slopes. They may rise abruptly from the plains to form a giant barrier or ascend
   gradually as a series of parallel ridges extending unbroken for great distances. Cliffs and precipices may be
   near vertical or even overhanging. Mountains may have isolated peaks, rounded crests, eroded ridges, and
   high plains. They may be cut by valleys, gorges, and deep ravines. High rocky crags with glaciated peaks
   and year-round snow-cover exist in mountain ranges at most latitudes along the western portion of the Americas,
   in Europe, and in Asia.

MOUNTAIN BUILDING
   1-3. Understanding the processes and the conditions under which mountains form helps us to understand
   their structures and hazards. The two primary mechanisms for mountain building are volcanic and tectonic
   activity. Volcanoes are constructed from lava and ash, which begin within the earth as magma. Tectonic
   activity causes plates to collide, heaving up fold mountains, or to pull apart and crack, forming fault-block
   mountain ranges.
TYPICAL MOUNTAIN STRUCTURES
   1-4. The massive slabs composing the outer layer of the earth are called tectonic plates. Their movement
   relative to each other creates earthquakes, volcanoes, ocean trenches, and mountain ridge systems. The
   different horizontal and vertical stresses that create mountains usually produce complex patterns. Each type
   of stress produces a typical structure, and most mountains can be described in terms of the following structures:
        • Dome mountains—a simple, upward bulge of the crust forms dome mountains. They are usually the
              result of the upward movement of magma and the folding of the rock layers overhead. Erosion may
              strip away the overlying layers, exposing the central igneous core.
        • Fault-block mountains—faulting, or cracking of the crust into large chunks, often accompanies
              upwarp, a broad low arching of the surface, which results in fault-block mountains. The motion of
              chunks along these faults creates various forms of mountains.
        • Fold mountains—tectonic forces, in which continental plates collide or ride over each other, have
              given rise to the most common mountain form: fold mountains. When erosion strips down the
              overburden of rock from folded mountain ranges, the oldest, central core is all that remains.
        • Volcanic mountains—along convergent plate boundaries, volcanic activity increases. As volcanic
              activity is forced underneath an overriding neighbor, continental crust melts and turns to magma
              within the mantle. Since it is less dense than the surrounding material, it rises and erupts to form volcanoes.
        • Complex mountains—most ranges are complex mountains with portions that have been subject to
              several processes. These processes occur at both the macro and the micro level. One massive fold
              can make an entire mountain peak; however, there are folds measured by rope length, and tiny folds
              found within a handhold.
EROSION AND GLACIATION
   1-5. Even as mountain massifs are being pushed up, they begin to crumble and wear away. The two main
   processes that shape mountains are erosion and glaciation.
   1-6. Erosion is when precipitation scours soil and loose rock from the steep slopes of mountains. Cycles of
   freeze-thaw exert tremendous force in cracks and fissures in the rock. These forces break apart softer rock
   and wash the fragments away down creeks and drainages, forming many of the gullies and smaller terrain
   features on the mountains.
   1-7. Glaciation is when glaciers are rivers of ice and rocks that slowly move down mountains. They form
   when the rate of snowfall exceeds the rate of melting in summer months. After accumulations over hundreds
   of years, the snow compresses into ice that can range from ten to several hundred feet thick. Glaciers can be
   small and only cover a portion of a mountain, or they can be massive with a series of glaciers covering a
   mountain range. They are a powerful force for carving and moving rock and form many of the large features
   we observe in the mountains.




26 November 2025                                    TC 3-97.61                                                        3
Chapter 1



TERRAIN FEATURES AND TERMS
    1-8. Common geologic terminology includes—
         • Summit, peak—the highest point.
         • Spire—a tall, narrow rock formation, resembling a steeple.
         • Ridge—a line of high ground with height variations along its crest.
         • Valley—low ground bordered on the sides by higher ground. A valley may or may not contain a
            stream course. A valley generally has maneuver room within its confines.
         • Hanging valley—a valley whose lower end is high on a sheer wall of a larger valley into which it flows.
         • Saddle—a dip or low point along the crest of a ridge. A saddle is not necessarily the lower ground
            between two hilltops; it may be a break along an otherwise level ridge crest.
         • Pass—any route from one valley over higher ground to another valley. Usually, a relatively low
            point along a ridge. Many regional synonyms exist to describe pass, such as the word notch in New
            England.
         • Col—the low point on a ridge joining two peaks. Glaciologists reserve this term for gaps of glacial
            origin, but others use it much more generally.
         • Cirque—a bowl-shaped valley high on a mountain, usually of glacial origin. Also referred to as
            simply a bowl.
         • Draw—like a valley, except that it normally is a less developed stream course. The ground slopes
            upward on each side and toward the head of the draw.
         • Gully—a channel caused by erosion, especially by water running down a slope. A gully is generally
            narrower and steeper than a draw.
         • Couloir—a narrow snow- or ice-filled gully.
         • Spur—a usually short, continuously sloping line of higher ground, normally jutting out from the
            side of a ridge.
         • Arête—a narrow, rocky spur.
         • Buttress—a prominent feature that juts out from a rock or mountain, like the buttress that supports
            the roof of a cathedral.
         • Gendarme—a steep-sided tower along a ridge, guarding or blocking the way.
         • Shoulder—a lateral protrusion on a mountain, or a point on the mountain where the slope changes,
            forming a convex shape.
         • Headwall—vertical or near-vertical section of slope at the uphill end (head) of a valley, ravine, or
            cirque.
         • Cliff—a vertical or near-vertical slope.
         • Ledge—a narrow, flat spot along an otherwise vertical face.
         • Snow field—a field of perennial snow.

SECTION II – MOUNTAIN TERRAIN COMPOSITION
    1-9. Mountain terrain composition can substantially affect the speed and safety of movement during military
    operations. An understanding of compositional factors is important to determine appropriate movement
    techniques, appropriate protective techniques, and realistic estimations of movement time.

VEGETATION
    1-10. Surface composition is highly variable in mountainous terrain. Slopes can be steep, broken, rocky,
    thickly vegetated, and ice or snow covered. Any of these conditions can have a significant impact on military
    operations, and often more than one of these conditions are found concurrently.
CLIMATE
    1-11. Major mountain ranges force air masses and storm systems to drop significant amounts of rain and
    snow on the windward side of the range. As air masses pass over mountains, the leeward (opposite of the
    windward side) slopes receive far less precipitation than the windward slopes. It is common for the climate
    on the windward side of a mountain range to be humid and the climate on the leeward side to be arid. This



4                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                          Mountain Environment



   phenomenon affects both coastal and inland mountains. As a result, vegetation and forest characteristics are
   different between these areas.
ARID REGIONS
   1-12. In areas receiving little rainfall, there may be little vegetation. Much of the terrain is composed of hard
   ground, which is firmly compacted, rocky soil. Any existing vegetation is minimal and provides minimal
   protection from the elements.
DENSE FOREST
   1-13. In most temperate mountain ranges, the lower elevations are covered in dense forest. These areas can
   provide good concealment and protection from weather. Steep slopes may require greater levels of fitness
   and more time to move through than woodlands in flat terrain, but the tactics, techniques, and procedures
   (TTP) for moving and fighting remain the same.
THICK BRUSH
   1-14. Near tree line, high winds, ice buildup, and poor soil cause the trees to grow in dense mats. The branches
   may grow together so tightly that Soldiers may have to walk above or crawl below the tangle of branches.
   Natural breaks, such as old rockslides, creek beds, and existing trails may provide corridors for movement.
   Concealment is excellent as the outline is broken well, but any movement can be easily visible.
   Small-diameter spruce and fir trees provide limited cover from small arms fire.
GRASSY SLOPES
   1-15. Higher in the mountains, soil depth and quality deteriorate, and conditions become too harsh for trees.
   Slopes with enough soil are often covered with grass tussocks and low shrubs. Passing above tree line, the
   first major change in hazards occurs. Without trees and vegetation, there is the possibility of long, tumbling
   falls that cannot be arrested. Grassy slopes are slippery after rain, new snow, and dew. After long, dry spells,
   clumps of slope tend to become fragile and break away. From a tactical standpoint, moving above tree line
   changes the exposure of our elements. Open areas can be observed from long distances. Limited cover means
   large elements can be decisively engaged in open areas by relatively small elements in advantageous terrain
   or by indirect fires directed by observation posts. Tactical maneuver above tree line favors small elements,
   using terrain masking and surprise.

ROCK
   1-16. Steep slopes have few features that hold soil. Where soil is washed away, there is only exposed rock.
   Rock comes in many forms and is classified by origin and mineral composition:
       • Igneous rocks—igneous rocks form from cooled magma. The two main categories are intrusive and
            extrusive:
             Plutonic (intrusive) rocks—slow crystallization from deeply buried magmas generally means
                 good climbing, since the minerals formed are relatively large and interwoven into a solid matrix.
                 Weathering develops protrusions of resistant minerals, which make for either a rough-surfaced
                 rock with excellent friction or, if the resistant crystals are much larger than the surrounding
                 matrix, a surface with numerous knobby holds.
             Granite—granite is a very hard rock and provides good climbing. It produces less rockfall than
                 softer rock, but when rock breaks away, it may be as large boulders. After a rain, granite dries
                 quickly. Most protection is found in cracks. Face climbing can be found; however, it is not
                 easily protected.
             Volcanic (extrusive) rocks—explosive eruptions eject molten rock so quickly into the air that
                 it hardens into loose aerated masses of fine crystals and uncrystallized glass (obsidian). When
                 this ash consolidates while molten or after cooling, it is called tuff—a weak rock that breaks
                 down quickly and erodes easily. Quieter eruptions, from which widespread lava flows from
                 large fissures, produce basalt. Basaltic rocks are fine-grained and often sharp-edged.
       • Sedimentary rocks—sedimentary rocks are born high in the mountains, where erosion grinds down
            debris and moves it down to rivers for transportation to its final deposition in valleys, lakes, or
            oceans. As sediments accumulate, the bottom layers are solidified by pressure and by mineral



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                   5
Chapter 1



             cements precipitated from percolating groundwater. Gravel and boulders are transformed into
             conglomerates, sandy beaches into sandstone, beds of mud into mudstone or shale, and shell beds
             and coral reefs into limestone or dolomite. Although, in general, sedimentary rocks are much more
             friable than those cooled from molten magmas, pressure and cementing often produce solid rocks.
              Chalk and limestone—chalk and limestone are slippery when wet. Limestone is usually solid;
                  however, conglomerate-type stones may be loose. Limestone has pockets, face climbing, and
                  cracks.
              Sandstone—sandstone is usually soft, causing handholds and footholds to break away under
                  pressure. Chocks placed in sandstone may or may not hold. Sandstone should be allowed to dry
                  for a couple of days after rain before climbing on it; wet sandstone is very soft. Most climbs
                  follow a crack. Face climbing is possible, but any outward pull breaks handholds and footholds.
                  Sandstone is usually difficult to protect.
        •    Metamorphic rocks—these are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been altered physically or
             chemically by the tremendous heat and pressures within the earth. After sediments are solidified,
             high heat and pressure can cause their minerals to recrystallize. Shale changes to slate or schist,
             sandstone and conglomerate into quartzite, and limestone to marble. These changes may be minimal,
             only slightly altering the sediments, or extensive enough to produce gneiss, which is almost
             indistinguishable from igneous rock. Higher degrees of metamorphism or metamorphism of the
             right rocks provide a solid climbing surface. Examples are slate and gneiss, which can be firm and
             brittle in the same area (red coloring indicates brittle areas). Rock fall danger is high, and small
             rocks may break off when pulled or when pitons are placed.
MOVEMENT ON ROCK
    1-17. As softer rock and materials are eroded, the remaining rock formations are often steeper and more
    prominent than the surrounding surfaces. These cliffs, buttresses, and rocky arêtes often form terrain features
    that can mask maneuver, and their weaknesses form the unlikely avenues of approach used for infiltration
    and attacks. Moving over rock is risky and the consequences of falling can be high. A fall often cannot be
    arrested and leads to death or injury. The movement skills for negotiating steep rock faces and the technical
    skills for protecting that movement comprise a major portion of mountaineering training.
SCREE
    1-18. Scree refers to small rocks, from pebble size to dinner-plate size. It accumulates in areas abundant with
    weak, brittle rock. These small stones do not settle into stable slopes. Climbing scree is inefficient because it
    is unstable, with each step sliding down as weight is placed upon it. Firmer footing may be found around the
    edge of rock outcroppings. Scree can be descended quickly by sliding on one’s feet but should be done so
    under control.
TALUS
    1-19. Talus refers to rocks larger than a dinner plate but smaller than boulders. They can be used as
    steppingstones to ascend or descend a slope. The stability of talus can vary. Time, exposure to weather, snow,
    and foot traffic all help to shift rocks into positions where they are more secure and dislodge insecure rocks.
    More recent rockfall is often less stable, and it is more likely that large rocks will be displaced as one moves
    through it. Rockfall can be a hazard, but the most prevalent hazard is loose footing, which causes lower
    orthopedic injuries. Ascending talus is more efficient than ascending scree and requires less energy.
BOULDERS
    1-20. Boulders are rocks that are larger than can be carried. They indicate good rock quality in the
    surrounding cliffs. In general, boulders form into relatively stable fields where Soldiers may need to hop
    from boulder to boulder and can do so without dislodging them. Boulders can be in precarious positions and
    can be catastrophically destructive if they roll. The large spaces between boulders and their solid nature can
    provide effective cover.
MANAGING ROCKFALL
    1-21. Blocks and scree at the base of a cliff can indicate recurring rockfall. Light-colored spots on the rock
    wall above may indicate the impact of falling rock or areas where large portions of rock have recently


6                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Environment



      detached. Avoiding boulder fields, talus, and cliffs that show extensive signs of rockfall is the best way to
      avoid the threat of rockfall. Gullies and couloirs, while offering breaks in steeper terrain, also act as funnels
      for falling rock or ice. When traveling suspect areas, alert the group of the hazard and choose a path that does
      not place Soldiers in a position below others who may dislodge rocks. In small groups, keeping close together
      prevents falling rock from generating enough force to cause harm. At other times, the best measure may be
      to use sheltered stances, exposing only one or two Soldiers to the hazard at a time. During thaws in the spring
      and early summer, timing may be the best tool. Avoid traveling in gullies and other areas prone to rockfall
      during the heat of the day, when rocks may be shifting positions.

RIVERS
      1-22. Mountains are home to several water sources, including freshwater springs, lakes, and streams.
      Mountain streambeds may be dry or contain a significant amount of water. Steep contours make for fast
      moving water; small streams can be dangerous to cross. Water level fluctuates rapidly with storm runoff or
      snowmelt. Flash floods are possible after heavy rain. The likelihood of a flash flood after heavy rain can be
      greater during spring snowmelt. A storm that produces heavy rain higher on the mountain could produce a
      flash flood lower on the mountain. It is important to be aware of this risk and plan accordingly.

SNOW
      1-23. In most of the mountain ranges on earth above 5,000 feet, snowfall potential exists year-round.
TYPES OF SNOW
      1-24. There are many different types of snow with their own unique characteristics. Each type presents
      various challenges during military operations.

New Snow
      1-25. New snow makes easy terrain slick and dangerous. Maneuvering elements leave tracks that show their
      routes and relative size. It makes roads impassable for units that cannot clear them of snow and with vehicles
      that are not equipped with tire chains for traction. The distance for foot movements is significantly reduced
      for troops without snowshoes, skis, and over-the-snow vehicles. Movements are slowed even for properly
      trained and equipped troops. Steep, snow-covered terrain presents the risk of avalanches.

Firm Spring Snow (Firm Snow)
      1-26. As snow goes through cycles of warming and cooling, it settles into a denser snowpack. A snowpack
      is the entire mass of snow covering a given area of terrain. Dense, old snow can provide a uniform surface
      that covers obstacles. The character of the snow can vary greatly with temperature and sun exposure. Snow
      is generally firm during the night and early morning, providing efficient travel but an increased risk of long
      sliding falls. The snow softens with warmer temperatures and direct sunlight.

Soft Snow
      1-27. Soft snow can be easier to negotiate without stiff boots and crampons, and the fall hazard is reduced.
      However, if it is too soft, travel becomes more difficult. Movement on steeper slopes requires an ice axe,
      crampons, and the necessary training with this equipment. (See chapter 6, section II.)
ICE
      1-28. Ice forms in a few different ways as described below. Any movement on ice demands crampons. (See
      chapter 6, section II.)
          • Alpine ice forms in steep, sheltered couloirs and on glaciers, where firm snow consolidates into a
               mass of ice. It forms in a plane at the angle of the slope. Even at moderate angles, it can be physically
               demanding due to the lack of stances for rest and the hardness of the ice.
          • Waterfall ice forms when ambient temperatures are cold enough to freeze water quickly and water
               flows or seeps over cliffs and exposed rock faces. Waterfall ice can form much steeper flows than




26 November 2025                                    TC 3-97.61                                                   7
Chapter 1



             alpine ice, often with freestanding vertical columns or overhangs where drips freeze quickly.
             However, waterfall ice also forms bulges and steps that allow stances to rest and place protection.
        •    Verglas is a thin sheet of ice that forms when rain or dripping water freezes on colder rocks. Verglas
             is too thin to climb like ice and makes conventional rock climbing impossible.
GLACIERS
    1-29. When enough ice accumulates in the peaks, it begins to flow down the mountain. Valleys in the high
    mountains may be buried under massive glaciers and present additional hazards, such as hidden crevasses
    and icefalls. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest
    passage through the more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. (See chapter 14 for information
    on glacial travel.)

SECTION III – TERRAIN ANALYSIS
    1-30. Terrain analysis is critical to every decision and task when planning an operation in mountainous
    terrain. Substantial experience moving and living in a wide variety of terrain is essential to effective terrain
    analysis. Military mountaineers can use the standard Army acronym for observation and fields of fire,
    avenues of approach, key terrain, obstacles, and cover and concealment (OAKOC) as a guide during terrain
    analysis.

OBSERVATION AND FIELDS OF FIRE
    1-31. Observation in mountains varies extensively due to weather and ground cover. The dominating height
    of mountainous terrain and sparse vegetation generally permits excellent long-range observation.
    Well-placed elements in the high ground can typically observe and affect much of the terrain. However,
    rapidly changing weather with frequent periods of high winds, rain, snow, sleet, hail, and fog can limit
    visibility. The rugged nature of the terrain often produces dead space at midranges.
    1-32. Low cloud cover at higher elevations may neutralize the effectiveness of operations established on
    peaks or mountaintops. High wind speeds and sound often mask the noises of troop movement. Several
    operations may need to be established laterally, in-depth, and at varying altitudes to provide visual coverage
    of the battle area.
    1-33. Conversely, the nature of the terrain can provide concealment from observation. This concealment can
    be obtained in the dead space. Mountainous regions are subject to intense shadowing effects when the sun is
    low in relatively clear skies. The high contrast from light to shaded areas considerably reduces visual
    sharpness within shaded regions. These shadowed areas can provide increased concealment when combined
    with other camouflage, and they should be considered in maneuver plans.
    1-34. Fields of fire, like observation, are excellent at long ranges. However, dead space is a problem at short
    ranges. Rocky, broken terrain favors dispersed teams that can cover the many approaches to their position.
    Range determination is deceptive in mountainous terrain. Soldiers must routinely train in range estimation in
    mountainous regions to maintain their proficiency.

AVENUES OF APPROACH
    1-35. The rugged nature of terrain creates many natural obstacles. Maneuver elements are constrained to the
    few movement corridors for which they have the appropriate training and equipment to negotiate. Mountains
    usually favor the defense. Units in dominating terrain can ward off large attacks easily. However, the
    difficulty of sustaining forces in the high ground, their exposure to bad weather, as well as the many
    approaches created by the rugged terrain means defending forces cannot cover all avenues of approach. They
    focus their limited combat power on the approaches from which they expect an attack. Historically, large
    attacks along easy approaches in the mountains have failed. Attacks are more likely to succeed by using
    troops that can exploit unexpected avenues of approach, with adequate reconnaissance, rehearsals, and the
    element of surprise.




8                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                           Mountain Environment



KEY AND DECISIVE TERRAIN
   1-36. Mountain warfare is a fight to control roads, and the lines of communication (LOCs) located in valleys.
   Controlling them enables the movement of road-bound critical supplies and heavy combat assets, such as
   tanks that must transit through the mountains to other fronts of the battlefield. The decisive terrain for control
   of these LOCs is often the passes. Here, the valleys narrow and rise, limiting the maneuver of armor and
   mechanized units. The terrain canalizes these forces into terrain dominated by the surrounding heights. Here,
   these assets experience degradation of their maneuver and firepower capability, making them vulnerable to
   attacks from mobile and light mountain infantry forces. The unit that holds this decisive terrain can protect
   its own heavy assets as it moves through mountainous terrain and destroys enemy assets attempting to take
   the same route.
   1-37. The high ground offers a tactical advantage to whoever holds it. In the valley, cover shrinks when
   engaged from an elevated position. On the heights, even relatively small cover gives protection from direct
   fires from the valley and using ridge crests allows units to maneuver while masked by terrain. However, the
   tactical advantage of holding high ground is also resource intensive. Occupying and then sustaining mountain
   positions require a significant commitment of support that may make long-term occupation difficult or
   impossible.

OBSTACLES
   1-38. Mountain terrain is defined by its rugged character. Cliff bands, steep gullies full of loose rock, and
   other natural obstacles exist throughout the terrain. All can be used to slow or canalize opposing forces into
   decisive engagement areas. In difficult terrain, fewer resources may be needed to improve obstacles.

COVER AND CONCEALMENT
   1-39. When moving in the mountains, outcroppings, boulders, heavy vegetation, and intermediate terrain can
   provide cover and concealment. The digging of fighting positions and temporary fortifications is difficult
   because soil is often thin or stony. Selecting dug-in positions require detailed planning. Some rock types,
   such as volcanic tuff, are easily excavated. In other areas, boulders and other loose rocks can be used for
   building hasty fortifications. In alpine environments, snow and ice blocks may be cut and stacked to
   supplement dug-in positions.
   1-40. Above tree line, lack of vegetation significantly reduces concealment. Movement requires careful
   terrain analysis and route planning, using terrain to mask movement from enemy observation. Hide sites and
   defensive positions built in locations with good observation angles are often exposed; they require careful
   camouflaging.

MOUNTAIN CLASSIFICATIONS
   1-41. The military uses two systems to classify mountain terrain: operational terrain levels and dismounted
   mobility classifications. Operational terrain levels describe the tactical advantages and disadvantages based
   on their difficulty to access and secure. The dismounted mobility classification describes the individual
   mobility skills required to move safely and effectively through that terrain. These classifications are crucial
   tools for planners and leaders. They enable the appropriate terrain analysis and help to facilitate planning
   feasible and realistic operations in mountain environments.
OPERATIONAL TERRAIN LEVELS
   1-42. Level I terrain is located at the bottom of valleys and along the main LOCs see table 1-1 and figure 1-2,
   page 10. These areas typically contain resources, population centers, or mobility corridors that are vital to
   mission success. Opening, blocking, or controlling these regions and LOCs is therefore always a tactical
   objective in mountain combat operations. At this level, maneuver space is restricted, but armored forces can
   operate effectively along valley roads and trails. Infantry and armored forces are typically task-organized
   together at this level to ensure freedom of movement and protection along LOCs. While armor provides
   mobility and firepower within the confines of the valley floor, infantry and other high mobility units secure
   adjacent high ground. Units operating in level I terrain must consider how higher terrain—particularly




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                   9
Chapter 1



     level II—can influence their mission, including exposure to enemy observation, fires, and maneuver from
     above.
     1-43. Level II terrain consists of the highlands that overlook and influence level I terrain. Level II terrain is
     often found between valley floors and the higher mountain peaks. Units occupy level II terrain because it
     provides a tactical advantage through observation, fires, and maneuver over the valleys below. In mountain
     operations, control of level II terrain, rather than the actual summit, often determines key terrain. However,
     units positioned in level II must also account for how higher level III terrain may allow enemy forces to
     observe, flank, or otherwise influence their position. Infrastructure in level II terrain is typically sparse or
     nonexistent. If present, roadways may include narrow roads or trails that follow ridgelines or cross saddles.
     Such roadways often serve as secondary LOCs.
     1-44. Level III terrain includes the dominant terrain of summit regions. These areas typically do not allow
     forces to directly influence level I terrain, but they may dominate or affect operations in level II. Operations
     in level III terrain are challenging due to extreme environmental exposure, limited infrastructure, and
     separation from adjacent units and logistical support. However, level III terrain can provide acclimatized
     troops with advanced mountaineering training with opportunities to support forces in level I and II terrain.
     Such supporting activities include flanking enemy positions, infiltrating along unexpected avenues of
     approach, and striking key vulnerabilities such as LOCs, logistics nodes, air defense sites, or command
     infrastructure.

DISMOUNTED MOBILITY CLASSIFICATION
   1-45. Most mountainous terrain severely restricts mobility. The dismounted mobility classification is a tool
   that rates the terrain based upon difficulty of movement and consequence of a fall and provides general
   guidelines on risk management. It uses the same categories as the Yosemite Decimal System (YDS), which
   is used to rate climbing in the United States. It is used across all types of mountainous terrain and defined as
   a rough framework for communicating the appropriate risk treatment and required technical systems and
   resources for negotiating the terrain. It is subjective, and risk treatment will vary based upon the group,
   surface conditions, and weather.
   1-46. 1st-class terrain is defined as gentle slopes or easy trails. This terrain is negotiated with simple walking
   techniques. This can be anything from established trails to cross-country movement over terrain with stable
   footing and moderate grades. Mobility challenges in this terrain may include dense vegetation, stream
   crossings, and challenging route planning. Risks are limited to navigation errors and hazards posed by
   stream-crossings, weather, and altitude. (See table 1-2.)
   1-47. 2nd-class terrain involves off-trail scrambling in steeper, more rugged terrain, often with extensive
   scree, talus, or boulder fields. Hands are often used for balance. Good physical conditioning is required, but
   no technical solutions are needed for safe movement. Route-finding skills are even more important for
   efficient and safe travel across or around terrain that is more difficult, vegetation, stream-crossings, and
   rockfall hazards. The risk of injury from slips and rockfall is moderate, but generally, the likelihood and
   consequence of a fall is low. Moving a casualty will generally require simple rope systems. (See table 1-2.)
   1-48. 3rd-class terrain requires scrambling. Hand and footholds are numerous and easy to find, requiring
   limited climbing experience. Movement may be easy, but falls can cause serious injury. Advanced
   route-finding skills are necessary to avoid difficult and dangerous terrain. Experienced mountaineers will
   usually travel unroped. Using fixed ropes or belays are required for Soldiers moving during limited visibility,
   bad weather, or when carrying heavy loads. All Soldiers moving in 3rd-class terrain should have training in
   individual mobility, good physical fitness, and proficiency with rope systems used. Route finding and risk
   decisions should be made by someone with formal mountaineering training. (See table 1-2.)
   1-49. 4th-class terrain requires moderate to difficult scrambling. Holds are numerous but must be tested and
   are frequently smaller and more difficult to find than in 3rd-class terrain. The terrain is often broken, with
   short, steep steps of less than 15 meters, interspersed with blocky ledges. It is often exposed. Serious injury
   or death can occur if an unroped fall occurs. Climbing should be protected by belays or fixed ropes. Advanced
   military mountaineers are required to find routes and provide belays or fix ropes for less experienced troops
   where necessary. It requires significant time and resources to manage risk for large elements. It is more
   efficiently traveled by small teams. 4th-class terrain is the most difficult terrain in which to evaluate and
   manage risk. (See table 1-2.)
   1-50. 5th-class terrain is climbing terrain. Significant injury or death can occur from an unroped fall.
   Climbing is protected by belay techniques and intermediate protection. Steep rock often requires that anchors
   be built with rock gear. Advanced military mountaineers are trained to lead climbs to negotiate this terrain.
   Large groups can descend through bands of 5th-class terrain more quickly by rappelling. Ascent requires
   more time and equipment, as well as proficiency in rope ascending across the entire element. (See table 1-2.)

     1-51. Operations conducted in 1st- and 2nd-class terrain require little to no mountaineering skills. Special
     teams may require some training and ropes for moving casualties. Operations in 3rd-, 4th-, and 5th-class
     terrain require a higher level of mountaineering skills throughout the element for safe and efficient
     movement. Elements moving through terrain obstacles are easily fixed. Operations moving through exposed
     terrain should have plans for maintaining security and for contingencies during the movement.

SECTION IV – MOUNTAIN WEATHER
     1-52. Weather presents its own hazards in the mountains. It also increases the hazards posed by terrain. On
     routes with snow or glacial hazard, variations in temperature and cloud cover can significantly affect speed
     and safety. Strong winds can make exposed ridges unclimbable. Rain, in addition to causing discomfort and
     potentially hypothermia, makes rock slick and increases the likelihood of a fall. Rain washing through debris
     in gullies increases the danger of rockfall. Summer thunderstorms move quickly and hammer exposed ridges
     and peaks with lightning.
     1-53. Bad weather increases hazard and physical discomfort. Civilian mountaineers plan climbs with
     “weather windows” to allow flexibility. Military mountaineers often have less flexibility in plans and
     timelines. Some weather hazards can be managed by more conservative terrain choices, additional
     cold-weather clothing and equipment, and training focused on producing self-reliant Soldiers who can endure
     poor conditions. Plans should be flexible with multiple layers of redundancy for sustainment. Bad weather
     may force early resupply or the adjustment of operations to accommodate the lack of ground and aerial
     resupply.

MOUNTAIN WEATHER FACTORS
     1-54. Weather analysis is the collection, processing, evaluation, and interpretation of relevant military aspects
     of weather. It is the evaluation of forecasted weather effects on operations. The military aspect of weather—
     visibility, wind velocity, precipitation, cloud cover, temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure—and
     their effects on operations remain the same as in other environments. However, elevation and terrain with
     significant relief create effects unique to the mountain environment. Weather in the mountains follows larger
     patterns, but local factors cause weather systems to produce more precipitation and make the effects of storms
     and instabilities greater and longer lasting. (See table 1-3, page 14.) (See ATP 2-01.3 for more information
     on weather analysis.)
ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE, TEMPERATURE, HUMIDITY
     1-55. Changes in atmospheric pressure are the underlying cause of many factors. Atmospheric pressure is the
     weight of the atmosphere in an area. As elevation increases, pressure is reduced, causing lower air density.
     Aircraft capabilities and human performance decrease. Sunlight is less filtered, causing quicker warming and
     cooling.
     1-56. Reduced pressure also affects temperature. Air temperature decreases as elevation increases in the
     mountains at the adiabatic rate or about 3 degrees (°) Fahrenheit (F) to 5 °F for every 1,000 feet of elevation
     gain. Cooler air holds less moisture. As air masses pass over mountains, they are lifted by the terrain—a
     process known as orographic lift. If the air cools to its saturation temperature, its water vapor condenses and
     becomes a visible cloud. Lenticular clouds, named for their lens shape, are cloud caps that often form above
     peaks because of orographic lift and precipitates such as fog, rain, or snow. This process increases the severity
     and length of storms and produces unique localized weather.
     1-57. Mountain air is incredibly dry. Dehydration is more likely in the mountains if Soldiers are not properly
     hydrated. (See chapter 3 for more information.)
VISIBILITY, CLOUD COVER, AND PRECIPITATION
     1-58. On clear days, high elevations provide opportunities to see great distances. However, minor
     atmospheric disturbances produce fog, clouds, and precipitation that reduce visibility. Weather systems that
     would not influence operations in the lowlands often do in the mountains. Clouds are common in mountain
     environments and may form quickly. Precipitation occurs more often on the windward side of mountain




12                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                         Mountain Environment



   ranges than on the leeward side. Snow is common in the mountains and may occur during any season at
   elevations above 1,500 meters (5,000 feet).
   1-59. Local thunderstorms often pass quickly but bring driving snow and sudden wind squalls. Lightning is
   common in mountain storms and normally discharges on high points and prominent features. Peaks, ridges,
   rock walls, isolated trees, fixed wire installations, cracks that guide water, cracks filled with earth, shallow
   depressions, shallow overhangs, and rock needles should be avoided; shelter should be obtained around dry,
   clean rock without cracks.
   1-60. Storms caused by widespread atmospheric disturbances often involve strong winds and heavy
   precipitation. These conditions may last several days longer than in the lowlands. Low temperatures, high
   winds, and blinding snow often accompany winter storms in alpine regions.
WIND VELOCITY
   1-61. Mountains more frequently create variation in wind than in most other environments. Valleys often
   protect Soldiers from strong winds, but the ridges and passes of mountains are seldom calm. Wind velocity
   generally increases with altitude and is intensified by mountainous terrain. Wind speed increases when winds
   are forced over ridges and peaks or when funneled through narrowing mountain valleys, passes, and canyons.
   (This is known as the Venturi effect.) Exposed mountainsides and summits are especially susceptible to
   strong winds. Topography usually controls local wind direction.
   1-62. When the wind speed is doubled, the force on an object buffeted by the wind is quadrupled; therefore,
   bivouacs or patrol bases should be established in areas not subject to extreme winds. Colder air temperatures
   along with wind produce wind chill. Soldiers in a static security posture in these conditions are more likely
   to experience cold-weather injuries. (See chapter 3 for cold-weather injuries.)
   1-63. Warming and cooling cycles cause local air movements. Valley breezes moving up a slope are more
   common in the morning and are known as anabatic winds; descending mountain breezes known as “katabatic
   winds” are more common in the evening.

PLANNING FOR WEATHER
      1-64. Mountain weather can be a dangerous obstacle to operations or a valuable aid, depending on how well
      it is understood and to what extent advantage is taken of its characteristics.
      1-65. Weather often determines the success or failure of a mission. Military operations plans must be flexible.
      The clouds that often cover mountaintops and fog that covers valleys are excellent tools for concealing
      movements normally made during darkness or in smoke. Limited visibility can be used as a combat
      multiplier.
      1-66. The safety of most high mountain regions, especially in winter, depends upon the change of a few
      degrees of temperature above or below the freezing point. Ease and speed of travel depend mainly on the
      weather. Terrain that can be crossed swiftly and safely one day may become impassable or dangerous the
      next due to snowfall, rainfall, or warmer temperatures; the reverse can happen just as quickly. The prevalence
      of avalanches depends on terrain, snow conditions, and weather factors.
      1-67. Weather affects Soldiers’ abilities to see enemies, terrain, and teammates, as well as their ability to
      move through the terrain. Access to weather information during the planning process drives tactical decisions.
      Whether patrolling or static, military mountaineers should constantly evaluate the following:
          • What is the weather currently?
          • What was the weather recently and when did it change last?
          • When is the next forecasted change coming?
          • How does it affect us?

WEATHER FORECASTING
      1-68. Reports from other localities and from any weather service, including the Air Force, Navy, or the
      National Weather Service, are helpful. Weather at various elevations may be quite different because cloud



14                                                    TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                          Mountain Environment



   height, temperature, and barometric pressure will all be different. There may be overcast and rain in a lower
   area, with mountains rising above the low overcast into warmer clear weather. To be effective, a forecast
   must reach the small-unit leaders who are expected to utilize weather conditions for missions. Normally
   located within a chief of staff intelligence office or battalion or brigade intelligence office and designated as
   a special staff officer, the U.S. Air Force staff weather officer provides and coordinates weather support and
   services. (See AR 115-10 and AR 5-25 for additional guidance.)
   1-69. Weather patterns form at the continental scale and involve many factors. Individuals on the ground
   cannot create weather forecasts from locally observed conditions and it is unrealistic to expect them to do so.
   It is critical that weather data produced at higher levels is pushed down to forces on the ground. However,
   individuals on the ground must recognize that there is inherent uncertainty in all forecasts, and local factors
   may produce unexpected conditions. Paying attention to changing trends can prevent Soldiers from being
   unprepared for changing conditions. Many of the trends that indicate changing weather are easily observed.
   1-70. Monitoring changes in barometric pressure provides one of the reliable indicators of changing weather.
   High-pressure systems bring cooler, drier weather. As air pressure rises, it prevents moisture from rising and
   forming in the atmosphere, allowing for clearer skies and cooler temperatures. Lower air systems bring
   warmer, wetter weather and atmospheric instability. As air pressure falls, it allows moisture to rise and
   condense, allowing clouds to form.
   1-71. Pay attention to key indicators of changes. Analog altimeters measure barometric pressure and can be
   used to identify an increase and decrease in pressure when stationary for a prolonged period. (See chapter 7
   for information on altimeters.)
DETERIORATING TRENDS
   1-72. Military mountaineers must pay careful attention to indicators of deteriorating weather trends. The
   following are common indicators:
        • Marked wind direction shifts. A high-pressure system wind flows clockwise. A low-pressure system
           wind flows counterclockwise. The closer the isometric lines are, the greater the differential of
           pressure and the greater the wind speeds.
        • Marked wind speed increases.
        • Changes in obstructions to visibility.
        • Increasing cloud coverage.
        • Increase in precipitation. A steady drizzle is usually a long-lasting rain.
        • Lowering cloud ceilings.
        • Marked cooler temperature changes, which could indicate that a cold front is passing through.
        • Marked increase in humidity.
        • Decrease in barometric pressure indicates a lower-pressure system is moving through the area. This
           can be measured using a digital or analog altimeter.
   IMPROVING TRENDS
   1-73. Predicting coming favorable weather conditions is important during operations planning. The following
   are common indicators of favorable weather trends:
        • Steady wind direction, which indicates no change in weather systems in the area.
        • Decreasing wind speeds.
        • Clearing of obstructions to visibility.
        • Decreasing or ending precipitation.
        • Decreasing cloud coverage.
        • Increasing height of cloud ceilings.
        • Changing temperature slowly gets warmer.
        • Decreasing humidity.
        • Increasing barometric pressure indicates that a higher-pressure system is moving through the area.
            This can be measured using a digital or analog altimeter.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                  15
Chapter 1



CLOUDS
     1-74. At the boundaries of major weather systems where different air masses collide, warm air is lifted into
     the atmosphere, causing clouds and precipitation. Fronts create distinctive cloud formations. Warm fronts,
     where the incoming warm air gradually displaces cold air below, present as steadily thickening and lowering
     clouds over a few days. Cold fronts create an uplift that is more violent and may come as a single, larger
     storm system.

High-Level Clouds
     1-75. High-level clouds (above 6,000 meters) are formed of ice crystals, with a fibrous structure and blurred
     outlines. The sky is often covered with a thin veil that partly obscures the sun or, at night, produces a ring of
     light around the moon. Cirrus clouds indicate moisture aloft and the approach of a traveling storm system.
     Precipitation is often 24 to 36 hours away. As a storm approaches, the high-level clouds thicken and lower.

Mid-Level Clouds
     1-76. Mid-level clouds (2,000 to 6,000 meters) appear more distinct than high-level clouds because of a
     mixed composition of water droplets and ice. Mid-level clouds often form in advance of a cold front. Puffy,
     mid-level clouds on a warm, humid summer morning are commonly followed by thunderstorms later in the
     day. “Fair weather” cumulus are clouds scattered rather than even in a blue sky and suggest arrival of high
     pressure and clear skies.

Low-Level Clouds
     1-77. Low-level clouds (below 2,000 meters) are mostly composed of water droplets. Most precipitation
     originates from low-level clouds because rain or snow usually evaporates before reaching the ground from
     higher clouds. Low-level clouds usually indicate impending precipitation.

Vertical Development (Cumulonimbus)
     1-78. Large, vertical development clouds often form on the steep, leading edge of a cold front. They can
     develop as individual towers or form a line of towers called a squall line. Their formation is fueled by
     vigorous convective updrafts. These storms tend to develop during the afternoon and early evening when the
     effects of heating from the sun are the strongest.

                                                Chapter 2
                          Training Military Mountaineers
   Operational success in complex, compartmentalized, and objectively hazardous terrain largely
   rests on the shoulders of a unit’s military mountaineers. Often, these are the only unit members
   with significant experience living and moving in mountainous terrain. Units with highly
   experienced mountaineers and well-developed mountain programs will be better prepared to
   engage in mountain warfare and will likely prove more successful. Military mountaineers serve
   as advisors for the development of such programs and trainers for mountain knowledge and
   skills; they also ensure safe training conduct in hazardous terrain. When used effectively,
   mountaineers provide their units with the ability to successfully live in extreme environments
   and move efficiently in terrain inaccessible to other units. Additionally, advanced and master
   military mountaineers serve as planners and advisors to commanders for combat operations in
   mountainous terrain. They are the primary means for a commander to lead units through
   complex terrain, emplace special teams at inaccessible points of domination, and conduct
   casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) in 5th-class terrain. The selection, formal training, and
   development of military mountaineers are critical to the effectiveness of all units operating in
   mountainous terrain.

SECTION I – LEVELS OF MOUNTAINEER
   2-1. Three doctrinal levels of military mountaineer correspond with increasing experience and formal school
   graduation requirements for qualification—basic, advanced, and master military mountaineers. Each level of
   mountaineer is expected to be capable of performing an increasingly complex set of skills and functions in
   preparing for and leading mountain warfare operations.
   2-2. Additionally, contemporary mountain operations and training have highlighted the need to identify what
   capabilities are necessary for all Soldiers in mountainous terrain, given that 100 percent of a unit achieving
   even basic military mountaineer qualification is likely impossible due to a unit’s operating tempo and
   personnel turnover. Soldiers belonging to units that anticipate participating in mountain operations who have
   not received formal mountaineer training will be referred to as mountain Soldiers. Additionally, some guiding
   criteria for selecting Soldiers for formal mountaineering training should be followed so that success is more
   likely.

CANDIDATES FOR FORMAL MOUNTAIN TRAINING
   2-3. Ideal military mountaineers are self-motivated, critical thinkers requiring minimal supervision and
   direction to succeed in assigned tasks. They are undaunted by difficulty or adversity and possess a strong
   desire to work and live in mountainous terrain.
   2-4. Although all Soldiers operating in mountainous terrain benefit from formal mountaineering training,
   opportunities for training are limited. Commanders should select Soldiers who possess characteristics, which
   allow them to both successfully pass courses and return with the ability to improve their unit’s mountain
   capability.
   2-5. Candidates should embody the following characteristics:
        • Independent and self-motivated.
        • Mentally and physically fit.
        • Sure-footed and agile (necessary for scrambling or climbing).
        • Comfortable with heights.
        • Experienced in living and working in a cold-weather environment.
        • Skilled at map reading and land navigation without electronic aids.
        • Quick learner of technical skills.



26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                                17
Chapter 2



     2-6. Leader candidates should possess the following characteristics:
          • Leadership experience in tactical operations up to their level of responsibility.
          • Capable of solving problems and taking initiative based on commander’s intent.
          • Possess teaching and mentorship skills.
          • Comfortable serving as advisors to senior leadership.
     2-7. Officer candidates should possess the following characteristics:
          • May serve in the future, or currently serve, as commander for a unit that will operate in mountainous
              terrain.
          • May serve in the future, or currently serve, as operations or training planner for a unit that will
              operate in mountainous terrain.

LEVEL 1: BASIC MILITARY MOUNTAINEER
     2-8. A basic military mountaineer is a Soldier who graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer
     Course. Basic military mountaineers have been trained in basic mountaineering techniques, such as
     fundamental mobility skills necessary to move safely and efficiently in mountainous terrain, and are
     also known as level 1 military mountaineers. Soldiers should be comfortable functioning in this hazardous
     terrain and extreme environmental conditions. They should be able to assist higher-level mountaineers in
     rigging and using all basic rope installations. Basic military mountaineers should be able to perform duties
     as the follower or second on a roped climbing team and be able to operate all basic rope systems. They may
     provide limited assistance and simple skills training to personnel unskilled in mountaineering techniques
     under the close supervision of higher-level mountaineers. Particularly adept Soldiers may be selected as
     members of special-purpose teams led and supervised by higher-level mountaineers. Risk mitigation
     decisions ultimately belong to commanders, but level 1 qualification should not be considered sufficient
     experience to inspect rigging without advanced mountaineer supervision.
     2-9. Units planning to operate in mountainous terrain should maximize the number of level 1 mountaineers.
     Leaders of units intending to operate in mountainous terrain should be, at a minimum, level 1 mountaineers.
     2-10. Basic military mountaineers are trained in the following mountain-specific skills:
         • Characteristics of the mountain environment (summer and winter).
         • Mountaineering safety.
         • Use, care, and packing of individual cold-weather clothing and equipment.
         • Care and use of basic mountaineering equipment.
         • Mountain bivouac techniques.
         • Familiarized with mountain communications.
         • Mountain travel and walking techniques.
         • Familiarized with hazard recognition and route selection.
         • Mountain navigation.
         • Basic medical evacuation (MEDEVAC).
         • Rope management and knots.
         • Natural anchors.
         • Familiarized with artificial anchors.
         • Belay and rappel techniques.
         • Establish and employ fixed ropes on simple terrain.
         • Climbing fundamentals.
         • Rope bridges.
         • Hauling and lowering systems.
         • Individual movement on snow and ice.
         • Mountain stream crossings.
         • First aid for mountain illnesses and injuries.
         • Familiarized with avalanche avoidance and rescue.
