                                                                                Training Military Mountaineers



         Note. Level 1 qualified personnel should be identified and prepared to serve as assistant instructors
         to train unqualified personnel in basic mountaineering skills. All high-risk training must be
         conducted under the supervision of qualified level 2 or 3 personnel.


LEVEL 2: ADVANCED MILITARY MOUNTAINEER
   2-11. An advanced military mountaineer is a Soldier who has graduated from the Basic Military
   Mountaineer Course and at least one of the Advanced Military Mountaineer courses. An advanced
   military mountaineer has been trained in advanced mountaineering techniques and is also known as a
   level 2 mountaineer. Operationally, an advanced military mountaineer is also known as an assault climber,
   which is a role assigned to a Soldier or team during tactical operations who is responsible for the
   location and establishment of technical routes in class 3 or higher terrain; ideally, a level 2
   mountaineer. A technical route is a route through steep or broken mountainous terrain that presents
   significant risk of fall injury and requires special movement techniques or ropes to ensure adequate
   safety for Soldiers moving through it. Ideally, assault climbers are level 2 mountaineers. Advanced military
   mountaineers are responsible for rigging, inspecting, using, and operating all basic rope systems. They are
   trained in additional rope management skills, knot tying, belay, and rappel techniques, as well as using
   specialized mountaineering equipment. Advanced military mountaineers can rig complex, multipoint anchors
   and high-angle raising and lowering systems. Level 2 qualification is required to supervise all high-risk
   training associated with level 1 skills.
   2-12. Units planning to operate in mountainous terrain should possess enough level 2 mountaineers to train
   lower-level personnel in mountain skills and lead small teams through hazardous terrain during operations.
   Company-level and higher unit leaders who possess level 2 training are better prepared to negotiate the
   challenges inherent in sustaining and moving their units in consequential terrain. Company-level and higher
   unit leaders better understand which training is appropriate and important to their personnel at all levels of
   mountaineering.
   2-13. Advanced military mountaineers are trained in the following mountain-specific skills:
       • Use specialized mountaineering equipment.
       • Conduct multipitch climbing on rock.
       • Conduct multipitch rappelling.
       • Establish and operate hauling systems.
       • Establish, employ, and supervise unit movement on fixed ropes on complex terrain.
       • Conduct roped movement techniques on moderate angle snow and ice.
       • Establish evacuation systems and perform high-angle rescue.
       • Recognize and evaluate terrain, weather, and hazards.
       • Perform avalanche rescue operations.
       • Perform rescue operations on mountainous terrain.
       • Perform glacier travel and crevasse rescue.
       • Conduct unit mountain skills sustainment and improvement training.

LEVEL 3: MASTER MILITARY MOUNTAINEER
   2-14. A master military mountaineer is a Soldier who has graduated from the Basic and Advanced Military
   Mountaineer courses and endorsed by the Master Mountaineer Board (MMB). A master military
   mountaineer is a Soldier extensively trained and experienced with mountaineering techniques who the
   commander appoints to serve as a subject matter expert. Master military mountaineers should be
   graduates of the Basic Military Mountaineer Course and Advanced Military Mountaineer courses.
   They possess all the skills of the advanced military mountaineer and have extensive practical
   experience in a variety of mountain environments in both winter and summer conditions. Level 3
   mountaineers should have well-developed hazard evaluation and safe route-finding skills over all types of
   mountainous terrain. Master military mountaineers serve as advisors to commanders and staff during
   planning on mountain warfare considerations across all warfighting functions. The master military
   mountaineer is the highest level of qualification and is the principal trainer for conducting mountain
   operations. The MMB is subordinate to the Army Mountaineering Board and endorses or suggests additional


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 19
Chapter 2



     training for Soldiers submitting packets. The MMB sets packet criteria to validate Soldier capability to
     perform the tasks in paragraph 2-16. The MMB’s endorsement assists commanders in appointing qualified
     Soldiers to perform level 3 tasks.
     2-15. Company-level units and higher that plan to operate in mountainous terrain should have one or more
     level 3 mountaineers assigned. Battalion-level units and higher should have at least one senior-ranking level 3
     mountaineer assigned to their operations staff sections to ensure commanders are informed of all mountain
     considerations that could affect operations.
     2-16. Master military mountaineers are knowledgeable and proficient in the following mountain-specific skills:
         • Develop and oversee unit mountain skills sustainment and improvement program.
         • Prepare route, movement, bivouac, and risk management.
         • Perform avalanche hazard evaluation and mitigation.
         • Plan and supervise high-angle rescue.
         • Organize and lead avalanche rescue operations.
         • Plan and supervise roped movement techniques on steep snow and ice.
         • Plan and supervise glacier travel and crevasse rescue.
         • Plan and conduct over snow mobility.
         • Conduct multipitch climbing on rock, snow, and ice.
         • Lead units over technically difficult, hazardous, or exposed terrain in both winter and summer conditions.

SECTION II – TRAINING INDIVIDUAL MOUNTAIN SKILLS
     2-17. Unit preparedness for operations in mountainous terrain is contingent on the effectiveness of the
     training program its commander implements. Commanders and trainers must understand how to prioritize
     mountain skill training, so skills are built in a progressive fashion that supports a unit’s collective task
     capability. General mountaineering skills and experience must be developed before complex technical skills
     and before collective tasks can be effectively performed. Attempting complex training in mountainous terrain
     before all participants are proficient in self-sustainment and basic mobility skills will likely cause a failure to
     achieve training goals and possibly serious injury or death.

UNIT-LEVEL TRAINING PROGRAMS
     2-18. Commanders anticipating operations in mountainous terrain should establish a mountaineering training
     program and program coordinator like a unit marksmanship program. An appropriate noncommissioned
     officer in charge (NCOIC) and officer in charge (OIC) should be tasked with this additional duty. The primary
     training coordinator (NCOIC) should be a level 3 master military mountaineer and senior noncommissioned
     officer with maneuver leader experience, as well as experience facilitating individual-, team-, and unit-level
     training events. The OIC should have a level 2 or higher qualification to create and manage a successful
     training plan and risk management process. Additionally, commanders should strive to maintain a cadre of
     formally trained level 1 and level 2 mountaineers comprised of experienced junior noncommissioned officers
     who can teach mountain skills and supervise high-risk mountain training. Commanders should carefully
     consider the number and distribution of this cadre throughout a unit. Spreading mountaineers throughout
     smaller units increases opportunities for them to teach skills to other Soldiers and incorporates them into
     smaller unit collective training events. Periodically, consolidated training should be conducted for each level
     of mountaineer, and unit commanders should plan collective training events that involve mountaineering
     techniques.
     2-19. Commanders at battalion level and higher should establish similar NCOIC and OIC additional duties
     for planning mountain operations and providing guidance and support to company-level trainers in
     accordance with (IAW) their intent for mountain capability. Ideally, an NCOIC at this level would be an
     accomplished mountaineer, with substantial experience leading Soldiers in the full range of mountainous
     terrain and environmental conditions, as well as having served as a lower-level unit mountain training
     coordinator. OICs at this level should be experienced level 2 mountaineers and should have either served as
     OICs of unit mountaineering training programs or the commander of a unit that developed one in the past.
     Since some mountain training is inherently high risk, battalion and higher-level commanders should establish
     clear risk mitigation guidance under the guidance of their master military mountaineer.



20                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                  Training Military Mountaineers



PROGRESSION OF MOUNTAIN SKILLS
   2-20. Mountain training planners must clearly understand how to prioritize the development of mountain skills.
   Three broad individual skillsets that are critical to developing a unit’s tactical effectiveness in mountainous
   terrain are—
        • Sustainment and survival in the mountainous environment skills—cold-weather clothing and
             moisture management strategies, bivouac techniques, and survival techniques.
        • Mobility skills—individual movement skills and surefootedness. These exist at the intersection of
             fitness and movement technique mastery.
        • Technical rope system skills—these comprise everything involved in the use of ropes and
             specialized equipment for protection, obstacle negotiation, and load movement.
SUSTAINMENT AND SURVIVAL SKILLS
   2-21. Units proficient in small group sustainment and larger unit resupply and communications TTPs have
   an overwhelming advantage over units that lack this experience in mountain environments, regardless of
   technical and tactical capabilities.
   2-22. While Soldiers must be comfortable living in an environment in which they are training or operating,
   this is particularly true in a mountainous, cold-weather environment. Soldiers struggling to stay warm are
   unable to focus on performing tasks that are more complex. All unit members must be familiar and acclimated
   to cold weather, otherwise unit members who are acclimated to the cold become occupied caring for those
   who are not. Typically, most of this training does not require high mountain terrain—just cold weather and
   terrain that is remote and difficult to access.
   2-23. As a unit gains proficiency in these skills, training locations should move into more difficult to access
   terrain, and periods of sustainment should increase. Eventually, moving into terrain at moderate to high
   altitude increases Soldier skill progressions and tasks become second nature. Typically, such training
   provides opportunities for the unit to develop collective sustainment, resupply, and communications TTPs,
   which are more important to successful operations in mountainous terrain than any other collective
   proficiencies.
MOBILITY SKILLS
   2-24. Mobility is critical to unit success in mountain warfare. High mobility skills allow units to outmaneuver
   their enemies no matter where they encounter them. The higher the skills, the more dominant terrain is
   accessible to the unit. The primary purpose of developing mobility skills is to increase the difficulty of terrain
   that Soldiers can move in unroped while carrying packs and combat loads. This expands the range of
   patrolling activities without the tactical disadvantage of using rope systems for fall protection, which is any
   anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber falls, should
   a fall occur.
   2-25. The hallmarks of individual movement skill proficiency are surefootedness and endurance. They
   describe a Soldier’s ability to walk, scramble, and climb safely without the need for protection. Fitness is an
   important component in developing mobility skills. General fitness infrequently translates to high mobility
   skill without specific movement technique training. After sustainment, these are the most important skills to
   build warfighting capability in mountainous terrain.
TECHNICAL ROPE SKILLS
   2-26. Technical rope skills are necessary for units to access and move in operational terrain above level 2.
   Although it is seldom necessary for large units to move in such high consequence terrain, small-specialized
   teams can use it to provide tremendous advantage for their parent units by doing so. Snipers, reconnaissance
   teams, fire support teams, forward observer teams, or special operations teams can use unlikely avenues of
   travel located there for concealment and position themselves on points of domination, which are inaccessible
   to the enemy. From there, they can provide real-time intelligence to commanders, direct air assets, indirect
   fires, or provide overwatch for troops moving through easier terrain that is vulnerable to enemy attack.
   Advanced military mountaineers with technical rope skills must guide them safely through such hazardous terrain.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  21
Chapter 2



     2-27. The unit requirement for personnel who are highly proficient in technical rope skills is relatively low.
     Technical rope skills, though complex to teach, are the lowest priority skills for units preparing to operate in
     mountainous terrain. This does not mean that these skills should not be taught but that other skills should be prioritized.
     2-28. Unit training programs should focus on training most Soldiers to low or moderate (level 1) mountaineer
     levels of rope use proficiency, and a minority of particularly interested and capable Soldiers to high
     proficiency (level 2).
SUSTAINMENT AND ENHANCEMENT TRAINING FOR MILITARY MOUNTAINEERS
     2-29. Formally, qualified military mountaineers provide training to non-qualified members and require
     sustainment and skills advancement training. The Basic Military Mountaineer Course successfully introduces
     graduates to the full array of level 1 skills and techniques but is only 2-weeks long and does not fully teach
     them how to integrate with level 2 mountaineers to maximize a unit’s mobility capability during the conduct
     of specific missions in mountainous terrain. The same is true for the Advanced Military Mountaineer Course.
     Graduates should have been exposed to all skills and techniques necessary to access all levels of terrain
     during military operations, but they should not be considered experienced. To be operationally capable, both
     levels 1 and 2 mountaineers require additional training experience fulfilling their roles and improving
     proficiency.

Individual Training for Untrained Mountain Soldiers
     2-30. Units with members who have experience in harsh environments and moving in steep terrain possess a
     significant advantage. Soldiers who are unprepared to live and move in the mountains will find it difficult to
     conduct combat operations there. Commanders should ensure all Soldiers in their formation are familiarized
     with the skills and knowledge outlined in paragraphs 2-34 through 2-40 when planning mountain operations.
     2-31. These Soldiers should be trained in foundational skills necessary for sustainment and mobility in
     mountainous terrain. These skills include characteristics and hazards of the mountain environment,
     cold-weather sustainment, basic minimalist bivouac techniques, rough terrain walking, load management,
     simple movement techniques, basic knot tying, and rope handling.
     2-32. Level 1 mountaineers, under the supervision of higher-level military mountaineers, should train
     untrained Soldiers IAW the commander’s mountaineering program.
     2-33. Units should create regular opportunities for untrained mountain Soldiers to integrate sustainment and
     mobility skills into their tactical training events.

Continued Individual Training for Level 1 Mountaineers
     2-34. Training for level 1 mountaineers should focus on improving sustainment skills, mobility skills,
     low-level technical skills, and assisting level 2 mountaineers in establishing technical rope systems.
     2-35. Level 2 mountaineers should provide technical sustainment and improvement training for level 1
     mountaineers IAW the commander’s mountaineering program and under the guidance of a level 3
     mountaineer.
     2-36. Units should create regular opportunities for level 1 mountaineers to integrate sustainment and mobility
     skills into their tactical training events. Examples are incorporating low-angle CASEVAC scenarios in rough
     terrain or using simple fixed lines to help squad movement on steep slopes into platoon situational training
     exercises.

Continued Individual Training for Level 2 Mountaineers
     2-37. Typically, level 2 mountaineers should be provided the time and resources to conduct sustainment and
     improvement training. This training should be planned and conducted under the guidance and supervision of
     level 3 mountaineers. Optimally, periodic, high-commitment mountain training events should be planned for
     level 2 and led by level 3 mountaineers. All training for level 2 mountaineers should focus on building
     experience in those skills that the commander determines necessary to perform operationally. In the absence
     of specific mission-essential task list tasks to focus on, level 2 training should concentrate on route selection,



22                                                       TC 3-97.61                                      26 November 2025
                                                                                    Training Military Mountaineers



    sharpening mobility skills, and climbing protective techniques in 5th-class terrain, leading small groups in
    4th-class terrain, and conducting technical rescue training. These should be conducted in both summer and
    winter environmental conditions.

Shadowing
    2-38. Whenever possible, level 2 mountaineers should participate in providing formal mountaineering
    training by shadowing or by being an assistant instructor for the Basic Military Mountaineer Course or
    Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. Opportunities to do so can be coordinated through the Army
    Mountain Warfare School in Vermont, the Northern Warfare Training Center in Alaska, and the 5th Ranger
    Training Battalion in Georgia. Participating in formal mountaineering training programs ensures level 2
    mountaineers are exposed to current techniques and training safety measures, provides experience with
    developing training programs, and helps prepare them for level 3 qualification and responsibilities.

Vertical Danger Area Ascent or Descent
    2-39. Units should occasionally create opportunities for level 2 mountaineers to integrate higher technical
    skills into tactical training events, such as a vertical danger area (VDA) ascent or descent task. A vertical
    danger area is steep terrain that significantly restricts a unit’s ability to maneuver, thereby putting the
    unit at significant tactical disadvantage should enemy contact be made while moving through the VDA.
    As units integrate linear danger area crossings into a field training exercise or live-fire exercise, they can also
    integrate a VDA ascent or descent task into a squad training lane. Training employs a unit’s level 2
    mountaineers, refreshes level 1 tasks, and adds a level of realism and rigor to an otherwise normal squad
    situational training exercise lane.

Continued Individual Training for Level 3 Mountaineers
    2-40. Even the most accomplished mountaineers require periodic sustainment training. Most often, this can
    be accomplished by participating in level 2 training. However, new mountaineering techniques are regularly
    developed, so whenever possible, level 3 mountaineers should undergo specialty training that is focused on
    increasing unit capability IAW the commander’s intent. Additional training in mountain rescue operations
    and avalanche forecasting may be particularly useful to units anticipating operations in more committing
    mountainous terrain. Opportunities exist for this at Army mountain training centers or through appropriately
    certified civilian mountaineering training organizations.

                                                  Chapter 3
                                   Environmental Injuries
   Operations in mountainous areas will expose Soldiers to a variety of harsh environmental
   conditions not found in lowland areas. Soldiers exposed to these conditions are at a heightened
   risk of becoming a casualty. This risk increases with lack of experience and training. Troops
   conducting operations in mountainous regions often encounter cold temperatures that can
   degrade physical performance, impact morale, and create cold-weather casualties. The lack of
   oxygen in high-altitude environments impairs many aspects of normal Soldier tasks. Soldiers
   may develop altitude illnesses that can produce debilitating symptoms and require immediate
   MEDEVAC. If not accounted for in the planning process, these conditions will negatively
   impact the mission. Soldiers will become fatigued sooner in this environment and must reduce
   their pace or lighten their load to remain healthy and effective. With experience and proper
   training, Soldiers will become more durable and lethal in this environment.

SECTION I – ENVIRONMENTAL INJURY PREVENTION
   3-1. Units operating in mountainous regions are exposed to various types of injuries and illnesses
   unassociated with other areas. Medical considerations are like those for other environments; however, there
   are some unique aspects of mountain operations to consider to provide effective support.

ILLNESSES AND INJURIES
   3-2. Most injuries in the mountain environment are orthopedic and soft-tissue injuries. These include sprains,
   strains, abrasions, contusions, and fractures. Skills in basic first aid are essential to all Soldiers operating in
   the mountains and should be reinforced with regular sustainment training. (See TB MED 505 for more
   information.) Medical personnel should receive training in identifying and treating these prior to deployment.

TREATMENT AND EVACUATION
   3-3. In harsh mountain weather, the most important course of action is to provide injured Soldiers with
   medical aid as soon as possible. Immediate first aid is given on site. Due to rough terrain, medical units can
   seldom reach unit aid stations by vehicle to evacuate casualties. Litter bearers must move casualties to the
   rear where they can be evacuated by ground or air to clearing stations. The victim must be protected from the
   weather and shock during transportation. Rendezvous points are coordinated with medical units as far
   forward as possible. All litter bearers must receive training in evacuation techniques and first aid. Lightly
   wounded personnel may need assistance to move over rough terrain. (See chapter 15 for CASEVAC TTP in
   mountainous terrain.)

INJURIES RELATED TO COLD EXPOSURE
   3-4. There are several common injuries associated with cold temperature exposure. Some are more
   commonly associated with hot weather but present just as serious a threat in cold conditions.
DEHYDRATION
   3-5. Dehydration is the loss of bodily fluids that prevents or slows normal bodily functions. This is usually
   caused by overexertion and improper water intake. Although the mechanism that causes dehydration is not
   specifically cold temperatures, the environment and the body’s natural response to the cold often lead to
   Soldiers becoming dehydrated. Dehydration precedes all cold-weather injuries and is a major symptom of
   acute mountain sickness (AMS). Dehydration contributes to poor performance in all physical activities, even
   more so than lack of food. Cold-weather requirements for water are no different from in the desert. In fact,
   they may exceed desert requirements because of the increased difficulty in moving with extra clothing and
   through the snow. At high altitudes, the air is dry. Combined with a rapid rate of breathing, as much as 2 liters



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                   25
Chapter 3



     of liquid may be lost each day through respiration. A Soldier needs about 3 to 6 liters of water each day to
     prevent dehydration when living and performing physical labor in a cold or mountainous environment.
     Leaders should monitor their Soldiers’ water intake, since motivation to drink cold water in a cold
     environment is low. Coffee and tea are diuretics and cause excessive urination, which contributes to
     dehydration. They should be avoided. However, providing other noncaffeinated hot liquids is a good way to
     encourage Soldiers to drink more water. The adequacy of liquid intake can best be judged by the color of
     urine and volume. Dark, amber-colored urine instead of light yellow or the absence of a need to urinate upon
     awakening from a night’s sleep is an indicator of dehydration. Thirst is not a good indicator of hydration.

Contributing Factors
     3-6. Factors that contribute to dehydration in cold weather are—
          • The thirst mechanism does not function properly in cold weather.
          • Water is often inconvenient to obtain and purify.
          • The air in cold climates and at high altitudes lacks moisture.
          • Cold causes frequent urination.

Symptoms
     3-7. Symptoms of dehydration include darkening urine, decreased amounts of urine being produced, dry
     mouth, tiredness, mental sluggishness, lack of appetite, headache, fainting, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, higher
     temperature, upset stomach, and unconsciousness. The symptoms of dehydration resemble those of
     hypothermia. To distinguish between them, open the victim’s clothes and feel the stomach. If the stomach is
     cold, the victim is probably hypothermic; if it is warm, the victim is probably dehydrated. However, this test
     is inconclusive since cold-weather dehydration can also lead to total body cooling. The cold environment
     may act as a diuretic and impair the body’s ability to conserve fluids. Cold diuresis is an increase in urine
     output, which is the body’s response to cold-weather immersion. This can contribute to dehydration, which
     is the precursor to several other cold-weather injuries, both freezing and non-freezing.

Treatment
     3-8. Prevent dehydration by consuming 3 to 6 liters of fluids each day (forced drinking in the absence of
     thirst is mandatory) and avoid caffeine and alcohol. Keep the victim warm and treat them for shock. In
     advanced cases, administer fluids by mouth if the victim is conscious. Ingesting snow will contribute to loss
     of body heat. Allow the victim to rest. If the victim fails to improve within 1 hour or is unconscious, evacuate
     to a medical facility immediately.
HEAT INJURIES
     3-9. Heat injuries, although associated with hot weather, can occur in cold-weather environments. Planning,
     periodically inspecting personnel clothing (ventilation) and equipment, balancing water and food intake, and
     resting can prevent most heat injuries.

Heat Cramps
     3-10. Heat cramps are muscle spasms that result from loss of large amounts of salt and water through
     exertion. Heat cramps are caused by an accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles and a loss of salt through
     perspiration.

Contributing Factor
     3-11. Strenuous exertion causes the body to rise in temperature and to produce heavy perspiration.

Symptoms
     3-12. Symptoms of heat cramps include pain and cramping in the arms, legs, back, and stomach. Victims
     sweat profusely and cannot quench their thirst.




26                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                          Environmental Injuries



Treatment
    3-13. Have the victim rest in a cool, shady area, breathe deeply, and stretch the cramped muscle as soon as
    possible to obtain relief. Loosen the victim’s clothing and provide cool water to drink. Monitor the victim’s
    condition and seek medical attention if pain and cramps continue.

Heat Exhaustion
    3-14. Heat exhaustion is rapid water and salt depletion that can occur after exposure to high temperatures or
    intense exertion. It is often accompanied by dehydration. Heat exhaustion may occur when Soldiers exert
    themselves in any environment and overheat. The blood vessels in the skin become so dilated that they reduce
    blood flow to the brain and other organs.

Contributing Factors
    3-15. Factors that contribute to heat exhaustion are strenuous activity in hot areas, troops that are not
    acclimated, inappropriate diet, and insufficient water or rest.

Symptoms
    3-16. Symptoms of heat exhaustion may resemble fainting but may also include weakness, dizziness,
    confusion, headache, cold clammy skin, and nausea. The victim may also have a rapid but weak pulse.

Treatment
    3-17. Move the victim to a cool, shady area and loosen clothing and boots. Have the victim drink water and,
    if possible, and if weather conditions are conducive, immerse the victim’s body in water to aid in cooling.
    Elevate the victim’s legs to help restore proper circulation. Monitor the victim’s condition, and seek medical
    attention if symptoms persist. Without proper intervention, heat exhaustion can lead to heat stroke.

Heat Stroke
    3-18. Heat stroke occurs when the core body temperature exceeds 104°F, commonly a result of prolonged
    exposure to or physical exertion at higher temperatures. Heat stroke is a life-threatening situation caused by
    overexposure to the sun. The body is so depleted of liquids that its internal cooling mechanisms fail to
    function.

Contributing Factors
    3-19. Factors that contribute to heat stroke are prolonged exposure to direct sunlight, overexertion,
    dehydration, and depletion of electrolytes.

Symptoms
    3-20. Symptoms of heat stroke include hot, dry skin; dizziness; confusion and incoherency; headache;
    nausea; seizures; breathing difficulty; a slow pulse; and loss of consciousness.

Treatment
    3-21. Cool the victim immediately and restore breathing and circulation. If the victim is conscious, administer
    water. If possible, and if weather conditions are conducive, submerge the victim in water to reduce
    temperature, treat for shock, and prepare for immediate evacuation.
SOLAR INJURIES
    3-22. Solar injuries can happen in warm or cold weather. These types of injuries can be just as incapacitating
    as most other injuries but usually are not fatal. Peak hours of ultraviolet (UV) radiation are between the hours
    of 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. Because of the long wavelengths of UV light, cloudy days can be more dangerous than
    sunny days. On sunny days, the Soldier takes more care due to the bright conditions. On cloudy days, the
    Soldier tends not to wear sunglasses or sunscreen.



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                 27
Chapter 3



Sunburn
     3-23. Excessive UV radiation from sunlight is a serious threat to military personnel operating in high
     mountain regions during daylight hours because of several factors increasing its damaging potential.
     UV exposure can cause significant short-term disability to military personnel through severe sunburn.

Contributing Factors
     3-24. Decreased UV filtering by the thinner atmosphere at high altitude causes an increased intensity of
     exposure (approximately 4 percent for every 1,000 feet of elevation increase) and a shift of the UV spectrum
     to more harmful short wavelengths. Reflection from snow and ice increases the intensity of exposure
     (approximately 75 percent of incident radiation is reflected). Soldiers vary greatly in their risk of sunburn
     based on their skin type and pigment.

Symptoms
     3-25. Symptoms of sunburn are painful, burning, red, or blistered skin with slight swelling. The skin may be
     warm to the touch. In severe cases, chills, fever, and headaches may occur.

Treatment
     3-26. Limiting skin exposure with clothes and sunscreen (sun protection factor 15 and above) will prevent
     most sunburns. Applying to skin areas that are normally shaded, such as the eyelids and under the chin, is
     necessary to reduce the likelihood of sunburn from light reflected off snow and rocks. Opaque agents, such
     as zinc oxide, red veterinary petrolatum, or titanium dioxide; can be used for high-risk body areas, such as
     the nose, lips, and tops of the ears. The agents should be used carefully in a tactical situation where they
     could make a Soldier more visible to opposing forces. Diagnosis, prevention, treatment, and prognosis of
     solar radiation injuries are the same as at low altitude. (See TB MED 505.)

Snow Blindness
     3-27. Snow blindness results when solar radiation “sunburns” the eyes. Snow blindness can occur in a few
     hours of exposure, and there is no sensation of abnormality other than brightness as a warning that eye
     damage is occurring.
     3-28. Using eyewear or goggles that block more than 90 percent of UV radiation will help prevent snow
     blindness. To prevent injury from reflected light, protective eyewear should have side shields. Additionally,
     eyewear should have a safety cord or strap to prevent it from being lost accidentally. If sunglasses are not
     available, opaque eye covering (for example, tape-covered eyeglasses) with narrow, horizontal slits provide
     adequate field-expedient eye protection.

Symptoms
     3-29. Eyes may feel painful and gritty, and there may be tearing, blurred vision, severe light sensitivity, and
     headache. Symptoms are worst for 6 to 8 hours after exposure and resolve in 48 to 72 hours.

Treatment
     3-30. Treating snow blindness involves patching the eye and controlling the pain. Cool compresses over the
     eyes help alleviate some discomfort. Dilating the pupil and using ocular antibiotics are helpful. Pain control
     may require oral analgesics, sedatives, or both. The prognosis is generally good, although snow blindness
     may take several days to resolve. The pain and visual decrements will require temporary, but significant, duty
     limitations. In severe cases, permanent damage can occur.
BLISTERS
     3-31. Blisters often only cause minor discomfort but can become severe enough to restrict a person’s physical
     activity and mobility temporarily. In some cases, friction blisters have developed into serious complications
     and infections requiring antibiotics and medical treatment. As one of the most common injuries to the military
     mountaineer, blisters present a notable adverse impact to mobility and mission readiness.



28                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                         Environmental Injuries



Contributing Factors
   3-32. Rough and sloped terrain increases friction generated between the skin and footwear during foot
   movements, leading to a higher incidence of blister development.

Symptoms
   3-33. Blisters are raised, painful, fluid-filled protrusions.

Treatment
   3-34. Before a blister forms or when a Soldier first notices one, cover a hotspot with moleskin (over the area
   and beyond it). Use tincture benzoin to help the moleskin adhere to and toughen the skin. Once a blister has
   formed, cover it with a dressing large enough to fit over the blister, and then tape it. Never drain blisters
   unless they are surrounded by redness or if draining pus indicates infection. If this occurs, drain the blister
   from the side with a clean, sterile needle. After cleaning with soap and water, gently press out the fluid,
   leaving the skin intact. Make a doughnut of moleskin to go around the blister and apply to the skin. For toe
   blisters, wrap the entire toe with adhesive tape over the moleskin. (Toenails should be trimmed straight across
   the top, leaving a 90° angle on the sides. This provides an arch, so the corners do not irritate the skin.)
CARBON MONOXIDE POISONING
   3-35. This is the replacement of oxygen in the blood with carbon monoxide, preventing adequate oxygenation
   of cells in the body.

Contributing Factor
   3-36. A contributing factor is inhaling fumes from burning fuel, such as fires, stoves, heaters, and running
   engines, without proper ventilation.

Symptoms
   3-37. Symptoms are like other common illnesses and include headaches, fatigue, excessive yawning, nausea,
   dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, and unconsciousness. Death may occur. Three visible symptoms are bright
   red lips, mouth, and inside of the eyelids.

Treatment
   3-38. Remove the victim from the source of contamination; administer oxygen, if available; and evacuate to
   a medical facility. Severe complications may develop even in casualties who appear to have recovered. If the
   victim is unconscious, administer rescue breathing and cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) as needed.

COLD-WEATHER CONSIDERATIONS
   3-39. Military mountain operations can occur in the coldest weather and with minimal logistical support,
   leaving troops under-equipped for hostile conditions. Individuals in these situations must rely on their prior
   training and strong leadership in cold stress management. This training can determine whether the mission
   will succeed or fail with either few or high casualty rates. Individuals in these situations often are not fully
   prepared, and, consequently, unit commanders and trainers must actively plan to prevent cold casualties.
   Soldiers need to be confident that they can master the environment by using preventive measures. Lessons
   learned from previous cold-weather deployments must be emphasized. Leaders must learn their unit’s
   capabilities and manage cold exposure relative to the provided guidance. Soldiers must be prepared to
   survive, move, and fight in winter conditions. Intense cold affects the mind as well as the body. Simple tasks
   take longer to perform and take more effort than in a temperate climate. When weather conditions become
   extreme, the problems of survival become more significant. Warmth and comfort become top priorities. The
   effects of extreme cold and the probability of injury are magnified by a lack of proper diet and sleep. The
   most important measure in preventing cold-weather injuries is the education of personnel and their leaders.




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                               29
Chapter 3



TYPES
      3-40. Cold injuries may be divided into two types: freezing and non-freezing. The freezing type is known as
      frostbite. The nonfreezing type includes hypothermia, chilblain, and immersion foot. Cold injuries result from
      impaired circulation and from cold and ice forming upon the tissues of the body. Temperature alone is not a
      reliable guide as to whether a cold injury can occur. Low temperatures are necessary for cold injuries to occur,
      but freezing temperatures are not. Wind speed can accelerate body heat loss under both wet and cold conditions.
PREVENTATIVE MEASURES
      3-41. Commanders should ensure the following measures are taken to prevent cold-weather injuries:
          • Soldiers’ uniforms are kept as dry as possible and are protected from the elements.
          • Soldiers are educated on proper use of clothing systems to avoid the effects of overheating and
              perspiration (layer dressing and ventilation).
          • The buddy system is used to watch for early signs of cold-weather injuries.
          • All Soldiers waterproof their equipment.
          • The rate of movement should be slow, deliberate, and careful. Soldiers should not move out at a
              force march pace and then be stationary after they have perspired heavily. Soldiers should not wear
              excessive cold-weather clothing while moving.
RISK FACTORS
      3-42. Several demographic, behavioral, and past history characteristics increase risk for cold-weather
      injuries.

Body Composition
      3-43. Individuals with a high amount of body surface area relative to their body mass (long and lean) lose
      more body heat in the cold than individuals with a small surface area relative to their body weight (short and
      stocky) do. The reason for this is that the principal means of heat loss in the cold is at the skin surface. This
      effect is somewhat reduced in short, stocky people because a large body mass maintains a constant
      temperature better than a small body mass.

Sex
      3-44. The peripheral (for example, hands and feet) cold-injury rate for female Soldiers is two times higher
      than the rate for males. Sex differences during cold exposure are almost entirely attributable to women’s
      generally greater body fat content and thicker fat layer under the skin compared to men of comparable age
      and weight. Women typically have a greater surface area but smaller total body mass (thus lower total body
      heat content) than men do.

Race
      3-45. African-American male and female Soldiers are two to four times more likely to suffer a cold-weather
      injury versus their Caucasian counterparts. This increased risk is consistent across all career management
      fields, which suggests that occupational exposure does not account for the differences between
      African-Americans and Caucasians. Differences between races may be due to cold-weather experience, but
      more likely they are due to anthropomorphic considerations (longer, thinner digits) and perhaps greater
      surface-area-to-mass ratio.

Fitness and Training
      3-46. Overall, physical training and fitness levels appear to have only minor influences on cold management.
      Fitter individuals can sustain more physical activity at a higher intensity and longer duration; therefore, they
      produce more heat from exercise for longer periods when compared to less fit individuals.




30                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                         Environmental Injuries



Fatigue
   3-47. Physical fatigue can impair shivering and peripheral vasoconstriction responses during cold exposure.
   Therefore, physical fatigue can increase the Soldier’s risk for hypothermia. Fatigued Soldiers cannot sustain
   sufficient activity levels to maintain body temperature during severe cold exposure.

Age
   3-48. Soldiers who are 45 years of age or older may be less cold tolerant than younger people, either because
   of a decline in physical fitness or because of reduced vasoconstriction and heat conservation in comparison
   to their younger counterparts.

Dehydration
   3-49. Dehydration can increase susceptibility to cold injury by decreasing the ability to sustain physical
   activity (particularly if accompanied by heat stress from exercising in heavy clothing) and, therefore,
   decreasing the ability to sustain thermal balance. In addition, dehydration might impair cognitive function
   and cause Soldiers to use poor judgment. Dehydration has not been shown to reduce peripheral skin
   temperatures and does not impair shivering.

Sustained Operations
   3-50. Exertional fatigue, sleep restriction, and underfeeding are common stressors during sustained
   operations and together impair a Soldier’s ability to maintain thermal balance in the cold. The metabolic heat
   production response degrades and impairs the ability to sustain exercise performance. Soldiers engaged in
   sustained operations also may make more judgment errors when tired and increase their exposure and risk of
   injury. A given cold stressor is more likely to induce cold injury after a long period of sustained operations
   compared to earlier in the operation. This emphasizes the need for planned rest, sleep, feeding, and recovery
   before conducting stressful operations in the cold.

Food and Nutrient Consumption
   3-51. Consuming too little nutrients can result in hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), which can impair
   shivering. Hypoglycemia contributes to an inability to sustain physical activity and the associated
   exercise-induced heat production during cold exposure. No food for 48 hours, even in the absence of
   hypoglycemia, results in an impaired ability to shiver and increased risk of hypothermia.

Alcohol
   3-52. Although alcohol may impart a sense of warmth, any peripheral vasodilation increases heat loss and
   the risk of hypothermia. Alcohol can cause hypoglycemia, which will decrease shivering responses and the
   ability to sustain physical work. In addition, alcohol blunts the senses and impairs judgment, so the Soldier
   may not feel the signs and symptoms of a developing cold injury. Soldiers must not consume alcohol while
   exposed to cold weather.

Nicotine
   3-53. Smoking or chewing tobacco can increase susceptibility to frostbite by increasing vasoconstriction in
   the periphery (for example, the hands). Heavy smokers (two to three packs per day) have a 30-percent higher
   incidence of peripheral cold injury, perhaps because nicotine reduces the body’s response to the cold.
   Smoking and chewing will be discouraged during cold-weather operations.

Previous Cold Injuries
   3-54. If Soldiers have had previous cold injuries, they are at higher risk for subsequent cold injuries.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                    31
Chapter 3



Associated Injury
     3-55. Injuries resulting in shock or blood loss reduce blood flow to extremities and may increase the injured
     individual’s susceptibility to cold injury, which, in turn, can accelerate shock.
COLD-WEATHER INJURIES
     3-56. A cold-weather injury is any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental
     conditions. Some of the most common nonfreezing cold-weather injuries are described in paragraphs 3-57
     through 3-75.

Hypothermia
     3-57. Hypothermia is the lowering of the body core temperature at a rate faster than the body can produce
     heat. Hypothermia may be caused by exposure or by sudden wetting of the body, such as falling into a lake
     or being sprayed with fuel or other liquid. Hypothermia can occur even on moderate days with temperatures
     of 40°F to 50°F with little precipitation if heat loss exceeds heat gain, and the Soldier’s condition can
     deteriorate. Hypothermia is classified as mild (core temperature above 90°F or 32°Celsius [C]) or severe
     (core temperature below 90°F or 32°C). An individual is considered “clinically hypothermic” when their core
     temperature is less than or equal to 95°F.
     3-58. Methods of heat loss:
         • Radiation—direct heat loss from the body to its surrounding atmosphere is called radiation heat loss.
             The head can radiate up to 80 percent of the total body heat output. On cold days, personnel must
             keep all extremities covered to retain heat. Heat loss from extremities accounts for the largest
             amount of heat lost from the body.
         • Conduction—direct transfer of heat from one object in contact with another (being rained on or
             sitting in snow).
         • Convection—loss of heat due to moving air or water in contact with the skin. Wind chill is
             convection cooling. Clothing that ventilates, insulates, and protects must control the layer of warm
             air next to the skin.
         • Evaporation—evaporation of perspiration causes heat loss. Wet clothing can cause heat loss by
             conduction and evaporation. Dressing in layers allows Soldiers to remove or add clothing as needed.
         • Respiration—when cold air is inhaled, the air is warmed, then exhaled, resulting in a significant
             source of heat loss.

Contributing Factors
     3-59. Factors that contribute to hypothermia are—
         • Dehydration.
         • Poor nutrition.
         • Diarrhea.
         • Decreased physical activity.
         • Accidental immersion in water.
         • Change in weather.
         • High winds.
         • Inadequate types or amounts of clothing.

Symptoms
     3-60. Body temperature refers to the core (rectal) temperature. Symptoms become progressively worse as the
     body temperature drops.
         • 96°F:
              Shivering (begins about 2° below normal body temperature).
              Uncontrollable shivering (about 96°F).
              Inability to care for self.
              Clumsiness (stumbling or falling).
              Slow reactions.


32                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                           Environmental Injuries



              Mental confusion.
              Difficulty speaking.
        •    95°F to 90°F:
              Sluggish thinking.
              Irrational thought.
              Apathy.
              False sense of warmth.
              Cold skin.
              Pale or bluish skin.
              Inability to perform simple tasks.
              Amnesia.
              Hallucinations.
              Decreased heart and respiratory rate.
              Weak pulse.
              Dilated pupils.
              Slurred speech.
              Visual disturbance.
        •    90°F to 85°F. Shivering may stop. In addition, a Soldier may experience—
              Irrationality.
              Incoherence.
              Loss of contact with the environment.
              Muscular rigidity.
              Disorientation.
              Exhaustion.
        •    85°F and below:
              Muscle rigidity.
              Unconsciousness.
              Comatose state.
              Faint vital signs.
              Faint or impalpable pulse.
              Breathing possibly too shallow to observe.

Prevention
    3-61. Prevent hypothermia by using the buddy system to watch each other for symptoms and consume
    adequate amounts of liquids, rest, and eat properly.

Avoidance
    3-62. Hypothermia can be avoided by dressing in layers, which permits easy additions or removal to prevent
    overheating, becoming too cold, or getting wet or windblown. If Soldiers are in a situation that precludes
    staying warm and dry, they should seek shelter. Eating sugary foods and physical activity helps to produce
    body heat.

Treatment
    3-63. Treatment methods vary based on the severity of the hypothermia. Mild cases—if Soldiers show
    symptoms of hypothermia, prevent additional heat loss by getting them into a shelter, if available; removing
    wet clothing; and replacing it with dry, insulated clothing. If they are capable, feed Soldiers fast energy food
    and hot liquids and increase their physical activity level to generate heat. If they are unable to move, insulate
    them from the ground, and consider directing warm Soldiers to share a sleeping bag (cover head) with injured
    Soldiers to transfer body heat. This method of warming can compromise warmer Soldiers’ core temperatures
    as well if they are not sufficiently fed, warm, and healthy. Make a diagnosis (for example, by obtaining a
    rectal temperature). Rehydrate the Soldier with warm liquids, sweets, and food. If the tactical situation allows,
    build a fire. Above all else, keep Soldiers conscious until their vital signs are normal, and seek medical
    assistance.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  33
Chapter 3



     3-64. Severe cases—if the victim is unconscious or appears dead without any obvious injury, prevent further
     heat loss. Avoid rapidly rewarming an unconscious victim, which can create problems. Evacuating as soon
     as possible is preferable. At all times, the victim should be handled gently so as not to cause the cold blood
     from the extremities to rush to the heart. Immediately transport the victim to the nearest medical facility.
     Field reheating is not effective and may be hazardous. Provide artificial respiration if breathing stops. If no
     pulse is detectable, be aware that in hypothermia there is often effective circulation for the victim’s
     hypothermic state. In such a case, cardiac compression (such as CPR) may be fatal. The exception is acute
     hypothermia with near drowning.
     3-65. Use the following treatment methods based on the severity of the victim’s hyperthermia:
         • Breathing warm, moist air is the fastest way to warm the inside of the body. If breathing steam is
             not possible, place tubing under the rescuer’s shirt so the victim will still breathe warm, moist air.
             This process can be done while on the move. In addition to breathing moist, warm air, the victim
             must be gradually rewarmed using external heat sources. Padded hot water bottles or heated stones
             should be placed in the armpits.
         • If conscious, the victim can be given warm, sugary drinks.
         • All bodily systems in hypothermia are brittle so treat the victim gently. While making these attempts,
             try to evacuate the victim. Severe complications may arise as the body temperature rises, which may
             result in cardiac arrest even though the victim seems to be doing well.

Immersion or Trench Foot
     3-66. The circulatory and nervous systems of the feet are damaged from prolonged exposure to cold and wet
     at above freezing temperatures. This can happen wearing boots or not. A Soldier may not feel symptoms until
     the injury has already begun.

Contributing Factors
     3-67. Factors that contribute to immersion or trench foot are—
         • Stepping into water that comes over the boot tops.
         • Not changing socks often enough.
         • Improper hygiene.
         • Prolonged exposure (3 to 5 days).

Symptoms
     3-68. Symptoms of immersion or trench foot include the sensation of tingling, numbness, and then pain. The
     toes are pale and feel cold and stiff. The skin is wet and soggy with the color turning from red to bright red,
     progressing to pale and mottled, and then grayish blue. As symptoms progress and damage appear, the skin
     becomes red and then bluish or black. Swelling may occur. Because the early stages of trench foot are not
     painful, Soldiers must be constantly aware to prevent it.

Treatment
     3-69. To prevent this condition, keep the feet dry and clean. Change socks often, drying the insides of boots,
     massaging the feet, and using foot powder. Drying the feet for 24 hours usually heals mild cases. Moderate
     cases usually heal within 3 to 5 days. The feet should be handled gently―not rubbed or massaged. They
     should be cleaned with soap and water, dried, elevated, and exposed to room temperature. Victims must stay
     off their feet and seek medical attention. Severe cases, when feet are not allowed to dry, are evacuated as a
     litter casualty.

Chilblain
     3-70. Chilblain (also known as pernio or kibe) is a superficial cold injury typically occurring after
     approximately 1 to 5 hours in cold-wet conditions, at temperatures below 50°F. A discolored rash or small
     red spots may appear on the skin, most often on the fingers but can commonly occur on the ears, face, and
     exposed skin. The lesions are swollen, tender, itchy, and painful. Upon rewarming, the skin becomes




34                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                           Environmental Injuries



    inflamed, red, and hot to the touch, and swollen with an itching or burning sensation that may continue for
    several hours after exposure.

Frostbite
    3-71. Frostbite is the freezing or crystallization of living tissues due to heat being lost faster than it can be
    replaced by blood circulation or from direct exposure to extreme cold or high winds. Exposure time can be
    minutes or instantaneous. The extremities are usually the first to be affected. Damp hands and feet may freeze
    quickly since moisture conducts heat away from the body and destroys the insulating value of clothing. Heat
    loss is compounded with intense cold and inactivity. Frostbite can be prevented with properly maintained
    and used clothing and equipment. The extent of frostbite depends on temperature and duration of exposure.
    Frostbite is one of the major nonfatal cold-weather injuries encountered in military operations but does not
    occur above an ambient temperature of 32°F.

Categories of Frostbite
    3-72. Superficial (mild) frostbite involves only the skin. The layer immediately below usually appears white
    to grayish with the surface feeling hard, but the underlying tissue is soft. Deep (severe) frostbite extends
    beyond the first layer of skin and may include the bone. Discoloration continues from gray to black, and the
    texture becomes hard as the tissue freezes deeper. This condition requires immediate evacuation to a medical
    facility.

Contributing Factors
    3-73. Factors that contribute to frostbite are—
        • Dehydration.
        • Below-freezing temperatures.
        • Skin contact with super cooled metals or liquids.
        • Use of caffeine, tobacco, or alcohol.
        • Neglect.

Symptoms
    3-74. Symptoms of frostbite vary and may include a cold feeling, pain, burning, numbness, and, in the final
    stages, a false sense of warmth. The skin first turns red, then pale. The skin may be bluish in color and then
    may appear frosty or waxy white. The skin may feel hard, be immovable over the joints and bony
    prominences, or be frozen. Identifying deep versus superficial frostbite is difficult to determine and often
    requires 3 to 7 days after rewarming for medical personnel to diagnose. Blisters, swelling, and pain may
    occur after thawing.

Treatment
    3-75. Using the buddy system is one of the primary ways to prevent frostbite. Buddies must watch each other
    for symptoms of frostbite and provide mutual aid if frostbite occurs. Frostbite should be identified early with
    prompt first aid care applied to prevent further damage:
         • Treat early signs of frostbite by rewarming with skin-to-skin contact or by sheltering the body part
            under the clothing next to the body. Do this immediately. If tissues have frozen, evacuate the victim
            before they thaw. If the feet are involved, evacuate the victim as a litter patient.
         • Thawing of a frostbitten victim is a hospital procedure. If the victim has frostbite with frozen
            extremities, protect the frozen parts and evacuate as a litter patient.
         • If frostbite is not recognized before it thaws, do not let the area re-freeze since this causes more
            damage. The most often affected body parts are the hands, fingers, toes, feet, ears, chin, and nose.
            If evacuating victims as a litter case is not possible and the body part has not yet thawed, have the
            victims walk out on their own. Walking out on frozen feet is better than having them thaw and
            refreeze. Self-evacuation may be tactically necessary. Walking on frozen feet does less harm than
            walking on thawed feet.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  35
Chapter 3



         •    If reheating is inevitable, do not overheat the affected body parts near flame; the warming
              temperature should not be greater than normal body temperature. Do not rub the parts; the
              crystallized tissues may break internally and cause more damage. Do not pop blisters; cover them
              with a dry, sterile dressing. Keep the victim warm (apply loose, bulky bandages to separate toes and
              fingers).
         •    Once a part is rewarmed, it will become painful. Pain may be managed with narcotic analgesics.
         •    Once the foot is rewarmed, it will swell and putting the boot back on will not be possible.

SECTION II – ALTITUDE EFFECTS, INJURIES, AND ACCLIMATIZATION
     3-76. As altitude increases, the overall atmospheric pressure decreases. Decreased pressure is the underlying
     source of altitude illnesses. Whether at sea level or 20,000 feet, the surrounding atmosphere has the same
     percentage of oxygen. As pressure decreases, the body has a much more difficult time passing oxygen from
     the lungs to the red blood cells and thus to body tissues. This lower pressure means lower oxygen levels in
     the blood and increased carbon dioxide levels.

ACCLIMATIZATION
     3-77. When the unit arrives at an operation area, all personnel require a period of conditioning and
     acclimatization. The schedule should allow for longer and more frequent periods of rest. The rigors of
     establishing an assembly area exhaust most personnel who are not acclimated. Water, food, and rest should
     be considered priorities, ensuring enough while individual metabolisms and bodies become accustomed to
     functioning at higher elevations. Since the acclimatization process cannot be shortened, and the absence of
     acclimatization hampers the successful execution of operations, planning for deployments to higher
     elevations should consider the following:
          • Above 8,000 feet, a unit should ascend at a rate of 1,000 to 2,000 feet per day. Units can leapfrog,
              taking extended rest periods.
          • Units should not resort to using pharmaceutical pretreatment with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors,
              such as acetazolamide. These drugs have side effects that mimic the signs and symptoms of AMS.
              Inexperienced medics may have difficulty recognizing the differences between the side effects of
              the drug and a condition that could possibly be life threatening. Additionally, these drugs are
              diuretics, which results in higher hydration levels (at least 25-percent increase per Soldier per day).
              These higher hydration levels create a larger logistical demand on the unit by requiring more water,
              more time to acquire water, more water purification supplies, and, if in a winter environment, more
              fuels for melting snow and ice for water.
          • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, are effective in treating mild and severe
              AMS. These drugs should accompany attached medical personnel because they can treat the Soldier
              suffering from AMS and, although rest may be required, evacuation may not be needed.
          • Do not move troops directly to high altitudes even if allowances can be made for inactivity for the
              first 3 to 5 days before mission commitment. Moving troops directly to high altitude can increase
              the probability of altitude sickness. Even if inactivity follows deployment, the incidence of altitude
              sickness is more likely than with a gradual ascent.

ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS
     3-78. AMS is the body’s response to physical distress from difficulty adjusting to lower oxygen levels at
     high altitude. AMS is a temporary illness that can affect any Soldier, regardless of mountaineering
     experience. Soldiers are subject to this sickness at altitudes as low as 5,000 feet. Incidence and severity
     increase with altitude and when quickly transported to high altitudes. Disability and ineffectiveness can occur
     in 50 to 80 percent of the troops who are rapidly brought to altitudes above 10,000 feet. At lower altitudes,
     or where ascent to altitudes is gradual, most personnel can complete assignments with moderate effectiveness
     and little discomfort.
     3-79. Personnel arriving at moderate elevations (5,000 to 8,000 feet) usually feel well for the first few hours;
     a feeling of exhilaration or well-being is typical. There may be an initial awareness of breathlessness upon
     exertion and a need for frequent pauses to rest. Irregular breathing can occur, mainly during sleep; these
     changes may cause apprehension. Severe symptoms—such as nausea, sluggishness, fatigue, headache,


36                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                        Environmental Injuries



   dizziness, insomnia, depression, uncaring attitude, rapid and labored breathing, weakness, and loss of
   appetite—may begin 4 to 12 hours after arriving at higher altitudes.
   3-80. A headache is the most noticeable symptom of AMS and may be severe. Even when a headache is not
   present, some loss of appetite and a decrease in tolerance for food occurs. Nausea, even without food intake,
   occurs and leads to less food intake. Vomiting may occur and contribute to dehydration. Despite fatigue,
   personnel are unable to sleep. The symptoms usually develop and peak by the second day. They gradually
   subside over the next several days so that the total course of AMS may extend from 5 to 7 days. In some
   instances, the headache may become incapacitating, and the Soldier should be evacuated to a lower elevation.
   3-81. Treatment for AMS includes the following:
       • Oral pain medications, such as ibuprofen or aspirin.
       • Rest.
       • Frequent consumption of liquids and light foods in small amounts.
       • Movement to lower altitudes (at least 1,000 feet lower) to alleviate symptoms, which provides for a
            more gradual acclimatization.
       • Realization of physical limitations and slow progression.
       • Practice of deep-breathing exercises.
       • Use of acetazolamide in the first 24 hours for mild to moderate cases.
   3-82. AMS is nonfatal, although if left untreated or further ascent is attempted, development of high-altitude
   pulmonary edema (HAPE) or high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) can be seen. Severe persistence of
   symptoms may identify Soldiers who acclimatize poorly and, thus, are more prone to other types of mountain
   sickness.

HIGH-ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA
   3-83. HAPE is a swelling and filling of the lungs with fluid, caused by rapid ascent. HAPE occurs at high
   altitudes and limits the oxygen supply to the body. HAPE—
         • Occurs under conditions of low-oxygen pressure, is encountered at high elevations (over 8,000 feet)
             and can occur in healthy Soldiers.
        • Can cause death. Incidence and severity increase with altitude. Except for acclimatization to altitude,
             no known factors indicate resistance or immunity. Few cases have been reported after 10 days at
             high altitudes. For Soldiers who remain at the same altitude, the incidence of HAPE is less frequent
             than that of AMS. No common indicator dictates how a Soldier will react from one exposure to
             another.
CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
   3-84. The following factors are associated with the development of HAPE:
       • A history of HAPE.
       • A rapid or abrupt transition to high altitudes.
       • Strenuous physical exertion.
       • Exposure to cold.
       • Anxiety.
SYMPTOMS
   3-85. The following symptoms are associated with the development of HAPE:
       • Progressive dry coughing with frothy white or pink sputum (this is usually a later sign) and then
           coughing up blood.
       • Cyanosis—a blue color to the face, hands, and feet.
       • An increased ill feeling, labored breathing, dizziness, fainting, repeated clearing of the throat, and
           development of a cough.
       • Respiratory difficulty, which may be sudden, accompanied by choking and rapid deterioration.
       • Progressive shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat (pulse 120 to 160 beats per minute), and coughing
           (compared to others who arrived at the same time to that altitude).




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                                37
Chapter 3



         •    Crackling, cellophane-like noises (known as rales) in the lungs caused by fluid buildup. A
              stethoscope is usually needed to hear them.
         •    Unconsciousness, if left untreated. Bubbles form in the nose and mouth, and death results.
PREVENTION
     3-86. HAPE is prevented by good nutrition, hydration, and gradual ascent to altitude (no more than 1,000 to
     2,000 feet per day to an area of sleep). A rest day, with no gain in altitude or heavy physical exertion, is
     planned for every 3,000 feet of altitude gained. If Soldiers develop symptoms despite precautions, immediate
     descent is mandatory to receive necessary treatment, rest, warmth, and oxygen. They should be quickly
     evacuated to lower altitudes. A descent of 300 meters may help; do not delay manual descent to await air
     evacuation. If untreated, HAPE may become irreversible and cause death. Cases that are recognized early
     and treated promptly may expect to recover with no aftereffects. Soldiers who have had previous attacks of
     HAPE are prone to second attacks.
TREATMENT
     3-87. Treat HAPE with—
         • Immediate descent (2,000 to 3,000 feet minimum), if possible. If not, then treat it in a hyperbaric
              chamber.
         • Rest (litter evacuation).
         • Supplemental oxygen, if available.

HIGH-ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA
     3-88. HACE is the accumulation of fluid in the brain, which results in swelling and a decrease in brain
     function that may result in death. HACE is caused by a rapid ascent to altitude without progressive
     acclimatization. Preventing HACE is the same as for HAPE. HAPE and HACE may occur in experienced,
     well-acclimated mountaineers without warning or obvious predisposing conditions. Both types of edemas
     can be fatal. When the first symptoms occur, immediate descent is mandatory.
CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
     3-89. The following factors are associated with the development of HACE:
         • Rapid ascent to heights over 8,000 feet.
         • Aggravation by overexertion.
SYMPTOMS
     3-90. Symptoms include mild personality changes, paralysis, stupor, convulsions, coma, inability to
     concentrate, headaches, vomiting, decrease in urination, and lack of coordination. The main symptom of
     HACE is a severe headache. Another manifestation of HACE is a headache combined with any other physical
     or psychological disturbances. Headaches may be accompanied by a loss of coordination, confusion,
     hallucinations, and unconsciousness. These may be combined with symptoms of HAPE. Victims are often
     mistakenly left alone since others may think they are only irritable or temperamental; no one should ever be
     ignored. The symptoms may rapidly progress to death. Prompt descent to a lower altitude is vital.
PREVENTION
     3-91. HACE is prevented by good nutrition, hydration, and gradual ascent to altitude (no more than 1,000 to
     2,000 feet per day to an area of sleep). A rest day, with no gain in altitude or heavy physical exertion, is
     planned for every 3,000 feet of altitude gained. If a Soldier develops symptoms despite precautions,
     immediate descent is mandatory to receive prompt treatment, rest, warmth, and oxygen. They should be
     quickly evacuated to lower altitudes. A descent of 300 meters may help; manual descent is not delayed
     awaiting air evacuation. If untreated, HACE may become irreversible and cause death. Cases that are
     recognized early and treated promptly may expect to recover with no aftereffects. Soldiers who have had
     previous attacks of HACE are prone to second attacks.

                                                              Environmental Injuries



TREATMENT
   3-92. Treat HACE with—
       • Supplemental oxygen.
       • Rapid descent and medical attention.
       • Use of a hyperbaric chamber if descent is delayed.
