                 Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment
   Units receiving mountain training show a marked advantage in harsh mountain environments
   than those that do not. Normal activities, such as navigating, communicating, and moving,
   require specialized techniques. To gain confidence and experience, Soldiers must conduct
   realistic mountain training. They should be expected to perform under any environmental
   conditions. Extended training exercises test the sustainment mechanisms in place for the unit
   and expose the Soldier to the isolation common to mountain operations. Training should reflect
   the harsh mountain environment and should focus on the following:
       • Fitness and nutrition.
       • Ability to survive and operate in a cold-weather environment.
       • Resupply methods.
       • Soldier load management.
       • Bivouac considerations.

SECTION I – PHYSICAL TRAITS OF THE MILITARY MOUNTAINEER
   4-1. Operations in mountainous terrain are extremely taxing on the human body. The combined effects of
   harsh weather, difficult dismounted movements, and elevation require Soldiers to be in superior physical
   condition. The more adapted Soldiers are to the conditions in which they fight, the greater chance they have
   of success in executing their mission. To adapt to the mountain environment, Soldiers must train in similar
   environmental conditions and simulate the physical workload of operations in mountainous terrain.
   Simulating the stresses of mountain warfare on the Soldier’s body in a training environment allows necessary
   adaptations to be made.

PHYSICAL TRAINING FOR THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
   4-2. Physical fitness training considerations can be broken down into two categories:
        • Fitness aspects, which are important to Soldiers’ abilities to perform in mountainous terrain.
        • Fitness training programs that should guide commanders in developing their unit’s capability to
           perform effectively in mountainous terrain.
INDIVIDUAL FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
   4-3. Operating in the mountains demands a higher level of fitness from the individual Soldier. Even basic
   movement techniques require a higher level of exertion and as the terrain becomes increasingly technical, so
   too does the physical demand. This; coupled with increased loads, adverse environmental conditions, and
   altitude effects; can render a Soldier with substandard fitness ineffective. The mountain Soldier must possess
   the capacity to reach the objective with the energy to fight while moving safely through hazardous terrain.
   4-4. A Soldier must demonstrate proficiency in many facets of fitness to prepare for mountain operations.
   Soldiers must have a holistic approach to their workout programming and selection. They should not focus
   entirely on one aspect of fitness. Mountain Soldiers must train for their job with a level of dedication like
   that of professional athletes training to compete. There are many similarities between mountain Soldiers and
   athletes, but there are key differences as well. Athletes train to compete in a known sport, governed by rules.
   Mountain Soldiers may be faced with unknowns and have a less defined concept of how they will need to
   perform during mountain operations. These differences drive the well-rounded, holistic approach to fitness
   required for Soldiers who may fight in mountainous terrain.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                41
Chapter 4



Aerobic Capacity
     4-5. Aerobic capacity allows the mountain Soldier to move for long periods and helps determine potential
     capacity of endurance for long movements. Aerobic capacity refers to the Soldier’s ability to use oxygen to
     create energy for extended periods. Dismounted movements and the carrying of a casualty in mountainous
     terrain are examples of tasks requiring endurance. Training in a low-intensity, high-volume manner
     conditions the aerobic energy system and develops the necessary levels of endurance. FM 7-22, table 6-2,
     covers training such as ability group runs, terrain runs, foot marches, and endurance training machines to
     help increase aerobic endurance for unit members.

Anaerobic Capacity
     4-6. Anaerobic capacity allows a Soldier to sprint or have high levels of exertion for a short period. Little
     oxygen is needed for this type of energy production. The anaerobic energy system can create large amounts
     of force for a short period. Mountain Soldiers require a high level of anaerobic capacity to move under fire
     and perform tasks that require a short burst of energy. Training in a high-intensity, low-volume manner
     conditions the anaerobic energy system and provides the necessary levels of explosive energy. FM 7-22,
     table 6-2, covers training such as 30:60s, hill repeats, and shuttle runs to help condition the anaerobic energy
     system of unit members.

Resistance Training
     4-7. Resistance training increases the performance of the muscle tissue found in Soldiers’ bodies and
     increases bone density. Properly trained muscle tissue protects Soldiers’ joints during mountain operations,
     leading to greater durability in this harsh environment. Resistance training can affect the body in different
     ways. Mountain Soldiers must use resistance training correctly. Soldiers who operate in mountainous terrain
     should avoid excess bulking of their muscle tissue as this decreases their endurance capabilities. Soldiers do
     not need large muscles to have strength; adequate strength can be developed using resistance training to gain
     lean muscle mass. Strength is primarily a function of the brain’s connection to the muscles (neuromuscular
     pathways), not the size of the muscles. Soldiers should use resistance training to increase the function and
     durability of the body, not aesthetics. This training should be designed to increase muscular endurance, lean
     muscle mass, and strength. A master fitness trainer can design training programs to help individual Soldiers
     and commanders achieve their desired results. FM 7-22, table 6-2, covers training, such as the climbing drill,
     push-up and sit-up drill, and the strength and conditioning circuit, to guide Soldiers through types of
     resistance training.
UNIT FITNESS CONSIDERATIONS
     4-8. The commander should develop a conditioning or training program to bring a unit to a level where it can
     operate successfully in mountain conditions. Training priorities should be established. As with all military
     operations, training is a major influence on the success of mountain operations. Fitness is the foundation
     upon which all other mountain skills are built. Proper levels of fitness increase the lethality and durability of
     Soldiers operating in mountainous terrain.
     4-9. A physical training program for operations in mountainous terrain should not be taken lightly. This type
     of program is time-consuming and requires buy-in from all levels of the deploying unit’s chain of command.
     Exercise equipment that allows for proper training should be obtained. Prior to conducting this training,
     Soldiers should assess their fitness levels. This assessment is an important tool for commanders and master
     fitness trainers to understand what is needed in the exercise program. Once an exercise program is generated,
     a unit may begin to train. The program should focus on increasing Soldiers’ physical abilities to perform their
     job in a tactical and mountainous environment.
     4-10. U.S. forces do not routinely train in mountainous terrain. Therefore, extensive preparations are needed
     to ensure individual and unit effectiveness. Units should be conditioned physically and psychologically
     before undertaking rigorous mountain operations. Units must work well as a team to cope with the terrain,
     environment, and enemy situation. Certain factors should be considered:
         • What are the climatic and terrain conditions of the area of operations?
         • How much time is available for conditioning and training?



42                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                         Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



       •    What additional personnel will accompany the unit? Will they be available for training and
            conditioning?
       •    What is the unit’s current level of physical fitness?
       •    Does the unit have master fitness trainers creating exercise programs specific to the mountain
            environment?
       •    Is there an exercise facility that will allow Soldiers to physically train themselves using the master
            fitness trainer’s program?
       •    What is the level of individual expertise in mountaineering?
       •    What type of operations can be expected?
       •    Which areas in the United States most closely resemble the area of operations?
       •    Are predeployment areas and ranges available?
       •    Does the unit have trainers with experience in mountain warfare?
   4-11. Physical capability is not solely gained during 1 hour per day in the gym. The participating Soldier
   must have the discipline to adhere to proper nutrition planning and get adequate rest. To maximize recovery
   during this period, Soldiers should sleep 8 to 9 hours during a 24-hour period to minimize the chance of
   injury and increase performance gains.

NUTRITION FOR THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
   4-12. The food Soldiers eat directly correlates to the energy levels they expend, including their ability to
   recover from strenuous activity as well as many other factors. An understanding of how different types of
   nutrients affect the body will help the Soldier eat better. Soldiers participating in an intense physical training
   program should not diminish their gains from the training with poor nutrition. When physical training and
   proper nutrition are combined, Soldiers have more success in achieving and sustaining the fitness required
   for operations in mountainous terrain.
HYDRATION IN THE MOUNTAIN ENVIRONMENT
   4-13. Water is vital to the health and performance of the mountain Soldier. Dehydration decreases cognitive
   and physical performance. Soldiers commonly face conditions, such as cold weather and high elevations, in
   mountainous terrain. Both elements affect the body’s ability to stay properly hydrated. A cold climate
   decreases the sensation of thirst and causes cold-weather diuresis (excessive urination). These both decrease
   fluid levels in the body and can lead to a performance-limiting state of dehydration. High elevation combined
   with cold temperatures can further dehydrate a Soldier. Less oxygen leads to an increased respiration rate.
   While breathing, Soldiers exhale water vapor. Rapidly breathing dry air decreases fluid in the body.
   4-14. Soldiers and leaders should ensure the availability and consumption of fluids. Hydrating before, during,
   and after periods of exertion allows for adequate levels of performance and acclimatization. Other factors
   necessary for maintaining fluid balance in the body include consuming appropriate levels of sodium,
   electrolytes, and other necessary nutrients. Bananas and other fruits are great examples of electrolyte rich snacks.
MACRONUTRIENTS
   4-15. Nutrients are compounds in foods essential to life that provide the body with energy and building blocks
   for repair and growth. Nutrients required in large amounts are called macronutrients. Proteins, fats, and
   carbohydrates are the three types of macronutrients that must be consumed in certain proportions to maintain
   a healthy body. These important nutrients allow the human body to perform and acclimate in mountainous
   environments.

Proteins
   4-16. Protein is a macronutrient responsible for maintaining and restoring muscles, providing key enzymes,
   and strengthening immunity. Protein also helps preserve lean muscle mass and increase strength and
   endurance. Protein serves many functions that support physical activity. Protein repairs muscle after exertion
   and creates energy during prolonged periods of submaximal exertion. The recommended requirement is
   0.8 grams of protein for every 2.2 pounds of body weight, but this can fluctuate with activity levels. Protein
   requires water for digestion and may facilitate dehydration. Proteins provide the body with about 4 calories
   of energy per gram.


26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                   43
Chapter 4



Fats
     4-17. Fats are critical to physical performance, recovery from exercise, and cardiovascular health. Fats are
     the body’s natural and most concentrated source of stored food energy. Main sources of fats are meats, nuts,
     butter, eggs, milk, and cheese. Fats should comprise 25 to 30 percent of the total daily caloric intake. Fats
     require more water and oxygen to digest than protein. Fats provide the body with approximately 9 calories
     of energy per gram. Fat is the most energy dense of the three macronutrients. It is harder for the body to use
     fat in an efficient manner to produce energy during periods of exertion. Fats are harder to digest at higher
     altitudes.

Carbohydrates
     4-18. Carbohydrates are the chief energy source for high-intensity physical activity, and they are important
     for meeting overall energy needs. Carbohydrates are an important source of calories and provide the body
     with dietary fiber and a variety of micronutrients. Nutritionally, the most useful sources of carbohydrates are
     foods, such as unrefined grains, vegetables, and fruit. Carbohydrates should comprise up to 50 percent of the
     total daily caloric intake. Carbohydrates provide the body with around 4 calories of energy per gram.
BALANCED DIET
     4-19. Eating a balanced diet provides the energy needed to conduct daily activities and to maintain internal
     body processes. A balanced diet containing adequate amounts of macronutrients, vitamins, and minerals
     ensures an efficient metabolism. Since operations in mountainous terrain are strenuous and demand
     high-energy use, a balanced diet is necessary. A proper diet requires Soldiers to be aware of how many
     calories they must consume. Soldiers of different ages, weights, and sexes have different nutritional needs.
     Caloric requirements differ between Soldiers, especially when accounting for levels of activity.
     4-20. Mountain Soldiers should take the time to understand their own caloric requirements. (See figure 4-1.)
     Individual variables coupled with a variety of environmental conditions, cold weather, or altitudes make it
     difficult to generalize a Soldier’s daily requirement, and it could range from 4,500 to 6,000 calories a day.
     4-21. Vitamins allow chemical reactions in the body to happen so that they may use the energy found in the
     three macronutrients. Without these reactions, the energy from the calories in the macronutrients cannot be
     turned into adenosine triphosphate that the cells in our body use for energy, allowing them to function.
     Vitamins and minerals are found in vegetables, fruits, and meats. There are many different micronutrients,
     and it can become hard to track ingestion of all types. Physically active Soldiers should pay special attention
     to consume adequate amounts of iron, vitamin D, and antioxidants through a balanced diet. If a diet deficient
     in fresh foods containing essential vitamins and minerals is not available during a deployment, vitamin
     supplements are a suitable substitute.


                    Resting Energy Expenditure (Calories Used at Rest)

         • Each Soldier’s resting energy expenditure is different.
         • It is important to know one’s resting energy expenditure to know how many calories
           to consume.
         • Resting energy expenditures can be multiplied by activity factors to get total caloric
           requirements for different levels of exertion. This is important to know to ensure
           Soldiers get proper nourishment while operating in challenging terrain. (See the
           Special Operations Forces Nutrition Guide, pages 4 to 5, for detailed information on
           performing these calculations.)


                                Figure 4-1. Individual caloric requirements

     4-22. Extra food should be carried in case resupply operations fail. Food should be lightweight, easy to digest,
     and be able to be eaten hot or cold. Meals, ready to eat meet these criteria and provide the basic food groups.



44                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                      Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   Commanders may consider supplementing meals, ready to eat with breakfast bars, fruits, juices, candies,
   cereal bars, and chocolate. Bouillon cubes can replace the required salt intake, and it can warm cold bodies
   and stimulate the appetite. Hot beverages of soup, juices, powdered milk, and cider should also be considered.
   Since coffee, tea, and hot chocolate are diuretics, consuming these beverages should not be relied upon for
   hydration (see AR 40-25).
   4-23. Calories from carbohydrates, protein, and fat digest, absorb, and metabolize at different rates in our
   body. The timing of nutrient intake will affect the individual’s physical, behavioral, and cognitive well-being.
   High-energy snacks help maintain performance during long movements. Soldiers should also consume a
   high-carbohydrate snack to replenish energy stores and maximize recovery immediately following foot
   movements or hard physical work.
   4-24. Certain drugs, medications, alcohol, and smoking have adverse effects on the circulation, perspiration,
   hydration, and judgment of Soldiers. They should be avoided, if possible, when operating in extremely cold
   conditions or at high altitudes.
NUTRITION OF ELEVATION
   4-25. Success in mountain operations depends on proper nutrition. Because higher altitudes affect eating
   habits, precautions must be taken. If possible, at least one hot meal each day should be eaten, which may
   require personnel to heat their individual rations. (See USARIEM TN-01/4 for more information on
   nutrition.)
   4-26. Soldiers can experience physiological acclimatization with abrupt ascents to high altitudes. The
   circulatory system works to provide the needed oxygen to the body. Large meals require the digestive system
   to work harder than usual to digest food. Large meals may be accompanied by indigestion, shortness of
   breath, cramps, and illness. Therefore, relatively light meals that are high in carbohydrates are best while
   acclimatizing at higher elevations. Personnel should eat moderately and rest before strenuous physical
   activity. Since fats and protein are harder to digest, less digestive disturbances may occur if meals are eaten
   before resting. A diet high in carbohydrates is not as dense in energy and may require eating more often.
   Consuming carbohydrates, beginning in the morning and continuing through mid-afternoon, are important in
   maintaining energy levels.

ACCLIMATIZATION
   4-27. The following elements are characteristic of nutritional acclimatization in mountain operations:
       • Weight loss during the first 2 to 3 days at high elevation.
       • Loss of appetite with symptoms of AMS.
       • Loss of weight usually stops with acclimatization.
       • At progressively higher elevations (greater than 14,000 feet), the tolerance of fatty or high-protein
           foods rapidly decreases. A high-carbohydrate diet may lessen the symptoms of AMS and may digest
           better than fat at high altitudes. (See USARIEM TN-01/4.)

FATIGUE
   4-28. Increased fatigue can cause Soldiers to become disinterested in eating properly. Decreased
   consumption can result in malnutrition because of the unpleasant taste of cold rations. Leaders should ensure
   that fuel tablets and squad stoves are available or that natural flammable materials are used, if possible.
   Although there is no physiological need for food to be hot, hot food does increase morale and a sense of
   well-being. Losing weight in the first few days can occur because of dehydration, metabolic changes, and
   loss of appetite. Carbohydrate-rich beverages, such as fruit juices and sports drinks, increase carbohydrates,
   energy, and liquid intake when the normal appetite response is blunted at altitude.

SECTION II – COLD-WEATHER SUSTAINMENT
   4-29. The ability to operate for extended periods in cold weather is an essential skill if a unit wishes to be
   successful in mountainous terrain. Individual skills and collective unit skills required for cold weather must
   be practiced before deploying to a cold region of the world. The skills required for survival in the cold must
   be known so they do not become the sole focus once the unit is faced with harsh conditions. For a unit to


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 45
Chapter 4



     accomplish its mission in cold, unforgiving weather, it must have the equipment necessary to live and operate
     in extreme conditions. Cold weather can affect many facets of daily life, from nutrition to clothing.

CLOTHING
     4-30. The clothing system refers to every piece of clothing placed against the skin (base layer), the insulating
     layers, and the outermost garments (shell), which protect the Soldier from the elements. When clothing is
     worn properly, the Soldier can function better; when clothing is worn improperly, Soldiers can develop
     hypothermia or frostbite. Wearing cold-weather clothing provides a barrier against weather and heat
     retention, moves moisture away from skin, dries quickly, and allows for adequate dexterity.
     4-31. Clothing for the cold-weather environment must manage Soldiers’ temperatures and control moisture.
     Clothing must be able to vent and breathe so a Soldier does not become overheated and perspire excessively.
     The clothing must also create insulation to shelter the Soldier from extreme temperatures. Clothing must
     manage moisture that comes from external sources, such as rain, or from internal sources, such as perspiration.
     4-32. One of the most effective ways to manage moisture from perspiration is to set a pace that limits exertion.
     In a cold-weather environment, patrols should move at a pace that will not saturate Soldiers’ insulating layers
     with sweat. Rest halts allow Soldiers an opportunity to adjust layers and control their own individual
     temperatures.
     4-33. Fitness, load, body composition, and metabolism all affect individual clothing needs. There should be
     room for individual variation in the wear of cold-weather clothing, but clothing decisions should be based on
     the principles of moisture management, trapped air spaces, and protection from the elements. The
     components of any clothing system can be broken down into the following general categories to match those
     principles.
BASE LAYER
     4-34. The base layer is a thin, lightweight moisture-wicking layer worn against skin and moves moisture
     away from the skin to prevent heat loss from conduction. Base layers should be constructed of wool,
     synthetic, or silk fabrics.
INSULATING LAYERS
     4-35. Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide
     additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat. Modern insulating layers allow moisture to move easily,
     and they trap air to increase the insulating factor. Several thin layers of insulation provide more warmth than
     one thick layer. Insulating layers should be constructed from wool, synthetic, or down fabrics. Insulating
     layers help Soldiers retain heat and not lose heat through convection.
SHELL
     4-36. The shell is the outermost layer worn. The shell is the primary barrier between the elements and the
     body and prevents outside moisture from getting in, while allowing inside moisture out. Shells must have
     some ventilation capacity to prevent overheating. There are two types of shells.
     4-37. A hard shell is generally more moisture and wind repellant and provides better protection against the
     elements at the cost of breathability. Soldiers cannot ventilate their bodies as well with a hard shell. The hard
     shell is a good outer layer to be worn in extreme conditions or static environments.
     4-38. A soft shell is a more breathable option. The soft shell is not as moisture and wind repellent as hard
     shells but is more breathable. The soft shell is a good outer layer to be worn when active as it provides better
     ventilation and breathability.

            Note. Cotton layers should NEVER BE WORN as any layer during operations in a cold environment.

GAITERS
     4-39. Gaiters protect the lower leg from snow, ice, mud, twigs, and stones. Using waterproof fabrics or other
     breathable materials laminated to nylon makes the gaiter an integral component of the cold-weather clothing



46                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                         Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   system. Gaiters are not presently fielded in the standard extended cold-weather clothing system and, in most
   cases, will need to be locally purchased. Gaiters are available in four styles:
        • Trail gaiters are short, typically extending just above the boot. They keep snow and debris out of
            boots in the spring and summer.
        • Alpine gaiters extend up to the knee and keep deep snow out of boots in the winter.
        • Expedition gaiters are thicker, designed to fit around a larger plastic mountaineering boot, and
            sometimes have added built-in insulation.
        • The integrated gaiter is a boot with a built-in gaiter, eliminating the need for a second piece of equipment.
HAND WEAR
   4-40. Even during the summer months, temperatures in the mountains can dip below the freezing point. While
   mittens are warmer than gloves, the finger dexterity needed to do most tasks makes gloves the primary
   cold-weather hand wear.
   4-41. The principles that apply to clothing also apply to gloves and mittens. A modular approach should be
   taken when wearing hand wear. (See figure 4-2, page 48.) They should provide moisture transfer from the
   skin to the outer layers―the insulating layer must insulate the hand from the cold and move moisture to the
   shell. The outer layer must be weather resistant and breathable. Both gloves and mittens should be required
   for all Soldiers during mountain operations, as well as replacement liners for both. This will provide enough
   flexibility to accomplish all tasks and keep the users’ hands warm and dry.
   4-42. Just as the clothing system is worn in layers, gloves and mittens work best using the same principle.
   Soldiers should have multiple sets of hand wear. They should have multiple thin liner gloves, intermediate
   climbing gloves, thicker gloves for working with carabiners in the extreme cold, trigger-finger mittens for
   using their personal weapon in the extreme cold, and thick mittens to protect their hands in the extreme cold.
   When outer layer gloves are removed, they can be placed in the jacket to keep warm.

Chapter 4




                            Figure 4-2. Modular cold-weather glove system

HEADWEAR
     4-43. Headwear in mountainous environments should take a modular approach as well. A single hat does not
     perform well in every condition; several hats should be available to mountaineers: a thin moisture-wicking
     hat to wear under the helmet or during active movements; an intermediate fleece cap for protection in cold,
     dry environments; and a heavy thick cap for extreme cold. For colder climates, a neck gaiter can be added.
     The neck gaiter is a tube of synthetic material that fits around the neck and can reach up over the ears and
     nose. For extreme cold, a balaclava can be added. This covers the head, neck, and face, leaving only a slot
     for the eyes. Worn together, the combination is warm and provides for moisture movement, keeping the
     wearer drier and warmer.
FOOTWEAR
     4-44. Soldiers may encounter various environmental conditions within relatively short distances in
     mountainous, plateau, and other highland areas. (See CTA 50-900.) In such places, clothing allowances that
     are adequate for adjacent lower areas may not provide sufficient protection for diverse highland areas;
     therefore, in these higher or more rugged areas, commanders may authorize, at their discretion, additional
     clothing items and special mountaineering equipment, as required.
     4-45. Mountain climates are colder than surrounding areas. Even in summer months, it may be necessary to
     equip troops with cold-weather boots. The intermediate cold-weather boot provides adequate protection for
     summer conditions in most mountain ranges with high elevation (2,500 to 4,000 meters) located in temperate




48                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                    Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   regions. It can be appropriate footwear for Soldiers whose mission only requires mobility in easy terrain.
   (See figure 4-3, page 50.)
   4-46. Leather mountaineering boots are designed to provide more capability in mountainous terrain. They
   are typically warmer and more water resistant than combat boots are. Rigid leather mountaineering boots
   provide better edging while climbing alpine rock. They also perform better when kicking steps in firm snow
   or wearing crampons. In general, a leather mountaineering boot with moderately stiff soles and upper section
   works well for most military mountaineering tasks. Although they are not available through the supply
   system, they can be a commercial, off-the-shelf purchase. (See figure 4-3, page 50.)
   4-47. During the winter months, most mountain ranges experience periods of extreme cold (–26°F to – 40°F).
   The extreme cold-weather boot (with vapor barrier [VB]) provides adequate protection from the extreme
   cold, but it is not an adequate platform for mountaineering tasks in these conditions. Plastic mountaineering
   boots provide a more versatile platform for any condition encountered in the mountains, while keeping the
   foot dryer and warmer. Plastic mountaineering boots are a double boot, consisting of a hard, plastic shell,
   and an inner insulating boot. The stiffness of the shell makes it compatible with crampons, snowshoes, and
   skis. The hard, plastic shell provides waterproofing, while the inner liner remains free of snowmelt, making
   it an ideal boot in wet conditions. Plastic mountaineering boots are the optimal footwear for extended
   operations in cold mountainous environments. (See figure 4-3, page 50.)

         Note. Maintenance of all types of footwear must closely follow the manufacturers’ recommendations.

                                    Figure 4-3. Mountaineering boots

SOCKS
     4-48. Socks cushion the foot, remove excess moisture, and insulate from cold temperatures. Improper wear
     and excess moisture can cause hot spots and blisters. Socks can be worn as a layered system:
         • The first layer should be a moisture-wicking material that moves moisture from the foot surface to
             the outer sock.
         • The outer sock should also be made of moisture-wicking materials but should be complemented
             with materials that provide cushioning and abrasion resistance.
         • A third layer can be added depending upon the climatic conditions:
              In severe wet conditions, a waterproof-type sock can be added to reduce the amount of water
                  that would saturate the foot. This layer would be worn over the first two layers if conditions
                  were extremely wet.




50                                                TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                      Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



               In extremely cold conditions, a VB sock can be worn either over both original pairs of socks or
                between the moisture-wicking layer and the insulating layer. If the user is wearing VB boots,
                the VB sock is not recommended.

EXTENDED COLD-WEATHER CLOTHING SYSTEM
   4-49. The extended cold-weather clothing system is the currently issued cold-weather clothing system. (See
   figure 4-4.)
        • Level 1: Base layer—a crewneck shirt constructed with a lightweight material that is highly
            breathable and has moisture-wicking properties. Kit includes two sets.
        • Level 2: Grid fleece (waffle)—a midweight long-sleeve shirt and elastic waistband drawers
            constructed with a heavyweight material, which offers stretch for increased comfort during
            movement, is highly breathable, and has moisture-wicking properties. Kit includes one set.
        • Level 3: Fleece jacket—a zipper jacket with raglan sleeves constructed with a material that creates
            air pockets that trap air and retain body heat, providing outstanding warmth without weight. This
            material also offers excellent breathability and the ability to dry quickly. However, this layer is not
            recommended as an outer garment for use during inclement or windy weather. Kit includes one
            piece.
        • Level 4: Wind jacket—a nylon or spandex jacket. It offers wind protection and environmental
            comfort with low weight and bulk and is quick drying. Kit includes one piece.
        • Level 5: Soft-shell jacket and trousers—constructed with a waterproof fabric, is quick drying, highly
            durable, and breathable. Kit includes one piece.
        • Level 6: Wet weather jacket and trousers—constructed with a two-layer waterproof and windproof
            fabric with sealed seams and is extremely breathable. Kit includes one piece.
        • Level 7: Extended cold-weather parka and trousers—three-layer construction that is fabricated with
            an outer layer, an insulation layer, and an inside layer of lightweight rip-stop material. They are
            water resistant, highly durable, and breathable. Kit includes one piece.

SECTION III – SMALL GROUP MOUNTAIN SUSTAINMENT AND SUBSISTENCE
   4-50. There is no one standardized way to plan for sustainment in mountain operations. Each mission has its
   own set of complications. Layers of contingencies should be built into the plan for sustainment. If one method
   fails due to any number of unforeseen circumstances, another method of sustainment must be ready to provide
   Soldiers with what they need. Gear that Soldiers carry must not be so heavy it makes them vulnerable.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 51
Chapter 4



     Methods to procure water must be available. Detailed coordination must be made with air assets to provide
     aerial resupply.

SOLDIER LOAD MANAGEMENT
     4-51. Operations in mountainous terrain require Soldiers to carry only mission-essential items as they move
     through challenging terrain. Individual Soldiers, small teams, and large units must be able to adjust their
     equipment. They must understand the fundamentals of cross-leveling essential equipment to avoid excess
     gear. Understanding and practicing these simple, yet often overlooked, skills can make a unit lighter, faster,
     and more lethal in mountainous terrain. No amount of training can change the body’s reaction to carrying
     excessive loads. Analyzing the situation and the level of risk are the keys to determining what is mission
     essential. All leaders should familiarize themselves with ATP 3-21.18, where they can access table 3-4, which
     is a helpful guide for leaders when planning loads for dismounted movements. (See chapter 6 for detailed
     information on load management to maximize mobility.)
CHOICE OF EQUIPMENT
     4-52. Mission requirements and unit standard operating procedures (SOPs) will influence the choice of gear
     carried, but the following lists provide a sample of what should be considered during mission planning.

Personal Gear
     4-53. Personal gear includes an emergency survival kit with signaling material, fire-starting material, and
     water procurement material. Pocket items should include a knife, whistle, pressure bandage, notebook with
     pen or pencil, sunglasses, sunblock and lip protection, map, compass, and altimeter.

Standard Gear
     4-54. Standard gear that can be individually worn or carried includes cushion-soled socks; combat or
     mountain boots, combat uniform and cap; load-carrying equipment with canteens, magazine pouches, and
     first aid kit; individual weapon; a large rucksack containing hard-shell top and bottom; insulating layers;
     helmet; poncho; and sleeping bag.

Mountaineering Equipment and Specialized Gear
     4-55. The element’s leadership should scrutinize mountaineering equipment. The equipment should allow
     Soldiers to move safely through any known technical terrain. Identifying hazards and obstacles during the
     planning phase is a crucial step to help determine the appropriate gear for the given mission. Required
     mountaineering equipment is never set in stone, and each patrol or mission may require different equipment.

Daypack
     4-56. When Soldiers plan to be away from the bivouac site for the day on a patrol or mountaineering mission,
     they carry a light daypack. This pack should contain—
         • Extra insulating layer.
         • Hard-shell layer, such as a waterproof jacket and pants or poncho.
         • First aid kit.
         • Flashlight or headlamp.
         • Canteen or water bottle.
         • Cold-weather hat or scarf.
         • Rations for the time away from the base camp.
         • Survival kit.
         • Improvised harness materials or climbing harness.
         • Necessary mountaineering equipment for technical terrain.
         • Gloves.




52                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                       Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



TEN ESSENTIALS
   4-57. Regardless of what equipment is carried, the individual military mountaineer should always carry
   10 essentials when moving through the mountains.

Navigational Tools
   4-58. Knowledge of the terrain and a well-developed route plan are the two most important tools for avoiding
   issues in the mountains. A map should be carried along with appropriate navigational aids like a compass,
   altimeter, and Global Positioning System (GPS) device.

Headlamp and Night Vision Devices
   4-59. Night vision devices are powerful tools for target identification and discrimination and are critical tools
   in the mountains. However, their narrow focal plane at close ranges is minimally helpful when scrambling in
   rough terrain. Light enables faster and safer movement and scrambling. Preventing enemy observation should
   always be a primary concern, but for maneuver in terrain that is masked from observation where risk of a fall
   is a greater threat, a light is valuable. Headlamps are also important for camp tasks, planning, and map work.

Sunglasses and Sunscreen
   4-60. In alpine or snow-covered terrain, sunglasses are vital for preventing snow blindness. Side shields,
   which minimize light entering from the side, permit ventilation to help prevent lenses from fogging. Each
   independent climbing team should carry at least one extra pair of sunglasses.

Extra Clothing
   4-61. Clothing is the primary protection from the environment and needs to match the conditions and the
   pace of a movement. Extra clothing includes the additional layers needed for static operations or enduring
   the long, inactive hours of an unplanned bivouac, such as the following:
        • Waterproof, breathable shells to protect from unexpected wind or precipitation.
        • Extra underwear to replace sweat-soaked underwear.
        • Extra hats or balaclavas.
        • Extra pair of heavy socks.
        • Extra pair of insulated mittens or gloves.
        • Extra insulation for the upper body and the legs (winter or severe mountain conditions).
   4-62. To back up foul weather gear, bring a poncho or extra-large plastic trash bag. A reflective emergency
   space blanket can be used for hypothermia first aid and emergency shelter. Insulated foam pads prevent heat
   loss while sitting or lying on snow. Finally, a bivouac sack can help by protecting insulating layers from the
   weather, cutting the wind, and trapping essential body heat.

Water and Water Containers
   4-63. These include wide-mouthed water bottles for water collection, hands-free backpack hydration
   systems, and a small length of plastic tubing for water procurement at snowmelt seeps and rainwater puddles
   on bare rock. Wide-mouth containers are easy to fill, easy to clean, and easy to clear out if ice forms.
   Hydration bladders are convenient, but they can break and have freezing issues in the tube.

First Aid Kit
   4-64. Small teams in the mountains often operate independently. In addition to the improved first aid kit,
   each Soldier should carry first-aid supplies to address common mountaineering injuries, such as punctures
   and abrasions with severe bleeding, broken bones, serious sprains, and blisters. Splinting material for
   stabilizing orthopedic injuries is an important addition.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                  53
Chapter 4



Lighter and Fire Starter
     4-65. Lighters are handy for starting fires, but they should be backed up by matches stored in a waterproof
     container with a strip of sandpaper. Fire-starting material is key to igniting wet wood for emergency
     campfires. Candles, heat tabs, and canned heat all work. These can also be used to quickly warm water or
     soup in a canteen cup. In alpine zones above the tree line with no available firewood, a stove works as an
     emergency heat source.

Knife
     4-66. A small folding knife is a helpful tool for its weight. It can be useful for cutting rope or cordage or for
     food preparation and shelter construction. A knife is important for first aid when improvising interventions
     with limited medical supplies. A multipurpose pocket tool is also helpful.

Repair Kit
     4-67. A repair kit should include—
         • Stove tools and spare parts.
         • Duct tape.
         • Patches.
         • Safety pins.
         • Heavy-duty thread or dental floss.
         • Sewing kit.
         • Cord or wire.

Extra Food
     4-68. Soldiers should carry one day’s extra worth of food in case of delay caused by bad weather, injury, or
     navigational error.
SMALL UNIT CROSS-LEVELING
     4-69. A small team of Soldiers must analytically look at the packing and choice of team gear. Everyone must
     be aware of essential-item locations. They must also ensure there is no unnecessarily redundant equipment.
     In challenging terrain, unnecessary weight slows Soldiers and reduces situational awareness.
SQUAD OR TEAM EMERGENCY PACK
     4-70. When a squad-sized element leaves the bivouac site, squad safety gear should be carried in addition to
     individual daypacks. This can be either loaded into one rucksack or cross-leveling among squad members.
     In the event of an injury, CASEVAC, or unplanned bivouac, these items may make the difference between
     succeeding and failing the mission. Squad safety gear comprises the following items:
          • Sleeping bag.
          • Sleeping mat.
          • Squad stove.
          • Fuel bottle.
          • Litter or packaging material.
     4-71. The following mnemonic, DROP, can help leaders ensure an appropriate load plan is achieved:
         • D—Determine level of mobility.
         • R—Reduce redundant or nonessential equipment.
         • O—Organize resupply.
         • P—Police Soldiers.

WATER PROCUREMENT
     4-72. Supplying adequate water to maintain hydration is a sustainment challenge. Fluids lost through
     respiration, perspiration, and urination must be replaced. However, water is heavy, and even a few days’




54                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                      Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   supply will overburden Soldiers. If the water supply is insufficient, then physical activity must be reduced.
   However, Soldiers cannot adjust permanently to a decreased water intake.
   4-73. Individual loads and support requirements can be reduced if small units can procure water from the
   environment. Water found in mountain streams and pools is often clean, but it cannot be assumed potable.
   Soldiers should be educated to drink water only from safe sources. Emphasis must be placed on the three
   rules of water discipline:
        • Only drink treated water.
        • Conserve water for drinking. Potable water in the mountains may be in short supply.
        • Do not contaminate or pollute water sources.
WATER SOURCES
   4-74. Water is scarce above the timberline. After setting up a perimeter, such as a patrol base, assembly area,
   or a defense; a watering party should be employed. Mountain streams, springs, rain, and lakes provide good
   sources of water. In areas where water trickles off rocks, a small piece of tubing can be used to fill canteens,
   or a shallow reservoir may be dug from which to collect water (after the sediment settles).
   4-75. Snow may be melted to procure water, which is a time-consuming process that requires significant fuel.
   Water should be collected at midday when the sun thaws the snow. In glaciated environments, fine particulate
   can be found in the runoff and should be filtered. After sundown, high mountain areas freeze. Storing water
   next to a Soldier or placing it in a sleeping bag at night can protect water from freezing.
BIOLOGICAL CONTAMINANTS
   4-76. Virtually all surface waters are microbiologically contaminated. There are three types of
   disease-causing microorganisms: protozoa, bacteria, and viruses.
   4-77. Protozoa are the largest of waterborne bugs measuring in the 1-micron range. Giardia and
   cryptosporidium are the most infamous of the group. The infective cysts and oocysts of protozoa are
   extremely robust and can survive for months in a water source. They thrive in domestic and wild animals, as
   well as humans. Cryptosporidium oocysts are known for their resistance to chemical treatment. Most
   disinfectants are ineffective, and the few that require long dwell times to do the job.
   4-78. Bacteria are an order of magnitude smaller than protozoa measuring in the 0.2-micron range. The most
   well-known bacteria are Escherichia coli (commonly referred to as E. coli); others include campylobacter,
   salmonella, and shigella. Bacteria are not as hearty, surviving in water for weeks instead of months. However,
   unlike protozoa and viruses, which require a host to multiply, some bacteria grow in water and are found in
   higher numbers than protozoa and viruses. Both animals and humans often carry bacteria, such as protozoa;
   as a result, many water sources are contaminated with bacteria. Beware of water sources near agricultural
   operations.
   4-79. Viruses—some notorious waterborne viruses are poliovirus, hepatitis, and norovirus. Waterborne
   viruses are very resilient and can survive for months in water. Viruses are generally species-specific; in other
   words, those that infect animals do not infect humans and vice versa. Because of this and the modern
   sanitation measures taken in developed countries, not as many water sources are contaminated with viruses.
   In developing countries with little or no sewage control, the opposite is true. However, as more people are
   becoming active outdoors, more rivers, lakes, and streams are at risk of viral contamination.
CHEMICAL CONTAMINANTS
   4-80. Filters and purifiers provide microbiologically safe drinking water. The carbon in the filters and
   disinfectant of the purifiers will adsorb or react with chemical contaminates, such as herbicides, pesticides,
   and volatile organic compounds. However, filters or purifiers will not protect from high chemical
   concentrations or heavy metal contamination. It is best to avoid water sources such as mining tailing ponds
   or those near agricultural operations.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 55
Chapter 4



WATER PURIFICATION
     4-81. Water should always be treated. No matter how clean the snow or water may appear, it should always
     be considered contaminated. There are many techniques to purify water, each with inherent advantages and
     disadvantages.
     4-82. Boiling kills biological contaminants but does not eliminate chemical contaminants. Filtration should
     also be used if chemical contaminants are suspected. To ensure all biological contaminants have been killed,
     let the water boil for 1 minute. This method requires time and fuel while allowing water to be treated away
     from the source.
     4-83. Chemical treatment can be accomplished with iodine or chlorine dioxide. These treatments are
     available commercially and come with instructions for proper use. Chemical treatment will kill almost all
     biological contaminants but are ineffective against cryptosporidium. It requires time for these chemical
     treatments to be effective, and, in cold temperatures, it takes longer. This method allows water to be treated
     away from the source and on the go.
     4-84. UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical
     contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants.
     Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy before use. This method can be used away from the source.
     4-85. Filters are compact and lightweight. They work by filtering out particulate, chemicals, and biological
     contaminants. Filters are not capable of removing any chemical contaminants that are dissolved in the water.
     Certain filters may not be able to filter out smaller biological contaminants as the pores of the filter are too
     large to remove them. These types of filters are designed to remove waterborne protozoa and bacteria but not
     viruses. The benefit of these types of filters is that water moves more rapidly through them. Filters that can
     filter smaller contaminants are often referred to as water purifiers. Water purifiers are designed to remove
     protozoa, bacteria, and viruses, offering a higher level of defense by combating all three. The drawback to
     these types of filters is that they filter water at a slower rate and may clog when filtering very cloudy water.
     Be sure to read the capabilities of the filter and treat the water with multiple methods, if necessary. Filters
     can freeze in cold temperatures if they are not properly cleared after use. In extreme temperatures, they may
     not operate at all. Filters require treating water at the source.

AERIAL RESUPPLY
     4-86. Movement of supplies by air is often the preferred method for remote, hard to reach locations. This is
     only possible when assets are available and the weather, terrain, and situation allow it. Air distribution in the
     mountains requires detailed planning, effective liaison, and a habitual relationship between the aviation crew
     and the ground unit. Direct communication between the unit and the air delivery asset is coordinated early in
     the planning process to help ensure proper delivery.
     4-87. Aerial resupply, though effective, is limited by weather, which must be permissive from the point of
     origin to the point of delivery, and all stops in-between. Fog, cloud cover, sudden storms, ice, and
     unpredictable air currents can shut down air support. Higher elevations will decrease aircraft lift capabilities.
     Temperature and air density at altitude restrict an aircrew’s ability to carry loads into the high mountains.
     Erratic weather conditions in the mountains will frequently prevent rotary- and fixed-wing aircraft from
     flying; this may last for multiple days.
     4-88. Suitable drop zones in the mountains are difficult to find. A common resupply delivery is accomplished
     by helicopters flying at a low altitude above the mountain terrain delivering unit-configured loads. Supplies
     should be packaged for immediate Soldier transport upon delivery. (For more information on options, see
     ATP 3-21.50, ATP 4-48, and supporting aviation assets.)

SECTION IV – BIVOUAC CONSIDERATIONS
     4-89. Mountainous regions often have strong turbulent winds, cold temperatures, and a general lack of
     concealment above the timberline. The wind overhead creates an extensive lee near the mountain. An inland
     wind blowing 50 miles per hour (mph) may not strike the ground for several kilometers after passing the edge
     of a cliff or a very steep slope. Such a lee is an attractive bivouac site from the standpoint of wind protection.



56                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                         Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   Note that such a lee area is often an area of maximum snow deposit. Frequent requirements to dig out
   vehicles, walkways, and weapons positions may offset the wind-free advantages of a lee site during snowfall
   or snow-blowing weather. Avalanche hazard areas must be avoided. Cold air is heavier than warm air and
   frequently settles in valleys. If tactically feasible, it is better to establish a bivouac up the hillside above the
   valley floor and below the timberline.

BIVOUAC SITE LOCATION
   4-90. The following are considerations for selecting a bivouac site in the mountains:
       • Cover and concealment—cover and concealment from air and ground observation is essential for
           the bivouac area. Forested areas pose few problems in comparison to areas above the tree line.
           Operations above tree line or at altitude may offer less cover and concealment. Bivouac may need
           to be established below tree line to support operations conducted above tree line.
       • Wind protection—protection from the wind is a prime consideration. Depending on the area of
           operations, bivouac site selections may vary due to the unpredictability of winds at elevation.
       • Ground condition—the condition of the ground is important. In warm conditions, bivouac should
           be located on hard ground. In snow-covered terrain, avoid digging to the ground, as this may collect
           water due to the thawing of the snow, or rain. A layer of snow should be left for ground insulation,
           comfort, and water absorption. The depth that is dug in will vary depending on the site selection and
           snow depth.
       • Construction materials—construction materials play an important part in selecting a bivouac. When
           reconnoitering an area, consider such things as the availability of firewood, water procurement, and
           snow for snow shelters.
       • Hazard awareness—bivouac sites must be protected from mountain-specific hazards that are not
           commonly encountered, such as rockfall, icefall, flooding, and avalanche-runout zones. These
           hazards are not always obvious so good awareness and vigilance must be used when selecting these
           sites in mountainous terrain.

GLACIER BIVOUAC PROCEDURES
   4-91. When locating a bivouac site or a gathering area where the team might need or want to unrope, at least
   one person will need to probe the area for hidden crevasses. (See chapter 14, section II, for detailed
   information on probing a potential bivouac site.)
   4-92. Once an area is determined to be safe, it must be marked to keep personnel within that area. Typically,
   wands are carried as flagging material specifically for this purpose. Water procurement sites (uphill) and
   latrines (downhill) must be determined for safety to avoid contamination.
   4-93. Multiple tent sites can be connected, which keeps tents closer together. Probe all areas between the
   tents if planning to move in those areas. Closer tents will make communicating between tent groups and rope
   teams easier.
   4-94. If there is a chance for severe storms with high winds, snow walls may be constructed to protect the
   tent site from wind. The walls can be constructed from loose snow piled on the perimeter, or blocks can be
   cut from consolidated snow layers. In deep, soft snow, digging 3 or 4 feet to find a consolidated layer will
   result in enough snow moved to build up decent walls around the tent site. For block construction, move the
   soft snow from the surface into the wall foundation areas (down to a consolidated layer of snow).

SHELTERS
   4-95. Operations in mountainous terrain require Soldiers to be familiar with a variety of bivouac shelter
   construction techniques. Ideally, purpose-designed shelters should be used. However, given the erratic nature
   of weather in mountainous terrain, Soldiers should also be prepared to improvise survival shelters for
   emergency bivouac situations that occur when carrying manufactured shelters is not feasible.
TENTS
   4-96. When selecting a tent, the mission must be defined to determine the number of people the tent must
   accommodate. The climate should also be taken into consideration. A tent used for warmer temperatures will



26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                   57
Chapter 4



     greatly differ from tents used in colder, harsher environments. Tent manufacturers offer many designs of
     different sizes, weights, and materials. Mountaineering tents are made of breathable or weatherproof material.
     A single-wall tent allows for moisture inside the tent to escape through the tent’s material. A double-wall
     tent has a second layer of material (referred to as a fly) that covers the tent. The fly protects against rain and
     snow, and the space between the fly and tent helps moisture to escape from inside. Before using a new tent,
     the seams should be treated with seam sealer to prevent moisture from entering through the stitching. The
     frame of a tent is usually made of an aluminum or carbon fiber poles. The poles are connected with an elastic
     cord that allows them to extend, connect, and become long and rigid. When the tent poles are secured into
     the tent body, they create the shape of the tent. Tents are rated by a relative strength factor; the speed of wind
     a tent can withstand before the frame deforms. Temperature and expected weather for the mission should be
     determined before choosing the tent.
FLOORLESS SHELTERS
     4-97. Floorless shelters are lighter and more packable than conventional tents. Soldiers can enter and exit the
     tent with boots on without bringing dirt into the tent or ripping the floor of a conventional tent. They can be
     pitched in many different types of terrain for many different uses. They can provide overhead cover while
     staying in a static position for a long period. They offer much more ventilation, allowing the use of a stove
     inside and no worry of spilling fuel onto the tent floor. Because floorless shelters are lightweight and easier
     to pack than conventional tents, it is possible to carry a much larger shelter. A tarp, poncho, or piece of house
     wrap makes a clean and dry floor area near the sleeping bags if the ground is damp. Floorless shelters do
     have some drawbacks. They are not suitable above the tree line due to the lack of anchoring and potential
     high winds. They need soil into which to drive the stakes. If extreme cold temperatures are encountered, they
     have much more ventilation and are inherently colder than a conventional tent. (See figure 4-5.)




                             Figure 4-5. Floorless shelter (10-man arctic tent)

EMERGENCY BIVOUAC SHELTERS
     4-98. The equipment that a Soldier carries, and the environment determine the type of shelter that can be
     built. Shelters can be built in wooded areas, open country, and barren areas. Wooded areas usually provide
     the best location, while barren areas have only snow as building material. Wooded areas provide timber for
     shelter construction, wood for fire, concealment from observation, and protection from the wind.

            Note. In extreme cold, do not use metal, such as an aircraft fuselage, for shelter. The metal
            conducts away from the shelter what little body heat the Soldier can generate.

     4-99. Shelters made from ice or snow usually require tools, such as ice axes or saws. Significant time and
     energy must be expended to build these shelters. Be sure to ventilate an enclosed shelter, especially if the



58                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                       Mountain Subsistence and Sustainment



   intent is to build a fire for warmth. Always block a shelter’s entrance, if possible, to keep the heat in and keep
   out the wind. Use a rucksack or snow block. Construct a shelter no larger than needed. This will reduce the
   amount of space to heat. A common error in cold-weather shelter construction is making the shelter so large
   that it steals body heat rather than helping conserve it.
   4-100. If possible, avoid sleeping directly on the ground. Lay down some pine boughs, grass, or other
   insulating material to keep the ground from absorbing body heat.
   4-101. Never fall asleep without turning off the stove or lamp. Carbon monoxide poisoning can result from
   a fire burning in an unventilated shelter. Carbon monoxide is a great danger. It is colorless and odorless. Any
   time there is an open flame, it may generate carbon monoxide. Always check for proper ventilation. Even in
   a ventilated shelter, incomplete combustion can cause carbon monoxide poisoning. Usually, there are no
   symptoms. Unconsciousness and death can occur without warning. Sometimes, however, pressure at the
   temples, burning of the eyes, headache, pounding pulse, drowsiness, or nausea may occur. The one visible
   sign of carbon monoxide poisoning is a cherry red coloring in the tissues of the lips, mouth, and inside of the
   eyelids. Soldiers must immediately be moved to fresh air if they begin to exhibit any of these symptoms.

Poncho Lean-To
   4-102. A poncho lean-to takes only a short time and minimal equipment to build. (See figure 4-6.) Material
   requirements are a poncho, 6 to 9 feet of rope or cord, 3 stakes about 12 inches long, and 2 trees or 2 poles
   that are 6 to 9 feet apart. Before selecting the trees or the location of the poles, check the wind direction to
   ensure that the back of the lean-to is facing into the wind.
   4-103. When using the lean-to for more than one night or if rain is expected, make a center support for the
   lean-to. Make this support with a line. Attach one end of the line to the poncho hood and the other end to an
   overhanging branch. Ensure there is no slack in the line.
   4-104. Another method for creating a center support is to place a stick upright under the center of the lean-to.
   However, this method restricts space and movement in the shelter.
   4-105. For additional protection from wind and rain, place some brush, a rucksack, or other equipment at the
   sides of the lean-to. To reduce heat loss to the ground, place some type of insulating material, such as leaves
   or pine needles, inside the lean-to. (See ATP 3-50.21 for more information.)

         Note. When at rest, Soldiers lose as much as 80 percent of their body heat to the ground.




                                         Figure 4-6. Poncho lean-to




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  59
Chapter 4



Field Expedient Lean-To
     4-106. In a wooded area that has enough natural materials, a field-expedient lean-to can be constructed with
     only a knife. It takes longer to make this type of shelter than it does to make other types, but it protects against
     the elements. It requires two trees (or upright poles) about 6 feet apart, one pole about 6 feet long and 1 inch
     in diameter, 5 to 8 poles about 9-feet long and 1 inch in diameter for beams; cord or vines for securing the
     horizontal support to the trees; and other poles, saplings, or vines to crisscross the beams. (See ATP 3-50.21.)
NATURAL SHELTERS
     4-107. Do not overlook natural formations that provide shelter. Examples are caves, rocky crevices, clumps
     of bushes, small depressions, large rocks on leeward sides of hills, large trees with low-hanging limbs, and
     fallen trees with thick branches. When selecting a natural formation, stay away from low ground, such as
     ravines, narrow valleys, or creek beds. Low areas collect the heavy cold air at night and are therefore colder
     than the surrounding high ground. Thick, brushy, low ground also harbors more insects. Check for ticks,
     mites, scorpions, stinging ants, and venomous snakes. Look for loose rocks, dead limbs, or other natural
     growth that could fall on the shelter. (See ATP 3-50.21.)

Snow-Cave Shelter
     4-108. The snow-cave shelter is an effective shelter because of the insulating properties of snow (See
     figure 4-7.) A snow-cave shelter requires significant time and energy to build, and during construction,
     clothing can become quite wet. Find a drift about 3-meters (the length of an avalanche probe) deep that can
     easily be dug into. While building this shelter, keep the roof arched for strength and allow melted snow to
     drain down the sides. Build the sleeping platform higher than the entrance. Separate the sleeping platform
     from the snow-cave’s walls or dig a small trench between the platform and the wall. This platform and a
     smooth ceiling will prevent the melting snow from dripping on clothing and equipment. The construction is
     especially important to ensure an efficient means of retaining heat. Ensure the roof is high enough to sit up
     on the sleeping platform. Block the entrance with a snow block or rucksack. The walls and ceiling should be
     at least 12-inches thick. Install a ventilation shaft. If there is no drift large enough to build a snow cave, a
     variation can be built by piling snow into a mound large enough to dig out. (See ATP 3-50.21.)

                                    Figure 4-7. Snow-cave shelter

Snow-Trench Shelter
   4-109. The snow trench is a hasty shelter designed to allow Soldiers to sleep below the snow and wind level
   while using the snow’s insulating qualities. To build a snow-trench shelter, follow the following steps:
       • Cut snow blocks about 1 foot by 1 foot by 2 feet and construct the walls by interlocking the snow
            blocks with overlapping placements. The walls should be slightly higher than the tent. At a
            minimum, build walls on the windward side of the tent site. Snow walls can also provide shelter
            from wind for food preparation and when using latrines.
       • In areas of compacted snow, cut snow blocks and use them as overhead cover. If not, use a poncho
            or other material. Build only one entrance and use a snow block or rucksack as a door.

LIGHTWEIGHT STOVES
   4-110. Lightweight stoves should be used during mountain operations to reduce Soldier load and as a
   cold-weather emergency risk mitigation measure. They should be issued at the team level and provide 3 to 4



26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                               61
Chapter 4



     Soldiers with the ability to rehydrate rations, melt snow into water, heat water to warm Soldiers with cold
     weather or other injuries, and generate heat in small shelters during emergencies.
     4-111. Soldier load can be greatly reduced by carrying lightweight stoves and fuel in winter environments.
     This is because they can create far more water by volume for the same carried weight than just carrying
     water. The actual amount varies dependent on altitude, temperature, and fuel type.
     4-112. Factors that should be considered when choosing lightweight stoves for mountain operations are
     weight, altitude, operational temperature, fuel availability, and reliability.
STOVE TYPES
     4-113. Most mountaineering stoves are either canister-fuel or liquid-fuel:
         • Canister-fuel stoves are simpler to operate than liquid fueled stoves. The gas, already pressurized,
             flows from the fuel canister into the burner, where it ignites, in the same manner as a domestic
             kitchen stove. Canister-fuel stoves are generally accepted as being more efficient for weight carried
             than liquid fuel. However, canister-fuel stoves are unreliable in cold temperatures. They are not
             recommended for use in freezing temperatures or at high altitudes.
         • Liquid-fuel stoves are more complex because the liquid fuel must be vaporized prior to burning. In
             many stoves, the priming pressure is generated by a small hand pump that forces air into the fuel
             container. Liquid-fuel stoves are typically capable of burning multiple types of fuel. They generally
             operate well in cold weather and at high altitude. Liquid fuel costs less than canister fuel. Some
             forms of fuel, such as kerosene or diesel, are readily available worldwide. Liquid-fuel stoves are the
             most widely used for mountaineering due to their wide versatility.
STOVE USE
     4-114. Stoves should be tested and maintained prior to operational use. Soldiers should be familiar with stove
     disassembly, cleaning, and troubleshooting prior to operational use. A repair kit and the tools needed to fix
     these stoves should always be packed together. The reliability of the stove has a huge impact on the success
     of the mission and the morale of personnel.
     4-115. When in use, hot stoves must be kept away from equipment and ammunition. At higher elevations,
     the heating times may be doubled. To conserve fuel, stoves, fires, and fuel tablets should be protected from
     the wind.
