                                             Avalanche
   World War I is remembered for the brutal fighting in the trenches in France and Belgium.
   However, in the fighting between Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Soldiers saw some
   of the most intense mountain fighting in human history. After the Italians checked the Austrian
   offensive through the passes of the Alps, both sides fought higher and higher into the
   mountains. Small, light units of mountaineers clashed over new ground high in the peaks, while
   the armies dug in on the peaks they had secured. Positions and paths were blasted out of the
   rock and carved through the glaciers to move personnel and materiel to the fighting in the
   heights.
   By the winter of 1916, the line had mostly stabilized, and both armies were hunkering down
   for winter. Both sides had established extensive networks of trails and camps to support their
   forward positions; however, much of the infrastructure had been built in avalanche paths. In
   the second week of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing
   massive avalanches across the range.
   Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records
   exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim picture. The lowest estimates place casualties
   at around 4,000 during the storm. Some records support numbers as high as 10,000. Today,
   their bodies are still melting out of the glaciers below.

SECTION I – AVALANCHE HAZARDS
   5-1. During winter months and throughout the year, snow covers the slopes. Steep, snow-covered terrain, in
   addition to mobility challenges and fall hazards, present the risk of avalanches. This hazard is easy to
   underestimate. It is not clearly visible, and, due to the complexity of the factors involved, there is a high
   degree of uncertainty, but the consequences of ignoring the hazard are high. Avalanches have taken the lives
   of more troops engaged in mountain warfare than all other terrain hazards combined.
   5-2. An avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between
   layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in
   the mountains during the winter, these instabilities in the snowpack may make large areas too dangerous for
   travel. These snow slopes may appear unthreatening but may have weak layers buried in the snowpack that
   can be easily triggered. Military elements may gravitate into avalanche terrain to avoid steeper technical
   terrain or enemy observation. Avalanches can generate incredible destructive force, destroying equipment,
   killing or burying Soldiers, and blocking key roads. Whether operating dismounted in high alpine terrain or
   as a mounted force in valley bottoms, units must be aware of avalanche hazards. They must incorporate the
   evaluation of avalanche danger into the planning process and learn to recognize and avoid hazardous terrain.
   (See figure 5-1, page 64.)




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               63
Chapter 5




                            Figure 5-1. Movement through avalanche terrain

AVALANCHE ELEMENTS
     5-3. Avalanches occur when the weight of accumulated snow on a slope exceeds the cohesive forces that
     hold the snow in place. There are three elements needed to create an avalanche: an unstable snowpack, terrain
     steep enough to slide, and a trigger that initiates the failure of bonds holding the snow in place.
SNOWPACK
     5-4. Layers of snow accumulate with each new snow or wind event. Variation in temperature and atmospheric
     conditions form layers with different types of snow crystals. These layers are subject to changes in texture
     and strength throughout the winter, as they are exposed to sun, wind, and temperature changes. Each layer in
     the snowpack will have distinct characteristics. Strong layers are made up of well-bonded, small, rounded
     grains. Weak layers are made up of larger, angular, poorly bonded grains.

Snowpack Concerns
     5-5. Instabilities are weaknesses within the snowpack as described below (see figure 5-2):
          • Weak layers—weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals
               can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming
               stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many
               avalanche cycles are due to weak layers that resist this change and retain their large grain size and



64                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                   Avalanche



           angular shape for long periods. These types of layers are known as “persistent” weak layers. These
           are common in prolonged colder temperatures.
       •   Weak bonds between layers—differences in the size and compositions of crystals between layers
           inhibit bonding. Large differences between layers are the primary source of instability.
       •   Bed surface—the bed surface is the surface over which a fracture and subsequent avalanche release
           occurs. Smooth, uniform sliding surfaces provide less friction to hold the snow in place. Examples
           are firm old snow layers, rain crusts, and sun crusts.




                                     Figure 5-2. Snowpack layers

Loading
   5-6. When instability exists in the snowpack, another important factor is the load placed on top of the weak
   layer. With the added weight of accumulated snow, it increases the shear forces within the snowpack:
        • New snow—during snowstorms, snowfall will rapidly increase the forces placed on the snowpack.
            Snowfall of more than 2.5 centimeters (cm) (1 inch) of snow an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot)
            of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during
            critical loading.
        • Wind loading—sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops,
            depositing it in sheltered features on leeward aspects. With high winds, even small deposits of new
            snow can produce significant loading. Top loading occurs when wind deposits snow over the top of
            a ridge. Side loading (or cross loading) occurs when snow is blown across the slope and deposited
            in gullies or on the leeward sides of ridges.
        • Rain—rain rapidly increases the load on the snowpack and erodes bonds between snow crystals and
            layers. After a period of sustained cold where weak layers have been preserved in the snowpack,
            rain can produce dense, wet avalanches that are very destructive.




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                               65
Chapter 5



TERRAIN FACTORS
     5-7. Terrain is the second factor that determines if an avalanche can occur. The character of a snowpack and
     opportunities for whether instabilities develop are determined by its elevation and aspect. A slope’s
     characteristics—slope angle, shape, and physical characteristics—determine the likelihood of a slide.
     Recognizing and avoiding avalanche terrain are the keys to managing avalanche risk.

Elevation
     5-8. Precipitation, temperature, and wind often vary significantly at different elevations. This results in
     differences in the snowpack, all of which influence the type, size, distribution, and sensitivity of avalanches.
     5-9. Increased precipitation—as weather systems are lifted over mountains (orthographic lift), the air cools
     and can hold less moisture, causing additional precipitation at elevation. Increased precipitation causes
     increased loads on the snowpack.
     5-10. Temperature—warming in the snowpack temporarily increases instability as bonds melt but improves
     stability when it re-freezes. Cooler temperatures at higher elevations inhibit stabilization. Instabilities can
     persist for much longer.

Aspect to Wind
     5-11. Sustained winds of 15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit
     it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the
     amount of snow that falls in sheltered locations. Slopes on the windward side have much of their new snow
     “scoured” off by the wind and are generally more stable than leeward slopes. Leeward slopes tend to form
     dangerous cornices and large, unstable slabs of snow.

Aspect to Sun
     5-12. Solar radiation causes drastic temperature swings in the snowpack. South-facing slopes can be
     dangerous on warm, sunny days immediately following storms. However, over time, these slopes stabilize
     as the added heat promotes bonding between layers. Snow on north-facing slopes does not stabilize as quickly
     and is more hazardous through most of the winter.

            Note. This effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.


Start Zone Characteristics
     5-13. The steepness of a slope, or its slope angle, is the primary factor that determines if an avalanche will
     occur. Most large avalanches occur on slopes between 30° and 45°. Slopes above 60° often do not build up
     significant quantities of snow because they are too steep. Snow will slide off as frequent, small sloughs.
     Under most conditions, slopes below 25° do not slide. (See figure 5-3.)




66                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                      Avalanche




                                          Figure 5-3. Slope angle

   5-14. The shape of the slope will also affect the forces within the snowpack, concentrating tension in specific
   areas where it requires less force to trigger an avalanche. (See figure 5-4, page 68.)
       • Profile or shape—
            Convex slopes. Slabs are most likely to fracture just below the bulge where stress is greatest.
                Convex rollovers have little support and are often steeper than the surrounding slope, making
                them a likely trigger point.
            Planar slopes. On these broad, smooth slopes, avalanches can happen anywhere. Slabs often
                fracture below cliff bands.
            Concave slopes. These slopes provide a certain amount of support through compression at the
                base of the hollow, but they are still capable of avalanching, especially on large slopes.
       • Anchoring—
            Boulders, trees, and ledges act as anchors and help hold the snow in place until they are buried.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                67
Chapter 5



                 Anchors can be areas of stress concentration because the snow upslope is held in place while
                  the snow below or to the sides are pulled downhill by gravity. For this reason, anchors can be
                  starting points for initial failure to occur, and fractures often run from tree to tree or rock to rock.




                                            Figure 5-4. Slope shape

Terrain Traps
     5-15. Terrain traps are features that increase the consequences of being caught in an avalanche. Examples
     include cliffs, gullies, creeks, lakes, trees, benches, or roads where debris will pile up, crevasses, or
     bergschrunds. Some terrain traps increase trauma during an avalanche. Others increase burial depth, making
     survival more unlikely.
TRIGGERS
     5-16. All avalanche triggers, whether caused by natural forces or human actions, are due to overloading the
     cohesive strength of the snowpack:
         • Natural—avalanches may be triggered by new snow, falling rock, snow, ice, or smaller avalanches.
              Solar warming erodes bonds and can trigger avalanches. Naturally occurring avalanches are a
              critical warning sign that the conditions for an avalanche exist on similar slopes. If natural
              avalanches are possible, human triggered avalanches are likely.
         • Human—most victims trigger the avalanches that kill them. People apply significant force to the
              snowpack. The impact of that force depends on snow density and distribution of force. A Soldier
              traveling on skis will not stress the snowpack as deep as a Soldier on foot will. Vehicles apply even
              more force. When a collapse occurs in a weak layer, it can propagate long distances up or across the
              slope.

TYPES OF AVALANCHES
     5-17. Avalanches can be categorized into two broad categories: loose snow and slab avalanches. (See
     figure 5-5, page 70.) Loose snow slides start with less snow and pick up more snow as they descend. Slab
     avalanches occur when one or more layers of cohesive snow break away as a unit and are generally more
     destructive.




68                                                   TC 3-97.61                                    26 November 2025
                                                                                                          Avalanche



   5-18. There are many variations of these types, each with distinct characteristics. These characteristics are
   defined by the structures within the snowpack, how an avalanche is released, and where it is found in the
   terrain. These avalanche problems guide group discussions, route planning, terrain choices, and the
   observations made during snowpack evaluation.
LOOSE-DRY AVALANCHES
   5-19. A loose-dry avalanche is a release of dry, unconsolidated snow. These avalanches occur within layers
   of soft snow near the surface of the snowpack. Loose-dry avalanches start at a point and entrain snow as they
   move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-dry avalanches include point-release
   avalanches or sluffs. Loose-dry avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers.
   Loose-dry avalanches are usually less dangerous than other avalanche problems but can be hazardous when
   combined with terrain traps, such as gullies, rocks, dense timber, cliffs, or crevasses. (See figure 5-5,
   page 70.)
STORM SLAB AVALANCHES
   5-20. A storm slab avalanche is a release of a soft cohesive layer (a slab) of new snow that breaks within the
   storm snow or on the old snow surface. Storm-slab problems last between a few hours and a few days but
   often stabilize quickly. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)
WIND SLAB AVALANCHES
   5-21. A wind slab avalanche is the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) formed by the wind. Wind
   transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind
   slabs are often smooth and rounded, sound hollow sometimes, and can range from soft to hard. Wind slabs
   form in specific areas and are confined to lee and cross-loaded terrain features. They can be avoided by
   sticking to sheltered or wind-scoured areas. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)
PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES
   5-22. A persistent slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of soft to hard snow (a slab) in the middle
   to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent weak layers can
   continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks, or even months, making them challenging to manage. As
   additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab on top of the persistent weak layer, this avalanche
   problem may develop into a deep, persistent slab. They can be triggered by light loads and last weeks after
   the last storm. The slabs often propagate in surprising and unpredictable ways, making this problem difficult
   to predict and manage, and require a wide safety buffer to handle the uncertainty. The best ways to manage
   the risk from persistent slabs are to make conservative terrain choices. (See figure 5-5, page 70.)

         Note. Storm slabs and wind slabs formed over persistent weak layers are also considered persistent slabs.

DEEP, PERSISTENT SLAB AVALANCHES
   5-23. A deep, persistent slab avalanche is a release of a thick, cohesive layer of hard snow (a slab), when the
   bond breaks between the slab and an underlying “persistent” weak layer, deep in the snowpack or near the
   ground. Deep, persistent slabs are difficult to trigger but are very destructive and dangerous because of the
   large mass of snow involved. Once developed, they can persist for months or an entire winter season. They
   are often triggered from areas where the snow is shallow and weak and are difficult to forecast and manage.
   (See figure 5-5, page 70.)
WET-LOOSE AVALANCHES
   5-24. A wet-loose avalanche is a release of wet, unconsolidated snow or slush. These avalanches occur within
   layers of wet snow near the surface of the snowpack but may quickly gouge into lower snowpack layers. Like
   dry-loose avalanches, they start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped
   avalanche. They often carve channels or paths through the snowpack to which subsequent avalanches are
   constrained. They move slowly but can contain enough mass to cause significant damage to trees, cars, or
   buildings. To avoid wet-loose avalanches, travel when the snow surface is colder and stronger. Plan
   movements to avoid crossing on or under very steep slopes in the afternoon. Move to colder, shadier slopes


26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                    69
Chapter 5



     once the snow surface turns slushy. Avoid steep, sunlit slopes above terrain traps, cliffs, and long steep slopes.
     (See figure 5-5.)
WET SLAB AVALANCHES
     5-25. A wet slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of wet snow (a slab) when the flow of liquid water
     weakens the bond between the slab and the surface below (snow or ground). They often occur during
     prolonged warming events or rain-on-snow events. Wet slabs can be very destructive. Avoid terrain where
     and when wet slab avalanche activity is expected. Give suspect slopes a wide safety buffer to handle the
     uncertainty. (See figure 5-5.)
CORNICE FALL
     5-26. Cornice fall is the release of an overhanging mass of snow that forms as the wind moves snow over a
     sharp terrain feature, such as a ridge, and deposits snow on the downwind (leeward) side. Cornices range in
     size from small wind lips of soft snow to large overhangs of hard snow that are 10 meters (30 feet) or taller.
     They can break off suddenly. Even small cornices can have enough mass to be destructive and deadly.
     Cornice fall can entrain loose surface snow or trigger slab avalanches. Cornices can never be trusted and
     avoiding them is necessary for safe travel. Stay well back from ridgeline areas with cornices. They often
     overhang the ridge edge; they can be triggered remotely. Avoid areas underneath cornices, especially during
     periods of significant warming. (See figure 5-5.)
GLIDE (FULL DEPTH) AVALANCHES
     5-27. A glide avalanche is a release of the entire snow cover at the ground surface. Glide avalanches can be
     composed of wet, moist, or almost entirely dry snow. They occur in very specific paths, where the slope is
     steep enough and the ground surface is smooth. They often occur on south-facing slopes during periods of
     strong sun and warm temperatures. They may be proceeded by full depth cracks (glide cracks), though the
     time between the appearance of a crack and an avalanche can vary between seconds and months. Predicting
     the release of glide avalanches is very challenging. Because they only occur on very specific slopes,
     avoidance is key to safe travel. Glide cracks and other glide avalanches are indicators. (See figure 5-5.)




                                    Figure 5-5. Avalanche problem types

FORECASTS
     5-28. In areas with extensive avalanche terrain and conditions, there are regional offices with staff members
     that monitor weather and snowpack conditions and produce forecasts to warn the public of avalanche hazards.



70                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                     Avalanche



   Forecasts are created using a combination of weather models, remote weather stations, snowpack data, and
   field observations. Forecasts use the North American Avalanche Danger Scale and add additional information
   regarding specific avalanche problems, location in the terrain, likelihood of triggering, and expected size.
NORTH AMERICAN DANGER SCALE
   5-29. The North American Avalanche Danger Scale is a tool used by avalanche forecasters to communicate
   the potential for avalanches to cause harm or injury to backcountry travelers. It converts the forecasters’
   projections of the size and distribution of avalanches and likelihood of triggering into travel advice. (See
   figure 5-6.)
AVALANCHE PROBLEM
   5-30. In addition to the danger rating, forecasters publish a more detailed discussion of the avalanche
   problem. The avalanche problem describes the types of potential avalanche, the expected location based on
   aspect and elevation, the likelihood of triggering, and the expected size. Specific avalanche problems with
   similar ratings on the danger scale may present differently and require different terrain choices. (See
   figure 5-7, page 72.)
USING THE FORECAST
   5-31. The forecast is a starting point to guide planning for patrols or missions. In addition, planners should
   consult a record of the season’s conditions and current weather. Group discussion, identifying the hazard,
   communicating recent observations, and planning routes with clear decision points are all part of the
   decision-making framework used to manage avalanche risk.

SECTION II – AVALANCHE RISK MANAGEMENT
     5-32. More than any other hazard faced in the mountains, avalanches pose the most significant threat of a
     catastrophic accident for an entire element. There is inherent uncertainty in any forecast, even those produced
     by avalanche professionals, and the consequence of being caught in an avalanche are high. The best control
     measure is avoiding all avalanche terrain. However, this is not always possible. In some mountain ranges,
     even valleys, roads, and railways are threatened by avalanches when dangerous weather conditions are
     present. Key terrain and approaches to it may be in avalanche terrain. Much of the time, the snowpack may
     be stable and safe for travel, but without an understanding of specific hazards and their locations in the terrain,
     units can be dangerously exposed.
     5-33. Education is the greatest tool for managing avalanche hazard. Unit commanders are responsible for
     implementing avalanche training. They must understand the hazards that Soldiers may be exposed to and
     ensure that subordinate leaders and Soldiers are prepared for those threats. Units should have designated unit
     members with formal avalanche training and education.

UNIT-LEVEL RESPONSIBILITIES
     5-34. Avalanche hazard shuts down large areas to maneuver. As part of their intelligence preparation of the
     battlefield, units need to analyze terrain, snowpack, and weather factors to develop a forecast for subordinate
     elements. Route planning, terrain selection, and risk decisions are all driven by a forecast.
     5-35. When training in the United States, units may have access to avalanche forecasts being generated at
     avalanche centers in our geographic regions. These forecasts identify the avalanche problems and locations
     in the terrain and assign them a danger rating based off the likelihood of triggering them and their size. These
     forecasts guide route planning and help to evaluate the overall risk. To develop an operational capability,
     units must identify and develop key personnel that can evaluate the hazards using weather data and snowpack
     observations within their area of operations.

MILITARY MOUNTAINEER RESPONSIBILITIES
     5-36. Route planning and decision making are the primary tools to reduce exposure and avoid avalanche
     prone terrain and being caught in an avalanche. The following skills are critical for travel in avalanche terrain:
         • Terrain analysis—military mountaineers must be able to use information from an avalanche forecast
              to identify and inform commanders of hazardous slopes and safe corridors within their area of
              operations. They must also recognize terrain traps. To travel safely below avalanche terrain, they
              must estimate run-out zones (how far an avalanche may travel before it stops). This can vary and is
              determined by snow cover and snow depth.
         • Route selection—routes with terrain angles that are less than 30° and greater than 45° should be
              identified, and care must be taken to ensure routes are not threatened by overhead avalanche hazard.
              The safest routes are on ridge tops, slightly on the windward side. Valley bottoms can provide safe


72                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                         Avalanche



            routes, but lines of travel must be far from the bottom of slopes, clear of any run-out zones. Avoid
            cornices from above or below. Take advantage of dense timber, ridges, or rocky outcrops as islands
            of safety. Use them for rest stops.
       •    Critical weather analysis—changes in the following weather factors that increase loads on the
            snowpack or erode bonds will directly contribute to increasing avalanche danger:
             Rain.
             Snowfall of more than 2.5 cm (1 inch) an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot) in 24 hours.
             New or recent wind loading.
             Rapid rise in temperature.
       •    Stability analysis—direct signs of instability, such as those noted below, should be viewed as clear
            evidence of immediate danger to Soldiers traveling in similar terrain:
             Evidence of avalanching and recent avalanches on similar slopes.
             Shooting cracks—a shooting crack is evidence of a slab or weak layer combination.
             Whoomphing sounds—hollow sounds when moving through the snow. These are evidence of
                 the collapse of a weak layer. On a steeper slope, a whoomph could trigger an avalanche.
       •    Deliberate triggering:
             Types—avalanches can be triggered using explosives. Soldiers can use recoilless rifles,
                 artillery, and mortars to trigger avalanches. Small charges of C4 explosive (1 to 2 kilograms)
                 with a time fuse are effective if Soldiers can drop the charge to a point in the slope that triggers
                 an avalanche.
             Uses—deliberate triggering can be used for force protection. Soldiers can trigger small
                 avalanches so that larger avalanches do not threaten key positions and infrastructures. Soldiers
                 can use avalanches to deny key terrain to the enemy, and to block roads and narrow passes.
                 Mountaineer Soldiers can use deliberate triggering of avalanches offensively to isolate elements
                 that they desire to engage with direct fire and indirect fire assets.
             Principles—understanding what cause avalanches and where they are likely to occur are useful
                 for selecting the best triggering locations. Choose a point of maximum tension in the snowpack
                 to detonate the charge.
       •    Planning and supervising avalanche training—leaders must ensure that all Soldiers operating in
            avalanche terrain practice and rehearse individual avalanche protective measures. They must be
            capable of coordinating and leading the rescue if someone is caught in an avalanche.
INDIVIDUAL RESPONSIBILITIES
   5-37. All Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain must be proficient in basic avalanche tasks. They must be
   able to travel in the terrain, be proficient with all equipment, and well drilled in tasks for companion rescue.
        • Travel techniques—just as battle drills are rehearsed for tactical movement, troops moving in
             avalanche terrain must practice and rehearse movement techniques for limiting exposure to
             avalanche hazard by—
              Having a planned and rehearsed communication strategy. Be deliberate when passing through
                  pockets of increased hazard.
              Zipping up clothing and other layers.
              Posting a spotter to observe the entire element as it passes through. Send one person across at
                  a time. Stop on islands of safety. All Soldiers should travel in the same track. Set the track high,
                  above potential start zones.
        • Avalanche safety equipment—every Soldier operating in avalanche terrain should be equipped with
             the three basic items of avalanche rescue equipment. They should be trained and rehearsed in their
             use.
              Shovel—to dig out the victim. It should be constructed of aluminum and collapsed or
                  disassembled in a pack where it is protected and will not be lost but easily accessed. E-tools are
                  insufficient for this purpose.
              Transceiver—an active radio-beacon transceiver designed for finding people buried under
                  snow. When turned on, it broadcasts a signal that other transceivers can locate with a range of
                  about 30 meters.
              Probe—a long pole used to confirm the location of an avalanche victim and to measure how
                  deeply they are buried.



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                   73
Chapter 5



         •    Survival—try to escape quickly out of the side of the avalanche. An alternative for if or when
              Soldiers are caught in the start zone and before debris gains speed is to arrest in the bed surface and
              let the snow flow past. If Soldiers are caught, they should discard equipment and attempt to swim
              to stay closer to the surface. If their head goes under the snow, they should shut their mouth and use
              their elbow to form an air pocket in front of their face by reaching across the body and grabbing the
              opposite shoulder strap of the rucksack. Many avalanche victims suffocate because their mouth and
              nose are plugged with snow. The opposite arm can be used to attempt to reach for the surface.
              Although often difficult to tell surface direction when tumbling, many victims have been quickly
              found when a rescuer found a hand or body part sticking out of the snow. When the snow stops, try
              to relax. If Soldiers feel themselves about to pass out, they should not fight it. Once unconscious,
              respirations are shallower, pulse rates slower, and body temperature lower, all of which help to
              conserve oxygen.
         •    Companion rescue—a fast, efficient transceiver search and shoveling are key to the survival of an
              avalanche victim. Avalanche rescue is covered in-depth in section III.
SNOWPACK EVALUATIONS
     5-38. Snowpack stability evaluation can be difficult in the absence of direct evidence, such as recent
     avalanches, whoomphing, or shooting cracks. It is also especially difficult when it has been several days
     since new loading has occurred (rain, new snow, wind-transported snow), several days without significant
     temperature changes, or in situations where a “persistent” weak layer exists in the snowpack. During these
     times, experienced Soldiers may use a multitude of tests to help determine stability and identify particularly
     dangerous terrain. These tests are limited, because their accuracy is localized to the vicinity and should only
     be used to determine where not to go. Typically conducted by master mountaineers, these tests require a high
     degree of skill and training both to perform and interpret; therefore, specific procedures are not covered in
     detail in this manual. Most of these tests require the digging of snow pits in safe locations that are specifically
     representative of terrain that is in question (same aspect and elevation). These snow pits can have a range of
     dimensions that can be modified depending upon the types and quantities of tests to be conducted; however,
     they are typically 2-meters across the slope by 1.5-meters up slope and dug to below the depth of any weak
     layers in question.
         • Layer identification—used to identify specific areas of concern within the snowpack, for example,
                layers with major differences in characteristics. This could be major differences in hardness,
                softness, gain size, and shape.
         • Shovel tilt—used to evaluate bonding between the most recent storm snow and the old snow surface.
                Also used to identify thin weak layers not found during layer identification. Limited to the top 45 cm
                of the snowpack.
         • Compression test—used to locate weak layers in the top 1 meter of snow and to provide an indication
                of triggering potential on nearby slopes with similar conditions.
         • Extended column test—used to test for the potential of crack propagation of a pre-identified slab or
                weak layer combination in the upper 1 meter of the snowpack.
         • Propagation saw test—used to test for the potential of crack propagation of a pre-identified slab or
                weak layer combination that is greater than 1-meter deep.
         • Rutschblock—used to test stability of pre-identified weak layers up to 1-meter deep with skis.
         • Explosives—used to test slopes and trigger slides in the top layers of the snowpack. Placement in
                the sensitive regions of the start zone is critical for getting a reaction.
         • Hasty tests (hand shear, pole plants, test slopes)—nonstandardized tests that can be used quickly
                while traveling in the terrain to determine signs of instability or to recognize when conditions are
                changing.
     5-39. Avalanches pose a significant threat to Soldiers operating in mountainous terrain. Unlike fall hazards,
     or weather conditions, avalanche hazard is not easily observed. If units wish to maintain the ability to conduct
     operations during winter months or in regions of the world with the possibility of snow throughout the year,
     they must develop the capability to assess avalanche hazard. This means identifying individuals for further
     training and education, incorporating avalanche forecasts into the planning process, and ensuring that all
     Soldiers operating in the terrain are equipped and trained for the avalanche threat.

SECTION III – AVALANCHE SEARCH AND RESCUE
   5-40. The primary risk mitigation tool in avalanche terrain is avoidance. In the planning phase, Soldiers
   should make every effort to patrol routes that avoid avalanche hazards. The planning phase includes having
   clear decision points from which to evaluate conditions and viable alternate routes. However, when
   evaluating an avalanche hazard, there is often a high degree of uncertainty. When mistakes are made, the
   consequences are high. Avalanches produce incredible energy. Soldiers caught in an avalanche may be
   injured or killed by blunt force trauma from collisions with rock, ice, and trees. If they come to rest with an
   intact air pocket, they may succumb to hypothermia or shock. However, most avalanche victims die from
   asphyxiation. Without an air pocket, unconsciousness may come in minutes, followed rapidly by permeant
   brain injury and death. Evidence has shown that after 15 minutes, the chances of surviving complete burial
   decreases from 90 percent to 30 percent. It is critical that all Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain are
   equipped with avalanche safety equipment and are drilled in companion rescue.

AVALANCHE SEARCH
   5-41. All individuals traveling into terrain in which avalanches could possibly occur must be familiar with
   and carry the following equipment: avalanche transceiver, lightweight shovel, and collapsible probe. Soldiers
   must be adequately trained in their use during avalanche rescue.
TRANSCEIVER
   5-42. Avalanche transceivers (beacons) are radio transceivers that emit a pulsed signal. (See figure 5-8,
   page 76.) When turned on, they broadcast a signal that other transceivers can locate within a range of
   approximately 30 meters. Other transceivers can be switched into a search mode to receive that signal and
   find transceivers buried under the snow. Soldiers should wear their transceiver over the top of their base
   layers but underneath insulating layers that may be removed or added throughout the course of the day.
   Soldiers should always wear their transceiver below a layer to protect it in case of an avalanche.
   5-43. Electronic interference has been shown to interfere with the range and accuracy of avalanche
   transceivers, especially in search mode. Manufacturers recommend that transceivers are worn 30 cm
   (12 inches) away from any radios, cell phones, and GPS devices to ensure that there is no metal or reflective
   material (such as meals, ready to eat wrappers) in the area around where the device is worn. This may not be
   possible when wearing combat equipment, but in a training environment, every effort should be made to
   adhere to manufacturer recommendations. In search mode, manufacturers recommend that Soldiers turn off
   all other devices and keep the transceiver at least 50 cm from other devices. If possible, Soldiers with radios
   and active electronic equipment should delegate transceiver searches to those without electronic equipment
   and radios.
SHOVEL
   5-44. Shovels suitable for avalanche rescue are lightweight and made of aluminum. They are durable enough
   to cut through dense avalanche debris but light enough to for Soldiers to carry while skiing or mountaineering.
   Soldiers can collapse or disassemble their shovel to carry it inside their pack. Soldiers should pack their
   transceiver, so it is quickly accessible. (See figure 5-8, page 76.)
PROBE
   5-45. Probes are used to confirm the location of a burial before digging. Probes are approximately 3-meters
   long. They collapse to fit disassembled inside a pack but deploy quickly with a pull of the connecting cable.
   They should lock into place automatically. Soldiers should carry their probes inside their pack in a location
   where it is protected and immediately accessible.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                75
Chapter 5




                               Figure 5-8. Individual avalanche equipment

GROUP CHECKS
     5-46. All Soldiers must be familiar with the group avalanche equipment functions check process before
     movement into avalanche terrain. All leaders must be familiar with conducting these functions checks to
     ensure that their unit is prepared to respond to an avalanche burial event. All Soldiers must be familiar with
     avalanche response actions. SOPs and rehearsals should be conducted in the same manner as battle drills.
PRECOMBAT CHECKS
     5-47. Soldiers must be trained and familiar with each equipment item and how it functions. Individual and
     team rehearsals, transceiver checks, and rescue drills are necessary:
         • Check that individual rescue equipment is functional and stowed appropriately.
         • Conduct verbal rehearsals of all avalanche tasks, movement through danger areas, and avalanche rescue.
TRANSCEIVER CHECK
     5-48. A group check confirms that each member of the element knows how to turn on the device and switch
     between modes, ensures that every device can receive and search for a signal, and that every device transmits
     a signal. Manufacturers recommended procedures for group checks might vary.
          • Locate an area away from other groups that may cause conflicting signals. Stand in a half circle an
               arm’s length or more apart, with the leader a few meters away in the middle of the group.
          • Turn transceivers on. As the transceivers power on, each individual confirms that the transceiver
               runs a self-check, and the display is ok. Note battery strength and report it aloud to the group. For




76                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                       Avalanche



            patrols or missions lasting less than 24 hours, battery life should be a minimum of 50 percent. For
            multi-day missions, each Soldier should begin with fresh batteries.
       •    Switch all transceivers to search mode. Silence indicates that everyone is ready and ensures that no
            transmitting units are in packs or sleds.
       •    The leader then switches to transmit/send and checks that each group member can receive a signal
            by walking toward each group member one by one while group members read their display aloud.
       •    Turn all units to transmit. The leader ensures that group members stow their unit for the day, secured
            under an outside layer, and 30 cm from a cell phone or radio.
       •    The leader returns to Search mode and confirms all group members are transmitting. The
            check-leader then switches to transmit mode and confirms to at least one group member, who also
            verifies that the leader’s device is transmitting and properly stowed.

AVALANCHE RESCUE
   5-49. Units must be prepared to conduct avalanche rescue when operating in avalanche terrain. Avalanches,
   especially those involving Soldier burial, will significantly affect tactical operations. Commanders must
   provide clear guidance regarding subordinate unit response to avalanche burial events during tactical
   operations. This guidance should cover avalanche victim rescue priority in relation to mission conduct,
   affected unit response SOPs, higher unit response capabilities and SOPs, and reporting expectations.
   Maneuver units must be capable of finding and digging out victims quickly. Unit commanders must plan for
   and be prepared to organize rescue operations for avalanche mass casualty events, as well as deliberate body
   location and recovery.
ORGANIZING THE RESCUE
   5-50. The normal chain of command may be broken if a leader is buried or separated. Everyone should be
   prepared to organize and take charge of a rescue. Every Soldier must be prepared to make critical decisions
   and tasks for an efficient and successful rescue.
       • Assess safety—determine if there is further avalanche hazard. If there is risk of secondary
            avalanches (hangfire), limit the number of personnel exposed to further hazard. Post a watch and a
            relay to maintain communications.
       • Headcount—get an accurate headcount to find out how many Soldiers are buried.
       • Report or call for help—do not waste time; report the accident to get resources moving if a Soldier
            needs them. If possible, delegate and leave a relay up high to maintain communications. Do not let
            radio operators in the rear or at a dispatch delay or interfere with the rescue.
       • Switch all transceivers to Search mode—physically ensure that all unit members have switched their
            transceivers to Search mode to avoid disrupting the searchers. Just one rescuer still transmitting will
            confuse the searchers and waste precious time.
       • Assign roles—in small teams, everyone may need to help with the transceiver search. In a larger
            group, assign some to search and others to prepare probes and shovels.
       • Determine where to search—the spotter should have been able to observe a point last seen. Search
            the fall line below the point last seen. Search the run-out zone and other areas of deposition, such as
            terrain traps. Search in line with equipment clues if they exist.
TRANSCEIVER SEARCH
   5-51. Transceiver searches involve three distinct phases: signal search, course search, and fine search.
       • Signal search—begin searching for a signal. Get all the searchers online with 40-meter spacing to
            ensure that the search ranges overlap across the entire search area. If alone, or covering a very wide
            search area, use a search pattern that covers the entire path. Movement should be rapid but
            deliberate. Keep eyes up, searching for physical clues. (See figure 5-9, page 78.)
       • Course search—once a signal is found, the transceivers change tones and light up with a distance
            and direction. Slow down and follow the arrow. Communicate with the other searchers, calling out
            the distance reading. At 10 meters, slow down even further. Ensure the transceiver aligns with the
            direction arrow. Continue moving slowly and bring the transceiver lower and closer to the surface
            of the snow. Avoid sudden movements or changes in orientation.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 77
Chapter 5



         •    Fine search—inside 3 meters, transition to a fine search. The transceiver should be moving in a
              plane just above the surface of the snow. Maintain orientation throughout the rest of the search. Do
              not twist or turn it. Continue the azimuth of approach until the numbers start to rise. Return to the
              low point, and search side to side, far enough to see the numbers rise, returning to the point with the
              lowest number.




                                           Figure 5-9. Signal search

PROBING
     5-52. Mark the lowest point with a foot or hand. Probe at the low point, perpendicular to the snow surface.
     Probing must be conducted with both hands. (See figure 5-10.) If no strike is felt, probe again 2 cm uphill
     and continue to probe in a spiral search pattern. Once a probe strike is achieved, do not remove the probe.
     This probe is a valuable reference point that must be visible to ensure Soldiers do not waste effort and energy
     during shoveling.




78                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                       Avalanche




                                            Figure 5-10. Probing

SHOVELING
   5-53. Upon probe strike, take 1 large step downhill, 2 steps for a deep burial (greater than 2 meters). Rescuers
   should excavate snow from the side so that they are not lifting snow out of a hole. They should dig towards
   the probe and throw the snow far away while shoveling as fast and hard as possible. If there is a large group,
   rotate personnel often. Those who are not shoveling in the hole should continue to move snow out of the way
   and widen and improve the platform the others are creating. Everyone must prepare to switch out often so
   that those shoveling are doing so at maximum capacity. (See figure 5-11, page 80.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 79
Chapter 5




                                              Figure 5-11. Shoveling

PATIENT CARE
     5-54. Work to clear the victim’s airway as soon as possible. Provide first aid and CPR as required. With long
     burials where there is a risk of hypothermia, move the patient gently. Move the patient to safe terrain and
     begin planning for evacuation.
PROBE SEARCHES
     5-55. Avalanche burials longer than 15 minutes can result in permanent brain damage and death. If victims
     are going to be saved, it is critical that it is done quickly. If the Soldier is not wearing a transceiver, the
     likelihood of finding them in time for survival is small.
     5-56. If transceivers are unavailable, it is likely there are no probes available either. Soldiers can use their ski
     poles with the basket removed to begin initial probing attempts. If there is any hope of success, searchers
     must focus their efforts on the most probable locations.
         • Start the search from the point last seen.
         • Look for equipment clues. Gloves, hats, ski poles, packs—all may give clues to the trajectory of the
               victim or may still be attached. Pull each out of the snow to confirm.
         • Most buried victims are carried to the place of greatest deposition, usually the toe of the slide. Any
               terrain features that catch and hold avalanche debris, such as outside curves, are also likely locations.
         • Vegetation, rocks, and other obstacles act as strainers and may catch or slow the victim.




80                                                    TC 3-97.61                                   26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Avalanche



PROBE LINES
   5-57. For body recovery of individuals without transceivers, it may be necessary to locate them using a probe
   line. A probe line is a systematic search, online, through the entire debris field. It is a slow process and
   requires many rescuers. A probe line is not appropriate when there is still an overhead avalanche hazard.
   5-58. There are two distinct probing methods: coarse probe and fine probe. Coarse probing is intended to be
   fast, with wide spacing of probe insertions. Fine probing involves close-spaced probing with an emphasis on
   thoroughness. The coarse-probe technique has about a 70-percent chance of locating the victim on a given
   pass, while the fine probe has closer to a 100-percent chance of locating the victim.

                                                 Chapter 6
                                       Mountain Mobility
   A unit’s ability to maneuver through difficult and hazardous terrain provides it with access to
   the most tactically advantageous areas in the mountains. Units with Soldiers trained to a high
   level of mobility can move further, faster, and more safely through all levels of terrain. Mobility
   skill is the primary tool to manage risk when there is a fall hazard. Rope systems and belays
   can be used to mitigate fall risk during movement but require more time to complete, more
   technical training to accomplish, and can result in increased exposure to enemy attack. By far,
   the greatest combat multiplier in the mountains is high mobility skill. Units anticipating combat
   operations should focus on building individual movement skills over nearly all other special
   technical or tactical skills.

SECTION I – INDIVIDUAL MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
   6-1. The speed at which the unit can move, the complexity of terrain they can negotiate unroped, and the
   violence of action they can muster as a team on the objective are all determined by the mobility of the unit’s
   weakest members. Properly equipped units with mobility skills are more likely to outmaneuver the enemy in
   physically demanding and hazardous terrain. Soldiers who have been trained in mobility techniques can take
   advantage of terrain above operational level 2. This provides commanders with access to the highest and
   most difficult to reach points of domination in their areas of operation. For those untrained in mountaineering,
   such terrain can prove too hazardous to move in. However, units well-trained to maneuver here can take
   advantage of reduced combat risks during all types of combat operations by owning ground that most enemy
   forces cannot access, granting them overwhelming tactical advantage. As a result, individual mobility skills
   training should always be a high priority for units anticipating these operations.

MOBILITY
   6-2. Individual mobility comprises many factors, the most important of which are fitness and movement
   techniques. Soldiers can increase their mobility by practicing the movement techniques specific to
   negotiating rough terrain. Soldiers build proficiency by approaching movement from a skill-building
   perspective, whether the movement is walking, scrambling, or climbing, and regardless of whether the
   surface is dirt, rock, snow, or ice. The hallmarks of mobility are balance, surefootedness, and net endurance.
   The results are reduced likelihood of slipping or falling, reduced energy expended, increased speed, and the
   ability to focus on other critical tasks. A reasonable goal for Soldiers is the ability to move confidently
   through 3rd-class terrain unroped, even when exposed to fall hazards that would result in significant injury
   or death.
BALANCE
   6-3. The most important aspect of mobility is balance. Soldiers who learn to move in such a way that their
   body is rarely out of balance will display a higher level of surefootedness and endurance than ones who have
   not mastered this skill.
   6-4. Moving in balance requires a basic understanding of how the human body moves, how gravity and other
   forces act upon it, and how to counteract them. In the beginning of skills development, Soldiers can build
   knowledge by paying attention to when they feel out of balance, such as when they are stepping around, over,
   or under small obstacles in their path. Carrying a pack or heavy tactical equipment high on the body will
   increase the effort required to stay in balance.
   6-5. As Soldiers begin to identify when movements put them out of balance, they should begin to experiment
   with adjusting body position, or foot placement, to maintain the feeling of being in balance. Early in training,
   achieving a less out-of-balance feeling may be the best a Soldier can achieve. Through practice, this will
   improve.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 83
Chapter 6



     6-6. The complexity or severity of the terrain will determine the difficulty of the movement techniques and
     body positions required. Techniques for 5th-class rock climbing are much less intuitive than those necessary
     for hiking, but the principles for building skill are the same for both, and across the spectrum of difficulty.
     6-7. With enough focus and practice, Soldiers will develop enough skill that moving becomes natural and
     requires little effort. At that point, they can focus on other mission critical tasks, such as navigation, security,
     communicating, firing weapon systems, moving casualties or any other complex tasks without the distraction
     of trying not to fall.
FITNESS
     6-8. Soldiers develop and improve their mountain fitness through strengthening muscles that move and
     stabilize the body. Although strength in some large muscle groups is useful to move the body uphill against
     the pull of gravity, muscles used in maintaining balance are far more important. Recovering from a slip or
     stumble requires far more energy than just maintaining balance and footing in the first place. Well-developed
     supporting and stabilizing muscles prevent these slips and stumbles and reduce the burden on large muscle
     groups. In this way, mountain Soldiers are better at controlling corrective movements and conserving energy,
     which reduces fatigue and results in greater endurance over the course of a movement. (See FM 7-22 for
     more information on training specific muscle groups.)
     6-9. Flexibility is another important aspect of fitness. Soldiers who are flexible have a greater range of
     movement. Soldiers with low flexibility may not be able to perform movements necessary to negotiate some
     obstacles. Soldiers should develop flexibility along with strength when training for mobility in the mountains.
     6-10. General combat fitness does not translate to mountain fitness. Ruck marching, especially over relatively
     level ground, does not develop the balance and flexibility necessary for movement over rough, broken, and
     steep terrain. Upper body mass developed through heavy body building regimens does nothing for
     dismounted mobility and little for scrambling and climbing. A holistic approach to fitness is necessary.
     Physical training plans must balance combat fitness and mountain fitness requirements to best prepare
     Soldiers for combat action.
     6-11. A Soldier’s role within the unit should be considered when training for the physical requirements of
     the mountains. An advanced military mountaineer who will be responsible for regular movement in 4th- and
     5th-class terrain requires a higher level of mobility than a machine gunner does.

MOUNTAIN WALKING
     6-12. Most terrain negotiated during combat operations in mountainous terrain requires only well-developed
     walking skills. However, this terrain is typically undeveloped, broken, steep and covered by loose dirt, rock,
     or snow. Surfaces are often slick. Heavy loads, nonuniform stride, and unpredictable footing challenge
     Soldiers moving in any of these conditions. Half of the battle for mountaineers is knowing where to step
     under these variable conditions to gain maximum traction, and the other half is knowing how to position their
     body to ensure their footing holds.
TYPES OF TERRAIN
     6-13. Typically, mountain-walking terrain is considered class 1 and 2 terrains, but these skills are equally
     important in terrain that is more difficult. Mountain-walking techniques provide the foundation for
     higher-level skills, such as climbing. They require the same level of focus and practice to master.
MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
     6-14. Quality footwear, such as mountaineering boots, reduces many risks associated with moving in
     mountainous terrain. Quality boots increase both mobility and security of footing and can reduce orthopedic
     injuries. Boots designed for mountaineering range in weight, breathability, flexibility, and in how well they
     interface with other equipment. The rand helps protect the toe area from sharp rock and standing water. They
     have a high enough upper boot to protect the wearer’s ankles from sharp rock and provide joint support
     against rolling. They have recessed soles made of softer rubber, a protective band around the forefoot, at least
     a partial shank, and are constructed with abrasion and water-resistant materials. Mountain boot soles are
     designed for traction on dirt and slick rock alike. Their stiffer, stickier rubber soles provide a significant
     advantage when climbing.


84                                                    TC 3-97.61                                   26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility



   6-15. Quality socks are more durable, help reduce blisters, better manage moisture, and dry faster than other
   materials.
   6-16. Good quality insoles are critical to reducing minor foot injuries, such as blisters, during movement in
   rough, rocky terrain that can interfere with mission completion if they progress untreated.
   6-17. Most Soldiers do not require special packs in walking terrain if they assemble their packs neatly and
   do not overload them.
   6-18. The rucksack is the issued, modular lightweight load-carrying equipment (MOLLE) pack. The carry
   harness should be adjusted to the body of the Soldier carrying it. Soldiers should place heavier items close to
   the frame. Heavy items attached to the outside of, or higher on the pack, increase strain on the Soldier and
   raise the Soldier’s center of gravity, increasing the effort required to stay in balance. Soldiers should remove
   large pouches that they usually attach to the outside of MOLLE packs to streamline the pack and reduce its
   likelihood of being caught on obstacles. Soldiers should use compression straps to prevent loads from shifting
   and throwing them off balance. They should use waist belts to support the weight on their hips and lower
   their center of gravity.
   6-19. Mountaineering packs are designed to be slimmer, taller, and lighter than Army packs. Typically,
   mountaineering packs are not designed with organization and accessibility in mind but rather to consolidate
   loads close to the body and to make movement and balance easier. They are generally less durable than Army
   packs; however, crossover packs, designed for remote mountain hunting, provide an excellent middle ground.
   The drawback of crossover packs is the high expense.
   6-20. Using assault packs when walking terrain can reduce the negative impact on Soldier mobility if loads
   are not too heavy. Their lack of a rigid frame means that they provide less support. If lashing items to the
   outside of the assault pack becomes necessary to carry all required items, then carrying a properly loaded
   MOLLE pack is probably less detrimental to the Soldier’s mobility.
GRASSY SLOPES
   6-21. Grassy slopes are usually composed of small tussocks of growth rather than one continuous field. When
   ascending, step on the upper side of each hummock or tussock, where the ground is more level. When
   descending a grassy slope, climbers should use the traverse technique because of the uneven nature of the
   ground. A climber can easily build up too much speed and fall if a direct descent is attempted. When
   traversing, the climber’s uphill foot points in the direction of travel. The downhill foot points about 45° off
   the direction of travel (downhill). This maintains maximum sole contact and prevents possible downhill ankle
   rollout.
MOUNTAIN WALKING
   6-22. Two critical skills in mountain walking are selecting foot placements and moving the body in a way
   that maintains balance with each step. (See figure 6-1, page 86.) These skills increase the security of foot
   placements and decrease slips. Surface characteristics vary greatly in mountains, and Soldiers should
   experiment with various features and surfaces in their operational environment. To obtain maximum traction
   on a given feature, Soldiers must position their bodies so that their weight pushes perpendicularly against the
   feature. Soldiers must reposition their body with each step to do this and should try to gain as much sole
   contact as possible to achieve maximum friction. As Soldiers become familiar with surface characteristics in
   their area of operation, they learn just how much friction is necessary for the footing to hold on various
   features such as the following:
        • Common microfeatures that can provide greater footings are flat spots, small divots, or depressions,
            the uphill side of stable rocks and tussocks, rough rock features, dry spots, rough or heavily featured
            rock, and stable compact dirt.
        • Common microfeatures that make traction more difficult to achieve and that should be avoided if
            possible are smooth features, loose dirt or small rocks, wet spots, and any surface covered with loose
            debris, such as leaves or small sticks.

     6-23. Selecting reliable foot placements is even more difficult while descending. This is primarily because
     they must be made dynamically (while stepping down) and often out of their ideal body position. This
     prevents the Soldier from testing the placement before committing weight. If a slip occurs, momentum
     increases the likelihood of a fall or tumble.


86                                                TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                             Mountain Mobility



   6-24. General techniques for ascending:
       • As terrain becomes steeper, routes should adopt a traversing or switchback pattern. This involves
           moving diagonally up and across a slope, then turning back and doing the same in the opposite
           direction as necessary. This switchback pattern reduces the intensity and demand on large muscle
           groups, slows the onset of fatigue, and allows Soldiers to maintain situational awareness. Charging
           in a straight line up a steep hill is more demanding, results in more extreme fatigue and longer
           recovery time, and increases the likelihood of slips, falls, and injury. This technique should be
           avoided unless speed is critical, and all members of the group are highly fit and experienced moving
           this way.
       • The rest step technique involves locking out the rear leg briefly with each step. This gives muscles
           a micro rest with each step and results in greater endurance over long movements. (See figure 6-2,
           page 88.)
       • Pressure breathing—this technique involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the
           lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the
           lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more space for oxygenated air. Second, the
           negative pressure created in the lungs makes it easier to pull lower pressure air into them when
           moving at higher altitudes.

                                       Figure 6-2. The rest step

     6-25. General techniques for descending:
         • Whenever Soldiers must use a questionable foot placement, they should identify a quick plan for
             how they will react prior to stepping down.




88                                              TC 3-97.61                             26 November 2025
                                                                                                   Mountain Mobility



        •   Soldiers should ensure they bend their knees when stepping down to reduce impact on their joints.
            Prolonged descents often prove painful, and they could sustain long-term damage if they do not take
            measures to protect their joints under heavy loads.
        •   Poles are helpful when descending. They make it easier to stay in balance and allow the arms to
            absorb or reduce much of the impact on lower extremity joints. Even one pole can be very helpful.
        •   When Soldiers are new to walking in the mountains, it takes more focus to do so effectively. They
            move slower, but they benefit by moving at a rate that allows them to remain in balance without
            slipping and stumbling. Additionally, they improve mountain walking skills when allowed to move
            a little slower during training, becoming faster and more efficient in the end. Leaders should look at
            every dismounted movement in training as an opportunity to improve.
   6-26. When a moderate pace is set, the need for rest halts decreases and the chance of personnel overheating
   lessens. Typically, shorter breaks taken more often are better than long breaks, especially in colder weather.
   However, leaders should consider fitness level, difficulty of the terrain, length of movement, speed, load, and
   level of fatigue when determining rest durations.
   6-27. During the first half-hour of movement, an adjustment halt should be taken. Soldiers will loosen or
   tighten bootlaces as needed, adjust packs, and add or remove layers of clothing.

Brush
   6-28. Brush is both a help and a hindrance. Brush-filled gullies can provide routes and rally points concealed
   from observation; on the other hand, steep, brushy terrain is hazardous to negotiate. Cliffs and steep ravines
   are hidden traps, and blow downs and thickets can obstruct travel as much as manmade obstacles. When
   brush must be negotiated, take the most direct route across the obstacle; look for downed timber to use as
   raised paths through the obstacle; or create a tunnel through the obstacle by prying the brush apart, standing
   on lower branches, and using upper limbs for support.

Dirt and Rocky Terrain
   6-29. Surfaces comprised of mixed dirt are very common in mountainous terrain. As the terrain gets steeper
   and rockier, it typically becomes rougher and looser. This may require slowing the rate of movement to one
   that is maintainable by the less fit and skilled or overburdened members of the group. If this is not done, they
   are at risk of falling out or injury while struggling to catch up.
   6-30. Hard ground is firmly compacted, rocky soil that does not give way under the weight of a Soldier’s
   step. It is usually found under mature forest canopy, in low brush or heather, and areas where animals have
   beaten out multiple trails. When ascending, employ the rest step to rest the leg muscles.
   6-31. Scree fields are comprised of loose rock approximately fist-sized or smaller, that are common in the
   mountains and are a challenge to ascend. The experience is like climbing sand, except that the loose rock can
   be rough on ankles and lower legs. Climbers should avoid ascending scree fields, if possible, as they demand
   the expenditure of much more energy than other surfaces. Soldiers should kick in with the toe of the upper
   foot so that a step is formed in the loose scree. After determining that the step is stable, the Soldier transfers
   weight to the upper leg, then steps up, and repeats the process with the lower foot. Traversing scree is very
   difficult, as the loose stones slide out from under the foot downslope with each step. On the other hand, they
   are often a good option for descent routes. Greater focus on maintaining balance is required since foot
   placements are invariably unstable. The best method for descending scree slopes is to come straight down
   the slope using a short shuffling step with the knees bent, back straight, feet pointed downhill, and heels dug
   in. When several climbers descend a scree slope together, they should be as close together as possible (one
   behind the other at single-arm interval) to prevent injury from dislodged rocks. Avoid running down scree as
   this can cause a loss of control.
   6-32. Talus fields are comprised of larger rocks. Often these rocks are loose and present a hazard to Soldiers
   moving through them. Soldiers must choose their foot placements carefully, often testing rocks to ensure
   they are stable. Typically, talus is easier to ascend than scree or loose dirt, but it is still demanding physically.
   Often it requires occasionally using hands for balance on steeper slopes. If a talus field is particularly
   unstable, then the switchback travel technique may not be appropriate for larger groups to use, as the risk of
   Soldiers higher on a slope knocking off a rock that hits Soldiers lower on the slope is potentially high.
