SCRAMBLING
     6-33. Scrambling is the act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking
     techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. It is perhaps
     the most dangerous means of mobility in which snow and ice are not present. At the lowest level, scrambling
     involves simply placing a hand or hands on features periodically to help maintain balance and improve
     efficiency during movement. At the higher level, scrambling involves Soldiers making multiple easy
     rock-climbing moves, followed by several steps walking, and repeating that sequence throughout an ascent.
     6-34. Typically, 3rd-class terrain is where Soldiers begin scrambling, but just exactly what terrain and terrain
     features require is determined largely by the mobility skill of the individual Soldier. Soldiers with
     low-mobility skill will need to use hands more often, especially if a fall risk is present, which will slow their
     movement. Soldiers with higher mobility skills need to use their hands less often for balance enabling them
     to move faster even when a fall risk is present.
     6-35. The higher the rock-climbing skill, the more quickly, efficiently, and safely Soldiers can scramble. The
     best way to train Soldiers to be better at scrambling is to provide rock-climbing training. Rock climbing is
     easier to protect with ropes and forces Soldiers to use better movement techniques even though rock-climbing
     training involves steeper and more difficult terrain.
SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
     6-36. Scrambling terrain can be some of the most dangerous terrain through which Soldiers can move. Often
     it is the low ground between higher terrain features or cliffs, subjecting it to falling object hazards and
     significant tactical disadvantage. Additionally, it can be exposed to fall hazards below.
     6-37. Good reconnaissance and route planning are critical for movements through scrambling terrain.
     Whenever possible, small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be sent to find the best route
     ahead of the main body.
     6-38. Maneuvering is incredibly difficult in terrain that requires a lot of scrambling. If enemy contact is a
     possibility, bounding overwatch must be used to ensure security during movement. Small teams may need to
     be sent forward to clear points of domination over the route. Sniper or machine gun overwatch positions may
     need to be established to cover movement through sections of terrain that is particularly exposed to enemy
     attack. All these security measures increase movement times significantly. (See ATP 3-21.50 for
     VDA-crossing TTP.)
     6-39. Two-point slings should be used to secure rifles close to the body. Heavier weapon systems, such as
     sniper rifles and machine guns, may need to be secured to rucksacks close to the body during sustained
     scrambling to allow Soldiers to use their hands freely for assistance.
SCRAMBLING CONSIDERATIONS
     6-40. There are no scrambling specific movement techniques, but greater care in selecting hand and footholds
     is often necessary given the nature of the terrain. Possessing rock-climbing skills (discussed later in the
     chapter) increases the efficiency with which Soldiers can scramble. Vegetation may appear to provide good
     handholds but may easily pull free. Large boulders or masses of loose rock may be knocked free without
     warning. Groups should move in such a way that Soldiers further back in the formation are not subject to
     rockfall from those above. Some scrambling terrain may require simple fixed lines to aid movement. This is
     even more likely during descending. These sites must be identified, planned for, and established prior to the
     main body arriving for efficiency. (See chapter 11 for more techniques for moving on ropes.)

CLIMBING ROCK
     6-41. Climbing rock, typically 4th- and 5th-class terrain, requires a very high level of skill, especially when
     done for sustained periods. The probability and consequence of falls are high, even under the best conditions.
     Rope systems are usually necessary to protect climbers from injury or death, slowing movement and reducing
     tactical maneuverability.
     6-42. Building rock-climbing skill increases the confidence and speed at which Soldiers can move unroped
     in easier terrain, even when subjected to higher fall consequence. Soldiers who possess moderate



90                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Mobility



   rock-climbing skills can maneuver more safely and efficiently unroped in easy terrain. This should be the
   goal for level 1 mountaineers. Soldiers with high rock-climbing skills can do the same in moderate terrain.
   This should be the goal for level 2 mountaineers.
   6-43. The basic principles of rock climbing are the same as walking in rough terrain; they are just more
   difficult to achieve, and the required movements less intuitive. Selecting hand and foot placements can be
   much more difficult, and the movements and body positions required for them to hold can be challenging to
   perform. Experience built through climbing terrain more difficult than would need to be accessed in military
   operations is the path to building rock-climbing skill.
CLIMBING EQUIPMENT
   6-44. Climbing shoes are small, lightweight, close-fitting shoes with a smooth, soft, rubber sole used by
   recreational climbers, which increase the precision in which weight can be applied to small rock features.
   They contain hook-and-loop fasteners or laces to secure to the foot, and they are designed for various levels
   of climbing difficulty. The tighter, stiffer, and more downcurved the toe is, the more difficult the terrain
   (YDS 5.9 and higher) for which they are designed. Typically, climbing shoes are not appropriate for military
   applications because they are much more uncomfortable to wear for long periods and unsuitable for walking
   even short distances. However, these are an excellent choice for advanced military mountaineers looking to
   improve their skills using established routes off military installations, where climbing with muddy boots may
   be frowned upon. A moderate climbing shoe that is comfortable for the Soldier to wear for long periods is
   sufficient in training and (rarely) operationally. Operationally, climbing shoes are only appropriate to small,
   assault climber teams that must guide or establish routes for others in the most difficult operational terrain.
   (See figure 6-3.)




                             Figure 6-3. Rock-climbing specific footwear

   6-45. The issued advanced combat ballistic helmet provides sufficient protection from head impacts during
   a fall and from small falling objects. However, it is not designed to absorb large impact from above, and its
   weight introduces substantial additional fatigue during sustained climbing. Rock-climbing helmets are very
   lightweight and are designed to protect the wearer against impact from falling objects but do not provide a
   means of mounting night vision devices. Plastic, tactical bump helmets offer a reasonable compromise for
   military rock climbers as they provide the best combination of top- and side-impact protection, the ability to
   mount night vision devices, and weight savings. Commanders must consider risks when determining
   headgear requirements for Soldiers during rock climbing. It is recommended that lead climbers use, at a
   minimum, a lighter-weight helmet. (See figure 6-4, page 92.)

                                        Figure 6-4. Climbing helmets

     6-46. The issued MOLLE pack is not suited for rock climbing. Its size, empty weight, and width interfere
     with movements necessary for even moderate climbing. When loaded, climbing may not even be possible.
     Soldiers climbing sustained rock routes may require a smaller lightweight pack to carry required items (for
     example, water, sensitive items, communications equipment) during the climb. Whatever packs are worn
     should be snugged to the body, and waist straps as well as chest straps worn to reduce the load from shifting
     during climbing and throwing the climber out of balance.
ROCK CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
     6-47. Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical.
     However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by shorter sections of 4th or easier 5th-class terrain.
     These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained
     units. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers can be used to establish fixed-rope routes for
     lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement. Accessing these points may be required to
     reach enemy defensive positions, establish observation posts, or position small teams conducting
     reconnaissance or forward observation of fires.
     6-48. Soldiers climbing 4th- and 5th-class terrain are typically unable to provide themselves sufficient local
     security during movement. Bounding overwatch in vertical terrain by small-specialized teams or
     VDA-crossing procedures must be performed by a larger unit to provide adequate security for climbing
     Soldiers. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more on VDA.) Small reconnaissance and surveillance teams may have to
     rely on careful technical route selection that provides concealment throughout the approach and the climb.
     Fortunately, 4th-class and easier 5th-class terrain often provide such opportunities for teams with the
     technical and mobility skills necessary to negotiate them.
CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION
     6-49. Before climbing, Soldiers should scan the rock for features that indicate that climbing the route is
     possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult a section of rock will be for them to complete.



92                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility



   Climbers should begin to form a plan for climbing the route and a plan to protect themselves with a rope
   system (when necessary) before leaving the ground. (See chapter 10 on how to protect climbers from fall hazards.)
   6-50. During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See
   chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.)
ROCK-CLIMBING TECHNIQUES
   6-51. The basic principles for rock climbing are the same as those for walking in rough terrain. They are
   finding and selecting suitable holds and positioning the body to achieve sufficient friction for continued
   movement. Due to the vertical nature of the terrain, hands must be used to aid Soldiers in maintaining balance
   and preventing them from tipping backward off the rock.
   6-52. Suspect rock-climbing holds should be tested to ensure they are secure by tapping with a hand or foot.
   Holds that move or shift should be avoided. This is common in undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain.

Maintaining Balance
   6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good
   use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable stance is essential.
   The body should be centered over the feet as much as possible. On lower angle sections of climbing, it should
   be positioned away from the rock face. Alternatively, it should be positioned closer to the rock face on steeper
   sections. This puts downward pressure on footholds, increasing their security. Smaller lower body
   movements are often less strenuous than larger ones, which take more effort to stay in balance.
   6-54. Rock climbing usually requires the use of handholds to maintain balance. Handholds can be large jugs
   that allow climbers to hold nearly their whole weight or tiny crimpers that only hold a fraction of their weight.
   Specific handhold techniques are discussed throughout this section. New climbers commonly overuse their
   arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of
   bad footwork.
   6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next
   hold. This can reduce the likelihood of a fall should one point of contact fail.

Types of Contact
   6-56. Though counterintuitive, often pushing rather than pulling is required during climbing. Using
   downward pressure involves pushing down on a feature with the hands to allow unweighting of the other
   hand or one foot for movement to the next hold. Using counterpressure involves pushing away from features
   to allow a hand or foot to be unweighted for movement. (See figure 6-5, page 94.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                  93
Chapter 6




                                Figure 6-5. Downward or counterpressure

     6-57. Occasionally, the holds available put the climber out of balance, but repositioning the body (usually by
     extending a leg to the left or right) improves the climber’s balance. This technique is called counterbalancing
     and often allows the climber greater reach. (See figure 6-6.) Often the climber can find a microfeature to
     touch or apply slight pressure to with the foot improving the security of the move.




94                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility




                                       Figure 6-6. Counterbalance

   6-58. Occasionally, the climber must switch hands or feet on a hold to make the next move. Sometimes the
   hold can be shared temporarily by two hands or feet, even if they are unsecure, while the lead hand or lead
   foot moves. Other times, the second hand or foot may need to use a temporary, perhaps less desirable hold,
   while the lead one moves.
   6-59. Dynamic moves are sudden, explosive moves where climbers throw themselves out of balance,
   potentially even losing contact with the rock, to reach another hold. These moves must be calculated carefully
   because failing to execute them perfectly usually results in a fall.

Slab and Face Climbing
   6-60. Slabs are typically smoother, lower angle rock features. They can be large or small. Comparatively,
   they provide the climber with few hands and footholds and require good footwork and balancing to climb.
   The primary technique used to climb them is smearing with the feet. This involves placing the sole of the
   boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then
   positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The closer climbers can get to pushing
   perpendicular to the rock, the more friction they will create. (See figure 6-7, page 96.) Hands are usually used
   to help balance by pushing against the rock. Any microfeature that can be found will improve the security of
   climbing slabby terrain. Climbing slabby rock helps build confidence in footwork and good balance skills.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 95
Chapter 6



     6-61. Face climbing is what is commonly associated with rock climbing. Face climbs are typically suitably
     featured rock faces (cliffs) where climbers employ a wide variety of basic moves to ascending. Climbers
     spend most of their time facing the rock, like climbing a ladder. Many footholds are small or sloped and
     require edging or smearing to be effective; others are larger. (See figure 6-8.) Many techniques for using
     handholds exist. (See figure 6-8.) Using knees should be avoided because they are more likely to slip than
     good footwear.
     6-62. Most slab or face climbing terrain appropriate to military operations can be climbed in combat boots,
     mountaineering boots, or approach shoes. Moderate to difficult climbs require climbing shoes. (See
     figure 6-9.)

Resting During Climbing
   6-63. Resting is critical during sustained rock climbing. Any opportunity to stand up and let go or lightly
   hold on with the hands should be taken. Sometimes the body or a body part can be wedged into a large crack,
   allowing the climber to relax. Often, the only rests available are between moves while looking for the next
   hold. When not actively moving, climbers should keep their weight on their skeletal system as much as
   possible. This means locking out legs or arms and providing muscles with a brief rest. Doing this is
   particularly important to preserve arm strength. Often one arm and the climbers’ feet can support their weight
   while they shake out the other arm and hand. (See figure 6-10, page 98.)

Specific Moves
     6-64. Mantling involves pulling down with both arms on the edge of a ledge type feature until the chest is
     ledge height, then transitioning to pushing down on the ledge while walking the feet up the face below. This
     move is common to climbing out of a swimming pool. (See figure 6-11.)




98                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Mobility



   6-65. Stemming involves placing the feet on features to the left and right of the body so that force is applied
   outward as well as down. Stemming is typically very stable and requires a relatively low amount of energy
   to maintain. (See figure 6-12, page 100.)
   6-66. Underclinging involves gripping an overhanging rock feature with the hands, palm up, and pushing
   against a lower rock face with the feet. Underclings can be very stable but can be quite strenuous and tiring.
   Occasionally, underlings are the only means of getting through a section of climbing. (See figure 6-13,
   page 101.)
   6-67. Liebacking involves using counterforce by pulling hard on a vertical or diagonal feature (such as a
   large flake) while pushing hard against the face of the rock. These moves are very strenuous because little or
   none of the climbers’ weights is supported by their feet. In fact, leg muscles are being used to push away
   from the rock, so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber’s hands are then walked up the feature
   while the feet are walked up the face. Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking
   easier and more secure. (See figure 6-14, page 102.)

Crack Climbing
      6-68. Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build
      proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more
      difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing
      involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See
      figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or
      fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side
      for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are
      larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. These climbs are difficult.




102                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility




                              Figure 6-15. Mixed face and crack climbing

Jamming
   6-69. A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning,
   twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam
   can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its
   position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often
   uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold.
   Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure.

Types of Hand Jams
   6-70. Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers
   bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically,
   leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of
   hand jamming.)



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                103
Chapter 6



      6-71. Fist jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are larger than those that work for hand jams. The
      same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for
      variations of fist jamming.)
      6-72. Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The
      same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the
      crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger
      muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See
      figure 6-18.)

Types of Foot Jams
      6-73. Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of
      the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure
      6-19.)
      6-74. Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.)

Types of Arm Jams
      6-75. Arm bars is a technique used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack
      and bending at the elbow to create a jam. (See figure 6-21, page 106.)
      6-76. Chicken wing is a technique also used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into
      the crack bent at the elbow and pushing against one wall of the crack with the hand to create a jam. (See
      figure 6-21, page 106.)

Dihedral and Chimney Climbing
      6-77. Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using
      counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous
      climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet
      to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly
      parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body.
      6-78. Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing.
      Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features.
      6-79. Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The
      basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with
      arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. (See figures 6-22 through 6-24, pages 107 through 109, for
      variations in chimney climbing techniques.) Often during chimney climbing, it is necessary to attach climbing
      packs to the harness hanging below the climber.

Traversing
   6-80. Traversing is moving laterally on the rock. This is often necessary because the features that make up a
   rock route are not always continuous or travel straight up a face. Traversing often involves a series of
   placement exchanges. Most traversing is done facing the rock.
   6-81. Hand traversing requires a ledge, flake, other horizontal feature, or a series of horizontally oriented
   large handholds. Climbers’ hands walk their way across the features while their feet walk their way across a
   face below. (See figure 6-25, page 110.)




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                              109
Chapter 6



      6-82. Steep traverse is a technique often used when handholds are not as good, but decent footholds are
      present. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and
      then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful.
      This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See
      figure 6-26.)




                                           Figure 6-25. Hand traverse

Topping Out or Gaining Ledges
      6-83. Topping out or gaining a ledge can be one of the more challenging parts of climbing. Often low holds
      located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling
      technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when
      moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges.
      A crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and
      counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26 for the proper technique.)

                                       Figure 6-26. Gaining ledges

Down Climbing
   6-84. Down climbing is far more difficult than climbing up and takes much practice to gain proficiency. This
   is largely because rock features are often difficult to identify from above. They are easily obscured by other
   features above them or even the climber’s body parts. However, down climbing is an important skill to
   practice, as it is often necessary to do in 3rd- and 4th-class terrain.
   6-85. Facing out is a technique used on low angle rock. Climbers face out and use their hands for stability
   behind and below their body while moving their feet down to the next hold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)
   6-86. Walking down a slab is a technique that involves simply walking down slabby rock while maintaining
   maximum friction and balance. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)
   6-87. Facing sideways involves climbers facing to the side and side stepping down to lower footholds while
   controlling and balancing their movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper
   rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)
   6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the
   rock. Climbers lower themselves down with their arms, keeping their body away from the rock so they can
   see footholds below, and then transition their weight onto the next foothold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.)




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               111
Chapter 6




                                          Figure 6-27. Down climbing

TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING
      6-89. Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope
      belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is
      relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not
      often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with
      concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers
      but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather
      than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills.
      6-90. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on
      more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces
      conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing
      and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer.
      6-91. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas.

SECTION II – MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE
   6-92. Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to
   movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under
   other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary
   for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain.

MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE
   6-93. Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However,
   identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced.
   Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions
   above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move
   through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a
   few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same
   level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like
   moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units
   that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others
   cannot.
EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE
   6-94. Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement.
   This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are
   varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering
   are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release
   for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill.
   Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one
   direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is
   necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required.
   Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.)




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  113
Chapter 6




                                       Figure 6-28. Alpine touring skis

      6-95. Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Modern snowshoes
      provide sufficient floatation and traction for moving through snow on fairly steep (class 2) slopes and should
      be small and light enough to pack, if necessary. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.)




114                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025

   6-96. Ski poles are typically used with snowshoes and skis to provide more lateral stability and balance. Ski
   poles can be used to provide excellent support for weapons systems during firing from the prone, kneeling,
   and standing positions.
   6-97. Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons,
   food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered
   before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the
   military supply system. These are designed to carry all group sustainment equipment (for example, tents,
   stoves, fuel) for a four- or ten-Soldier group. These come with a cover and rigid poles, convenient for
   dragging up and downhill. (See figure 6-30, page 116.)

                                           Figure 6-30. Ahkio sleds

      6-98. Crampons attach to the Soldier’s boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types:
      general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less
      aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice
      climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more
      rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons
      work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with
      issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.)




                                            Figure 6-31. Crampons

      6-99. Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The
      two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. General
      axes are designed for steep snow and hybrid axes are designed for steep snow and low-angle ice climbing.
      Ice axes have an adze to the rear of the pick for chopping snow and ice. (See figure 6-32.)

                                                                                            Mountain Mobility




                                       Figure 6-32. Mountain axes

   6-100. Ice tools are modified ice axes designed for steep ice climbing. They are much more aggressive and
   curved to help obtain solid sticks in hard vertical ice and over bulges. They are less effective in snow than
   general or hybrid axes because of their short length. Ice tools can include an adze or a hammerhead. Hammers
   are used for placing pitons during mixed climbing. (See figure 6-33, page 118.)

MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN
      6-101. Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain.
      Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether
      the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial
      obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in
      them prior to engaging in combat operations.
      6-102. Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper
      than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military
      mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing
      rope systems for larger units. (See chapter 11 for establishing fixed-rope systems for troop movement in steep
      terrain and ATP 3-21.50 for crossing VDA TTP.)




118                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Mobility



MOVEMENT OVER SNOW
   6-103. Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of
   movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the
   easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these
   often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain.
   6-104. Techniques for moving over snowy surfaces change IAW slope and surface conditions. Some soft
   snow increases physical strain but can increase the security of foot placements. During movement, breaks
   should be taken more frequently and for shorter durations in cold weather to assist with moisture
   management. This helps prevent overheating, which can cause problems once movements stop. Snow deeper
   than calf-height makes movement difficult without skis or snowshoes. Hard-packed snow slopes requiring
   special techniques and equipment or falls that could result in serious injury or death are likely.
   6-105. A thorough analysis of avalanche threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could
   be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. All Soldiers moving in
   potential avalanche terrain must be equipped with avalanche protective equipment and trained in its use, as
   well as avalanche response procedures. (See chapter 5 for more information on avalanche considerations.)
BOOT PACKING
   6-106. The boot-packing method requires the least amount of training and special equipment. The same
   techniques can be used in mountain walking; however, there is often less traction. During the boot-packing
   method, Soldiers move slower and minor slips and falls should be expected. In deeper soft snow, Soldiers
   should step in the tracks left by the Soldier in front of them. This packs them into hard steps and makes
   movement less difficult. Rotate lead Soldiers to prevent fatigue.
   6-107. Crampons are strongly recommended for moving on hard-packed slopes. However, if crampons are
   not available, there are a few techniques to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking
   involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which
   improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a third point of contact, allowing the body to gain more
   traction. The axe is typically held by its head in the uphill hand, with the pick to the rear (cane position).
   Steps can be cut into the slope using the axe’s adze to improve foot placement security. (See figure 6-34,
   page 120.) This technique is effective for short distances but is very time-consuming.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               119
Chapter 6




                                            Figure 6-34. Step cutting

GLISSADING
      6-108. Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated
      position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend
      appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific
      conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as
      trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to
      allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice
      surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not
      caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide.
      6-109. Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft
      against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at
      the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe
      pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on
      their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it
      deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the
      snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same
      glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide.




120                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Mobility




                                          Figure 6-35. Glissading

FLATFOOTING
   6-110. Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement
   over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key
   principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface.
   This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe
   movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency.
   Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons.
   (See figure 6-36, page 122.)
   6-111. Crampons substantially increase the security of foot placements when used properly. However,
   walking in them forces the Soldier’s gait to change and can take some practice getting used to. They must be
   sized properly and snugged tight to the boot, so Soldiers’ boots do not slide around in the crampon introducing
   instability to their foot placements.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               121
Chapter 6




                                           Figure 6-36. Flatfooting

Ascending
      6-112. Lower-angle slopes can be ascended using a diagonal traverse or switchback technique. More security
      can be gained from pointing the toe downhill some when placing the foot. Mountain axes or an ice tool can
      also be used in cane position the same way previously mentioned. (See figure 6-37.)
      6-113. As terrain gets steeper, maximizing crampon point contact with the surface becomes more difficult.
      Footwork techniques used in rock climbing, such as edging, are very insecure when wearing crampons. They
      should not be used. Ankles must be rolled somewhat downhill to ensure crampon points are embedded in the
      surface. Turning the downhill foot so that the toe points downhill increases security by making it easier to
      engage the crampon points on the outside edge of the foot.




                               Figure 6-37. Ice axe uses in low-angle terrain




122                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                                                 Mountain Mobility



   6-114. To obtain secure foot placements, lean the body away from the slope to increase pressure on crampon
   points. This becomes more important as surface conditions get firmer. Generally, it is easier to stay in balance
   and achieve solid foot placements by taking smaller steps. Moving diagonally up slope makes this easier to execute.
   6-115. Flatfooting, using a mountain axe in a cross-body position. To perform this technique, the Soldier
   stands sideways to the slope. The mountain axe head is held in the downhill hand and the shaft held low in
   the uphill hand. The uphill foot is placed perpendicular to the slope and the downhill foot is placed similarly,
   but with the toe pointed downhill as much as comfort demands. The axe spike is then forced into the
   snowpack uphill from the feet far enough so that most of the Soldier’s weight is transitioned onto it. This
   provides balance and security during foot movement. The downhill foot is moved across and placed above
   the uphill foot. If the crossover step is too awkward, it can be moved to a position just below the uphill foot,
   but this method is less efficient. The Soldier’s weight is then transitioned onto the newly placed foot so that
   the uphill foot may be moved upslope. The process is then repeated, starting with replacing the axe uphill
   and the Soldier moves in a generally diagonal path up the slope. (See figure 6-38.)




                       Figure 6-38. Flatfooting with axe in cross-body position

   6-116. Flatfooting using a mountain axe in anchor position. The footwork is the same for this technique as
   when using the axe in a cross-body position. However, the axe is held by the shaft like a hammer and swung
   so that the pick is embedded into the uphill slope. The axe can then be “climbed” by walking the hands up
   the shaft while the feet work their way up the slope. (See figure 6-39.)




                         Figure 6-39. Flatfooting with axe in anchor position



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  123
Chapter 6



      6-117. Front pointing involves kicking into the slope with the toe of the boot so that all front crampon points
      become embedded in the surface. The Soldier leans forward slightly locking the ankle so that the sole of the
      foot is held perpendicular to the slope. If the heel is too low or too high, or only the large front points are
      embedded, then the foot placement will be less secure and may fail. The Soldier stands up on the placement
      using hands or mountain axe for balance and repeats kicking in with the other foot higher on the slope. This
      process is repeated as the Soldier generally moves straight up the slope. The front-pointing technique is very
      effective and allows for faster movement in steep terrain but is more physically taxing. The Soldier’s calf
      muscles become fatigued quickly using this technique. The front-pointing technique is most effective for
      ascending short, steep sections of terrain. (See figure 6-40.)




                                          Figure 6-40. Front pointing

      6-118. Front pointing with a mountain axe in dagger positions involves Soldiers holding the axe by the head
      with the adze and thumb facing them. The pick is then forced into the slope in a hammer-fist motion (high
      dagger). Once placed, Soldiers walk their feet up the slope, using front pointing as high as they can go. A
      low dagger technique can be used to allow climbing higher than a high dagger allows by transitioning the
      hand to the top of the axe head and pushing down on it for balance. The process is then repeated, moving
      straight up the slope. (See figure 6-41.)

   6-119. Front pointing with mountain axe in anchor position involves holding the axe by the shaft and
   swinging it like a hammer so that the pick is embedded into the slope higher above the Soldier. The axe is
   then used as holds for both hands as Soldiers climb the slope with their feet using front pointing. (See
   figure 6-42.)




                     Figure 6-42. Front pointing with axe in anchor positions

Descending
   6-121. Slips and slides should be considered very likely on moderate to steep terrain, especially if surface
   conditions are hard. Rope systems may be used to mitigate the risk of injury, but they do not make movement
   faster or easier. Efficient movement requires good flatfooting skills.
   6-122. Moderately steep slopes can be descended by simply using a diagonal traverse or switchback pattern
   down the slope. This may require rolling the ankle more than usual to force all crampon points into the snow.
   The downhill foot can be turned so that the toe points downhill to reduce strain and add security during
   movement. The mountain axe is used in any of the positions described above to aid with balance and prepare
   the Soldier for self-arrest. Edging technique is ineffective; Solders should not attempt this technique. (See
   figure 6-44, page 128.)
   6-123. Steeper slopes require descent facing downhill and relying heavily on a mountain axe for balance and
   security. Soldiers must bend their knees to lower their center of gravity and position their weight over their
   crampons. Depending on the slope angle and surface hardness, the mountain axe should be used in one of
   the positions described below:
        • Using the mountain axe in cross body position, while driving the spike into the slope behind the feet
             is a very secure method of moving down steep slopes when executed properly. During movement,
             most of the weight is supported by the mountain axe and the feet are moved forward in short
             deliberate steps. In hard surface conditions, crampons need to be stomped into the ground to ensure
             points are set. Weight is then transitioned over the feet, the axe moved down and reset. (See
             figure 6-44, page 128.)
        • In addition to the positions already discussed, the mountain axe can be used in support position
             while descending. This is when it is carried in one hand, head oriented uphill and pick facing down,
             while the Soldier moves down the slope facing downhill. The axe is held in this position so that the
             Soldier can quickly plant the pick into the snowpack for security, as necessary. If this is done, the
             axe provides a handhold to assist in making one or two moves that are more difficult. This can be
             repeated for longer sections that are more difficult than necessary. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)
        • If more security is needed, then the Soldier can transition to using the axe in the anchor position,
             allowing both hands to grip the axe and a more secure pick placement. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)
   6-124. Using the mountain axe in cross body position, while driving the spike into the slope behind the feet
   is a very secure method of moving down steep slopes when executed properly. During movement, most of
   the weight is supported by the mountain axe, and the feet are moved forward in short deliberate steps. In hard
   surface conditions, crampons need to be stomped into the ground to ensure points are set. Weight is then
   transitioned over the feet; and the axe moved down and reset.
   6-125. In addition to the positions already discussed, Soldiers can use the mountain axe in its support position
   while descending. Soldiers carry the axe in one hand, head oriented uphill and pick facing down, while
   moving down the slope, facing downhill. The axe is held in this position so that the Soldier can quickly plant
   the pick into the snowpack for security, as necessary. Carrying the axe this way provides a handhold to assist
   in making one or two moves that are more difficult. This can be repeated for longer sections that are more
   difficult, as necessary. (See figure 6-44, page 128.)
   6-126. If more security is needed, the Soldier can transition to using the axe in the anchor position, allowing
   both hands to grip the axe for a more secure pick placement.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                127
Chapter 6




                                     Figure 6-44. Descending steep slopes

SELF-ARREST
      6-127. Self-arrest is a technique intended to stop a short fall before it turns into a long, sliding, tumbling fall.
      Soldiers that will be moving on moderate to steep snow slopes unroped must be issued a mountain axe at a
      minimum and trained to proficiency in self-arrest techniques. There is little margin for error in executing
      self-arrest on steep slopes with firm surface conditions. Self-arresting should not be considered an adequate
      protective measure when slipping and falling risk is determined to be likely. Good movement skills are still
      the primary risk mitigation for moving unroped.
      6-128. Soldiers should carry the axe in the cane position with the pick to the rear in the uphill hand. The
      instant Soldiers fall, they must commit to self-arresting immediately. The technique is executed by bringing
      the mountain axe into position at the center of chest, with the hand on its head and pick facing away. The
      lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of
      action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not centered under
      the body, it is difficult to apply adequate force to achieve this. The less aggressive and curved design of the
      ice axe pick is meant to prevent it from biting into the surface too well, where momentum would cause it to
      be ripped out of the falling Soldiers’ hands. Rather, it is designed to stop the Soldier gradually. For this
      reason, picks that are more aggressive like those found on tools meant for ice climbing are less effective for
      this. If crampons are not worn, the Soldier can also dig toes into the snowpack to assist stopping the slide.
      Careful attention must be paid not to allow the spike of the axe to dig into the snow while sliding. If this
      happens, the Soldier could be flipped over backwards and thrown into a tumble. Recovering from a tumbling
      is unlikely. (See figure 6-45.)
      6-129. When self-arresting with crampons on, Soldiers must bend their knees during the slide, so the crampon
      points do not catch and cause a tumble. Legs must remain bent until sliding has stopped. Front points can
      then be planted to reduce the likelihood of a slide resuming.
      6-130. To self-arrest while sliding on the back, the Soldier must bring the axe into position at the center of
      the chest, then roll in the direction of the axe head until on the stomach, and then drive the pick into the snow.
      6-131. To self-arrest headfirst face down, the Soldier must reach downhill to the same side as the axe head,
      plant the pick, pivot the body around the pick, and swing the legs downhill.
      6-132. Self-arrest headfirst, on the back, is the most difficult. Here, the Soldier must plant the pick, twist and
      roll toward the pick, swing the legs downhill, and roll the chest toward the pick.

SNOWSHOES AND SKIS
   6-133. Snow deeper than calf height typically requires more floatation than crampons provide for efficient
   movement to be possible. Skiing is the most efficient technique for moving over deep snow but requires
   substantial training to become proficient. Snowshoeing is less efficient but is relatively easy for Soldiers to learn.
   6-134. Moving in snowshoes provides good floatation and traction in deep snow. Poles should be used to
   maintain balance while moving. More practice is necessary if the terrain is rough, rocky, or strewn with
   obstacles. Soldiers should practice with operational loads to proficiency.
   6-135. Skiing involves using climbing skins on flat terrain and while ascending. Heels are released during
   movement. Traversing or switchback techniques should be used when ascending slopes. Poles should be used
   to help with balance, especially when carrying a pack. Slopes can be descended slowly with skins on, or skins




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                   129
Chapter 6



      can be removed for rapid decent. Well-trained skiers can move very quickly in steep terrain. The historical
      effectiveness of ski troops is well documented.

ICE CLIMBING
      6-136. Ice climbing is demanding and requires specialized equipment and techniques. Waterfall ice develops
      in the bottom and along the steep sides of drainages, such as gullies and couloirs. (See figure 6-46.) Alpine
      ice can develop in the same areas or in glacial features that are more open. (See figure 6-47.) These terrain
      features may provide the easiest routes for ascending and descending steep mountains.




                                           Figure 6-46. Waterfall ice




130                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                              Mountain Mobility




                                          Figure 6-47. Alpine ice

   6-137. All the hazards associated with rock climbing exist for ice climbing, as well as additional ones,
   including avalanches and icefalls. Icefall is always a real threat to ice climbers and personnel located below
   them. This is particularly true during warmer temperatures as hanging ice features can break off and fall
   naturally. Ice climbers are at higher risk of injury during a fall due to the sharp tools and crampons used in
   climbing. Even short falls can result in a tool accidentally puncturing the climber’s body, or a crampon
   catching on a feature during the fall and causing lower extremity injuries.
   6-138. Climbing ice usually requires the use of rope systems for protection even when climber’s skills are
   high due to the consequences of falling.
ICE CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS
   6-139. Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical,
   especially when covered in ice. However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by short sections of
   low or steep angle waterfall ice. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points
   of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced mountaineers can be used to establish
   fixed-rope routes through this terrain for lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement.
   6-140. Typically, Soldiers climbing ice are unable to provide themselves with sufficient, local security during
   movement. Bounding overwatch in vertical terrain by small-specialized teams or VDA-crossing procedures
   must be performed by a larger unit to provide adequate security for climbing Soldiers. (See ATP 3-21.50 for
   more on VDA crossing.) Small reconnaissance and surveillance teams may have to rely on careful technical
   route selection that provides concealment throughout the approach, the climb, and the top out. Fortunately,
   the terrain in which ice develops often provides such opportunities for teams with the technical and mobility
   skills necessary to negotiate it.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               131
Chapter 6



ICE CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION
      6-141. Before starting to climb, Soldiers should study the face of the ice flow for features that indicate that
      climbing the route is possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult an ice flow will be for
      them to climb and how reliable protection placements will be. Climbers should form a plan for climbing and
      protection using rope systems (when necessary) before leaving the ground. (See chapter 10 for how to protect
      climbers from fall hazards.)
      6-142. During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See
      chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.)
BASIC ICE CLIMBING TECHNIQUES
      6-143. Compared to rock climbing, ice climbing movement techniques are relatively simple. The most
      difficult part is learning how to place tools and crampons into the ice so that they hold the climber’s weight,
      and then moving in balance so as not to dislodge them or waste energy. The keys to efficient ice climbing
      are a reliable and secure tool, crampon placements, and staying in balance during movement.
      6-144. Complicated movement techniques are rarely necessary in ice climbing.

Using Ice Tools
      6-145. The purpose of the tools in ice climbing is to provide climbers with handholds to hang from while
      moving their feet and for maintaining balance while moving the body. Whenever possible, each tool
      placement should be secure enough to hold the climber’s entire body weight.
      6-146. Modern ice tools should be held loosely by the grip, with the heel of the hand wedged into the hook
      or stop at the bottom of the shaft. This feature allows the climber to hang without squeezing. When done
      properly, the climber’s weight can be held with just moderate pressure from two or three fingers around the
      grip. (See figure 6-48.)
      6-147. Some force must be used when swinging ice tools, but how they are swung is more important than
      how hard it is. Placing tools starts with positioning the climber’s hips close to the ice creating space to swing
      the tool. This becomes more important as the ice gets steeper. The tool is swung in an overhead arc with a
      flick of the wrist as the pick is about to strike the ice.
      6-148. Ideal tool placements are as high as the climber can comfortably reach and as close to the centerline
      of the body as possible. Low features, or small depressions, are the best targets for tool placements. If a
      placement is not secure enough after one swing, climbers should swing again aiming for the same spot until
      they are confident that it will hold their entire weight.
      6-149. Ice tools can be removed from the ice by gently tapping upward on the adze or hammer to loosen the
      pick in the ice. If the tool is too low in relation to the upper body, it can be gripped by the head and wiggled
      up and down to loosen.




132                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility




                                         Figure 6-48. Ice tool grip

Using Crampons
   6-150. Crampons must be sharp, correctly sized, and tight. Vertical ice or technical crampons are preferred,
   but not always necessary.
   6-151. Crampon placements on low-angle ice are used in the same manner as flatfooting with occasional
   front pointing. The hard surface of the ice requires more effort to ensure crampon points are set securely in
   the ice before committing weight to them. Edging techniques are insecure on ice.
   6-152. When using crampon placements on moderate and steeper ice flows, front pointing is used
   exclusively. Climbers must move their lower body away from the ice during crampon placement. Good front
   point placements are those in which all front points are in solid contact with the ice and the foot is
   perpendicular to the surface. (See figure 6-40, page 124.) Low spots in the ice, the top of small features
   sticking out of the ice, and the tops any step-like features are the easiest spots to place crampons. Climbers
   must ensure that the sole of their boot remains perpendicular to the surface of the ice (for example, heel is
   not too high or too low), or front points may lever out of the ice.

Body Positioning and Moving Efficiently
   6-153. The basic body position for ice climbing is a triangle, with crampons placed about shoulder width
   apart, and tools placed in a staggered vertical pattern close to the centerline of the body. Body weight should
   be centered under the higher ice tool. This puts the climber in balance. The climber must resist the urge to
   place tools parallel with each other or wide in relation to the body. When this is done, the position causes the



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                133
Chapter 6



      climber to become out of balance during tool removal, causing the climber’s body to open or swing toward
      the remaining tool placement. (See figure 6-49.) This could cause a fall.
      6-154. The basic movement sequence starts from the position described in this paragraph. (See figure 6-50.)
      Climbers hang from a high tool placement and walk their feet up the ice as high as they can go. They return
      to a stable stance and push their body upward with their legs. Once erect, the low tool is removed. Climbers
      then place it as high as possible as close to the centerline of the body, and the sequence is repeated.
      6-155. With practice, the above sequence becomes more fluid, and steps are combined for efficiency.
      However, focusing on this sequence helps new climbers to learn what being in balance feels like. Once they
      develop basic proficiency, they can adjust the technique for their body type and can better negotiate more
      complex ice features.
      6-156. Occasionally, moving diagonally left or right of the high tool is necessary or more efficient than
      straight up above the climber. In this case, the high ice tool is placed as high as necessary in the direction of
      travel. Climbers then adjust their feet laterally back into line with the high tool to maintain balance, then
      climb their feet up as previously described. With practice, the lateral foot movement can be skipped, and
      climbers can just climb toward their high tool and back into position.




                                       Figure 6-49. Basic body position



134                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility



Special Moves
   6-157. Stemming is the same as in rock climbing and provides the same benefits. The opportunity to do this
   is created by a groove feature running vertically up and down the ice. Climbers kick their crampons
   diagonally into the sides of the feature for very secure foot placements. Stemming makes climbing steep ice
   much easier.
   6-158. Climbing over ice bulges is challenging because maintaining a high tool for balance is not always
   possible. The high tool must be placed low in relation to the body on a horizontal feature. Feet must then
   walked up the lower face as close to the lip of the bulge as necessary for the climber to step onto the top of
   it. Crampon placements can be difficult because the bulge may block the climbers’ line of sight with their
   feet. This series of movements is strenuous for the arms because it forces the climber to lean back away from
   the ice more than normal so as not to topple forward. (See figure 6-50.)
   6-159. Traversing is challenging because it requires the climber to move deliberately out of balance and then
   back into balance with each move. The lead hand places a tool far to the side in the direction of travel. The
   climber then makes a short move in that direction. The rear tool is then moved into a new position closer to
   the centerline of the body. The climber then moves toward the lead tool again until it is close to the centerline
   of the body. The lead tool is then moved to a position further in the direction of travel and the sequence
   repeats. (See figure 6-50.) Another more advanced technique involves leap frogging the tools across the ice
   face to provide successive high tool placements. This requires changing hands on the high tool with each
   move and passing the rear tool to the lead hand before the next tool placement is made. With either technique,
   there is a strong likelihood that a tool could be pulled sideways and out of the ice. The climber must always
   pull straight down when traversing.
   6-160. Down climbing ice is tricky but can be done on lower angle ice by Soldiers with strong skills. Down
   climbing steep ice is very difficult since the ice flow usually blocks the climbers’ view of their feet and
   transitioning over bulgy features during descent may prevent climbers from even positioning their body to
   make effective crampon placements.




                                    Figure 6-50. Climbing over bulges

MIXED CLIMBING CONSIDERATIONS
   6-161. Mixed climbing involves climbing terrain that is made up of both rock and ice features. Ice tools are
   used as described earlier in ice features but are also used to hook rock features or wedge into cracks. This
   kind of 5th-class climbing requires very high rock and ice climbing skills.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 135
Chapter 6



      6-162. Climbing difficult mixed routes is impractical for military operations. However, easy to moderate
      mixed climbing (3rd- and 4th-class) is often necessary in alpine terrain. At the very least, transitioning back
      and forth between climbing low angle ice and snow and scrambling on rock in a cold environment is often necessary.
TRAINING FOR ICE CLIMBING
      6-163. Beginner ice climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope
      belay techniques (see chapter 10, section III). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of ice
      climbing is typically moderate risk and high payoff for developing mobility skill for small numbers of
      participants, if sufficient time is allotted. Top rope ice climbing sites are typically small or spread out.
      Training large groups effectively is difficult without special manufactured ice-climbing facilities. This is
      primarily due to the cold-weather environment in which ice develops. Ice climbing training should be planned
      along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging
      for climbers, but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to improve their skills. A
      motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills.
      6-164. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on
      more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in multi-pitch settings that more accurately reproduces
      conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing
      and route-finding skills critical to the advanced military mountaineer.
      6-165. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas.

SECTION III – LOAD MANAGEMENT FOR MOBILITY
      6-166. Overburdened Soldiers cannot move safely or efficiently in steep unstable terrain. The amount of
      weight Soldiers carry and how they carry it directly affects their ability to move safely and efficiently. The
      heavier the load carried; the greater the Soldier’s capability is reduced. This results in slower movement and
      the potential for injury in rough or steep terrain. Unbalanced or loosely packed loads have the same effect.

LOAD MANAGEMENT
      6-167. Load management is the act or strategy of planning and packing loads to reduce negative
      impacts on Soldier physical performance. Excessive loads reduce movement speed, increase the likelihood
      of orthopedic and lower back injury, and significantly increase the risk of falling in high-consequence terrain.

PLANNING
      6-168. When planning packing lists, leaders must consider the level of mobility necessary during movement
      first. Once identified, loads should be reduced IAW it. Commanders should consider modifying requirements
      for the protective posture for Soldiers operating in difficult terrain. When Soldiers must move dismounted in
      mountainous terrain, plate carriers, lower profile armor plates, and lower profile tactical load-bearing
      harnesses can allow them to move further, faster, and more efficiently, resulting in increased maneuver
      capability. Trends of past enemy engagements in a unit’s area of operation should be considered to determine
      if ammunition and other munitions requirements could be reduced. Equipment used infrequently must be
      considered for reduction or removal entirely from standard packing lists. “Ounces equal pounds,” and units
      that try to carry equipment for every contingency are less mobile and less effective in rugged terrain. (See
      chapter 4 for general load management guidance.)
      6-169. Sleds should be used when heavy loads must be carried over snow-covered terrain. Their use reduces
      Soldier fatigue and allows for rotating load-bearing responsibilities throughout a movement. Additionally,
      Soldiers can then drop most of their load when contact with the enemy is made while retaining essential
      survival items in their pack.
      6-170. In steeper less stable terrain, packs should be loaded with heavier objects lower than normal to assist
      with balance by lowering the Soldier’s center of gravity. Heavy or loose items should not be attached to the
      outside of packs, as they could shift and cause a fall.




136                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                               Mountain Mobility



SCRAMBLING AND CLIMBING LOAD MANAGEMENT
   6-171. Load planning for Soldiers who need to climb rock or ice is a difficult task. The difficulty of the
   climbing they must conduct, protective systems needed to prevent fall injury, and fitness must all be
   considered before packing lists are developed. Leaders must be open to developing different packing lists for
   different teams IAW the mobility level their mission requires. It is likely that only items necessary to the
   mission may be carried out to make easy climbing feasible. Lead climbers, who are at risk of long falls, may
   only be able to carry what is necessary to fulfill their role during the climb (for example, finding routes in
   technical terrain and establishing protective systems for follow-on troops). Any additional equipment they
   may need might need to be cached, hauled through the terrain, or carried by follow-on personnel.
   6-172. Climbers may require smaller packs that allow for greater range of motion when climbing.
   Occasionally it is necessary for them to attach their pack to their harness, hanging below, or between the legs.
   6-173. Weapons must be slung on the back or to the side of the pack during sustained climbing. Lead climbers
   may need to leave weapons behind or carry smaller weapons, such as pistols, during particularly difficult
   sections of climbing to reduce fall risk. Follow-on Soldiers who are protected by rope systems would then
   carry their weapon through the section.
