                                                  Chapter 7
                       Navigation in Mountainous Terrain
   The goals, strategies, and tools available to Soldiers for navigation in mountainous terrain are
   no different from other types of terrain. However, mountainous terrain makes using those tools
   to stay on course much more difficult. Additionally, straying off course while navigating in this
   terrain can prove extremely hazardous and detrimental to mission success. The difficulty of
   planning routes and calculating movement timelines also increases significantly with the
   steepness and complexity of terrain. Soldiers and leaders who learn how to mitigate these
   challenges effectively can not only successfully navigate in mountainous terrain but also better
   use the terrain for cover and concealment.

SECTION I – MILITARY LAND NAVIGATION IN NONTECHNICAL
  MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN
   7-1. Navigation is the process of determining one’s present position, locating a target objective, and selecting
   and following a route between these two points. Navigation consists of three distinct stages: orientation,
   navigation, and route finding.
   7-2. Orientation is simply figuring out exactly where one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain
   features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation.
   7-3. Navigation determines the objective’s location and the direction from the Soldier’s starting point to the
   objective. The same skills and equipment used in orientation are essential for good navigation.
   7-4. Route finding is picking the best line of travel IAW METT-TC (I); mission, enemy, terrain and weather,
   troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations, and the
   commander’s intent. Good route finding in mountainous terrain requires solid terrain analysis, clear priorities
   for route selection, an understanding of group members’ levels of fitness and mobility skill, unit capabilities
   for technical movement, and mission-specific requirements. Examples of priorities for route selection are
   navigability of terrain, tactical advantage and disadvantage throughout the movement, concealment
   throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement.
   7-5. Perhaps the single, most important factor in navigation through mountainous terrain is the ability to
   identify and analyze terrain. Navigators must be able to create an accurate mental model of the terrain to be
   moved through from a map or satellite imagery. The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they
   will be at avoiding hazards, selecting tactically advantageous or concealed routes, and planning paths that
   minimize fatigue. This ability can only be developed effectively through route planning and movement in
   such terrain. Skill at land navigation in level terrain does not necessarily translate to skill in mountainous
   terrain. (See TC 3-25.26 for more information on general navigation techniques.)

NAVIGATIONAL EQUIPMENT
   7-6. The following equipment should be considered for use when planning for or navigating in mountainous terrain:
        • Maps and protractors.
        • Imagery (satellite, aerial, or surface taken).
        • Compasses.
        • Altimeters.
        • GPS devices.
MAPS AND PROTRACTORS
   7-7. Ideal topographical maps for mountain navigation are those of sufficient scale and detail to depict terrain
   features accurately. This may require using larger-scale maps usually requested for military operations and




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  139
Chapter 7



      may require carrying more map sheets to cover all terrain in any operation. For larger-scale maps, a smaller
      contour interval can make terrain analysis easier.
SATELLITE AND AERIAL IMAGERY
      7-8. Additional imagery of complex terrain can be very useful to a navigator for route planning. However,
      top-down satellite imagery often is not as useful as topographical maps. Aerial or surface photographs of
      specific terrain features can be incredibly useful for finding and planning routes through complex terrain.
COMPASSES
      7-9. The lensatic compass is most used and can be employed in a variety of ways for either day or night
      navigation. It can be used as an effective tool for navigating the mountains. The primary benefits of a lensatic
      over adjustable declination compasses are durability, inclusion of a mil-radian scale, and availability in the
      military supply system.
      7-10. Ideal compasses for navigation in mountainous terrain are ones that have an adjustable declination. The
      user can adjust the compass to compensate for the difference between magnetic and grid north. This
      eliminates the conversion step usually required when obtaining navigational azimuths, thereby reducing time
      and probability of math errors. These types of compasses also usually come with illuminated north-seeking
      arrows, built-in protractor, and even magnifying glasses incorporated into the design. They are typically
      lighter than traditional military compasses and are the most widely used compasses by mountaineers. These
      compasses typically do not include scales in mil-radians and are usually plastic in construction, making them
      less durable than metal compasses.
ALTIMETERS
      7-11. Altimeters are valuable pieces of navigational equipment used by experienced navigators in
      mountainous terrain. They are rarely used in flatter terrain types. Most Soldiers have not been exposed to
      them or trained in their use. Altimeters provide navigators with elevation information for their location
      without requiring GPS satellite signal. This information turns contour lines on a map into reliable linear
      features that can be followed, used as progress markers during movement, or as known points when they
      intersect with other clearly identifiable linear terrain features.
      7-12. Modern altimeters are most commonly digital and typically come in wristwatch form, though they are
      available as stand-alone digital devices. Battery life must be considered when using these devices.
      Nonelectronic analog altimeters are also available, typically as stand-alone devices. Digital altimeter devices
      also have a digital compass feature. Most mountaineers use digital watch altimeters.
      7-13. Altimeters use a barometer incorporated into their design to measure the weight of air above the device.
      Since air pressure drops uniformly as elevation is gained, it can be used to read altitude by means of the
      altimeter’s scale or digital display, marked in feet or meters of elevation above sea level.
      7-14. Changes in the weather are usually accompanied by air pressure changes, which are reflected in the
      altimeter. As the air pressure drops due to the approach of inclement weather, for instance, the displayed
      elevation rises by a corresponding amount. This means that a barometric pressure change of 1 inch of mercury
      equals roughly 1,000 feet of elevation. If the altimeter displays an elevation gain of 300 feet, a loss of
      barometric pressure of 0.3 inch has occurred, and bad weather should be expected.
      7-15. Because the altimeter is sensitive to changes in air pressure, it must be recalibrated whenever a point
      of known elevation (summits, saddles, stream-trail intersections, survey monuments, and so forth) is reached.
      This is especially important when weather fronts are moving rapidly through the area.
      7-16. Altimeters are currently available in the military supply system. (See appendix C for national stock numbers.)
GLOBAL POSITIONING SYSTEMS
      7-17. The GPS is a highly accurate tool that can calculate user location by using a satellite constellation
      system. It can determine the latitude, longitude, and elevation of the user. Location information is also
      displayed in military grid coordinates.




140                                                    TC 3-97.61                                   26 November 2025
                                                                           Navigation in Mountainous Terrain



   7-18. The GPS provides precise steering information, as well as position locations. The receiver can accept
   many checkpoints entered in any coordinate system by the user and convert them to the desired coordinate
   system. The user then calls up the desired checkpoint, and the receiver displays direction and distance to the
   checkpoint. The receiver can also compute the approximate travel time to the next checkpoint.
   7-19. Because the GPS does not need visible landmarks to operate, it can provide position (accurate to within
   5 meters) in darkness or on featureless terrain. GPS also does not compound navigational errors as compass
   use can.
   7-20. GPS devices and satellites communicate via radio waves, so anything that blocks light reduces or blocks
   the effectiveness of the signals. The more unobstructed the view of the sky, the better the system performs.
   Although the GPS can be used in any terrain, it performs best in more open areas, such as the desert. Heavy
   cloud cover and precipitation, such as snow or rain, can interfere with or block GPS signals.
   7-21. Because the GPS requires horizon-to-horizon views for good satellite reception, its utility can be
   limited in the mountains. Canyons, deep valleys, saddles, and steep mountainsides are all problematic. Good
   locations to get satellite reception are high points or wide-open areas, such as ridgelines, spurs, summits,
   plateaus, and wide valleys.
   7-22. When using GPS in regions with questionable surveying and mapping products, the operational datum
   of the local maps must be reconciled with the datum used in navigational and targeting systems. Identify the
   spheroid and datum information on the pertinent map sheets and then check that the GPS receiver has the
   compatible datum loaded. If not, then contact the intelligence staff office for updated datum or maps.
   Otherwise, the GPS will show different locations than those on the map.
   7-23. Cold temperatures (50°F and below) and high elevations will adversely affect the GPS’s operation due
   to the batteries and the liquid crystal diode screen freezing. Soldiers can improve battery life and overall
   performance by placing the GPS inside their parka or coat.
   7-24. The best use of the GPS is to supplement, back up, or verify the accuracy of other navigational
   techniques. GPS should never solely be relied on to navigate in mountainous terrain.

NAVIGATIONAL TECHNIQUES
   7-25. When planning movement through mountainous terrain, all possible techniques should be considered
   for use. Typically, the best approach is a combined use of all the above tools to identify and navigate
   efficiently IAW the mission and commander’s intent. No single technique is a universal solution to every
   situation. Navigating requires putting varied emphasis on tools at different times along the route. The one
   skill used in mountain navigation that remains critical is terrain analysis and association.
DEAD RECKONING
   7-26. Because of the complex nature of mountainous terrain, dead reckoning is usually of limited value on
   most movements. Broken or sheer terrain can make it impossible to follow a precise azimuth for any
   significant distance. Furthermore, doing so may put significantly more strain on personnel as it may require
   traveling up and down or boxing around numerous large terrain features. The compass is generally employed
   more to support terrain association and to orient the map than as a primary navigational aid. Dead reckoning
   can be a useful and necessary tool under certain conditions, such as periods of limited visibility. Heavy fog,
   snowy, or whiteout conditions may prevent the use of other more effective techniques. Using dead reckoning
   under these conditions requires the development of a detailed limited visibility navigational plan. This plan
   must be followed precisely to prevent wandering off course into potentially hazardous terrain.
TERRAIN ASSOCIATION
   7-27. Terrain association is the process of creating a mental model of what terrain features look like from
   what is depicted on a map so that they can be identified and used to guide navigation during movement. This
   skill is critical in mountainous terrain. Once proficiency is developed, navigation in terrain of significant
   relief can be easier than in flatter terrain, because every feature stands out as a landmark.
   7-28. The most efficient way to increase skill and proficiency with terrain association is through practice
   navigating in areas of significant relief. The mnemonic SOSES (shape, orientation, size, elevation, slope)



26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               141
Chapter 7



      approach to considering terrain features is especially valuable in mountainous terrain association and should
      be practiced extensively (see TC 3-25.26). Terrain identification and association training should be
      incorporated into all land navigation training for Soldiers who are likely to operate in mountainous terrain.
      7-29. Terrain association allows Soldiers to identify navigational aids while planning to ensure the navigator
      does not stray off course. The following are some examples of navigational aids:
          • Checkpoints are easily identifiable terrain features to either side of a route, or linear features crossing
               a route, which are used to determine distance traveled. These can be hilltops, saddles, streams, or
               ridgelines, to name a few. Manmade features are less reliable due to lack of permanence.
               Checkpoints are typically used to mark the end of a leg of a route.
          • Handrails are easily identifiable linear features that run parallel with the navigator’s route, or leg of
               a route. They can be roads, streams, valleys, draws, or even distant ridgelines. During movement,
               they can be paralleled to a checkpoint or the objective. Navigational corridors are very large handrail
               features, such as valleys.
          • Attack points are easily identifiable features within 200 meters of an objective where area navigation
               ends and point navigation starts. Attack points should be located on a feature that is easy and quick
               to navigate to, such as a hilltop or prominent feature. From the attack point, the navigator can slow
               down movement speed to increase navigational accuracy for the final short movement into the
               objective. Often, it is best to use dead reckoning from the attack point to ensure navigational
               accuracy is maintained.
          • Expanded objectives are large features that contain the actual objective, such as a large hill. The
               navigator can easily navigate to the hill from far off and then reorient to move to the precise
               objective.
          • Catching features and elevation backstops are used to provide a limit of advance to prevent
               navigators from overshooting their objective. Some examples of catching features include stream,
               draw, elevation, or even movement time.
ALTIMETER NAVIGATION
      7-30. Altimeters help the navigator in several ways. They aid in orientation, in computing rates of ascent or
      descent, during resection, and in weather prediction.
      7-31. Altimeters allow any elevation line on a map to be used as a linear feature. Navigators can plan the legs
      of their route that run perpendicular to elevation lines. Navigators can then easily track progress as they
      ascend or descend by referencing their current elevation during movement. In the same way, elevation lines
      provide checkpoints and catching features to ensure the navigator does not ascend or descend too far.
      Navigators can also plan the legs of their route to run parallel to elevation lines on large terrain features. The
      navigator only needs to ascend or descend to the desired elevation, then turn, and follow it toward the
      objective or next checkpoint. Again, this is done by checking the altimeter occasionally to ensure they stay
      at the desired elevation while moving.
      7-32. Altimeters can confirm terrain association assumptions during movement. Anytime navigators are
      standing on an easily identifiable terrain feature, they can cross-reference data displayed on the altimeter with
      the terrain feature they think they are on using a map. If both numbers match, then the navigator is at the
      correct location.
      7-33. Altimeters are also useful in reestablishing navigators’ locations if they are unsure of it via modified
      resection. This is done by obtaining a back azimuth to their location from an easily identifiable terrain feature,
      then drawing it on a map. Wherever that line crosses the contour line corresponding to the elevation, their
      altimeter reads their location.
      7-34. Most altimeters allow the user to track and record elevation related data, such as ascent and descent
      rates, as well as overall elevation gain and loss. This data can help leaders more accurately plan route
      movement times in the future.
      7-35. Altimeters can be used as barometers to assist in weather prediction. Although GPS provides
      triangulated altitude, it does not use a barometer to do so and, therefore, cannot monitor weather. Altimeter
      weather prediction only works if the altimeter remains in a static position for a significant period (for
      example, several hours or more). Most digital devices have a barometer function, allowing the user to track



142                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                            Navigation in Mountainous Terrain



   the increase and decrease in pressure. These indicate changing weather conditions, whereas no or little
   increase or decrease indicates stable weather trends.

ROUTE PLANNING
   7-36. Careful map reconnaissance, knowledge of the enemy situation, terrain analysis of the operational area,
   and an accurate assessment of the unit’s capabilities are all key parts of the planning process. Route planning
   in the mountains proves to be difficult, and often the original route selection changes during movement due
   to the restrictive nature of this terrain. Always use METT-TC (I) to maximize advantages of routes used in
   military operations and carefully weigh costs and benefits of route decisions. Additionally, weather and
   surface conditions impact route decisions greatly.
MISSION FACTORS
   7-37. The mission and commander’s intent must be considered when planning routes in the mountains.
   Establish priorities for route characteristics IAW their impact on the mission. Some common examples of
   route selection priorities are navigability of terrain, tactical advantage or disadvantage throughout the
   movement, concealment throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement. For example, if a
   strong security posture is required, speed may need to be sacrificed in favor of moving through tactically
   advantageous terrain that is more difficult. In other circumstances, the opposite may be true. Ultimately, route
   planners must possess a clear understanding of how their route selection decisions may affect the mission.
ENEMY SITUATION
   7-38. There are several factors to consider when assessing the enemy’s capabilities. Some of which include
   range of weapons, effectiveness of indirect fires, level of mobility and capabilities in mountainous terrain. If
   the enemy force is better prepared to maneuver in the mountains, they have a marked advantage, and route
   selection must be scrutinized.
TERRAIN FACTORS
   7-39. Topographic map reconnaissance provides the primary source of information concerning the area of
   operations. A 1:25,000 map depicts greater detail than a 1:50,000 map and should be used whenever possible.
   Because examining the micro terrain is important for mountain operations, even larger-scale maps are
   desirable. Higher detailed nonmilitary maps may be useful, if available. Aerial, oblique angle, and
   photographs give details not always shown on maps (crags and overhangs). Sketch maps supplement other
   sources of information, but they should not be relied on for accuracy since they are seldom drawn to scale.
   Along with sketch maps, verbal descriptions, documented information gathered from units previously in the
   area, or published sources, such as alpine journals or civilian climbing guides, may help. Forest service,
   logging, and mining company maps provide additional information, often showing the most recent changes
   to logging trails and mining access roads. Standard military topographic maps are generally accurate graphic
   depictions of the operational area.
   7-40. Ensure map marginal information is reviewed for each new map used. The legend may contain
   mountain-specific symbols. Ensure map datum matches GPS datum, if used.
   7-41. Enemy capabilities and recent activity in the area provide important information for determining
   concealed routes.
   7-42. OAKOC should be used to analyze mountainous terrain during route planning. Typically, considering
   OAKOC from the enemy’s perspective is important. Additionally, mountain-specific hazards, such as falling
   rock or ice, loose, slick or ice-covered footing, avalanche threat, crevasse presence, and fall hazard, should
   all be considered when selecting routes.
        • Observation and fields of fire—in mountainous terrain, the easiest lines of movement are often
            exposed to observation from great distances. Good analysis of potential enemy positions and activity
            must be considered prior to using open or silhouetting terrain for movement.
        • Avenues of approach—when route planning, it is important to consider avenues of approach to
            positions that dominate terrain a route may run through. There is usually high ground around
            Soldiers in the mountains. Easily accessible dominating terrain is the most threatening to units on
            the move.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                143
Chapter 7



          •    Key terrain—when selecting routes, key operational terrain must be identified. Often key terrain is
               easier and allows nontechnical movement through and around very difficult terrain. These features
               are more likely to be observed by the enemy from positions that dominate them.
          •    Obstacles—broken rocky terrain, ice-covered slopes, cliff bands, rivers, ravines, and avalanche
               terrain can easily restrict or halt movement. These obstacles often require tactical movement
               techniques to maintain effective security (for example, traveling and bounding overwatch).
               Technical mobility skills, equipment, and systems for safe movement are also a result. If the terrain
               is severe or restrictive enough, VDA-crossing techniques may need to be employed to ensure unit
               security during certain legs of the route, which are a substantial operational undertaking.
          •    Cover and concealment—often folded and broken terrain provides good cover and concealment,
               even though it is more difficult to move in and maintain command and control. Draws, gullies,
               couloirs, and ravines often provide great concealment from a distance but also may contain water,
               loose rock, thick vegetation, and may be exposed to the hazard of falling objects or observation from
               high ground above.
      7-43. Other resources may greatly assist in selecting appropriate routes in mountainous terrain. Open-source
      mapping programs developed for mountain navigation provide useful tools for route finding and planning.
      Some provide detailed slope angle imagery that can help determine difficulty of movement, and valuable
      avalanche risk information that is not easily identified on a topographical map. In cases of extreme terrain
      complexity, advanced military mountaineers may need to be tasked with route finding or reconnaissance
      missions just to identify the possibility of a route existing through a given area.
      7-44. Terrain also has a huge impact on the effectiveness of communications systems. Many terrain features
      block or reduce communications ranges in the mountains. The capabilities of the group’s radios must be
      considered. Routes may need to be adjusted to ensure line of sight with higher or adjacent units is maintained,
      or to periodically gain high points to hit communications windows.
TROOPS FACTORS
      7-45. Route planners must have a solid understanding of the fitness, mobility skills under load, tactical
      movement proficiency, technical proficiency, and morale of their group members to adequately plan routes
      through the mountains. These factors determine what terrain is passable, passable with protective systems,
      or impassable, and how much time is required to do so.
CONSIDERATIONS FOR WINTER CONDITIONS
      7-46. Winter route planning can be far more difficult than in other seasons. This is primarily due to the
      presence of more difficult snow-laden and ice-covered surfaces. Cold temperatures and the additional hazards
      that come with accumulated snow and ice may also present some challenges. Even just a few inches of snow
      or occasional icy patches significantly slow movement, especially if the correct equipment is not used.
      Soldiers operating in these conditions should be issued special equipment necessary for moving over ice and
      snow IAW surface conditions. Movement times and risk of injury increase significantly in steeper terrain if
      the correct mobility equipment is not used. See chapter 6 for a detailed description of this equipment and its
      uses. Some of these techniques require significant practice to achieve proficiency, and the level of proficiency
      increases as the severity of the terrain and conditions increases.
      7-47. The following must be considered when planning routes in winter conditions:
          • Weather conditions affect the chosen route. During calm weather, a Soldier’s rate of movement is
              significantly faster than during periods of inclement weather. In windy conditions, routes on the
              leeward side of terrain features are usually preferred, so long as they do not pose an avalanche risk.
          • Avalanche danger zones must be identified by map review and data gathered during route planning.
              Routes should not be planned through avalanche danger areas unless necessary for the mission. In
              that case, experienced personnel should conduct in-depth analysis of avalanche risk prior to
              movement.
          • Vegetation can aid or hinder movement. Thickly forested areas usually have a deep snowpack. Trees
              provide shelter from the wind, but footing can be less reliable due to brush and small trees holding
              up a layer of snow that collapses when weighted, making movement arduous. Avalanches are still
              possible on forested slopes with an angle of 30° to 45°.



144                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                             Navigation in Mountainous Terrain



       •     Lower angled snow-covered water features can provide valuable navigation aids and easy
             movement routes, especially if personnel are proficient skiers. Runoffs sometimes provide the only
             feasible routes through steep, thickly vegetated terrain.
       •     Individual movement abilities affect rate of movement, limit choice of terrain, and route. All
             personnel must be proficient in the mobility skills (for example, crampon use, snowshoeing, or
             skiing) required by the surface conditions. Greater fitness is required to move in winter conditions
             than other seasons.
       •     Moisture output during movement should be considered when planning routes in cold temperatures.
             The rate of movement and the strenuousness of ascending slopes directly increase sweating, which
             can have a significant impact on the ability for personnel to stay warm when they stop movement.
             More frequent, shorter breaks should be planned, as opposed to fewer longer breaks, to reduce the
             need to up-dress and down-dress, and help personnel shed heat periodically.
   7-48. The following conditions and characteristics of cold weather and mountainous regions make accurate
   navigation difficult:
       • In winter, short hours of daylight, fog, snowfall, blizzards, whiteouts, and drifting snow, especially
            above tree line, drastically limit visibility. At times, an overcast sky and snow-covered terrain create
            a phenomenon called flat light, which makes recognizing irregularities in the terrain extremely
            difficult.
       • Heavy snow may completely cover existing tracks, trails, outlines of small lakes and similar
            landmarks. Because the terrain looks quite different in winter from that in summer, Soldiers must
            pay careful attention when identifying landmarks, both on the ground and from aerial photographs.
       • Avoid handling maps, compasses, and other navigation instruments in low temperatures with bare
            hands. Exposing bare skin to these conditions increases the risk of frostbite. (See chapter 3 for
            information on cold-weather injuries.)
       • Maintaining pace count is extremely difficult in winter and mountain environments. Thick
            vegetation and rough, steep slopes hamper attempts at accurate pace counts.
   7-49. Whenever there is a possibility of extremely limited visibility during movement, a whiteout navigation
   plan should be developed ahead of time and disseminated to every Soldier in the patrol. They should include
   numerous checkpoints and record the distance, azimuth, and end elevation for each leg. Guidance should be
   disseminated regarding rendezvous and rally points procedures. The easier the terrain each leg covers, the
   easier the plan is to follow blind. Waypoints can be entered manually into most GPS devices as well for those
   low-visibility circumstances where they can still connect to satellites. Note that accuracy may be negatively
   affected by fog or precipitation even if they do function. (See table 7-1 for an example.)

TIME CONSIDERATIONS
   7-50. Movement in mountainous terrain requires a lot more time than in many other terrain types. Route
   planners must understand how all the factors above affect the rate of their group’s movement so that they can



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 145
Chapter 7



      make route selection decisions that meet mission timelines. Accurately predicating movement times can only
      be achieved through building experience by moving in a wide range of mountainous terrain under a wide
      variety of conditions. Ideally, experience is developed through realistic unit training in similar terrain.
      7-51. Movements in mountainous terrain are often measured in time rather than distance units because
      elevation gain, elevation loss, and surface conditions can be bigger factors. To do this, first measure the map
      distance. This distance plus one-third is a good estimate of actual ground distance. Add 1 hour for each
      1,000 feet of ascent or 2,000 feet of descent to the time required for marching a map distance.
      7-52. Computing movement rates in the mountains is extremely difficult, especially when there is snow
      cover. Since snow can be expected in the mountains for most months of the year, units should have some
      experience in basic snow travel. The following rates are listed as a guide (see table 7-2). Rates are given for
      movement over flat or gently rolling terrain for individuals carrying a rifle and loaded rucksack.
                                       Table 7-2. Time-distance formulas
                Movement Technique                     Unbroken Trail                        Broken Trail
       On foot (no snow cover)                  2.0 to 3.0 kph (cross-country)        3.0 to 4.0 kph (trail walking)
       On foot (less than 1 foot of snow)               1.6 to 3.2 kph                       2.0 to 3.2 kph
       On foot (more than 1 foot of snow)               0.4 to 1.2 kph                       2.0 to 3.2 kph
       Snowshoeing                                      1.6 to 3.2 kph                       3.2 to 4.0 kph
       Skiing                                           1.0 to 5.6 kph                       4.8 to 5.6 kph
       Skijoring                                              N/A                            3.0 to 24 kph
       Legend: kph–kilometers per hour, N/A–not applicable

      7-53. Combined Soldier loads that exceed 50 pounds per Soldier can be expected to slow movement
      significantly in mountainous terrain. Given the increased weight of extra ammunition for crew-served
      weapons, basic military mountaineering gear, and clothing for mountain travel, it becomes obvious that
      Soldiers will carry weights well over that 50-pound limit. Units should conduct cross-country movements in
      the mountains with the expected rucksack and tactical load out to develop more accurate movement time
      data.
      7-54. Deep snow significantly reduces movement speeds and requires either snowshoes or skis to be practical
      for anything but the shortest movements.

SECTION II – NAVIGATION IN TECHNICAL MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN
      7-55. Technical terrain is defined as terrain that requires ropes and specialized mountaineering equipment to
      increase security and reduce the consequences of falling. Navigation on this type of terrain can be very
      difficult. Safe travel requires careful analysis and a greater level of experience. Given the capability, however,
      units can own and operate in areas that may be off limits to the enemy.

RECONNAISSANCE
      7-56. For small teams with advanced skills, the variable nature of technical terrain makes detailed
      reconnaissance an invaluable tool. Although Soldiers must be particularly skilled at decision making and
      on-the-fly problem solving, information obtained during reconnaissance can greatly reduce the challenges of
      navigation.
      7-57. Collecting information about the terrain before initiating movement is helpful to determine special
      equipment needs as well as movement techniques that may be required. Turnaround points, egress routes,
      and contingency plans should be identified to account for changing timelines, weather conditions, or
      unexpected enemy presence. Visually observing the terrain from as many angles as possible with the use of
      optics aids the mountaineer to identify specific features, such as cracks, ledges, cliff bands, and other
      landmarks, for travel. It may be used to determine rock quality and identify the presence of objective hazards.
      7-58. When a physical recon is not practical, several tools assist the mountaineer with interpreting terrain
      and identifying potential routes. A combination of sources is best.



146                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                            Navigation in Mountainous Terrain



   7-59. Maps can be used to assess terrain, establish distances, elevation, and general timelines. They are
   helpful for identifying key landmarks and potential weaknesses in the terrain that may allow for travel. Maps
   may not be up to date and may not always accurately reflect the ever-changing mountain landscape. Usually,
   micro terrain is not well represented on a military map, especially in mountainous terrain.
   7-60. Satellite imagery is useful for identifying specific objective hazards, degree of cover and concealment,
   and for visualizing possible routes through steep terrain. If the imagery is recent, it may provide supplemental
   information if using an older map to verify the terrain and hazards. Imagery may also identify terrain that is
   not always identified on a map, for example, a scree or talus field.
   7-61. Photos taken before or during movement are helpful for detailed technical navigation and can be used
   for future reference. They are particularly useful for remembering locations of small landmarks, intersections,
   and exposed or hazardous sections of terrain. Keep in mind that ridges and faces in photos often appear
   steeper than they are.
   7-62. Using time estimating tools, such as the Munter method (see appendix B, section III), can assist in
   making accurate timelines in nontechnical terrain. However, timelines through technical terrain are difficult
   to accurately calculate, and extra time must be allotted to these sections. The timeline is determined based on
   the accuracy of the information collected, the conditions, and the skill and ability of the unit. The more
   experience an individual has moving in technical terrain, the more accurate their time estimations.

ROPED MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
   7-63. Using roped movement techniques is an important decision that greatly affects the speed and efficiency
   of an element in technical terrain. Techniques described in chapter 10, such as fixed ropes, lead climbing,
   simultaneous climbing (known as simul-climbing), and rappelling may be necessary. Techniques are dictated
   by the terrain, weather, conditions, skill level, equipment available, and the tactical situation. Terrain that
   varies in difficulty may require the group to change movement techniques often to maintain efficiency. The
   best options create a balance of speed and security.

ROUTE FINDING
   7-64. Individual mobility skills play a huge factor in determining the feasibility of movement in technical
   terrain. Good route finding requires continually assessing terrain in relation to the climbing skill of team
   members. Information gathered during reconnaissance can often be inaccurate or incomplete once in the
   terrain and requires quick decision making and problem-solving ability.
   7-65. Keep established landmarks in sight and move through terrain that allows for protection when and
   where fall hazards exist. Prioritize ridges and buttresses rather than faces and gullies when possible. This
   reduces exposure to rockfall and keeps Soldiers in position to observe the surrounding terrain. Gullies often
   look easier but are more difficult to assess and have looser terrain and generally more objective hazard.
   7-66. A common route-finding mistake is climbing rock that appears easy but is loose or does not offer solid
   anchors or good options for protection, when other options are available. Another is misinterpreting the
   difficulty level of the terrain and climbing to the point where reversing direction becomes too difficult.
   Recognizing when one is “off route” early in the process is the key to avoiding serious injuries and major
   time delays. Any of these mistakes, when combined, can quickly lead to mission failure.
   7-67. Soldiers must have experience with both success and failure when navigating in technical terrain to
   build the foundation of experience required to be effective on complex missions in the mountains. Time spent
   focused on planning, analyzing terrain, and executing technical movements while managing risk is invaluable
   to both the individual Soldiers and the unit.
   7-68. Soldiers should be familiar with using collective data on established climbing routes found in
   guidebooks and online resources (see appendix B). Soldiers can train stateside and develop many of these
   critical skills, while intentionally selecting objectives within their ability level and with reasonable margins
   of safety. These resources contain route descriptions that include approach and decent information, rock
   quality, recommended rope strategies, topos, photographs, and more.
   7-69. Commanders must understand that these skills take time to develop and that a degree of investment is
   necessary to create mountain Soldiers capable of such tasks.

                                                Chapter 8
                      Knot Tying and Rope Management
   The rope is a vital piece of equipment to the mountaineer. It is used to address many of the
   problems and hazards encountered in the mountains. When climbing, rappelling, or building
   rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment.
   Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology,
   knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance.

SECTION I – TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS
   8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin
   of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment
   fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced
   when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer’s lifecycle recommendation.
   8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized
   standard. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine
   Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing
   equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment
   recognized throughout the world. In Europe, the European Conformity, or Conformité Européene (CE), and
   the European Committee for Standardization establish standards across all industries. They publish standards
   that align with the UIAA standards for all climbing and mountaineering equipment produced in Europe. The
   United States has no specific standards, but American manufacturers have their equipment tested to receive
   UIAA certification. Any equipment used for mountaineering should be marked with either the UIAA safety
   label or the CE standard that it meets.

ROPES AND CORDS
   8-3. Ropes and cords are Soldiers’ lifelines in the mountains. Soldiers should understand the types of ropes
   and cords and their applications. All ropes and cords used in mountaineering and climbing today are
   constructed with the same basic configuration. The construction technique is referred to as a kernmantle rope,
   which is a rope constructed with a load-bearing core of twisted synthetic fibers and a protective outer sheath
   of interwoven synthetic fibers. The core of fibers provides the strength of the material, which is protected by
   a woven sheath like parachute cord. (See figure 8-1.)




                              Figure 8-1. Kernmantle rope construction


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               149
Chapter 8



      8-4. There are many types of fibers and ropes that each have unique characteristics, making them suitable for
      specific tasks. The two main categories of rope are static and dynamic. Military mountaineers need to be able
      to differentiate between the two and know how each rope should be used.
STATIC ROPE
      8-5. A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling,
      lowering, and anchor systems construction. It has a core (kern) that is laid straight, giving it low stretch (2 to
      8 percent). They are constructed with a tightly woven sheath (mantle) and are more durable than dynamic
      ropes. Static ropes are preferred for rappelling, rescue operations, load hauling, and rope installations. They
      should never be used in situations where the rope is shock loaded (for example, lead climbing). Typical
      diameter for static rope is between 9 and 11 millimeters (mm). Static rope is issued in 600 feet (183 meters)
      spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the
      recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. The tensile strength for the
      9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope is approximately 6,000 pounds. The length needed is dependent
      on the specific task being conducted. A 45-meter (150 feet) static has been the standard military length since
      the introduction of nylon ropes, but some tasks or obstacles may require a longer rope. The length of rope
      over 100 meters is a challenge to carry and manage.
      8-6. The military purchases black static ropes to prevent a static rope from being mistaken for a climbing
      rope; however, static ropes are manufactured in all colors and patterns. A rope of unknown history or
      construction should not be used for any application.
DYNAMIC ROPE (CLIMBING ROPE)
      8-7. A dynamic rope is a kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect
      climbers from fall injuries. All climbing should be protected with dynamic ropes. Even short falls on static
      rope can cause serious injury. Standards for climbing ropes are established by the UIAA, and all climbing
      ropes should be certified.
      8-8. Dynamic ropes come in various diameters, but for most military applications, 9 to 10 mm provide a good
      compromise of durability and weight. The climbing ropes issued in the assault climbing team kits (ACTKs)
      are 60-meters long but can be cut shorter to meet mission or training requirements. Military climbing ropes
      are usually produced with olive drab or tan sheaths.
CORD
      8-9. Cord is thinner in diameter than rope. All cord is static and constructed in the same kernmantle structure
      as larger rope. It is used for constructing anchors, as well as most components in technical rope systems.
      Military mountaineering applications work best when Soldiers use 6- to 7-mm diameter cord. It is issued to
      units on a 200-meter spool and then cut down. It is commonly used in two configurations. Most
      mountaineering tasks can be accomplished with these two lengths. Units that conduct operations that require
      ascending a rope or extensive glacier travel may cut additional cords to length for specific tasks:
           • Cordelette—6-meters long, any appropriate joining knot for anchor construction and general use.
           • Prusik cord—1.8-meters long, joined with a double fisherman’s bend, for friction hitches.

WEBBING AND SLINGS
      8-10. Webbing is a flat or tubular nylon material that ranges in widths from 9 to 25 mm and has many uses
      in mountaineering. (See figure 8-2.) This material comes on a spool; it can be cut to a desired length for
      various purposes. It can be joined or presewn to form slings.
      8-11. Slings are presewn or tied loops of webbing. (See figure 8-3, page 152.) A sling is often attached to a
      harness to act as a personal safety, to extend a rappel device, or attach to a fixed rope. A sling rigged with
      two carabiners is a runner. Lead climbers use runners to clip the climbing rope to pieces of protection. Most
      sewn slings are 60 cm and are usually made of nylon.
          • Sewn slings are made in several lengths: 30 cm, 60 cm, 120 cm, and 180 cm.
          • Sewn slings are also manufactured with high-strength, low-stretch materials. These are lighter than
               nylon, do not absorb water, and are more resistant against UV deterioration. However, they are very




150                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Knot Tying and Rope Management



            static, exhibit very low-melting points, and are not recommended for use as personal safeties or
            friction hitches.
   8-12. If sewn slings are unavailable, tubular webbing can be used to create tied slings. Tubular webbing can
   be cut to length 175 cm (69 inches) and joined with a water knot to create a sling that is 60 cm (24 inches).
   Tied slings can be used for any task as sewn slings but require additional inspection. Tied slings can also be
   untied and retied around anchors and are more adjustable than sewn slings. Tubular webbing can also be used
   to create expedient harnesses.

CARABINERS
      8-13. A carabiner is a D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in
      mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope. A carabiner is
      one of the most versatile pieces of equipment available to the mountaineer. This simple piece of gear is the
      critical connection between anchors, ropes, and mountaineers. (See figure 8-4.)
      8-14. Most carabiners are constructed of aluminum. Carabiners are produced in several different shapes. Oval
      carabiners were once popular for general mountaineering because their symmetry makes them good for many
      purposes. Most carabiners used today are offset D-shaped carabiners, which offer the best compromise of
      weight to strength and ease of clipping and racking. (See figure 8-4.)




152                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                          Knot Tying and Rope Management




                                  Figure 8-4. Carabiner components

   8-15. A carabiner’s design allows it to be loaded in opposite directions along the spine. (See figure 8-4.)
   When loaded improperly, the strength of a carabiner is reduced significantly. When using a carabiner, care
   should be taken to avoid cross loading the carabiner across the gate and spine and to avoid tri-loading. (See
   figure 8-5, page 154.)
   8-16. There are two types of carabiners used in mountaineering: the locking carabiner and the nonlocking
   carabiner.
LOCKING CARABINERS
   8-17. Locking carabiners feature a barrel-shaped sleeve that prevents the gate from opening. They are used
   where an accidental carabiner opening could cause system failure. Any live load should be attached to an
   anchor with a locking carabiner. Locking carabiners are used for rappel hook ups, personal safeties, and the
   primary attachments in most rope systems. (See figure 8-5, page 154.)




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                              153

                                   Figure 8-5. Improper carabiner loading

NONLOCKING CARABINERS
      8-18. Most carabiners do not lock. Locking mechanisms add weight and slow the manipulation of carabiners.
      Nonlocking carabiners are used in most mountaineering applications. They should be used where there is
      more than one attachment and accidental gate opening will not cause system failure.

SECTION II – BASIC TERMINOLOGY
      8-19. Understanding basic terminology is important when learning how to tie knots. The terms explained in
      this section are the most common in military mountaineering. (See figure 8-6, page 156.)

RUNNING END
      8-20. A running end is the loose or working end of the rope.

STANDING END
      8-21. The standing end is the static, stationary, or nonworking end of the rope.




154                                                  TC 3-97.61                            26 November 2025
                                                                           Knot Tying and Rope Management



BIGHT
   8-22. A bight of rope is a bend in the rope in which the standing end is parallel to the running end and the
   rope does not cross itself.

LOOP
   8-23. A loop is a bend of the rope in which the rope crosses itself. When the running end crosses over the top
   of the standing end, it is an overhand loop. When the running end crosses under the standing end, it is an
   underhand loop.

TURN
   8-24. A turn wraps around an object, providing 360° contact.

ROUND TURN
   8-25. A round turn wraps around an object one and one-half times so that the running and standing end are
   parallel. A round turn is used to hold an anchor or knot in place.

HALF HITCH
   8-26. A half hitch is a turn with the running end crossing over the standing end.

TAIL
   8-27. The tail is the excess portion of the running end of the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot
   requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A
   safety knot is a backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose.

DRESSING
   8-28. Dressing a knot is arranging all the knot parts, removing unnecessary kinks, twists, and slack so that
   all rope parts of the knot are secured and tight.

SETTING
   8-29. Setting a knot is removing all unnecessary slack from the knot. This ensures that the knot is tight and
   minimizes the chances of the knot becoming untied.

SECTION III – KNOT TYING AND CONSIDERATIONS
      8-30. The term knot is commonly used to describe numerous categories. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope
      that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some
      purpose. Sometimes it is referred to as a “hard knot” since its condition will remain intact until actively
      untied. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its
      integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Yet, for simplicity, they are generalized into a single category.
      Knots should never be considered permanent. It is possible that they can loosen or become less secure under
      certain conditions. Knots should be inspected regularly. Many knots can accomplish the same task; therefore,
      it is important to understand these considerations when choosing the appropriate knot to tie.

TYPES OF KNOTS
      8-31. There are several broad types of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should
      be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum.
BENDS
      8-32. Bends are used to join the ends of rope, cord, or webbing. When tied correctly, they are considered safe
      and strong enough for many applications. Specific joining knots should be used for certain situations and
      applications. Take care to learn the purpose of each joining knot and to have a clear understanding of where,
      when, and why to use each one.
HITCHES
      8-33. Hitches are like knots but are tied around another object or rope. Without an object like a carabiner or
      another rope, a hitch would not retain its form and fall apart.



156                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                             Knot Tying and Rope Management



FRICTION HITCHES
   8-34. A friction hitch is a type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily
   while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. Friction hitches grip the rope
   while under load, but they can be moved along the rope when unloaded. There are several friction hitches,
   each with different applications. Using the wrong friction hitch can be dangerous or create additional
   problems.
LOOP KNOTS
   8-35. Loop knots are used to create fixed or adjustable loops in rope or webbing. Some loops are directional
   to prevent the distortion of a knot when loaded.
SPECIALTY KNOTS
   8-36. These knots do not fit the above criteria but are still useful to know. They may only serve one specific
   purpose for mountaineering.

KNOT TYING CONSIDERATIONS
   8-37. There are several factors to consider when selecting knots for use or training. Military mountaineers do
   not need to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able
   to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in
   mountaineering rigging, selecting simpler knots that are easier to tie, untie, and inspect are preferable to
   complex specialty knots, even if the complex knot is a little more effective. When considering teaching knot
   tying techniques to Soldiers and new military mountaineers, knots that are easier to teach and learn are
   preferred, as are multipurpose knots. Ultimately, the number and complexity of knots that military
   mountaineers may need to be proficient with increases as the scope and complexity of their technical
   mountaineering responsibilities and duties increase.
STRENGTH
   8-38. Introducing a knot reduces the rope’s strength by a quarter to almost half of its original strength. Certain
   knots retain more strength than others do. This depends on knot structure. (See table 8-1 for some examples
   of the remaining rope strength associated with common knots.)
              Table 8-1. Knotted kernmantle rope retained strength (single strand)
                                      Type of Knot               Rope Strength
                                     No knot                     100 percent
                                     Clove hitch                 60 to 65 percent
                                     Water hitch                 60 to 70 percent
                                     Figure eight                75 to 80 percent
                                     Overhead                    60 to 65 percent
                                     Bowline                     70 to 75 percent
                                     Two half hitches            60 to 70 percent

EASE OF TYING OR UNTYING
   8-39. Choosing a knot based on its strength alone is not always the best choice. Using knots that are easy to
   tie and teach are ideal. The ability to untie knots after being loaded is important for the reuse and recovery of
   that material.
EASE OF INSPECTION
   8-40. Efficiently inspecting knots is important to ensure they have been tied properly and safely. Choosing
   knots that are difficult to inspect or that can easily be tied incorrectly heightens the chance of human error
   and increases risk.




26 November 2025                                   TC 3-97.61                                               157
Chapter 8



CONSERVATION OF MATERIAL
      8-41. Using as little material as possible is the desired end state in knot tying. Some knots use more material
      than others do even if they accomplish the same purpose. It is important to recognize this when choosing the
      appropriate knot for a given application.

KNOT TYING TECHNIQUES
      8-42. More knots exist that are useful to military mountaineering. It is not feasible to include them all in this
      training circular. Those presented below were selected to cover the full range of military mountaineering
      applications as simply as possible. Versatility, ease of tying, untying, and teaching were the primary factors
      considered for selection.
OVERHAND SAFETY KNOT
      8-43. An overhand safety is commonly used in conjunction with other knots to make them more secure. Some
      knots loosen when subject to varying tension and therefore need a backup. (See figure 8-7.)




                                 Figure 8-7. Overhand and inline figure eight

INLINE FIGURE EIGHT
      8-44. The inline figure eight is a common initial step in tying figure-eight family knots. (See figure 8-7.)
FIGURE-EIGHT SLIP KNOT
      8-45. The figure-eight slip knot forms an adjustable bight in a rope. (See figure 8-8.)




158                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                         Knot Tying and Rope Management



Tying the Knot
   8-46. Refer to the following steps to tie a figure-eight slip knot:
       • STEP 1. Form a 12-inch bight at the end of the rope.
       • STEP 2. Hold the center of the bight in the right hand. Hold the two parallel ropes from the bight in
           the left hand about 12 inches up the rope.
       • STEP 3. With the center of the bight in the right hand, twist two complete turns clockwise.
       • STEP 4. Reach through the bight and grasp the running end of the rope. Pull another bight (from the
           running end) back through the original bight.
       • STEP 5. Pull down on the standing end of the rope and dress the knot down.
       • STEP 6. If the knot is to be used in a transport tightening system, secure the adjustable bight with a
           half hitch.




                                   Figure 8-8. Figure-eight slip knot

Checkpoints
   8-47. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • The knot is in the shape of a figure eight.
       • Both ropes of the bight pass through the same loop of the figure eight.
       • The sliding portion of the rope is the long working end of the rope.

FIGURE EIGHT ON A BIGHT (FIGURE-EIGHT LOOP)
      8-48. The figure eight on a bight is used to form a fixed loop in a rope. (See figure 8-9.) In certain situations
      or systems, this knot can be tied with two bights to form two fixed loops (double figure eight on a bight).
      This is achieved by folding the cord or rope to form two bights and prior to tying the figure eight.

Tying the Knot
      8-49. The following steps are used to tie the figure eight on a bight:
          • STEP 1. Form a bight in the rope about as large as the diameter of the desired loop.
          • STEP 2. With the bight as the working end, form a loop in rope (standing part).
          • STEP 3. Wrap the working end around the standing part 360° and feed the working end through the
              loop. Dress the knot tightly.




                                       Figure 8-9. Figure eight on a bight

Checkpoints
      8-50. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
          • The loop is the desired size.
          • The ropes in the loop are parallel and do not cross over each other.
          • The knot is tightly dressed.
FIGURE-EIGHT RETRACE (REROUTED FIGURE EIGHT)
      8-51. The rerouted figure-eight knot produces the same result as a figure-eight loop. However, by tying the
      knot in a retrace, it can be used to tie into a harness or fasten the rope to objects. (See figure 8-10.) It is also
      called a figure-eight retrace. This is the preferred method to tie into a climbing rope.

Tying the Knot
      8-52. The following steps are used to tie a figure-eight retrace:
          • STEP 1. Tie an inline figure-eight knot, leaving a long enough running end to go around the object
              or through the harness, and then back through the knot. Leave this knot loose to allow the rope to
              be routed back through itself easily.
          • STEP 2. Take the running end and place it through the attachment point on a harness or around
              an anchor.
          • STEP 3. With the running end, insert the rope back through the loop of the knot in reverse.
          • STEP 4. Retrace the knot around the wrap and back to the standing part.
          • STEP 5. Remove all unnecessary twists and crossovers; dress the knot down.

                                                                          Knot Tying and Rope Management




                               Figure 8-10. Rerouted figure-eight knot

Checkpoints
   8-53. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • A doubled rope runs side by side in the shape of a figure eight.
       • The knot forms a fixed loop around a fixed object or harness.
TWO-LOOP FIGURE EIGHT
   8-54. The two-loop figure eight is used to form two adjustable, fixed loops in a rope. (See figure 8-11,
   page 162.) This knot is useful because it forms two independent loops that are easily adjustable to different
   lengths.

Tying the Knot
   8-55. The following steps are used to tie a two-loop figure eight:
       • STEP 1. Using a doubled rope, form an 18-inch bight in the left hand with the running end facing
           the left.
       • STEP 2. Grasp the bight with the right hand and make a 360° turn around the standing end in a
           counterclockwise direction.
       • STEP 3. With the working end, form another bight, then place that bight through the loop just formed
           in the left hand.
       • STEP 4. Hold the bight with the left hand, and then place the original bight (moving toward the left
           hand) over the knot.
       • STEP 5. Dress the knot down.

                                     Figure 8-11. Two-loop figure eight

Checkpoints
      8-56. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
          • There is a double figure-eight knot with two loops that share a common locking bar.
          • The two loops must be adjustable by means of a common locking bar.
          • The common locking bar is on the bottom of the double figure-eight knot.
DIRECTIONAL FIGURE EIGHT
      8-57. The directional figure-eight knot forms a single, fixed loop in the middle of the rope that lays back
      along the standing part of the rope. (See figure 8-12.)

Tying the Knot
      8-58. The following steps are used to tie a directional figure eight:
          • STEP 1. Create an overhand loop, with the loop facing the opposite direction of the finished knot.
          • STEP 2. With the overhand loop formed, tie a figure-eight knot around the standing part.
          • STEP 3. When dressing the knot down, the running end and the bight must be together.




162                                                TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                         Knot Tying and Rope Management




                                 Figure 8-12. Directional figure eight

Checkpoints
   8-59. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • The loop should be large enough to accept a carabiner but no larger than a helmet-size loop.
       • The tail and bight must be together.
       • The figure eight is tied tightly.
ALPINE BUTTERFLY
   8-60. The alpine butterfly knot forms a single, fixed loop in the middle of the rope. (See figure 8-13,
   page 164.) The knot can be loaded in either direction or is easy to untie after use.

Tying the Knot
   8-61. The following steps are used to tie an alpine butterfly knot:
       • STEP 1. Take a bight of rope and twist it 360°.
       • STEP 2. Using the end of the bight, bring it up and back toward the two standing ends that exit at
           the back of the twisted bight just created. Careful to avoid untwisting the bight while doing this.
       • STEP 3. Bring the bight back through the portion of the twisted bight that created a hole where the
           first twist in the bight is located. Pull the bight through that hole.
       • STEP 4. Next dress down and tighten the knot.

                                       Figure 8-13. Alpine butterfly knot

Checkpoints
      8-62. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
          • The knot should have a bight of rope exiting two opposing bights of rope.
          • The opposing bights should be clean and untwisted.
FIGURE-EIGHT BEND
      8-63. The figure-eight bend is used to join the ends of two ropes of equal or unequal diameter up to a 5-mm
      difference. (See figure 8-14.) This joining knot should be the primary knot used to join cord. It can be untied
      after loading, which allows the material to be used for other applications.

Tying the Knot
      8-64. The following steps are used to tie a figure-eight bend:
          • STEP 1. Form a bight in the running end of the rope.




164                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                        Knot Tying and Rope Management



       •   STEP 2. With the other hand, grasp the running end (short end) and make a 360° turn around the
           standing end.
       •   STEP 3. Place the running end through the loop just formed creating an inline figure eight.
       •   STEP 4. Route the running end of the other rope back through the figure eight starting from the
           original rope’s running end. Trace the original knot to the standing end.
       •   STEP 5. Remove all unnecessary twists and crossovers. Dress the knot down.




                                   Figure 8-14. Figure-eight bend

WATER KNOT
      8-66. The water knot is used to attach the ends of webbing. (See figure 8-15.) The water knot is also known
      as a ring bend or tape knot.

Tying the Knot
      8-67. The following steps are used to tie a water knot:
          • STEP 1. Tie an overhand knot in one of the ends.
          • STEP 2. Feed the other end back through the knot, following the path of the first strand in reverse.
          • STEP 3. Draw tight and pull all the slack out of the knot. The remaining tails must extend at least
              4 inches beyond the knot in both directions.




                                           Figure 8-15. Water knot

Checkpoints
   8-68. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • There are two overhand knots, one retracing the other.
       • There is no slack in the knot, and the working ends come out of the knot in opposite directions.
       • There is an approximate 4-inch tail.
FLAT OVERHAND
   8-69. The flat overhand is used for joining two ropes that are being used to rappel. (See figure 8-16.)
   Additionally, it is used as a stopper knot at the end of the ropes to prevent Soldiers from rappelling off the
   end of the ropes.

Tying the Knot
   8-70. The following steps are used to tie a flat overhand:
       • STEP 1: Hold both strands 24 inches from the end of the ropes.
       • STEP 2: Tie an overhand knot with both strands.
       • STEP 3: Dress the knot down, ensuring there are no twists in the knot, and it is hard to touch.
       • STEP 4: Lastly, ensure that there is a minimum 18-inch tail for both strands of rope.




                                       Figure 8-16. Flat overhand

Checkpoints
   8-71. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • A double overhand dressed without twists.
       • Minimum 18-inch tails.


26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               167
Chapter 8



          •    Knot should be hard to the touch, not loose, or sloppy.
DOUBLE FISHERMAN’S KNOT
      8-72. The double fisherman’s knot is used to join the ends of a rope of the same diameter. (See figure 8-17.)
      Once loaded, it can become very difficult to untie. Avoid using this knot if it must be untied after use.

Tying the Knot
      8-73. The following steps are used to tie a double fisherman’s knot:
          • STEP 1. With the working end of one rope, tie two wraps around the standing part of another rope.
          • STEP 2. Insert the working end (step 1) back through the two wraps and draw it tight.
          • STEP 3. With the working end of the other rope, which contains the standing part (steps 1 and 2),
              tie two wraps around the standing part of the other rope, routing the wraps in the opposite direction
              as the first knot (the working end in step 1). Insert the working end back through the two wraps and
              draw tight.
          • STEP 4. Pull on the opposing ends to bring the two knots together.




                                    Figure 8-17. Double fisherman’s knot

Checkpoints
   8-74. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • Two double overhand knots securing each other as the standing parts of the rope are pulled apart.
       • Four rope parts on one side of the knot form two X patterns; four rope parts on the other side of the
           knot are parallel.
       • Ends of rope exit knot opposite each other with approximately 4-inch tails.
SQUARE KNOT
   8-75. The square knot is used to join the ends of rope of equal diameter while under tension. (See figure 8-18,
   page 170.) This joining knot should only be used when it is impossible to tie a more secure joining knot like
   the figure-eight bend or double fisherman’s knot.

Tying the Knot
   8-76. The following steps are used to tie a square knot:
       • STEP 1: Holding one working end in each hand, place the working end in the right hand over the
           one in the left hand.
       • STEP 2: Pull it under and back over the top of the rope in the left hand.
       • STEP 3: Place the working end in the left hand over the one in the right hand and repeat step 2.
       • STEP 4: Dress the knot down and secure it with an overhand knot on each side of the square knot.

BOWLINE
   8-78. The bowline is used to tie the end of a rope around an anchor. It may also be used to tie a single fixed
   loop at the end of a rope. (See figure 8-19.)

Tying the Knot
   8-79. The following steps are used to tie a bowline:
       • STEP 1. Bring the working end of the rope around the anchor, from right to left (as the climber faces
           the anchor).
       • STEP 2. Form an overhand loop in the standing part of the rope (on the climber’s right) toward the
           anchor.
       • STEP 3. Reach through the loop and pull up a bight.
       • STEP 4. Place the working end of the rope (on the climber’s left) through the bight and bring it back
           onto itself. Now dress the knot down.
       • STEP 5. Form an overhand knot with the tail from the bight.




                                        Figure 8-19. Bowline knot

Checkpoints
   8-80. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
       • The bight is locked into place by a loop.
       • The short portion of the bight is on the inside and on the loop around the anchor (or inside the fixed
           loop).
       • There is an approximate 4-inch tail after tying the overhand safety.

TRIPLE BOWLINE (THREE-LOOP BOWLINE)
      8-81. The triple bowline is used to tie the middle or a bight of rope around an anchor. (See figure 8-20.)

Tying the Knot
      8-82. The following steps are used to tie a triple bowline:
          • STEP 1. Form a bight. Route the bight around the anchor.
          • STEP 2. With the right thumb facing toward the body, form a doubled loop in the standing part by
              turning the wrist clockwise. Lay the loops to the right.
          • STEP 3. With the right hand, reach down through the loops and pull up a doubled bight from the
              standing part of the rope.
          • STEP 4. Place the running end (bight) of the rope (on the left) through the doubled bight from left
              to right and bring it back on itself. Hold the running end loosely and dress the knot down by pulling
              on the standing parts.
          • STEP 5. Safety it off with a double overhand knot.




                                          Figure 8-20. Triple bowline

Checkpoints
      8-83. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:
          • There are two bights held in place by two loops.
          • The bights form locking bars around the standing end.

                                                                           Knot Tying and Rope Management



       •    There is an approximate 4-inch tail (bight) after the double overhand safety knot is tied.
       •    The running end (bight) must be on the inside of the fixed loops.
BOWLINE ON A BIGHT (TWO-LOOP BOWLINE)
   8-84. The bowline on a bight is used to form two fixed loops in the middle of a rope. (See figure 8-21.)

Tying the Knot
   8-85. The following steps are used to tie a bowline on a bight:
       • STEP 1. Form a bight in the rope about twice as long as the finished loops will be.
       • STEP 2. Form an overhand loop with both strands.
       • STEP 3. Pass the bight up through the loop.
       • STEP 4. Fold the bight, passing the entire knot through, until the bight is around the standing ends.
       • STEP 5. Dress the knot down so that the bight is tight around the standing ends, and the loops are
           adjusted to the desired size.

PRUSIK
      8-90. The prusik is a friction hitch that can be loaded in either direction. When force is applied to this friction
      hitch, it is very difficult to move or loosen. It can be tied with the middle or end of a cord.

Tying the Knot
      8-91. The prusik can be tied with a cordelette to an installation rope. An installation rope is the primary
      load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system. A minimum of three turns should be used for this knot. The
      closer in diameter the cordelette is to the installation rope, the more turns may be required for the knot to
      function. Ideally, there should be a 3-mm difference in diameter between the cordelette and installation rope.
      Always check to see if the prusik grabs prior to operation.

Middle-of-the-Rope Prusik
      8-92. The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-23):
          • STEP 1. Double the cord, forming a bright, with the working ends even. Lay it over the installation
              rope so that the closed end of the bight is below the installation rope and the remaining part of the
              rope (working ends) is the closest. Spread the working end apart.
          • STEP 2. Reach down through the 12-inch bight. Pull up both working ends and lay them over the
              installation rope. Repeat this process twice more, making sure that the working ends pass in the

            middle of the first two turns. Now there are six turns and a locking bar working across them on the
            installation rope.
