End-of-the-Rope Prusik
   8-93. The following steps are used to tie an end-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-24, page 176):
       • STEP 1. Take approximately 1 meter of cord and place it over the installation rope.
       • STEP 2. Form a complete round turn in the rope.
       • STEP 3. Cross over the standing part of the cord with the working end of the cord.
       • STEP 4. Lay the working end under the installation rope.
       • STEP 5. Form a complete round turn in the rope, working back toward the middle of the knot.
       • STEP 6. There are six turns and a locking bar running across them on the installation rope. Dress
           the wraps and locking bar down. Ensure they are tight, parallel, and untwisted.
       • STEP 7. Finish the knot with a bowline with the tail, ensure both strands have tension on it and
           running end of the prusik knot cannot be pulled through and undo the knot.

      8-95. The autoblock creates a friction hitch that is releasable even when force is applied. (See figure 8-25.)

CLOVE HITCH
    8-104. The clove hitch is an anchor knot that can be used in the middle of the rope as well as at the end. (See

    8-106. The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope clove hitch (see figure 8-28, page 180):

MUNTER HITCH
   8-109. The Munter hitch is used to form a mechanical belay. (See figure 8-30, page 182.) The Munter hitch
   produces friction, reducing the force required to hold a fall. It can be used to belay a climber going up or to

Tying the Knot
   8-110. The following steps are used to tie a Munter hitch:
       • STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down about 12 inches apart.

           with the left hand.

           the loop.

           the locking carabiner.

      8-113. The following steps are used to tie a super Munter hitch:

MUNTER MULE KNOT
   8-115. The mule knot is used to create an easily releasable anchor knot in conjunction with a Munter hitch.

   8-116. The following steps are used to tie a Munter mule knot:

       • STEP 4. Dress the slipknot down against the Munter hitch.

FIELD EXPEDIENT HARNESS
   8-124. The field expedient harness creates a seat harness out of tubular webbing used for climbing or
   rappelling. (See figure 8-36, page 188.) This improvised harness is more secure than the rappel seat and will
   not come loose while climbing. The field expedient harness can also be used in rescue to secure a patient not
   wearing a harness. Either 1- or 2-inch tubular webbing is acceptable for use.

Constructing the Harness
   8-125. The following steps are used to tie a field expedient harness:
       • STEP 1. Find the middle of a 25-foot section of tubular webbing and form a bight.
       • STEP 2. Pass the bight between the legs from rear to front and pull it up to beltline level.
       • STEP 3. Wrap the right and left tails of webbing around each respective leg from rear to front
           ensuring that the tails do not cross over one another.
       • STEP 4. Pass the tails through the bight at belt level and wrap them back onto themselves.
       • STEP 5. Wrap the remaining lengths of webbing around the body above the hips and continue to
           wrap in the opposite directions until enough is remaining to tie a square knot with safeties.
       • STEP 6. Join the tails together just above the hip offset from front of the body on either side of the
           body using a square knot with overhand safeties.

SECTION IV – ROPES: PREPARATION, CARE, INSPECTION, COILING,
  CARRYING, AND THROWING
   8-127. The service life of a rope depends on the frequency of use, applications (rappelling, climbing, rope
   installations), speed of descent, surface abrasion, terrain, climate, and quality of maintenance. Ropes may
   fail if misused, placed over sharp edges, or not properly inspected prior to use.

PREPARING ROPES
   8-128. The mountaineer must select the proper rope for the task to be accomplished according to type,
   diameter, length, and breaking strength. It is important to prepare all ropes before departing on a mission.
   Avoid rope preparation in the field.
PACKAGING
   8-129. New rope comes from the manufacturer in different configurations, boxed on a spool in various
   lengths, or coiled and bound in some manner. New ropes should be carefully unspooled or uncoiled to avoid
   kinks and prevent tangling.

Coil
   8-130. A coil is a secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling.

Precut
   8-131. Precut ropes are usually packaged in a protective cover, such as plastic.
SECURING THE ENDS OF ROPE
   8-132. If still on a spool, the rope must be cut to the desired length. All ropes fray at the ends unless they are
   bound or seared. Both static and dynamic rope ends are secured in the same manner. The ends must be heated
   to the melting point to attach the inner core strands to the outer sheath. By fusing the two together, the sheath
   cannot slide backward or forward. Ensure that this is only done to the ends of the rope. If the rope is exposed
   to extreme temperatures, the sheath could be weakened, along with the inner core, reducing overall tensile
   strength. The ends may also be dipped in enamel or lacquer for further protection.

CARE AND MAINTENANCE
   8-133. The rope is a climber’s lifeline. The rope must be maintained and used properly. Climbers should use
   the following general guidelines when handling ropes:
        • While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension.
            If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and inspect often.
        • Never allow one rope to continuously run over another. The friction causes the nylon to melt.
        • Never leave a rope knotted or tightly stretched for longer than necessary. Doing so reduces the
            strength and life of the rope over time.
        • UV radiation (sunlight) tends to deteriorate nylon over long periods. This becomes important if rope
            installations are left in place for months.
        • Do not step on or drag ropes on the ground unnecessarily. Small particles of dirt grind between the
            inner strands slowly cutting them.
        • All ropes should be washed periodically to remove dirt and grit and rinsed thoroughly. Army-issued
            rope washes are made from short pieces of modified pipe that connect to any faucet. Pinholes within
            the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the
            washer.
        • Ropes should not be stored wet. Dry wet ropes by uncoiling and hanging them in large loops off the
            ground. Never dry a rope with high heat or in direct sunlight.
        • When not in use, ropes should be loosely coiled and hung on wooden pegs rather than nails or other
            metal objects. Storage areas should be relatively cool with low-humidity levels to prevent mildew




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                 189
Chapter 8



               or rotting. Rope may also be loosely stacked and placed in a rope bag and stored on a shelf. Avoid
               storage in direct sunlight, as the UV radiation deteriorates the nylon over long periods.
          •    Inspect the rope before each use for frayed or cut spots, mildew or rot, or defects in construction
               (new rope).
          •    Do not mark ropes with paints or allow them to touch oils or petroleum products. Some of these
               weaken or deteriorate nylon.
          •    Never subject the rope to high heat or flame. Heat and flame significantly weaken rope.
          •    Never use a mountaineering rope for any purpose except mountaineering.
          •    Each rope should have a corresponding rope log DA Form 5752-R (Rope Log [Usage and History]),
               which is also a safety record. On the form, annotate use, terrain, weather, application, number of
               falls, dates, and so on. Annotate each time the rope is used on the form. DA Form 5752-R is
               authorized for local reproduction on 8 1/2- by 11-inch paper.

INSPECTION
      8-134. Ropes should be inspected before and after each use, especially when working around loose rock or
      sharp edges.
          • Although the core of the kernmantle rope cannot be seen, it is possible to damage the core without
              damaging the sheath. Check a kernmantle rope by carefully inspecting the sheath before and after
              use while the rope is being coiled. When coiling, be aware of how the rope feels as it runs through
              the hands. Immediately note and tie off any lumps or depressions felt.
          • Damage to the core of a kernmantle rope usually consists of filaments or yarn breakage that results
              in a slight retraction. If enough strands rupture, a localized reduction in the diameter of the rope
              results in a depression that can be felt or even seen.
          • Check any other suspected areas further by putting them under tension (the weight of one person,
              approximately 185 pounds standing on a prusik tensioning system is about maximum). This
              procedure emphasizes the lump or depression by separating the broken strands and enlarging the
              dip. If a noticeable difference in diameter is obvious, retire the rope immediately.
          • Many dynamic kernmantle ropes are quite soft. They may retain an indentation occasionally after
              an impact or under normal use without any trauma to the core. When damage is suspected, patiently
              inspect the sheath for abnormalities. Damage to the sheath does not always mean damage to the
              core. Inspect carefully.

COILING AND CARRYING ROPE
      8-135. Use the butterfly or mountain coil to coil and carry the rope. Each is easy to accomplish and results
      in a minimal number of kinks, twists, and knots later during deployment.
BUTTERFLY COIL
      8-136. The butterfly coil is the quickest and easiest technique for coiling. (See figure 8-37.)

Coiling
      8-137. To start the butterfly coil, grasp both ends of the rope and begin back stacking, ensuring the ends of
      the rope are not buried at the bottom of the stack. Find the center of the rope and form a bight. With the bight
      in the left hand, grasp both ropes and slide the right hand out until there is approximately one arm-length of
      rope. Place the doubled rope over the head, draping it around the neck and over the shoulders. Ensure that it
      hangs no lower than the waist. Soldiers ensure the rest of the doubled rope is in front of them and continue
      making doubled bights and placing them over the head in the same manner as the first bight. Coil alternating
      from side to side (left to right, right to left) while maintaining equal-length bights. Continue coiling until
      approximately two arm-lengths of rope remain. Remove the coils from the neck and shoulders and hold the
      center in one hand. Wrap the two ends upwards around the coils with a minimum of three complete wraps,
      ensuring that the first wrap locks back on itself.




190                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Knot Tying and Rope Management



Tie Off and Carrying
   8-138. Take both strands from the tails of the rope, forming a double bight and pass it through the apex of
   the coils. Pull the loose ends through the doubled bight and dress it down. Ensure that the loose ends do not
   exceed 2 meters. In this configuration, the coiled rope is secure enough for hand carrying or carrying in a
   rucksack or for storage. To carry on the body, place the butterfly coil on the back, with one tail over each of
   the shoulders, bring back directly under the arms and wrap at least once around the body, ensuring to capture
   all the coils. Secure the ends with a square knot, which does not need overhand safeties. (See figure 8-37 for
   a farmer’s tie off.)




                            Figure 8-37. Butterfly coil with farmer’s tie off

MOUNTAIN COIL
   8-139. To start a mountain coil, grasp the rope about 1 meter from the end with one hand. Run the other hand
   along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Grasping the rope firmly, bring the hands together, forming
   a loop, which is laid in the hand closest to the end of the rope. This is repeated, forming uniform loops that
   run in a clockwise direction, until the rope is completely coiled. The rope may be given a one-quarter twist
   as each loop is formed to overcome any tendency for the rope to twist or form figure eights.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               191
Chapter 8



      8-140. To finish the mountain coil, form a bight about 30-cm long with the starting end of the rope and lay
      it along the top of the coil. Uncoil the last loop and, using this length of the rope, begin making wraps around
      the coil and the bight, wrapping toward the closed end of the bight. Make six to eight wraps to adequately
      secure the coil, and then route the end of the rope through the closed end of the bight. Pull the running end
      of the bight tight, securing the coil.
      8-141. The mountain coil may be carried in either the pack (by forming a figure eight), doubling it and placing
      it under the flap, or by placing it over the shoulder and under the opposite arm, slung across the chest.
      (Figure 8-38 shows how to coil a mountain coil.)




                                            Figure 8-38. Mountain coil

COILING CORDS AND SLINGS
      8-142. Length of cord, webbing, or rope less than 8 meters may be coiled so that they can be hung from the
      harness. Hold the ends of the cord or the joining knot in the left hand. Coil the doubled rope into 6- to 8-inch
      loops until an approximate 12-inch bight is left. Wrap that bight around the coil, ensuring that the first wrap
      locks on itself. Wrap until there is just enough bight left to feed through the bights formed at the top of the
      coil. Dress it down tightly. Now the piece of rope or webbing may be hung from a carabiner on the harness
      or attached to a gear sling and slung over the shoulder. The same can be done with slings.
UNCOILING, BACK STACKING, AND STACKING
      8-143. When the rope is needed for use, it must be uncoiled and back stacked on the ground properly to avoid
      kinks and snarls. Choose a location that is clear of sharp rocks, sticks, or other items that could damage the
      rope or cause snarls when deploying the rope. Also, avoid wet or muddy areas. When these locations are
      unavoidable, using a tarp, poncho, or rope bag to place under the rope when stacking can provide protection.
      8-144. Untie the tie off and lay the coil on the ground. Single back stack the rope to minimize kinks and
      snarls. (This is also useful when moving the rope a short distance and coiling is not desired.) Take one end
      of the rope in the left hand and run the right hand along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Next, lay
      the end of the rope in the left hand on the ground, ensuring that the standing end of the rope is laid off to the
      side and is not buried under the stack. With the left hand, regrasp the rope next to the right hand and continue
      laying the rope on the ground.
      8-145. The rope should be laid or stacked in a neat pile on the ground to prevent it from becoming tangled
      and knotted when throwing the rope, feeding it to a lead climber, and so on. This technique can also be started
      using the right hand.

THROWING THE ROPE
      8-146. Before throwing the rope, it should be back stacked to prevent it from tangling during deployment.
      The bottom end of the rope should be anchored to prevent complete loss of the rope over the edge when it is
      thrown. Several techniques can be used when deploying a rope.



192                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                               Knot Tying and Rope Management



   8-147. If the cliff is steep enough, it may be unnecessary to throw the rope. Back stack the rope down the
   cliff face. The rope is less likely to be carried by the wind or to be caught in trees. It is more likely to be hung
   up on ledges and shrubs on the face than when thrown. The rope should be thrown at a low angle and blocky
   terrain.
   8-148. To throw the rope, take the strand on the top of the stack and begin to create butterfly coils in the
   dominant hand. Create enough coils so that there is sufficient weight to carry the rest of the rope down when
   it is thrown. It is time consuming and almost never necessary to coil the entire length of rope to throw it. The
   rope is best thrown underhand and slightly up and out from the edge. Throwing the rope too high could cause
   it to be hung up in tree branches. At a training site where there may be people below, the thrower should
   confirm that no one is below and sound off with the following warning as they throw: ROPE.
   8-149. When windy weather conditions prevail, adjustments must be made. In a strong crosswind, the rope
   should be thrown angled into the wind so that it lands on the desired target. The stronger the wind, the harder
   the rope must be thrown to compensate. If the wind is too strong, sometimes it is best to single back stack
   the rope in a pack. The first Soldier who descends the rope should guide it down the fall line. During the
   descent, the rope is stacked in such a way that it exits cleanly from the pack to avoid becoming tangled.
   Another technique is to coil the rope freely on the shoulders of the first Soldier, allowing it to easily uncoil
   as the Soldier descends.
   8-150. This Soldier needs to incorporate a hands-free backup during the rappel to allow stopping and using
   both hands to manage the rope, if necessary.

                                                  Chapter 9
                      Anchor Selection and Construction
   Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path
   to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for
   mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in
   different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are
   found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to
   assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This
   chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are
   building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection
   in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most
   mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting
   anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging
   techniques with which they are familiar.

SECTION I – GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT
   9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of
   sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point
   in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance
   to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or
   fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of
   the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation
   of all systems.
   9-2. Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist
   any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the
   pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its
   proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a
   platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge.
   This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees,
   roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that
   an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor’s
   strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until
   sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an
   anchor should never be in question.
   9-3. Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as
   possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in
   various types of rope systems and cause an anchor to be shock loaded. It is best to avoid any circumstances
   that may lead to this as shock loading results in very high forces on the anchor.

SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS
   9-4. Single-point anchors are the simplest in mountaineering and serve as the building blocks for more
   complicated anchors. If a single feature, object, or piece of equipment is to be used as an anchor, there must
   be no doubt that it is both strong enough and secure enough to hold if shock loading were to occur. The same
   goes for all rigging used in building the anchor. Correctly tied master points, locking carabiners, and double
   nonlocking carabiners opposite and opposed must be used for all points of connection. (See figure 9-1,
   page 196.)




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                  195
Chapter 9




                              Figure 9-1. Opposite and opposed carabiners

      9-5. If using opposite and opposed carabiners in place of a locking carabiner, ensure they are properly
      configured. (See figure 9-1.)
      9-6. Single-point anchors are created by simply tying cordage or webbing around something of sufficient
      strength to form an adequate anchor.
      9-7. There are three basic methods of attaching webbing slings to single-point anchors: single loop (drape)
      with the webbing joined around the anchor, basket hitch (wrap), and the girth hitch. (See figure 9-2.)




196                                                TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction




     Figure 9-2. Single-point webbing anchors: single loop, double bight, and girth hitch

   9-8. There are two basic methods to create single-point anchors using joined cordelette. They are the basket
   hitch and master point. (See figure 9-3, page 198, and figure 9-4, page 199.)
   9-9. A cordelette can also be doubled before tying a basket hitch. This keeps the attachment point closer to
   the anchor. Round turns can also be added around the anchor to hold the anchor in place. Certain specific
   situations require this (for example, a high redirect). (See figure 9-3, page 198.)
   9-10. A knot can be incorporated in the basket hitch to create a master point. A master point is the loop
   created from the knot that is incorporated into the anchor. It serves as an attachment point for carabiners for
   building rope systems or belays. This can be created by creating a fixed loop with a figure-eight or overhand
   knot.
   9-11. The master-point technique should be used if there is any chance the material could be cut on sharp
   rock edges when the cord is wrapped around a rock. The knot isolates the individual strands creating
   redundancy so if an individual strand were to break, the entire anchor would not fail.
   9-12. A master point is also useful for creating a clean and easily identifiable working point for use with
   multiple carabiners.

MULTIPOINT ANCHORS
   9-13. Multipoint anchors are more than one fixed object joined with technical rigging to form an anchor
   system capable of suspending the weight or arresting the fall of an attached load. They become necessary as
   suitable single-point anchors become scarce. This not only provides greater anchor strength but also adds
   redundancy or backup because of the multiple components. Multipoint anchors are used frequently in
   mountaineering. It requires a strong understanding of anchoring principles, creativity, and experience
   applying them in the field to ensure adequacy.




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                             199
Chapter 9



ANGLE CONSIDERATIONS
      9-14. When using only two anchor points, it is extremely important to recognize the angle that is created.
      Imagine holding two ends of a rope with a 5-gallon water can in the middle. It would be very difficult to hold
      the can up with the rope straight at 180°. It would be much easier to support the weight of the water can if
      the two rope ends were almost touching in the middle. As the angle between anchor components increases,
      so does the force that is felt by each anchor. (See figure 9-5.)




                Figure 9-5. Ideal angle required between anchor points to reduce force



200                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                        Anchor Selection and Construction



SELF-EQUALIZING ANCHORS
   9-15. A self-equalizing anchor is a multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor
   component to a shared attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull
   changes during use. (See figure 9-6, page 202.) Self-equalizing anchors are rarely necessary in
   mountaineering as the direction of pull rarely changes, and there is the possibility of extension and shock
   loading if a component fails.




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                             201
Chapter 9




            Figure 9-6. Self-equalizing anchor




202                     TC 3-97.61               26 November 2025
                                                                          Anchor Selection and Construction



PRE-EQUALIZED ANCHORS
   9-16. A pre-equalized anchor is the preferred type of multipoint anchor used in mountaineering. The anchor
   distributes the weight of the load among each individual anchor component using fixed and independent
   strands. (See figure 9-7.) Multipoint anchors orient all strands together pointing in the direction that the
   anchor will be loaded. A pre-equalized anchor prevents extending and shock loading the anchor if an
   individual component fails. An anchor is pre-equalized by tying a master point using an appropriate loop
   knot in the webbing or sling.
   9-17. The mnemonic EARNEST-H can be used as a guide to build optimal and efficient multipoint anchors.
   Multipoint anchors should be—
       • E—equalized: Each component of the anchor shares the load evenly. Nonlocking carabiners are
           typically acceptable links between soft materials here.
       • A—angle: The angles between the strands of individual components should not exceed 90°, if
           possible. The goal is to minimize multiplying forces as shown in figure 9-7.
       • R—redundant: The entire anchor system is not reliant on a single anchor component. Rigging of the
           cord is such that if a single strand breaks or is cut, the entire anchor would not fail. Redundancy is
           achieved by tying a master point.
       • NE—no extension: If one leg of the anchor does fail, the anchor does not extend, causing shock
           load to the rest.
       • S—solid: This is the big picture look at the anchor system. Ensure that there are no problems with
           how the individual segments work together, that the larger feature comprising the anchor is strong
           and secure, and that the whole thing is appropriate for the intended anchoring application. Anchor
           components should not all be placed in the same feature.
       • T—timely: This is meant to remind mountaineers to remember efficiency when building anchors.
           The fastest and simplest anchor system to build that meets the above criteria is the best.
       • H—high: This is not required, but if it can be achieved while meeting all the above criteria, then it
           is strongly recommended. Anchors with master points between waist and shoulder height make
           operating any attached system significantly easier and more efficient.




                                    Figure 9-7. Pre-equalized anchor

SECTION II – TREES
      9-18. Tree anchors should be considered for use first. They are usually strong and often simple to construct
      with minimal use of equipment. Trees are already in place and simply require a method of attaching the rope.
      However, they should be carefully studied and evaluated for stability and strength before use. Sometimes the
      rope is tied directly to the anchor, but under most circumstances, a cord or sling is attached to the tree and
      then the climbing rope is attached to the sling with a carabiner.

CONSIDERATIONS
      9-19. The following are considerations for using trees as anchors for mountaineering rope systems:
          • In rocky terrain, trees usually have a shallow root system. This can be evaluated by pushing on the
              tree to see how well it is rooted. If there is concern that a tree may be pulled over when loaded,
              another anchor should be selected. If this anchor is the only option, the rope should be anchored as
              low as possible to reduce leverage.
          • When evaluating a tree for suitable strength, strive for a diameter at the base of the tree of at least 8
              inches.
          • In the summer months, it may be easy to determine if a tree is alive. The best indicator can be leaves.
              However, even trees that have fallen over may still grow leaves if they are still partially rooted.
              Ensure that a concentrated effort is made to evaluate the tree.
          • In the winter, certain trees do not have leaves. This may make it difficult to establish if they are
              alive. Look at the tree trunk for signs of extensive rot, woodpecker holes, or fungus growing on the
              tree trunk. Trees that have no leaves in the winter can still be checked to see if they are alive. The
              tree will have buds at the ends of small twig branches that will turn into next year’s leaves. Major
              deformities, cracks, or damage are also an indicator that the tree may not be a viable anchor.
          • Use padding on soft, sap-producing trees to keep sap off ropes and slings.

ROPE ANCHORS
      9-20. The climbing or installation rope can be tied directly to the tree anchor using several different
      techniques. (See figure 9-8.) This requires less equipment but also sacrifices some rope length to tie the
      anchor. The rope can be tied to the anchor using an appropriate anchor knot, such as a bowline or triple
      bowline. Round turns can be used to help keep the rope in position on the anchor and reduce the likelihood
      of it slipping on the trunk.




204                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction




                     Figure 9-8. Anchoring a rope to a single-point tree anchor

HIGH-STRENGTH TIE OFF (TENSIONLESS HITCH)
   9-21. A high-strength tie off is a single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope
   strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing
   the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. It is used to anchor
   the rope on high-load installations used for bridging and traversing. (See figure 9-9, page 206.) The wraps of
   the rope around the anchor absorb the tension of the installation and keep the tension off the knot and
   carabiner. The anchor is usually tied with a minimum of three wraps, more, if necessary, to absorb the tension.
   A smooth anchor may require several wraps, whereas a rough barked tree might only require a few. The rope
   is wrapped from top to bottom without crossing strands so that it can be untied under tension, if desired. A
   fixed loop is placed into the end of the rope and attached loosely back onto the rope with a locking carabiner.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                205
Chapter 9




                                      Figure 9-9. High-strength anchor

MULTIPOINT TREE ANCHORS
      9-22. When there are multiple tree anchors available that do not meet the criteria for a single-point anchor,
      then multiple trees should be used. Using multiple anchors incorporates redundancy in case one anchor fails.
      The same principles for multipoint anchors apply for trees and all other anchors. If using only two trees for
      anchors, then the angle created between the two trees should be less than 90° as described in paragraph 9-14,
      page 200.

BUSHES AND SHRUBS
      9-23. Bush and shrub anchors are not recommended for use unless there are no other options, and a technical
      task cannot be avoided. An advanced-level mountaineer should be present to evaluate the rigging and strength
      of the anchor. They are constructed by equalizing many small bushes and shrubs together into a master point
      using cordelettes, slings, and anchor ropes. As with trees, the anchoring rope is placed as low as possible to
      reduce leverage on the anchor. All vegetation should be healthy and well rooted to the ground. It cannot be
      overstated that the strength and security of bush and shrub anchors cannot be easily assessed for strength.

SECTION III – ROCK ANCHORS

BOULDERS AND ROCK PROTRUSIONS
      9-24. Boulders and rock protrusions make ideal anchors. (See figure 9-10.) Rock features should not be used
      as anchors if they can be moved by pushing or kicking it or sound hollow or detached when tapped. The


206                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                              Anchor Selection and Construction



   surface a boulder rests upon should be inspected to ensure the boulder does not slide when force is applied
   to it. Rock protrusions should be a solid mass of rock. Crumbly or loose rock formations are not typically
   sufficient anchors. Talus and scree fields are an indicator that the rock in the area is not solid. All areas around
   the rock formation that could cut the rope or sling should be padded. It is also wise to consider the
   consequences if the rock were to dislodge.




                       Figure 9-10. Boulders and protrusions used as anchors

CHOCKSTONES
   9-25. A chockstone is a rock that is wedged in a crack that narrows downward. (See figure 9-11, page 208.)
   Chockstones should be checked for strength, security, crumbling and should always be tested before use. All
   chockstones must be solid and strong enough to support the load. They must have maximum surface contact
   and taper with the surrounding rock to remain in position. Chockstones are often directional; they are secure
   when pulled in one direction but may pop out if pulled in another direction.




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                  207
Chapter 9




                              Figure 9-11. Chockstone used in a construction

TUNNELS, ARCHES, AND PINCH POINTS
      9-26. Tunnels and arches are holes formed in solid rock. If viable, they provide one of the more secure natural
      anchor points as they can be pulled in any direction (See figure 9-12.) A natural anchor is a natural fixed
      object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured and is of
      sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. A sling is
      threaded through the opening hole and secured with a joining knot or girth hitch. The load-bearing hole must
      be strong and free of sharp edges (pad, if necessary). A pinch-point anchor is used the same way as arches or
      tunnels; it is just formed by a pinch point between two large boulders, allowing a sling or cordelette to be
      tied around it. Boulders comprising a pinch point need to be large enough and secure enough to ensure they
      do not move when a force is applied. Sometimes a little digging in snow or earth provides a pinch-point
      anchor where no other options are available.




208                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction




                            Figure 9-12. Natural tunnel or hole in the rock

ARTIFICIAL ROCK PROTECTION
   9-27. Artificial rock protection is anything used to protect a climber or anchor a rope system and is not part
   of the natural environment. The evolution of artificial protection started with handmade pieces of metal called
   pitons. Now there are several companies that manufacture various lightweight artificial protection. There is
   fixed and removable protection. Fixed protections are bolts and pitons; they are left in the rock for future use



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                209
Chapter 9



      and can be difficult to remove. Removable protection refers to spring-loaded camming devices (known as
      cams), chocks, and other specialty protection that is easily recoverable after use.
      9-28. Artificial protection is used to construct anchors in various ways. Anchors may be comprised of a
      combination of artificial protection and other objects, such as a tree or a boulder. The combinations are
      endless. However, when building anchors made with only artificial protection, multiple pieces are required.
      No single piece of artificial protection is considered adequate to comprise an anchor. A minimum of two
      components are needed to provide redundancy in the case of bad placement, poor rock quality, or any other
      factor causing a piece to fail.

PITONS
      9-29. Pitons have been in use for over 100 years. Although still available, pitons are not used as often as other
      types of artificial anchors due primarily to their impact on the environment. Most climbers prefer to use other
      artificial anchors rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still
      have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely
      strong and secure anchor option when placed properly. They are particularly useful during rocky alpine
      descents, when an ice axe with a hammer is already carried and natural rappel anchors are scarce.
      9-30. One piton is not considered strong or secure enough to serve as a single belay or system anchor. When
      establishing an anchor using multiple pitons, they should be placed in different cracks or features. A single
      piton can also be combined with other viable natural anchoring methods, if available.

            Note. Properly placing pitons requires significant practice to master, which should be conducted
            in training scenarios involving backup systems to protect the trainee should a placement fail.

ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
      9-31. Some advantages with using pitons are—
          • Depending on type and placement, pitons can support multiple directions of pull.
          • They are less complex than other types of artificial anchors.
          • Pitons work well in thin cracks where other types of artificial anchors do not.
      9-32. Some disadvantages with using pitons are—
          • During military operations, the distinct sound created when hammering pitons is a tactical
              disadvantage.
          • Due to the expansion force of emplacing a piton, the rock could spread apart or break, causing an
              unsafe condition.
          • Pitons are more difficult to remove than other types of artificial anchors.
          • Pitons leave noticeable scars on the rock. They are prohibited in most established climbing areas.
          • Pitons are easily dropped if not tied off when being used.
PITON PLACEMENT
      9-33. Properly positioning or placing pitons is critical. (See figure 9-13 for examples of piton placement.)
      Usually, a properly sized piton for a rock crack will fit one-half to two-thirds into the crack before being
      driven with the piton hammer. This helps ensure the depth of the crack is adequate for the size piton selected.
      As pitons are driven into the rock, the pitch or sound that is made will change with each hammer blow,
      becoming higher pitched as the piton is driven in.
      9-34. Test the rock for soundness by tapping with the hammer. Driving pitons in soft or rotten rock is not
      recommended. When this type of rock must be used, clear the loose rock, dirt, and debris from the crack
      before driving the piton completely in.
      9-35. While it is being driven, attach the piton to a sling with a carabiner (an old carabiner should be used, if
      available) so that if the piton is knocked out of the crack, it is not lost. The greater the resistance overcome
      while driving the piton, the stronger and more secure the anchor is. The quality of the rock around the crack
      a piton is placed into also greatly affects the strength and security of the anchor. The piton should not spread
      the rock, thereby loosening the placement.

   this is not optimal, occasionally there are no other options. Instead of attaching to the piton hole, webbing
   should be attached to the shaft with a girth hitch as close to the rock face as possible to reduce leverage on
   the piton. (See figure 9-14, page 212.)

      while applying steady pressure. Pulling out on the attached carabiner eventually removes the piton. (See

REUSING PITONS
   9-38. Soft iron pitons that have been used, removed, and straightened may be reused, but they must be
   checked for strength. In training areas, pitons already in place should not be trusted since the weather loosens
   them in time. Also, they may have been driven poorly the first time. Before use, test them as described above
   and drive them again until certain of their soundness.

         Note. Fixed artificial anchors, such as pitons and bolts, are not widely accepted for use in all areas
         because of the scars they leave on the rock and the environment. They are often left in place and
         are unnatural fixtures in the natural environment. For training, consider local laws and courtesies
         for each area of operation.

BOLTS
      9-39. A bolt is a type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or
      glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. Bolts are often used in fixed-rope
      installations and in aid climbing where cracks are not available. Bolts provide one of the most secure means
      of establishing protection.
      9-40. Some bolts have rings attached for easy retrievable rappelling, clip-in points for top rope climbing,
      chains to aid in establishing tope rope climbing anchors, or other special-purpose attachment points.
      9-41. There are two primary types of bolts: expansion bolts and glue-in bolts. Both involve drilling a hole
      into a rock face, cleaning out dust and debris, and inserting a bolt. The difference is in how the bolt is secured
      in the hole:
           • Expansion bolts use a sleeve that expands as it is tightened. The sleeve expands against the walls of
                the hole to prevent it from coming out. (See figure 9-16.)
           • Glue-in bolts are held in place by a high-strength adhesive. Glue-in bolts are used in softer, porous
                rock, such as sandstone. Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support
                expansion bolts. Its porous structure allows the glue to expand deep into the rock around the original
                hole. (See figure 9-17, page 216.)

                   Figure 9-16. Expansion bolt

ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
      9-42. Some advantages of using bolts in anchor construction are—
          • Extremely strong and secure when installed properly.
          • Very easy to use for climbing protection when already installed.
          • Very easy to use in multipoint-anchor construction when already installed.
      9-43. Some disadvantages of using bolts in anchor construction are—
          • Extremely time consuming to install relative to other artificial anchoring devices.
          • Require the mountaineer to use both hands and hang during installation.
          • Require special, relatively heavy tools (for example, drills, hammers, wrenches) to install.
          • Noisy to install.




216                                                TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                Anchor Selection and Construction



INSTALLATION AND USE
   9-44. There are enough differences in bolts available on the market that mountaineers should refer to
   manufacturers’ instructions for installing bolts. Installing bolts permanently alters the rock. The climbing
   community has strong ethics regarding the placement of bolts. Ethics and regulations vary regionally, but in
   all areas, it is unacceptable to add bolts to existing climbs. Any bolting should be done with the consensus of
   the climbing community.
   9-45. When using existing bolts as climbing protection or as part of an anchor system, mountaineers should
   inspect them for anything indicating compromise. The first thing that should be inspected is the rock on
   which it will be placed. Bolts are only as strong and secure as the quality of the rock. The hanger should not
   be rusty or loose. Loose hangers can indicate the bolt being insecure, or the hole has not been drilled deep
   enough to secure the hanger to the rock’s face. If the nut holding a hanger can be tightened to a point, then it
   is viable. If it keeps spinning, the bolt should not be used or at the very least backed up with additional protection.
   9-46. Many chock picks (sometimes referred to as nut-tools) have a hex cut out in them that can be used like
   a wrench to tighten loose bolts. A chock pick is used in lead climbing to aid a follow-on climber in removing
   protection. (See figure 9-18.)




                                            Figure 9-18. Chock pick

CHOCKS
   9-47. The principles for using devices commonly called chocks, nuts, or stoppers are the same as with
   chockstones above. They are designed to work in smaller cracks, easier to place, and more secure. (See
   figure 9-19, page 218.) The direction of pull must be considered carefully when using chocks.




26 November 2025                                   TC 3-97.61                                                   217
Chapter 9




                                              Figure 9-19. Chocks

ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
      9-48. Using chocks in anchor construction has the following advantages:
          • Tactically quiet installation and recovery.
          • Usually easy to retrieve and, unless severely damaged, are reusable.
          • Light to carry.
          • Minimal rock scarring as opposed to pitons.
          • Sometimes can be placed where pitons cannot (expanding rock flakes where pitons would further
              weaken the rock).
      9-49. Using chock in anchor construction has the following disadvantages:
          • May not fit in thin cracks, which may accept pitons.
          • Often provide only one direction of pull.
          • Practice and experience are necessary to become proficient in proper placement and removal.
PLACEMENT
      9-50. The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of
      appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum
      surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull.
      9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose
      rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the
      crack, and then select a chock to fit it.
      9-52. When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock.
      A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. A chock that sticks partly out of
      the crack is avoided.
      9-53. All chocks used for lead climber protection should include a soft material extension, such as a runner,
      to prevent the rope from wiggling the chock out of placement.



218                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction



   9-54. Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the
   placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight.

CAMMING DEVICES
   9-55. Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are
   ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an
   outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no
   constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force
   is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed.
   9-56. Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during
   loading, they cannot exit the crack.
   9-57. Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages
   and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly.
SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES
   9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to
   mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that
   oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible
   stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed
   to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down.
   9-59. Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an
   expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to
   carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings
   to help the user select the correct size for use.
   9-60. Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An
   exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them. A
   single camming device is usually placed for intermediate lead-climbing protection. Suboptimal placements
   or rock features require additional pieces to achieve an acceptable anchor.
ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
   9-61. The advantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below:
       • They are much faster to place and remove, for creating anchors or as points of protection while lead
           climbing.
       • They require only one hand to place, so the mountaineer can hold on to the rock with the other.
       • They are easy to insert and remove when placed properly.
       • They can be more forgiving than other anchor devices if the direction of pull changes.
       • They provide many possibilities for rigging multipoint anchors.
       • They do not damage the surrounding rock.
   9-62. The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below:
       • They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck
           camming device that is difficult or impossible to remove.
       • They are much more expensive compared to other types of anchors.
       • They can be heavy and bulky to carry.
       • They have the potential to generate enough outward mechanical force to damage the surrounding
           rock and compromise the anchor when loaded.
PLACEMENT
   9-63. To place cams, find a uniform, parallel spot in the crack where the rock is clean and solid. Retract the
   lobes by pulling back on the trigger. Gently insert the camming device and release the trigger so the lobes
   expand to fit the crack. The spring mechanism works to hold the camming device in place. Ideally, the lobes




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               219
Chapter 9



      should be open between 10 percent and 80 percent of full expansion. (See figure 9-20 and figure 9-21,
      page 222.)
      9-64. Avoid overcamming, which can make the unit difficult or impossible to remove, or undercamming,
      which results in too little surface area contact and reduced stability. The unit should also be placed deep
      enough to not break the edge of the crack but not so deep that the trigger mechanism cannot be reached.
      9-65. Orient the stem to point in the direction from which the camming device is loaded.
      9-66. Inspect the final placement to ensure the angle of the lobes in relation to each other is even and within
      the acceptable range.
      9-67. An extension using a runner may be added between the camming device and climbing rope to reduce
      likelihood it walks out of position during lead climbing.
      9-68. Single cam placements can be used for fall protection while lead climbing. Multiple cam placements
      can be equalized together with cordage or webbing to create load-bearing anchors.
      9-69. To remove cams, simply pull the trigger mechanism and gently remove the device.

SECTION IV – ICE ANCHORS
      9-70. Fall protection and anchors can be constructed in alpine or waterfall ice using specialized ice screws.
      Occasionally, natural ice features can be found allowing anchor construction without them.

TYPES OF ICE ANCHORS
      9-71. Ice anchors consist of ice pillars, ice screws, and V-threads. Except for the case of large ice pillars, ice
      anchors should incorporate two or more anchor points to be strong and secure enough.

ICE PILLARS, ICE SCREWS, AND V-THREADS
      9-72. Ice pillars often form in steep alpine terrain. It is sometimes possible to pass a length of cordage or
      webbing around the whole mass of ice and create a single-point anchor in the same fashion as a rock
      protrusion or tree. (See figure 9-22.) Ice pillars should be totally frozen to the ground, comprised of dense,




222                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction



   crack-free ice, and greater than 1 foot in diameter to use as a single-point anchor. Smaller pillars may be used
   as part of multi-point anchors.
   9-73. Occasionally, ice pillars can be created in ice features, such as sufficiently thick ice curtains where
   there is a hollow space behind, and a hole can be broken through a thin section with a mountain ax. Then an
   anchor can be established as above. Care must be taken not to damage the selected ice mass when creating a hole.




                                           Figure 9-22. Ice pillar

ICE SCREWS
   9-74. The ice screw is the most common type of ice protection. An ice screw is a threaded tubular screw with
   teeth on the end. Some screws have longer hangers or handles, which allow them to be easily twisted into
   position by hand. Ice screws come in various lengths for use in various ice thicknesses. Newer ice screws
   come manufactured with a twist knob on the hanger for easier placement.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                223
Chapter 9



      9-75. The security of an ice screw is determined by the quality of the ice in which it is placed. The thicker
      and denser the ice is, the stronger it is. Thinner ice, aerated ice, or ice with air pockets is weak; mountaineers
      should avoid this sort of ice. Deep, thick ice is generally bluish in color, while ice that has air pockets is often
      white in color. It takes significant experience to judge the strength of ice, but even a novice can learn much
      about ice quality by the resistance felt when placing the ice screw. Air pockets are felt as a reduction in
      resistance. The more resistance, the denser the ice. The longer the core grows as it is screwed in, typically
      the better the ice. (See figure 9-23.) Evaluate the integrity of the ice structure. If possible, avoid fracture lines,
      the apex of ice bulges, and ice blocks that are not attached to a main flow.




             Figure 9-23. Long ice core protruding from screw indicates good ice quality

      9-76. One ice screw in quality ice is sufficient to protect a lead climber. Two or more ice screws must be
      placed in quality ice to create a secure anchor. (See figure 9-24.) The same principles apply for creating
      multipoint anchors for ice screws. If the ice quality is suboptimal, then additional screws should be
      incorporated.




224                                                     TC 3-97.61                                    26 November 2025
                                                                           Anchor Selection and Construction




                           Figure 9-24. Multipoint ice anchor construction

Advantages and Disadvantages
   9-77. The advantages of using ice screws in anchor construction are that they—
       • Can be placed almost anywhere in an ice flow.
       • Can be placed with one hand.
       • Fastest protection to place in ice.
   9-78. The disadvantages of using ice screws in anchor construction are that they—
       • Are bulky and difficult to carry in large numbers.
       • Require difficult and tedious maintenance to keep sharp because of the double angle and curvature
           of the teeth.
       • If not removed and cleared correctly, ice can freeze in the core of the screw, rendering it useless.

Placement
   9-79. Ensure all rotten ice is cleared away from the surface.
   9-80. Hold the hanger end of the screw, and press teeth against the surface at an approximately 90° angle to
   the ice with a twisting motion. An acceptable range is +/–20°. (See figure 9-25, page 226.) Typically, several
   twists are necessary to get it started. The screw is started when it does not fall out of the ice. This is more
   easily done at about waist level for leverage, especially if the footing is poor.
   9-81. Once started, fold out the screw’s knob or handle, and twist in a circular motion clockwise until the
   hanger is tight to the ice. Fold knob or handle down and out of the way. Avoid overturning the screw once it



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               225
Chapter 9



      has become tight. If the screw is tight and the hanger is not pointed downward, back the screw out enough to
      achieve a downward hanger. The screw should be tight and secure; the threads in contact with solid ice are
      what absorb any force placed on the screw.
      9-82. Clip a carabiner to the hanger, then incorporate into a multipoint anchor or clip rope when lead climbing.
      9-83. Remove the ice by folding out the knob or handle and spinning counterclockwise. Clear any ice out of
      the tube so that it does not freeze.
      9-84. Melting of the ice around a screw must be considered. The effective time or strength of an ice screw
      placement are limited. The screw will heat from solar radiation, or the ice may crack or soften. Solar radiation
      can be nearly eliminated by covering the screw with ice chips once it has been emplaced. If repeated use is
      necessary for one installation, such as top roping, the screws should be inspected frequently and relocated
      when necessary. When an ice screw is removed, the ice that has accumulated in the core of the screw must
      be cleared immediately.




                                       Figure 9-25. Ice screw placement

V-THREADS
      9-85. An ice anchor can be improvised using one long screw. This is particularly useful when the climber is
      short on ice screws or does not want to leave ice screws behind while rappelling. V-threads are common in
      fixed rope construction in snow and ice. Vertical or horizontal V-thread anchors can be created depending
      on the nature of the ice flow. Multiple V-thread anchors may be created and joined to create a secure ice
      anchor when ice quality is suboptimal. (See figure 9-26.)




226                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                              Anchor Selection and Construction




                                       Figure 9-26. V-thread anchors

Advantages and Disadvantages
   9-86. The advantages of using V-threads in anchor construction are that—
       • They can be placed almost anywhere in an ice flow.
       • They require very little to build many of them.
       • Their gear placed in the ice is expendable.
   9-87. The disadvantages of using V-threads in anchor construction are—
       • Compared to other ice anchors, it takes a long time to construct, and two are necessary for a strong
           and secure anchor.
       • They require a fair amount of experience to use appropriately.

Placement
   9-88. Place a long (19+ cm) ice screw into quality ice at a 60° angle to the ice face, and then remove it,
   creating a borehole the length of the screw.
   9-89. Use the length of this ice screw to measure how far away from the first hole (either vertically or
   horizontally) a second hole should be bored.
   9-90. Bore another 60° angle hole in the opposite direction as the first so that it intersects the first at the back
   of the hole, creating a roughly triangular column of ice.
   9-91. Pass a piece of cordage or webbing through the tunnel created and tie it off with an appropriate knot to
   complete the anchor. Usually a V-thread tool is used to fish the cordage or webbing out of the hole.
   9-92. V-thread tools can be made from a wire coat hanger by cutting the length of wire, bending one end into
   a small hook and the other into a handle (See figure 9-27, page 228.)




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                  227
Chapter 9




                                Figure 9-27. Constructing a V-thread anchor


SECTION V – EARTH ANCHORS
      9-93. Using improvised earth anchors becomes necessary when naturally existing anchors, such as trees, are
      unavailable. These anchors are created using materials that are readily available. The strength of these
      anchors depends on the material used, the depth, and the density of the earth in which they are placed. The
      art of constructing and placing good earth anchors requires a great deal of practice and experience. It is
      especially important to load earth anchors in a slow and steady manner. It is also important to ensure the
      direction of the pull is low and does not pull up on any component of the earth anchor.

DEADMAN ANCHOR
      9-94. A deadman is an effective means of building an anchor in earth or snow when there are no other natural
      anchors available. A deadman is constructed by digging a trench perpendicular to the direction of pull and
      placing a lengthy solid object with a sling or cordelette attached into it. A thinner slot is cut into the ground
      in the direction of pull and bisecting the trench to form a T-shape. The attached cordelette or webbing is then
      routed through this slot in the direction of pull.
      9-95. The object is then buried. A rope or rope system can then be attached to it. The strength of a deadman
      anchor is determined by the density of soil it is placed into. The security of it is determined by the depth of
      the trench. Objects such as lengthy rocks, sticks, poles, and mountain axes can be buried.

PICKET HOLDFAST
      9-96. A picket holdfast can be constructed in the absence of suitable existing anchors. It requires three
      suitable pickets that can be made from sturdy sticks at least 3 inches in diameter and 3-feet long. The pickets
      can also be improvised from sturdy metal stakes or poles, if available. It is best to sharpen one end of each
      wooden stick or picket, so they are easily driven into the ground. (See figure 9-28.)
      9-97. Next, drive the pickets in line with the load a safe distance from the edge. Drive the pickets
      approximately 2-feet apart from each other at a 45° angle leaning away from the edge. The pickets should be
      driven into the ground at least half their total length.
      9-98. Attach the rear picket at its base with a cord. Then attach the other end at the top of the middle picket.
      Using a clove hitch here will make it easy to adjust so there is equal tension on the pickets.
      9-99. Repeat this process from the middle picket to the front picket, then attach a cord to the front picket at
      its base and create an attachment point for the anchor.

                                       Figure 9-28. Picket holdfast

SECTION VI – SNOW ANCHORS
   9-100. Snow anchor effectiveness is determined by the density of the snow into which they are built. Two or
   more snow anchor points can be equalized into a multipoint anchor if strength and security are questionable.

PICKETS AND ICE AXES
   9-101. Pickets and ice axes may be used as snow anchors. The picket should be driven into the snow at 10°
   to 15° off perpendicular from the lower surface. If the picket cannot be driven in all the way to the top hole,
   the carabiner should be placed in the hole closest to the snow surface to reduce leverage. The picket may also
   be tied off with a short loop of webbing or rope girth hitched low on the picket. (See figure 9-29, page 230.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               229
Chapter 9




                                     Figure 9-29. Snow picket placement

      9-102. When the snowpack is loose or it is suspected that a single picket cannot act as a sufficient anchor,
      then use multiple pickets if available. (See figure 9-30.) If the snow picket goes into the snow with ease,
      consider placing it in the deadman orientation to maximize strength and surface contact. If the snow picket
      requires pounding to place in vertically, the placement is most likely solid. The same general principles apply
      to constructing this multipoint anchor as any other. Ensure that each picket shares the load equally. They can
      be placed in succession similarly to the picket holdfast described in section V in this chapter or in a reverse
      V-shape shown in figure 9-31, page 232. If the snow is extremely loose, it may be better to build a deadman
      anchor that is dug in quite deeply where there is firmer snow.

                                  Figure 9-30. Multipoint snow anchor

   9-103. In softer snow conditions, both snow pickets and mountain axes can be used effectively in constructing
   a deadman anchor in the same fashion that they are constructed in earth (described in paragraphs 9-93 through
   9-99, page 228). Longer objects, such as skis, can be used for increased strength. (See figure 9-31, page 232.)

   most reliable compared to all other techniques described. (See figure 9-31, page 232.) This is the most simple

BOLLARD ANCHOR
      9-104. This is an artificial anchor shaped generally like a horseshoe. (See figure 9-32.) It is formed from
      either ice or snow and constructed by either cutting with an ice axe or stamping with the boots. When
      constructed of snow, the width should not be less than 10 feet. In ice, this width may be narrowed to 2 feet,
      depending on the strength of the ice. The length of the bollard should be at least twice the width. The trench
      around the horseshoe should be stamped as deeply as possible in the snow and should be cut not less than
      6 inches into the ice after all rotten ice is removed. The backside of the anchor must always be undercut to
      prevent the rope from sliding off and over the anchor.
      9-105. This type of anchor may be used for fixed ropes or rappels. It must be inspected frequently to ensure
      that the rope is not cutting through the snow or ice more than one-third of the length of the anchor. If it is, a
      new anchor must be constructed in a different location.
      9-106. A horseshoe anchor constructed in snow is always precarious; its strength depends upon the prevailing
      texture of the snow. For dry or wind-packed snow, the reliability of the anchor should always be suspected.
      The backside of the bollard can be reinforced with ice axes, pickets, or other equipment for added strength.
      A snow-T trench is an example of a horseshoe anchor. (See figure 9-31.)
