                                               Chapter 10
                             Rope Systems for Climbing
   There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence,
   where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting
   in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain.
   Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and
   Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive
   positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently,
   the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful
   offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and
   under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders
   hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these
   types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing.

SECTION I – RISK MITIGATION
   10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined
   by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure
   to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the
   exposure to compromise by enemy forces.

MANAGING RISK
   10-2. Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for
   managing risk change with the terrain and situation.
   10-3. Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment,
   such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by
   rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above
   one another.

REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL
   10-4. The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the
   consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause
   severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood of a fall.
JUDGEMENT
   10-5. The safety of a mountaineer comes from the ability to read the terrain. Judge the rock, snow, or ice,
   and see where it can be climbed and where it cannot. This includes identifying features and weaknesses that
   can be linked together. Judgement is developed through time spent climbing in a controlled environment and
   through experience and mentorship.
TECHNIQUE
   10-6. Soldiers must possess the physical ability to make the moves, use footholds, and maintain balance as
   each move is made. As with judgement, climbing technique is the product of extensive training.
LOAD
   10-7. Increased Soldier load rapidly increases the difficulty of climbing, even in easy terrain. Operations in
   the mountains are subject to the mindset that occupying high terrain requires more equipment for sustaining
   life than at lower elevations. However, to maintain maneuverability, the Soldier’s load must be reduced.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               235
Chapter 10



      Soldiers conducting offensive operations, reconnaissance patrols, or any maneuver in high-consequence
      terrain need to travel light.
FOOTWEAR
      10-8. Proper footwear will enhance the military mountaineer’s ability to move safely and efficiently through
      the rugged terrain found in the mountains. (See chapter 4 for footwear considerations.)
ROPE
      10-9. Ropes are used to reduce the consequence of a fall. Ropes can be fixed in place to manage or reduce
      the consequences of a fall (see chapter 11) or can be used to provide belays (see section III in this chapter).

SECTION II – CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED
      10-10. Moving unroped is the fastest and most efficient method of moving through terrain. It requires little
      equipment and is quiet. Team members can move together, making communication quiet and easy. In
      instances where the greatest hazard is not falling, but rock or icefall, impending severe weather threat, enemy
      observation, or failing to meet an operational timeline, moving unroped may be the safest way to move. (See
      figure 10-1.) Moving unroped in terrain above 3rd-class should only be done after thorough risk analysis has
      been conducted and speed has been identified as a critical control measure for managing overall operational
      risk.




                                    Figure 10-1. Soldier moving unroped

      10-11. Moving unroped should only be done in 4th-class terrain or lower. It should never be considered in
      5th-class terrain.
      10-12. Moving unroped exposes Soldiers to very high consequences in the event of a fall and could have
      catastrophic results including death. A rescue or body recovery in this terrain would likely become its own



236                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                     Rope Systems for Climbing



   operation. Moving unroped should not be the default choice. The risk of a fall must be balanced against the
   other hazards. If the choice is made, there are measures to manage the risk.
       • Target likelihood—maximize the use of every control measure to reduce the likelihood of a fall.
            Everyone in the team should have good movement skills. Loads should be reduced to the essentials.
            The team should be wearing appropriate footwear for climbing.
       • Conservative route selection—the difficulty of the route must be within the comfort zone of the
            entire group. It is necessary to have the ability to adjust to a more conservative movement strategy,
            which requires harnesses to be worn and rope accessible.
       • Route planning—use all available tools to build route plans. Often, climbing unroped goes badly
            not because a route is too difficult, but because a climber ends up off route in more difficult terrain.
       • Pace—climb at a slow, deliberate pace. An easy pace allows full focus on the movement.
       • Attention—keep attention focused on the climbing. Every foothold and handhold are critical. Stop
            often and assess the terrain ahead. Do not commit to features to which a Soldier cannot back off.
       • Communication—a nontechnical risk management tool is coaching. Communicating a hazard
            focuses awareness on the hazard. During a movement, check in with group members and reassess
            their comfort with the risks at rest halts and decision points.
       • Descent plan and tools—down climbing is more difficult than climbing up. Always have a
            multilayered descent plan and a rope and equipment to get down.
       • For most units, there is limited terrain where climbing unroped may be appropriate. Average combat
            loads are heavy and issued combat boots are poorly suited for climbing. Limited steps of 3rd-class
            terrain, without exposure, are the upper limit for most units, and even then, should be assessed and
            managed carefully. Without individual mobility training and teams selected for their movement
            proficiency, there is a high risk of someone falling.


                                                 WARNING
               • Never climb unroped in 5th-class terrain.
               • Climbing unroped in 4th-class terrain requires high skill,
                 extensive experience, and superior confidence. Unroped
                 climbing is only an option when the need to move quickly due
                 to exposure to enemy or environmental hazards exceeds the
                 risk of an unroped fall.
               • Unroped climbing is a high-risk activity that requires a
                 deliberate risk mitigation process and commander approval.



SECTION III – BELAYED CLIMBING
   10-13. A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier’s fall should
   one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays.

TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING
   10-14. When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed
   climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member
   is always anchored and providing a belay for the other.
TOP ROPE CLIMBING
   10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope
   is run through an anchor at the top of a climb and kept relatively snug to avoid longer falls. It is a training
   tool used to teach climbing technique. (See section IV for more information on top rope climbing.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 237
Chapter 10



LEAD CLIMBING
      10-16. As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is
      climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall
      protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection
      and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is
      prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay
      second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section
      of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length
      (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag
      and aid communication.
      10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because
      they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed
      before the rope begins to come tight, so it is still imperative that leaders have good movement skills. The
      second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always
      has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V
      for more information on lead climbing.)
      10-18. Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in
      darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and
      provides the greatest margin of safety.
AID CLIMBING
      10-19. If the climbing is too difficult for the leader, aid climbing is a climbing technique in which standing
      on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward
      progress. (See figure 10-2.) Aid climbing is when climbers use anchors and protection to support their weight
      as they climb. In a recreational setting, climbers on big walls may do extensive aid climbing, with webbing
      ladders called etriers (or aiders) that can be clipped to pieces of rock protection and climbed, and daisy chains
      or webbing tethers, to hang from. Aid climbing can also be as simple as pulling on pieces of protection to get
      through difficult sections of what would otherwise be a free climb.
      10-20. Aid climbing is slow. It may take hours to climb one pitch. Aid climbing requires significantly more
      rock protection. An aid rack may have three times the equipment used by leaders to protect themselves.
      Advanced military mountaineers should be familiar with aid climbing but expect to improvise the tools to
      make it happen.




238                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                     Rope Systems for Climbing




                                         Figure 10-2. Aid climbing

Simul-climbing (Running Belay)
   10-21. Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while
   attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing,
   where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb
   simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces
   of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance,
   but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber.
   Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3,
   page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten
   ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag.
   10-22. When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only
   use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. If rockfall or icefall is a


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 239
Chapter 10



      concern, it is not appropriate because the second is exposed to anything dislodged by the leader.
      Simul-climbing is best suited for easy alpine ridges where rocks fall off the feature. Simul-climbing is an
      appropriate technique for easy climbing, 3rd class through easy 5th class, with well-matched partners.
      10-23. Simul-climbing is a technique used when the environmental or tactical situation presents a greater
      threat than the fall hazard. Simul-climbing sacrifices some level of fall protection to gain speed of movement.




       Figure 10-3. Simultaneous climbing: two Soldiers climbing together with intermediate
                                     protection from falling

                  • Only highly experienced advanced or master military
                    mountaineers are qualified to simul-climb. They should only
                    simul-climb in terrain that is well below their ability level, when
                    speed is needed due to enemy contact, or when environmental
                    hazards outweigh the risk of a long-roped fall.
                  • Simul-climbing is a high-risk activity that requires a deliberate

Short Roping
   10-24. Short roping is a technique that may have some use in training military mountaineers. (See figure 10-4,
   page 242.) Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers
   in easy but exposed terrain. The climbing rope is shortened to just a few meters, and the leader holds the rope
   close to the other’s harness and the two move together. Short roping cannot arrest a fall. It manages risk by
   putting the senior mountaineer close to the other climber, where the senior mountaineer can coach and model.
   If someone slips, leaders pull the rope connected to their harness to prevent the slip from becoming a fall.
   The only anchor is the senior mountaineer’s stance. Short roping is appropriate only in terrain where leaders
   are confident climbing unroped and do not need their hands to climb.
   10-25. Short roping has limited application for military mountaineers. Short roping requires practice and the
   leader’s full attention. In an operational environment, the military mountaineer’s focus must be forward,
   looking for upcoming hazards or enemy contact. All Soldiers operating in the mountains, especially those
   working in small teams, should have the mobility skills to move in easy terrain.


                                                WARNING
               • Only highly experienced master military mountaineers are
                 qualified to short rope. They should only use short rope as part
                 of a formal risk management process that identifies short
                 roping as the appropriate risk mitigation method for the
                 circumstances of the movement.
               • Short roping is a high-risk activity that requires a deliberate
                 risk mitigation process and commander approval.

                                           Figure 10-4. Short roping

Short Pitching
      10-26. Experienced leaders often combine short pitching with short roping as they manage less experienced
      Soldiers in 4th-class terrain. It is used when leaders need to use their hands to climb and cannot provide
      security with a short rope. Leaders place others in a safe position, and then scramble up the more technical
      section to a stance. From above, they can anchor or brace themselves to provide a belay as they climb. Often,
      because 4th-class terrain is more stepped, with plenty of ledges and stances, the leader can use simpler belay
      techniques and anchors than when rock climbing in 5th-class terrain and use a much shorter rope.
      10-27. Most of the military mountaineer’s time is spent avoiding the steepest and most difficult terrain.
      Operationally, they are more likely to use terrain where short pitching and simul-climbing would be most
      efficient. The techniques used in short pitching are faster than belayed climbing in longer pitches. A shorter
      rope helps with communication and fast transitions.
      10-28. Short pitching requires training and practice in techniques to become safe and efficient. These
      techniques may not be as commonly practiced as other belay techniques, but they still have a place in alpine
      terrain, with good stances, and in positions where the second will not be stuck, hanging from the belay.
      10-29. Hasty belays may be necessary during short pitching where anchoring options that are more
      substantial are not available. (See figure 10-5.) These involve leaders using their own body, positioned in a
      good stance, as the anchor or partial anchor. Ideally, the leader is also attached to a back-up anchor of some
      type, even if it does not meet the usual standards for a climbing anchor. This technique should only be used




242                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                    Rope Systems for Climbing



   by experienced advanced military mountaineers when operationally necessary or when no other secure
   anchoring or belaying technique is possible.




                                         Figure 10-5. Hasty belay

Shortening the Rope
   10-30. When climbing in variable terrain, most pitches are short. This type of terrain is usually associated
   with 4th-class terrain. A full-length climbing rope is often too long and slows every transition with extra rope
   management. Teams may choose to carry shorter ropes if the terrain can be descended easily without long
   rappels, or they may choose to shorten their full-length climbing rope. Ropes are typically shortened for
   simul-climbing, short roping, and short pitching.

Kiwi Coil
   10-31. The Kiwi coil is the most common method of shortening a rope for climbing. (See figure 10-6,
   page 244.) After a climber ties into the end of the rope, the rope is coiled in a circular fashion, and then put
   over the shoulder of the climber. To secure this coil, a bight is run through the belay loop and around the
   coils. The bight is then tied off to the strand going to the other climber with an overhand on a bight, and a
   carabiner secures the bight to the harness. After the rope is shortened, team members can begin movement
   and adjust the length between them as necessary. Since the climber is tied into the end and the rope was
   shortened towards the other climber, it is easy to adjust the distance between climbers. This distance between
   climbers is usually dictated by the terrain. To lead a longer pitch, the coils can be removed from around the
   body. To stay closer to one another, the rope can be shortened.

                                             Figure 10-6. Kiwi coil

OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
      10-32. The various strategies and techniques described above for moving while roped will compromise speed
      and security. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus.
      As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line.
      Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the
      movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a
      fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military
      mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability
      to react are critical if enemy contact is expected.

SECTION IV – TOP ROPE CLIMBING
      10-33. A top rope is a belay in which both rope ends are on the ground and the rope runs up to the top of the
      cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while
      the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than a
      short distance. This system also enables the belayer to lower the climber back down to the ground after
      completing the climb. (See figure 10-7 for an example of top rope climbing.)




244                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing




                                     Figure 10-7. Top rope climbing

   10-34. A top rope is a training tool. It allows Soldiers to learn the fundamentals of tying in and belaying and
   to practice individual climbing techniques without the consequences of a long leader fall or unroped fall. It
   allows one instructor to coach and supervise both the climber and the belayer. It also facilitates learning the
   climbing technique because all participants can observe one another.

EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS
   10-35. The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. Equipment used for
   any mountaineering training should meet these standards as outlined in chapter 8 and appendix C.
HELMETS
   10-36. Helmets will protect a Soldier from rockfall and debris. They also offer some protection from impacts
   in a swinging fall. Climbing helmets are lightweight and certified to standards set by the UIAA.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               245
Chapter 10



      10-37. Most units do not have access to climbing helmets. The combat helmet, while not rated or designed
      for impact protection from rockfall or in climbing falls, is already issued to most Soldiers and provides
      adequate protection.
HARNESS
      10-38. There are many types of climbing harnesses. Harnesses must be made and tested to UIAA standards,
      and users must ensure that wear and use conforms to manufacturer recommendations. The high-angle
      mountaineering kit (HAMK) is issued to units where most Soldiers have no formal mountaineering training.
      The harness that was selected for the HAMK (see figure 10-8), is a harness with a single, reinforced tie-in
      portion. It is a simpler harness than most recreational climbing harnesses. It is one-size fits all and easy to
      put on and inspect. It has one gear loop on the left side, which can be used to rack equipment. When worn, it
      should be tight around the waist, with the leg loops snug enough to take some of the force while falling or
      sitting into the harness.
      10-39. If harnesses are not available, tubular webbing can be used to make field expedient harnesses,
      although this is not preferred. Soldiers must ensure their seats are tied correctly, and military mountaineers
      acting as safeties must carefully inspect several more points. This introduces several more points for human
      error.
      10-40. The rappel seat (Swiss seat) should not be used as a climbing harness as it is not designed for this
      purpose. In addition to being uncomfortable, it quickly loosens with repeated loading and unloading.




246                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                  Rope Systems for Climbing




                     Figure 10-8. High-angle mountaineering kit harness tie-in

ROPE
   10-41. Dynamic ropes are used for all climbing training. Dynamic ropes stretch and reduce the peak impact
   force felt by a climber in a fall. Falls while top roping should not generate as much force as a lead fall;
   however, if slack develops in the belay, such as from a stuck rope or slow belayer, there is potential for
   generating significant force.
   10-42. Top rope training puts significant wear and tear on ropes. New climbers fall often, and because a rope
   may be used on the same climb for the entire day, there may be significant wear in the same sections of rope.
   Heavy-duty climbing ropes in the 10-mm range are recommended for top rope training. The 10.2-mm
   dynamic rope included in the ACTKs provides good durability.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                              247
Chapter 10



PREPARATION
      10-43. Advanced and master military mountaineers should plan and supervise mountaineering training that
      involves roped climbing and rappelling. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and
      equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training.
SITE RECONNAISSANCE
      10-44. Visit the training area before the scheduled training date and conduct a rehearsal or walkthrough with
      key personnel. This will help proof the plan, identify hazards, and develop controls. It is also an opportunity
      to save time with set up by identifying anchors and cleaning the area of loose rock or other hazards ahead of
      time.
TIME MANAGEMENT
      10-45. Ensure the training plan provides ample time to cover movement, set up, demonstrations, and training
      time. Extra time for contingencies is often needed.
COMMUNICATION
      10-46. All key personnel should have reliable communication with each other to communicate changes to
      hazards or conditions or to coordinate the response to emergencies.
PARTICIPANT-TO-INSTRUCTOR RATIO
      10-47. Ensure an adequate number of trained personnel are available to effectively supervise the given
      number of participants. In cases where there are only one or two trainers working with a much larger group,
      it may be necessary to limit the number of Soldiers being trained at one time.
ORGANIZATION OR PLACEMENT OF KEY PERSONNEL
      10-48. Critical points must be identified, and key personnel must be placed or distributed to facilitate
      supervision of the training site.
EMERGENCY AND MEDICAL EVACUATION PLANS
      10-49. Emergency and MEDEVAC plans must include special equipment and must consider the nature of
      the terrain in the training area. These plans must be rehearsed to ensure the viability of the plan.

TRAINING SITE CONSIDERATION
      10-50. The following are important considerations when managing a top rope training site.
EASE OF ACCESS
      10-51. The top of the cliff must be accessible to safely establish the anchors and hang ropes. Otherwise, a
      climb may have to be led prior to rigging. The bottom of the cliff must be easily accessible for the group and
      have adequate space to safely move around and store equipment.
LENGTH OF CLIMBS
      10-52. The length of the climbs must be less than half the length of the available ropes. Longer climbs can
      be used by joining two ropes together but is more complex and should be avoided, if possible, when working
      with beginners.
DIFFICULTY
      10-53. Ensure the difficulty of climbing is appropriate for the Soldiers. A common mistake is to use climbs
      that are too difficult for Soldiers to learn the basic movement skills and establish confidence. It is best to have
      a variety of difficulty levels available.




248                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing



DISTANCE BETWEEN CLIMBS
   10-54. Climbs should be far enough apart so that climbers are not falling on or swinging into other climbers;
   however, they should not be so far apart that supervision and control are hindered. With climbs in close
   proximity, the instructor can often maintain adequate supervision of more than one climb.

TRAINING SITE ANCHORS
   10-55. Anchors at training sites are built stronger and more redundant than others used in climbing. A top
   roping anchor is used for long durations of time and is often out of the user’s sight. It either is loaded
   frequently, with climbers falling or as each climber is lowered back down to the ground. Extra care should
   be taken to avoid sharp edges and add padding where necessary.
LOCATION OF ANCHORS
   10-56. Anchors should be located directly above the climb. If the anchor is not above the climb, during a fall
   climbers will pendulum, swinging across the face until they are in line with the anchor. This is more
   pronounced the closer to the top the climber gets.
CONSTRUCTION OF ANCHORS
   10-57. Anchors must be strong and redundant. Developed climbing areas often have bolted anchors at the
   top of climbs. A top roping anchor can be built with these with a cord as for other applications. (See
   figure 10-9.) Locking carabiners may be substituted for non-locking carabiners to ensure that the anchor is
   secure, even if it is checked only a few times during the training day. If anchors are unavailable at the cliff
   edge or are not in line with the top of the climb, static rope can be used to extend anchors out over the edge
   of the cliff and create a master point that is in line. Anchor ropes should be at least 9.5 mm in diameter.




                                 Figure 10-9. Top rope climbing set up

INSPECTIONS
   10-58. Inspection is one of the most critical components of any technical mountain training event. Many
   accidents can be attributed to lack of inspection or instructor error during the inspection process. Level 2 or



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               249
Chapter 10



      higher military mountaineers should inspect all rigging. The site should be organized in such a way that
      participants are unable to climb or proceed towards edges or dangerous terrain without first being inspected.
      Trainers must have a clear, logical sequence to follow when conducting inspections, whether it is anchor
      points, harnesses, tie-ins, rappel hook ups, or other. These should be conducted hands-on, not viewed from a
      distance.

TOP ROPE BELAY
      10-59. Top rope training develops two main skills. One is the individual mobility skill of the climber. The
      other is belaying. Belaying is the most important for safe training.
POSITIONING THE BELAYER
      10-60. The best position to catch a fall is directly below the anchor. The belayer will be pulled straight up
      and not off-balance. However, belayers should be offset enough so that the climber will not fall on them.
      They should also be positioned so that the rope will not interfere with climbers as they climb the route or
      entangle the climber in the event of a fall. The belayer should be protected from hazards, such as falling rock
      or ice. They should be placed into a protected feature under a roof or bulge or offset out of the path of any
      falling objects.
ANCHORING THE BELAYER
      10-61. Anchoring belayers can keep them from being pulled off their stance during a fall. It is not always
      necessary, but the decision not to anchor should be deliberate. It is recommended that the belayer is anchored
      when—
          • Belayers are inexperienced and may lose control of the belay if they are pulled up.
          • The climber severely outweighs the belayer.
          • It is necessary to keep them from being pulled into hazards and obstructions.
BACK-UP BELAYER
      10-62. Using back-up belayers can achieve several things. Back-up belayers improve the overall security of
      the climbers, since it decreases the likelihood that a Soldier could be dropped to the ground. Back-up belayers
      help to convey the importance of the belay when learning is first taking place and keeps additional Soldiers
      occupied and focused when unit trainers are working with large numbers of participants. To provide a
      back-up belay, one Soldier stands just behind the primary belayer, on the brake-hand side, and keeps
      additional control of the rope while making sure not to interfere with the primary belayer’s movements.
BELAYING WITH A TUBE-STYLE DEVICE
      10-63. A belay device acts as a brake on the climbing rope by applying friction to it. The device, plus the
      belayer’s braking hand, keeps tension on the rope in the event of a fall and helps protect the climber at the
      other end. It is an essential device for climbing safety.
      10-64. Tube-style devices are the most used belay devices. (See figure 10-10.) They are lightweight, simple,
      and do not twist the rope. The brake position with a tube-style device is down, with the brake hand below the
      device, creating two sharp bends in the rope that provide the necessary friction. Attention must be paid to the
      belay technique, as there is very little friction outside of the brake position.
          • Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness or into the belay loop. Thread a bight
               of the climbing rope through the tube slot of the device opposite the side of the keeper loop. Attach
               both the bight of rope and the keeper loop to the carabiner and lock the gate.
          • To take in the rope, grasp the brake strand a few inches from the device and with the thumb pointed
               towards the device. Reach out and place the guide hand on the load strand with the thumb pointed
               up. Pull down with the guide hand and up with the brake hand simultaneously until the brake strand
               is approximately 1 foot away from the waist. Return the brake strand immediately to the brake
               position (below the device). Move the guide hand down to the brake strand just underneath the brake
               hand and slide the brake hand back to within a few inches from the device. Reach back up to the
               load strand with the guide hand and repeat.
          • Never let go of the brake strand. The climber’s life depends on it.



250                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                Rope Systems for Climbing



       •   To lower the climber, remove all slack from the system. Hold the brake strand in the brake position
           with both hands, and feed rope slowly back through the device until the climber is safely on the
           ground. (See figure 10-11, page 252.)




                       Figure 10-10. Top rope belay with tube-style device




26 November 2025                             TC 3-97.61                                              251
Chapter 10




                                  Figure 10-11. Tubular device belay action

BELAYING WITH A MUNTER HITCH
      10-65. The Munter hitch is rarely used for top roping, but for units that are not fielded mountaineering kits,
      it provides an adequate belay. It has the advantage of requiring no extra equipment and maintaining a
      sufficient level of friction to stop a fall with the brake strand in a variety of positions. Its main disadvantage
      is that it twists and kinks the rope.
           • Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness. Tie a Munter hitch in the climbing
                 rope and clip it into the carabiner for either a right-hand or a left-hand brake. Lock the carabiner.
           • To take in rope, grasp the brake strand with the brake hand a few inches away from the Munter hitch
                 and with the thumb pointed up. Pull down with the guide hand and up with the brake hand
                 simultaneously until the brake hand is just below the guide hand. With the guide hand, grasp both
                 ropes just above the brake hand, and then slide the brake hand back down to its original place, a few
                 inches from the Munter hitch. Reach back up the rope with the guide hand, and repeat.
           • During a fall, the bight of the Munter hitch will pass from the brake side of the carabiner to the
                 guide-hand side. The hitch creates enough friction for the belayer to easily hold the climber’s body
                 weight. The brake position for the Munter hitch is with the brake strand and the load strand parallel.
           • Never let go of the brake strand.
           • To lower the climber back down, place both hands on the brake strand and feed the rope slowly
                 back through the Munter hitch until the climber is safely on the ground. (See figure 10-12.)

            Note. Do not put the brake hand too close to the Munter hitch. Fingers caught in the Munter hitch
            could cause a mountaineer to lose control of the brake, dropping the climber.

                                  Figure 10-12. Munter belay technique

CLIMBING COMMANDS
   10-66. Using standardized verbal climbing commands is a necessary safety protocol to ensure both members
   are ready before any actions are taken. Commands while top roping also teach proper communication before
   introducing lead climbing, where communication may occur over a much longer distance. Clear
   communication minimizes the chance of human error and helps to ensure safe operation of the belay. All
   commands must be preceded by the other Soldier’s first or last name, like a radio transmission, to gain the
   other Soldier’s attention. This is especially important at training sites where there are multiple top rope climbs
   set up nearby to avoid confusion.
   10-67. Units and schoolhouses should develop their own SOPs to determine appropriate commands. Consider
   the following when choosing these terms:
        • Avoid using terms that sound alike or may be confused with another word (for example, GO, SLOW,
            and WHOAH may sound like NO and vice versa).
        • Avoid using words that are not definitive (for example, GOOD is a vague term that does not define
            any specific action).
   10-68. Table 10-1, page 254 lists common terms that are widely used. To manage risk and avoid confusion,
   consider these commands as the bare minimum associated for top rope climbing. Units or schoolhouses may
   add additional commands if they feel they are necessary to help further mitigate risk.

                                         Table 10-1. Climbing commands
        Belayer                Climber                               Command Description
                          THAT’S ME            This command is said when the climber feels tension from the rope
                                               as the belayer takes all the slack out of the system. This command
                                               is intended to let belayers know that they have tension to the
                                               climber and the rope is not caught somewhere.
 BELAY ON                                      This command is given when all slack between the climber and
                                               belayer has been taken out of the rope, and the belayer has control
                                               of the break strand with at least one hand.
                          SLACK                The climber may use this command to release some tension in the

SECTION V – LEAD CLIMBING
      10-69. Lead climbing is where a roped team has one climber take the lead while the other climber follows.
      While ascending the route, the lead climber periodically connects the rope to protection for safety in the event
      of a fall. This protection can consist of permanent bolts to which the climber clips quick draws, or removable
      protection, such as nuts and cams. One of the climbers below the lead climber acts as a belayer. The belayer
      gives out rope while the lead climber ascends and stops the rope when the lead climber falls or wants to rest.
      10-70. In military mountaineering, the primary mission of a roped climbing team is to fix a route with some
      type of rope installation to assist movement of less trained personnel in the unit. This duty falls upon the most
      experienced climbers in the unit, usually working in two- or three-man groups or teams. Even if the climbing
      is for another purpose, roped climbing should be performed whenever the terrain becomes difficult and exposed.
      10-71. Units or schoolhouses should develop their own SOPs for lead climbing commands and establish
      alternative means of tactically communicating actions while lead climbing. Examples of climbing commands
      are described in table 10-1 in the top rope section.

EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS
      10-72. The ACTK contains the equipment necessary for lead climbing operations and includes
      mountaineering harnesses, chocks, and cams in a wide variety of sizes, locking and nonlocking carabiners,
      dynamic climbing rope, webbing and accessory cord, ascenders, and belay devices. The specific use of this
      equipment is described in chapters 8 and 9.
      10-73. The snow and ice mobility kit (SIMK) is designed to outfit a platoon with safety and mobility
      equipment for operations in snow- and ice-covered mountainous terrain. This kit will be required if moving
      through this type of terrain and the specific use of this equipment is described in chapters 6 and 15.



254                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing



HELMETS
   10-74. As outlined in chapter 6, lighter weight or climbing-specific helmets offer several advantages and are
   recommended for lead climbers.
HARNESS
   10-75. The ACTK contains three basic mountaineering harnesses. These harnesses are a bare minimum, and
   lead climbing in any type of field expedient harness is not recommended. Lead climbing requires much more
   gear than general mountaineering tasks, so harnesses with additional features can increase efficiency and
   functionality. (See figure 10-13.) Typical features of harnesses well-suited for lead climbing are—
        • Adjustable leg loops with buckles.
        • Four or more gear loops designed to hold extra gear.
        • Thick and durable padding increases comfort when spending a long time in the harness.
        • Extra lumbar padding helps to stabilize the lower back and waist.




                   Figure 10-13. Climbing harness tie-in and equipment racking

ROPE
   10-76. Lead climbing can be protected by different rope systems. The UIAA develops safety and testing
   standards for mountaineering equipment. It sets standards for three different types of climbing rope: single
   ropes, half ropes, and twin ropes.

Single Ropes
   10-77. Single ropes are the most common type of climbing rope. Diameters can range from 8.9 to 11.1 mm.

Half Ropes
   10-78. Half ropes are a set of two ropes that are clipped separately into points of protection. This reduces
   friction and rope drag during long wandering routes and serves as a second rope for longer rappels. The
   disadvantage to half ropes is the increased complexity required for both the climber and belayer to manage
   these ropes separately. The diameters for half ropes can range from 8 to 9 mm. Half ropes are used for a party
   of two in wandering alpine terrain, on rock, or on ice.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               255
Chapter 10



Twin Ropes
      10-79. Twin ropes are also a set of two ropes, but both strands are clipped into each point of protection and
      managed as one rope. Diameters for twin ropes range from 7 to 8 mm. Twin ropes are primarily used on
      routes needing two ropes for rappels.

            Note. Some ropes may hold more than one, or all, of these certifications, which can add to
            confusion during rope selection. Weight, versatility, and durability should be the primary
            considerations. In most cases, lightweight, single ropes offer the best balance of these factors.

PROTECTION
      10-80. The amount of protection the lead climber brings depends upon the character of the climber and the
      skill of the lead climber. In easy alpine terrain, the rack may be just a few pieces of rock gear to protect
      exposed steps and make simple anchors. Protecting sustained, multipitch rock may require a rack of doubles,
      two sets of the entire size range of cams.
      10-81. The presence of pre-established anchors or bolts found in some commonly used training areas are
      some of the biggest variables in protection. Climbing a route that has bolts placed for protection, known as
      sport climbing, provides security and allows the climber to carry less equipment. Sport climbing is useful for
      training purposes only. Sport climbing provides a safe way to introduce climbers to lead climbing and allows
      more experienced climbers to work on climbing terrain that is more difficult without having to place
      traditional protection.
      10-82. In winter and alpine environments, ice screws must be incorporated.
ROCK SHOES
      10-83. Rock shoes are specialized pieces of equipment that are only necessary when moving through difficult
      technical terrain. The practical application of this equipment is limited operationally but can greatly enhance
      climbing training and should be utilized when building Soldiers’ skillset in rock climbing. These specialized
      shoes provide more friction, support, and precise footwork, allowing the Soldier to move more effectively
      through the terrain. (See figure 10-14.) It is a common misconception that climbing is about upper-body
      strength. Climbing requires a lot of upper-body strength, but the legs typically propel the climber up the wall.
      The reason Soldiers fall while learning how to rock climb is typically some failure of their foot placement.
      While lead climbing, especially when learning, rock shoes are invaluable in managing risk by increasing the
      security of foot placements and reducing the likelihood of a fall.

                   Figure 10-14. Rock-climbing shoes

BELAYING A LEAD CLIMBER
      10-84. Belayers must first identify a place to stand when belaying that is free from rockfall or other objective
      hazards they can trip over or be pushed into. Belayers must also achieve an adequate stance or brace their
      body positions to help absorb the energy from a lead fall. They should consider attaching themselves to an
      anchor near the ground to help prevent being pulled off their stance and losing control of the belay. (See
      figure 10-15.) The climbing rope should then be back stacked, and both climber and belayer will tie into the
      appropriate ends of the rope.
      10-85. The best position to catch a fall is directly below the first piece of protection. Belayers will be pulled
      straight up and not lose their balance. However, they should be offset enough so that the climber will not fall
      directly on them. The belayer should be positioned so that the rope does not interfere with the climber as they
      climb the route, and they do not become entangled in it in the event of a fall.
      10-86. As the leader climbs, the rope is fed out ensuring that climbers have full freedom to move, and they
      are not hindered by the rope. Ensure that there is always a slight sag in the rope, but no more. Anticipate the
      climber’s movements and be prepared to feed rope out quickly when protection is being clipped. If belayers
      cannot see the climber, they must feel the climber through the rope. Unless the climber says otherwise, the
      belayer can slowly give slack on the rope as the climber proceeds on the route. The belayer should keep just
      enough slack in the rope so the climber does not have to pull it through the belay. If climbers want a tighter
      rope, they can call for it. If belayers notice too much slack developing in the rope, they should take in the
      excess rope quickly. It is the belayers’ responsibility to manage the rope, whether by sight or touch, until the
      climber tells them otherwise.
      10-87. To catch a fall, immediately drop the guide hand down next to the brake hand and lock the rope off in
      the brake position. Bend the knees slightly to help absorb the impact.




258                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing




                                Figure 10-15. Belaying the lead climber

LEAD CLIMBER
   10-88. Lead climbers have a lot to consider while climbing. A lead climber is the first climber to negotiate
   a route, for whom a top belay is not possible, and who assumes the most risk of injury in a fall. They
   should spend sufficient time reviewing the various techniques available for protecting themselves and their
   followers before selecting one, as well as preparing their equipment for efficient use before beginning a
   climb.
RACKING
   10-89. The protection the lead climber brings with them is referred to as the rack. The term racking is simply
   the process a climber goes through to prepare the equipment for climbing. Racking should be organized so
   the right gear can be found and accessed quickly. Equipment should be spread out between a gear sling over



26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               259
Chapter 10



      the shoulder and the gear loops on the harness. The specific location and order of placement of the protection
      falls to personal preference, but there should be a logical sequence to the process.
CLIMBING
      10-90. The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most
      experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. They
      must ensure that the route is well within their climbing ability and that of the second climber (“second”). The
      lead climber carries most of the climbing equipment to place protection along the route and set up the next
      belay. The leader must also ensure that the second has the necessary equipment, such as a chock pick, to
      remove any protection that the leader may place.
      10-91. The leader is responsible for emplacing protection frequently enough and in such a manner that if
      either the leader or the second should fall, their fall is neither long enough nor hard enough to result in injury.
      The leader must also ensure that the rope is routed so that it can run freely through the protection placements,
      thus minimizing friction, or rope drag.
      10-92. The other member of the climbing team, the second, is responsible for belaying the leader, removing
      the belay anchor, and retrieving the protection placed by the leader between belay positions (also known as
      cleaning the pitch).
      10-93. The leader continues the route until either a designated belay location is reached, or the near end of
      the rope is reached. At this position, the leader sets an anchor, connects to the anchor, and says OFF BELAY.
      The belayer remains attached to the anchor until the command BELAY ON is given.
      10-94. Leading a difficult pitch is the most hazardous task in roped climbing. Lead climbers may be exposed
      to potentially long, hard falls. They must exercise keen judgment in selecting routes, placing protection, and
      routing climbing rope through the protection. Every effort should be made to keep the climbing line as direct
      as possible to the next belay to allow the rope to run smoothly through the protection with minimal friction.
      Protection should be placed whenever the leader feels it necessary to prevent hazardous situations and before
      moving past a difficult section.
PLACING PROTECTION
      10-95. Generally, protection is placed from one stable position to the next. If the climbing is difficult,
      protection should be placed more frequently. If the climbing becomes easier, protection can be placed farther
      apart, saving hardware for difficult sections. On some routes, an extended diagonal or horizontal movement,
      known as a traverse, is required. As leaders begin this type of move, they must consider the second’s safety
      as well as their own. The potential fall of the second will result in a pendulum swing if protection is not
      adequate to prevent this. The danger comes from any objects in the swinging path of the second.
REDUCING ROPE DRAG; USING RUNNERS
      10-96. No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the
      protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between
      carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience;
      severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can
      be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result
      in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so
      the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this
      by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary
      direction. The runner is attached to the protection while the rope is clipped into a carabiner at the opposite
      end of the runner. Extending placements with runners allows the climber to vary the route slightly while the
      rope continues to run in a relatively straight line.




260                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                 Rope Systems for Climbing




                   Figure 10-16. Use of runners to extend and reduce rope drag

   10-97. Not only is rope drag a hindrance, but it can also cause undue movement of protection as the rope
   tightens between any out of line placements. Rope drag through chock placements can be dangerous. As the
   climber moves above the placements, an outward or upward pull from rope drag may cause correctly set
   chocks to pop out, even when used correctly. Passive protections, like chocks, are especially prone to
   wiggling loose as the rope pulls on the cable attachment. All wired chocks used for leader protection should
   be extended to reduce the chance of the rope pulling them out. (See figure 10-17, page 262.)




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                              261
Chapter 10




                  Figure 10-17. Proper extension of cams and chocks using runners

CLIPPING TECHNIQUE
      10-98. Clip the climbing rope into a point of protection by reaching down and grabbing the rope between the
      thumb and index finger. Use the middle finger to stabilize the carabiner at the protection or runner, and use
      the thumb and index finger to clip the rope in. Alternately, the rope can be held between the middle and index
      finger and clipped in as shown in figure 10-18. Ensure the gate of the carabiner faces out (not towards the
      rock), and the rope is clipped in the direction of travel to prevent the rope from potentially becoming
      unclipped in a fall. Recreational climbers typically do all their clipping while hanging onto rock holds as
      much as they can; however, as a Soldier not worried about preserving the free climbing style, simply grab
      the point of protection and hang onto it while clipping the rope and runner into it. This may provide better
      temporary hold or provide a much-needed rest.




262                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing




                               Figure 10-18. Proper clipping techniques

BELAYING A SECOND CLIMBER
   10-99. Typically, one climber takes the lead while belayed from below, moves up the route to the next ledge
   or desired spot, and then sets up a new anchor and belay. This distance between these belays is known as a
   pitch. The length of a pitch is limited to the length of available rope and convenient, suitable to belay
   positions.
   10-100. In most cases, the leader attaches to the anchor with either separate sling material or by using the
   climbing rope with a clove hitch and locking carabiner. Using a clove hitch in the climbing rope itself has
   the distinct advantage of allowing more room and material to fine tune the distance between the anchor and
   the cliff edge to enable better communication with the climber below. The leader then uses the command of
   OFF BELAY. Once the belayer has removed the belay, enabling the rope to run freely, the belayer would
   use the command BELAY OFF. The leader then pulls in all the remaining rope until it is tight with the second.
   Once an appropriate belay is set up, the leader uses the command BELAY ON letting the second know that
   it is safe to climb.
   10-101. Many techniques can be used to belay the second, depending upon the terrain, difficulty of the
   climbing, availability of anchors, and likelihood or consequences of a fall. The second is essentially on a top
   rope, with a snug rope being maintained throughout the climb.
INDIRECT BELAYS
   10-102. An indirect belay occurs when a leader is anchored and belays the second off the harness with either
   a Munter hitch or tube-style belay device. While this does work, it has several drawbacks. It can oftentimes
   be quite awkward in the event of a fall that pulls the belayer down towards the ground or if there is a climber
   who is struggling and hanging excessively on the rope. The belayer is forced to hold the rope in the brake
   position with much or all the climber’s weight pulling in a downward direction on the harness. Additionally,


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               263
Chapter 10



      should belayers need to tie off the climber and escape the belay for any reason, several steps would be
      required to free themselves from the system. For these reasons, this technique is only preferred when using
      an anchor that is suspected to be weak. With a weak or bad anchor, belayers’ bodies, in this case, act as the
      primary anchor with the other simply backing them up. Once again, a good, braced position is necessary. The
      preferred technique otherwise is to always use direct belays.
DIRECT BELAYS
      10-103. Belaying directly off the anchor allows any forces to be transmitted solely to the anchor so that the
      belayer is not pulled in any direction and cannot become trapped in the system should problems arise. Direct
      belays are also generally more comfortable and give the belayer freedom to move while maintaining control
      of the brake rope. This can be done either using a Munter hitch or using a plaquette-style belay device in
      guide mode. In either case, the first step is for the climber to attach to the anchor and shout, OFF BELAY.
      Pull the remainder of the rope up until the second shouts, THAT’S ME. Then use one of the following belay
      methods: the Munter hitch or the autolocking tubular device in guide mode.

Belaying with the Munter Hitch
      10-104. Using a Munter hitch as a belay is quick, easy to tie, and can be used to easily lower the second back
      down, if necessary. It is an alternative in case a Soldier does not have a belay device. Attach a locking
      carabiner to the anchor master point, pull the slack out of the rope to the climber below, and tie a Munter
      hitch with the climbing rope. (See figure 10-19.)
      10-105. Place the guide hand on the load strand and the brake hand on the brake strand a few inches away
      from the Munter hitch, ensuring both thumbs are pointing towards the anchor. To take in rope, hold firmly
      and slide both hands towards each other until they meet. With the guide hand, grab both strands of rope just
      beneath the brake hand, then slide the brake hand back up to within a few inches of the Munter hitch. Slide
      the guide hand back down and repeat. Care should be taken to ensure that the brake hand does not get so
      close to the Munter hitch that a thumb or finger could be sucked in and pinched during a fall.




264                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                   Rope Systems for Climbing




                             Figure 10-19. Belaying using a Munter hitch

Autolocking Tubular-Style Device
   10-106. The tube-style belay or rappel devices issued in the Army mountain kits can be used in guide or
   autolocking mode. To use this device in autolocking mode, a locking carabiner is clipped through the metal
   loop and attached to an anchor. A bight of rope is then fed into the device, with the climber’s strand on top,
   and a second “braking” locking carabiner is clipped through the device’s carry wire and the bight of rope.
   One locking carabiner is used to attach the device itself to the anchor, and a second is used as a braking
   carabiner after the rope is fed through the device. The shape and orientation of the device allows rope to pass
   smoothly through it in one direction, but lock off in the opposite direction, being pinched around the stock
   of the braking carabiner. (See figure 10-20, page 266.)
   10-107. To use the device, attach it to the anchor with a locking carabiner in the appropriate spot. Then feed
   a bight of rope into the device, paying close attention to the diagram on its side. Clip an additional locking
   carabiner around both the rope and the keeper, ensuring again that the brake strand is between the Soldier’s
   body and the load rope. Pull down on the load rope to make sure it is rigged correctly and locks off in the



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               265
Chapter 10



      correct direction before shouting ON BELAY. To take in rope with a device in guide mode, use the same
      technique described above for the Munter hitch.
      10-108. One advantage of these devices over the Munter hitch is that they do not require holding power on
      the part of the belayer because they lock off automatically, oftentimes allowing the belayer to multitask at
      the anchor. They can also be used when using half or twin ropes or when belaying two seconds
      simultaneously on two separate ropes. They are particularly useful in these situations or if the climbing is
      difficult and the second is expected to be hanging a lot. A disadvantage is that since it only allows rope to
      pass through in one direction, giving “slack” or lowering a climber back down requires additional training.

            Note. Never use a device in standard tube-style mode to belay directly off the anchor.




            Figure 10-20. Belaying a climber using an autolocking device in guide mode

ROPE MANAGEMENT WHILE BELAYING
      10-109. Pay careful attention to ensure that rope taken in when belaying the second is stacked or coiled neatly
      to make the belay transition easy and to ensure that it does not fall down the cliff and become tangled or
      caught.




266                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                     Rope Systems for Climbing



On Ledges
   10-110. On small or large ledges, it is usually possible to stack the rope in a neat pile as it is pulled through
   the belay. This allows for an easy transition and for smooth rope feeding.

At Hanging Stances
   10-111. At hanging belay stances, it may be necessary to stack the rope back and forth over the tie-in strand
   as the Soldier pulls rope through the belay. If this is done, the rope should be looped back and forth in large
   bights (not so long as to becoming caught on things below). If the second becomes the new leader for the
   next pitch, these bights should start big and gradually become smaller. This allows the rope to feed out
   without becoming tangled during the next lead. If the original leader leads the next pitch, the rope may have
   to be restacked over the second’s tie-in strand when they reach the anchor. Another option is to stack the rope
   back and forth over a leg or foot. However, feet tend to get shifty when belaying during a long lead, which
   can lead to dropping the rope where it could possibly become stuck or jammed below.
ROPE TUG COMMANDS
   10-112. Sometimes yelling cannot be heard when the climber and belayer are far apart. This is especially true
   in windy conditions or if the climber is around a corner, above an overhang, or at the back of a ledge. It may
   be necessary to use a series of tugs on the rope in place of the standard voice commands. To avoid any
   possible confusion with interpreting multiple rope tug commands, use only one. Rope tug commands may
   also have a tactical application where noise discipline is particularly important. Units or climbing teams
   should develop their own SOPs for rope tug commands. These commands should always be discussed and
   confirmed prior to a climb.
TRAINING CONSIDERATIONS FOR LEAD CLIMBING
   10-113. Due to the high consequences involved, advanced and master military mountaineers must plan and
   supervise mountaineering training that involves lead climbing. They advise the commander on training
   requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. Lead climbing
   training is particularly demanding of trainers and supervisors. For inexperienced climbers, a 2:1 ratio is often
   required. Supervision of climbing training must be thorough and deliberate. A large part of this supervision
   is inspecting every component of the rope system. The ability to balance the rigid process of supervision and
   inspection with the soft skills of mentorship and coaching can help maximize the safety and value of the
   training.
   10-114. Assess the mental readiness of the climber. The fear of heights is real and is not something that can
   be ignored. A Soldier becoming panicked while lead climbing can create hazardous situations and may
   dissuade the Soldier from continuing further climbing training.
   10-115. Consider climber skill when selecting routes for training. Climbs should be challenging but
   achievable with a couple of tries. Routes for new climbers should not exceed intermediate difficulty (see
   appendix A for more on climbing classification). A common mistake is to place Soldiers on climbs that are
   too difficult, steep, or strenuous, where they cannot first focus on the processes. Established bolted climbs
   are often an excellent place to begin lead climbing training. Traditionally protected routes can be attempted
   after proficiency has been achieved with these. For initial training, the length of climbs is ideally less than
   half the length of the available ropes to allow quick transitions to rappel and maximize repetitions. These
   shorter lengths also make it easier for the supervising trainer to ascend next to the climber when necessary.
   10-116. Soldiers should already be proficient at placing protection, clipping ropes into protection, belaying
   leaders, belaying follow-on climbers, and constructing multipoint anchors. These skills can often be practiced
   on the ground in advance.
   10-117. Mock lead training is a useful tool to prepare Soldiers for lead climbing. Mock leading occurs when
   a Soldier climbs a route on top rope while also leading up with another rope. This allows the Soldier to focus
   on placing protection, clipping, and managing the rope on lead with the security of having a top rope as
   backup in case of a fall.

SECTION VI – ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES
      10-118. In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging
      from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be
      compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question
      as to security.

BODY BELAYS
      10-119. Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely
      and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the
      rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope
      is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with
      the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and
      slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body
      belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center
      of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is
      its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are
      disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers’ bodies, serious
      rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also
      generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall
      farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced
      position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.)




268                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                    Rope Systems for Climbing




                                          Figure 10-21. Hip belay

SHOULDER BELAY
   10-120. A shoulder belay is a way to add a level of friction to the rope as the belayer pulls it tight with a
   climber below. The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the
   body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short
   steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where
   the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber
   below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is
   kept tight with the climber below. The belayer’s body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at
   the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22,
   page 270.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                269
Chapter 10




                                         Figure 10-22. Shoulder belay

      10-121. A terrain belay can be used when there is a feature that the rope can go around and create enough
      friction to arrest a fall or lower a load. The natural feature must be solid and not have sharp edges. Terrain
      belays are an effective means of belaying a climbing partner, but they require good judgement. When using
      a boulder or horn of rock, the belayer must ensure the rope will not slide off the rock in the event of a fall
      and that the rock is wedged securely. Trees are another good example of a natural object that can be used as
      a terrain belay. (See chapter 9 for more information on tree selection.) (See figure 10-23.)




270                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
