                                       Figure 10-23. Terrain belay


SECTION VII – CLIMBING IN A TEAM OF THREE
   10-122. Level 2 mountaineers are trained to work as a team of two. There are numerous examples of when
   it may be beneficial to work and move as a team of three. Moving as a team of three has added complexity
   and much more challenging rope management at each belay. To progress into managing two ropes, a climber
   must first become proficient in managing one.
   10-123. It is good for military mountaineers to have options for roped travel through terrain with changing
   hazards. The mountaineer must constantly assess terrain and hazards and fluidly adapt the technique to
   mitigate those hazards as best as possible. Time is always against mountaineers, and efficient transitions from
   one roped movement style to the next are important. A mountaineer should not default to using one style of
   movement for all types of terrain and should know how to properly apply different roped movement
   techniques to different terrain.

CATERPILLAR
   10-124. Caterpillar technique is usually the first technique learned for managing a party of three. The lead
   climber and second climber tie into the ends of one rope. The second also ties into another rope with the third
   climber. The leader leads as usual, clipping protection, and then builds an anchor and belays the second.
   Rather than cleaning the protection, the second climbers remove their rope and clip the second rope into the
   protection. Once the second climber is anchored, the leader then belays the third climber.
   10-125. Climbing while using the caterpillar technique is often slower than other techniques. It can take the
   party twice as long to cover a pitch in some situations but is the simplest method of managing a party of
   three. It builds on the skills already used for two-party climbing, with only slightly more complex rope and
   station management. This technique also reduces the workload on the following climbers.

END ROPING
   10-126. In easy terrain, two climbers can tie into the end of the same rope. One ties into the end of the rope,
   the second attaches with a cow’s tail and a bight of rope long enough that they can move up and down
   independent of the climber below. (See figure 10-24, page 272.) It is tied with an overhand on a bight loop


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               271
Chapter 10



      with a 30-cm bight. This bight should be far enough from the other climber that the two do not interfere with
      each other as they climb, usually about 4 meters. The second attaches to the cow’s tail with a clove hitch
      around two opposite and opposed locking carabiners. This is almost as fast as climbing in a party of two.
      Rope management is simple for the leader and no different from climbing in a party of two. The two followers
      can be clove hitched into the anchor on the rope between them, securing them both. The followers can also
      coach and assist each other with the climbing.
      10-127. This is only appropriate in easy terrain, where there is little risk of a fall. It is used primarily in
      4th-class terrain.




                           Figure 10-24. Clipping to a cow’s tail and end roping

            Note. When attaching to a rope to climb, the preferred method is to be tied directly into the rope.
            Locking carabiners can unlock and open if they are not being monitored, and while climbing, they
            may end up in a position where they can be cross loaded. When clipping into a rope to climb, it
            should be with two lockers, opposite and opposed, and with a knot that secures around the
            carabiners to keep them oriented correctly.


PARALLEL
      10-128. For parallel technique, the lead climber ties into both ropes and the two followers tie into the other
      ends. The leader leads on one strand, clipping it into the protection. The second rope can either be clipped
      into the protection as well, clipped into just specific pieces as directional, or routed on a separate line,
      depending on the terrain and the hazards. (See figure 10-25.) At the anchor, the leader sets up to belay the
      two followers.
      10-129. Belay devices with a guide mode (plaquette or autolocking) can be used to belay two climbers, on
      two ropes, simultaneously. For rock climbing, with little rockfall hazard, both followers often climb together,
      offset enough so that they do not fall onto each other. Where loose rock is a concern or when ice climbing,
      this must be managed differently, often one climber climbing at a time, either for the whole pitch, or bounding
      from sheltered stance to sheltered stance. (See figure 10-26.)

   10-130. Rope management is more difficult with two ropes and two climbers moving simultaneously.
   Organization at the belays requires additional thought, ensuring that the followers are anchored in a manner
   that the ropes are not twisted, and both strands feed up from them.
   10-131. The parallel technique is used frequently. In steep terrain, it is often the fastest way to move as a
   party of three. However, to avoid complications, it requires mastery of the basics and practice.




                               Figure 10-25. Parallel climbing two stands




                 Figure 10-26. Belaying two climbers with an autolocking device

FIXED STRANDS
   10-132. It is also possible for leaders to fix the strand of rope they led onto the anchor at the top. This frees
   up leaders from any belaying responsibilities and allows them the ability to provide security, if necessary.
   This concept of the leader fixing strands of rope after leading a pitch provides many options for moving
   Soldiers through terrain. Leaders are not limited to just fixing the strand of rope they led on. They can pull


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 273
Chapter 10



      up the rope, fix the middle, and have two strands for others to ascend if the rope reaches. The leader could
      trail another rope and fix it in another location after having reached the top. Having second climbers ascend
      rather than climb removes any possibility of a second not being able to reach the top due to a lack of climbing
      ability. The second would then ascend the rope rather than climb on belay. It is not appropriate in all terrain
      due to various terrain hazards. The weighted rope can dislodge loose rock. The rope is easily damaged or cut
      if it runs over a sharp edge while the followers ascend. (See chapter 11 for more information on ascending
      ropes.)

                                             Fixed Ropes
   Fixed ropes are an important part of military mountaineering as they facilitate the movement
   of Soldiers through rugged terrain. Fixed ropes allow large groups of Soldiers to safely access
   terrain that provides tactical advantage over the enemy. They have proven useful in past
   conflicts. During World War II, they were successfully used during Operation Neptune
   (commonly referred to as D-day) and the famous assault on Riva Ridge by the 10th Mountain
   Division. Proficiency in using fixed ropes allows units to overcome mobility limitations and,
   therefore, achieve greater lethality in mountainous terrain.

SECTION I – BASIC FIXED-ROPE TECHNIQUES
   11-1. A fixed rope is any rope system attached to at least one anchor that can be used to improve security
   and efficiency of movement through difficult terrain that subjects Soldiers to a fall hazard. They can be used
   for ascending, descending, or traversing across steep terrain in which a fall hazard exists. They may simply
   provide Soldiers with a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet
   of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to
   fall. They can be used to assist the movement of small teams to large units. They allow units to overcome
   mobility limitations and access tactically advantageous terrain.

FIXED-ROPE CONSIDERATIONS
   11-2. Fixed ropes should be used whenever a group of Soldiers cannot move safely through a section of
   terrain unroped. Fixed ropes are usually the most efficient means of protecting groups larger than team sized,
   especially if the groups have not received advanced military mountaineering training. Common factors
   contributing to the necessity of building fixed ropes are fall hazard, slippery surfaces, limited visibility, heavy
   loads, low mobility skills, and fatigue.
   11-3. The two basic types of fixed-rope systems are simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate
   anchors. Both types have applications in every class of terrain. Simple fixed ropes are anchored only at the
   top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top.
   Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more Soldiers to
   move on them simultaneously and the path to change directions. Each type is determined by route and
   availability of anchors along it, the number of Soldiers to use the system, and the type of available equipment
   to attach to it.
   11-4. All types of fixed ropes are built from the top down over, or through, terrain obstacles. However, fixed
   rope installation teams may need to ascend terrain using other techniques prior to building a fixed-rope
   system. (See chapter 10.)
   11-5. Units planning to use fixed ropes must establish installation teams capable of locating routes, moving
   safely through various terrain obstacles, and building a variety of installations. They should be led by
   advanced military mountaineers but may be assisted by basic military mountaineers. These teams should be
   experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the
   task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them.
   11-6. In a tactical environment, any terrain that requires a fixed rope should be considered a VDA, which is
   steep terrain that puts a unit moving through it at significant tactical disadvantage. The process for
   establishing even the simplest fixed rope comes at the cost of time and exposure to enemy attack. Adequate
   security must be established prior to deploying the installation team. In complex terrain, security teams may
   need to be adjusted or leap-frogged forward if fixed-rope systems cover large pieces of terrain. Emplacing
   security teams in a complex terrain may require high-mobility skills as well as substantial time. Typically, it
   is best to approach fixed-rope terrain from above because security is more easily established on higher




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  275
Chapter 11



      ground. But that is rarely possible. Units that anticipate building fixed-rope systems for movement in a
      combat environment should be well-rehearsed in crossing VDA TTP. (See ATP 3-21.50.)

SIMPLE FIXED ROPES
      11-7. A simple fixed rope is a rope that is anchored at the top of steep terrain that can be used to increase
      safety or efficiency of movement up or down. The method of anchoring the rope is determined by anchor
      features available but can be as simple as a bowline tied to a tree or as complex as a multipoint anchor
      established with rock-climbing gear. The principal benefit of simple, fixed ropes is their simplicity and speed
      of construction.
      11-8. Simple fixed ropes are typically established by one mountaineer climbing the obstacle, dragging a rope,
      and then anchoring it at the top. They can also be established by approaching the top of a steep obstacle by
      some other means, anchoring a rope, and lowering the other end down for others to use.
      11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path
      straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for
      a large enough loading and unloading platform to manage the site safely. Using a friction hitch or mechanical
      progress capture to attach to the rope provides increased security during movement.
EASY TERRAIN
      11-10. Short 2nd- or 3rd-class slopes with low fall consequence can be negotiated using simple fixed ropes
      without the necessity of attaching to the rope. Soldiers using the fixed rope simply grasp the rope with the
      thumb downward and use it in a hand-over-hand fashion to assist with balance. (See figure 11-1.) This
      technique is appropriate when there is an increased likelihood of fall but low consequence. Usually this means
      short slopes that Soldiers could easily negotiate normally, but slippery conditions, fatigue, or heavy loads
      increase the chance of a fall. Knots can be added to increase the security of Soldiers moving on the rope,
      making it less likely their hand slips on the rope.




                             Figure 11-1. Simple fixed rope use in easy terrain




276                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Fixed Ropes



MODERATE TERRAIN
   11-11. Short sections of steep 3rd or 4th class with higher fall consequence can be negotiated by attaching to
   simple fixed ropes with a progress capture, such as a prusik or other mechanical rope-grabbing device. This
   technique requires Soldiers to wear some type of harness. A significant drawback to this technique is that it
   takes a lot of time to move a group of Soldiers. Only one Soldier can move at a time on a rope, and time is
   lost during attachment and detachment. (See figure 11-2, page 278.)

Prusik Technique
   11-12. A common technique involves tying a prusik on the rope with a cordelette, then tying a fixed loop in
   the other end of the two tails. Clip the fixed loop to the harness with a locking carabiner. The optimum length
   of the attachment is one outstretched arm.
   11-13. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the rope as a handhold for balance,
   sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip.
   11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points
   because friction hitches cannot be easily or safely transitioned past intermediate anchors.

Mechanical Ascender Technique
   11-15. It is also possible to use a rope-grabbing device, such as a mechanical ascender, to create a progress
   capture for Soldiers moving on fixed ropes. These devices are easier and faster to use but require every
   Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has limited uses. They should be used when fixed rope ascents are
   planned for large groups in moderate terrain.
   11-16. Mechanical ascenders are devices shaped like a handle that can be attached to a rope by means of a
   toothed cam. It can slide in one direction on a rope but not the other. When weighted, the camming
   mechanism activates and grips the rope. Soldiers can attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along
   fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2,
   page 278). Ascenders should never be dynamically loaded as their teeth could damage the rope. Ascenders
   are included in the Army ACTK, but Solders can use other similar ascenders to ascend fixed ropes. Some are
   much lighter but are less easy to use. Advanced military mountaineers should familiarize themselves with
   the options available and units should obtain those best suited to the mountaineering tasks they must perform.
   11-17. To use a mechanical ascender, attach it to the fixed rope. Then girth hitch a sling to the harness and
   clip it to the ascender with a locking carabiner. (See figure 11-2, page 278.)
   11-18. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the ascender as a handhold for balance,
   sliding it up to capture progress and prevent fall in the case of a slip.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               277
Chapter 11




                    Figure 11-2. Simple fixed-rope attachments in moderate terrain

VERTICAL TERRAIN
      11-19. Moving on simple fixed ropes in terrain where significant sections are very steep or vertical requires
      rigging that is more complex. These rigging techniques provide secure attachment to the rope and aid
      movement up the rope. (See paragraphs 11-36 through 11-52, pages 282 through 286, for more information
      on ascending techniques.)

FIXED ROPES WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS
      11-20. Larger or more complex sections of steep terrain require fixed ropes with intermediate anchors to
      ensure adequate safety and efficiency of movement. This may involve various sections of 3rd, 4th, or even
      5th-class terrain. The principal difference between simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate
      anchors is the use of intermediate anchor points to create independent sections and changes in direction of
      travel. This allows the movement route to follow the easiest, safest, and most efficient path. This type of
      fixed rope is commonly used along exposed ridges and narrow mountain passes.
      11-21. Advanced or master military mountaineers with substantial experience are required to establish fixed
      ropes with intermediate anchors, but they can be assisted by basic military mountaineers.
FIXED-ROPE CONSTRUCTION WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS
      11-22. The primary guiding principles for building a fixed rope with intermediate anchors are that they
      provide adequate fall prevention while maximizing the speed at which Soldiers can move using them.

Path
      11-23. Establishing a fixed rope with intermediate anchors starts with thorough terrain analysis and route
      finding. When selecting a path for the rope, mountaineers must consider the anchor options available,
      difficulty of movement on the route, and any other objective hazards present. The characteristics of the
      Soldiers who use the fixed rope are also useful information. Particularly, what their mobility and technical
      skill levels are and what equipment they have for attaching to the rope.


278                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Fixed Ropes



Intermediate Anchors
   11-24. Terrain and vegetation determine the equipment mountaineers need to build the fixed rope. Heavily
   vegetated terrain or broken rocky terrain may only require cordelettes, slings, and carabiners. Slabby or steep
   rock faces require cams, nuts, and other lead climbing protection to build anchors. Intermediate anchors must
   be built robust enough to support the weight of a fall by the number of Soldiers who will move on each
   section at a given time. When possible, anchors should be built at about waist height in places where good
   footing is possible so that transitioning past anchors is easier for Soldiers moving on the fixed rope (See
   figure 11-3 for common methods of attaching ropes to single component anchors.)

Rope Section Slack
   11-25. Fixed-rope sections do not have a standard amount of slack. There should be enough slack to allow
   Soldiers to follow the easiest path through terrain without adding fall risk. Sometimes a lot of slack is
   necessary to go around an obstacle or steep section. This is usually better than running a tighter rope over
   these things, because going around is easier, which reduces the chance of a fall. Other times, a section may
   need to be tight to reduce fall distance, such as traversing across a cliff on a narrow ledge.




                 Figure 11-3. Intermediate anchors in moderate terrain, example

ATTACHMENT AND MOVEMENT
   11-26. The method for movement on fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is as important as how they are
   constructed. Two primary methods exist for use in steep terrain: the two personal safeties method and the
   ascender-carabiner method. Choosing between the two is a tradeoff between not carrying heavier
   single-purpose items and having more security during movement. The two personal safeties method requires
   no special equipment but cannot eliminate fall risk for a Soldier. The ascender-carabiner method prevents
   falling but requires each Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has little other use. Both techniques have
   their place, and both must be considered for use when planning fixed-rope movements.


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               279
Chapter 11



Two Personal Safeties Method
      11-27. This method involves having two separate girth hitched slings attached to the tie-in portion of the
      harness with a single nonlocking carabiner in each. The carabiners are then attached to the fixed rope. Always
      keep the two carabiners attached to the rope unless they move past an intermediate anchor. To move past an
      intermediate anchor, clip one carabiner at a time above the anchor. When both carabiners are above the
      anchor, continue movement. (See figure 11-4.)
      11-28. The two personal safeties method is appropriate for situations where the fall consequence is high, but
      the likelihood is low. It can be used up to 4th-class terrain under good conditions (such as good surface
      conditions, moderate mobility skills, light loads, well-rested, high visibility) provided that intermediate
      anchors are appropriately spaced to prevent serious fall injury. Since falls using this method are only stopped
      by the last anchor a Soldier passed, there is always a chance of injury. This should be considered carefully
      before choosing it.




                              Figure 11-4. Two personal safeties attachment




280                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                       Fixed Ropes



Ascender-Carabiner Method
   11-29. The ascender-carabiner method is the fastest and most secure way to travel up very steep fixed ropes.
   It is preferred when fall risk is substantial or sections of the fixed rope are long, because the ascender captures
   the Soldiers’ progress as they move.
   11-30. To use this technique, girth hitch two slings into the harness. Clip one nonlocking carabiner into one
   extension. Clip a mechanical ascender to the other extension with a locking carabiner.
   11-31. Ascend in the same manner as with simple fixed ropes. To move past the intermediate anchor, clip
   the nonlocking carabiner above the anchor, and then move the ascender to above the carabiner on the fixed
   rope. (See figure 11-5.)
   11-32. This method is appropriate when both fall consequence and likelihood are high. It can be used in
   terrain up to 4th class under any conditions. It is the best method when surface conditions are slippery, loads
   are heavy, mobility skills are low or Soldiers are fatigued, during low visibility, and when intermediate
   anchors cannot be established to prevent fall injury.




                                Figure 11-5. Ascender-carabiner method



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  281
Chapter 11



FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN
      11-33. Fixed ropes are sometimes necessary for moving in vertical terrain during complex rescue operations
      or other special operations in permissive or nontactical environments. They are rarely practical for tactical
      operations, given their extreme exposure to enemy observation and direct fire. However, vertical terrain is
      not always avoidable during combat operations, and there are historical examples of their use during pivotal
      cliff assaults. Vertical terrain is the most extreme example of VDA. Soldiers moving on vertically fixed ropes
      require well-established overwatch security since they are totally exposed and can do little but ascend the
      fixed rope.
      11-34. Moving on fixed ropes in vertical terrain requires Soldiers to possess the equipment and skills
      necessary to ascend rope, relying entirely on their attachment to it to prevent fall. Efficient ascending requires
      specialized equipment.
CONSTRUCTING FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN
      11-35. Fixed ropes in vertical terrain are constructed in the same fashion as moderate terrain; however, they
      take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes
      in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build
      the system top-down. However, this is rarely possible. Typically, they must be established from the bottom
      up by advanced military mountaineers employing lead climbing techniques to get the rope to the top. This
      process is time-consuming and inherently risky.
ASCENDING TECHNIQUES
      11-36. Many situations may require a Soldier to ascend a rope in very steep or vertical terrain. Soldiers must
      be prepared and equipped to do so when operating in 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Typically, ascending rope is
      a more efficient technique than climbing for moving followers over hard climbing terrain, to include those
      members of small assault climber teams.
      11-37. The techniques described below are for single strands of rope, so it is imperative that appropriate
      measures are taken to pad the rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they
      should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement.
      11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall,
      and whenever rappellers find their rope does not reach the ground.

Prusik Ascent
      11-39. Two prusiks can be used to ascend rope. One prusik is tied to the fixed rope using a cordelette at
      approximately forehead height. A fixed loop is tied in the hanging tails to create an attachment point at about
      waist level. This is then secured to the harness with a locking carabiner. Another prusik is tied to the fixed
      rope at about waist level. The hanging tails are then tied to one or both feet using any appropriate knot to
      form a foot stirrup. (See figure 11-6.)
      11-40. The upper prusik serves as the “progress capture,” during ascent, by holding the Soldier up, while the
      lower friction hitch serves as the “progress” or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid
      up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing
      down and behind them with their leg, while sliding the upper hitch as high as possible. They then rest in the
      harness from the upper hitch and continue. Safety knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch
      and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against
      failure of the friction hitch to grab. This technique should be considered an improvised technique for use when
      ascending is not expected.




282                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                     Fixed Ropes




                                        Figure 11-6. Prusik ascent

Prusik Ascender Method
   11-41. Mechanical ascenders are a one-directional device used to capture progress along a rope and assist
   climbers as they ascend steep, vertical, or free-hanging terrain. They can be substituted for one or both hitches
   described in prusik ascent. They make ascending efficient and fast.
   11-42. To use an ascender as a progress capture, attach it to the rope at about head height. Girth hitch a sling
   or cordelette to the harness, and then use a locking carabiner to secure the other end to the bottom of the
   ascender, forming an arm-length extension between them. Commonly, a nonlocking carabiner is clipped
   around the rope through the top of the ascender for added security. This prevents the device from twisting
   off the rope.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 283
Chapter 11



      11-43. To create the progress with an ascender, attach it to the rope at about waist height. Girth hitch or use
      any carabiner to attach a sling or cordelette to the bottom of the carabiner and tie it to one or both feet using
      any appropriate knot. The movement process is the same as described above for prusik ascent.
      11-44. There are dozens of devices available that work the same as an ascender. Ensure the rope type and
      diameter are appropriate for the device used, as most mechanical devices have a specified range of acceptable
      use. Read all manufacturers’ instructions to ensure safe use.
      11-45. Stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch or device and attached to the
      harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against the rope grabs slipping.
      This technique should be used when ascending is planned but not enough ascenders are available for Soldiers
      to be issued two.

Double-Ascender Method
      11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for
      ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each ascender with a
      locking carabiner. Both ascenders are then placed on the rope. A cordelette or sling also hangs off each
      ascender and is girth hitched to the user’s harness, creating two attachment points to the rope. (See
      figure 11-7.)
      11-47. To use the system, the Soldier places a foot in each etrier (or stirrup) and slides the upper ascender up
      the rope. This upper ascender is easier to move because the Soldier’s weight is on the lower ascender. The
      lower ascender is moved up next, while the upper ascender supports the Soldier’s weight. Sometimes it is
      necessary to slightly release the camming mechanism before moving an ascender.
      11-48. It is also recommended to tie back-up knots periodically in the same manner as prusik ascent.
      11-49. This technique is the most efficient and is recommended for use whenever ascending is a planned
      movement technique.

SPECIAL TECHNIQUES AND CONSIDERATIONS
   11-50. There are too many considerations for using and improving fixed ropes to cover them all in this
   training circular. However, the following techniques should be considered for use with fixed ropes.

Weapon Management
   11-51. Unless enemy attack is imminent, weapons should be slung to the rear, allowing Soldiers to scramble
   more easily in difficult terrain. Heavier weapons, such as sniper weapon systems, mortars, and machine guns,
   may need to be attached to the top of rucksacks.




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                              285
Chapter 11



Improving Steps
      11-52. Soldiers are less likely to fall and move more quickly if they have good footing. Hard snow is
      especially easy to carve steps into and can allow Soldiers to move with less exertion on their calf muscles.
      Carving steps should be done first in steeper sections and, as time allows, in other areas too. Platforms can
      also be made where Soldiers are transitioning past intermediate anchors. If a Soldier can easily stand near an
      intermediate anchor, they can clip around it much faster. This greatly lessens the time required for the group
      to navigate terrain where objective hazards may be present.

Etriers or Slings at Difficult Steps
      11-53. The hanging of a sling or etrier (for use as a hand or foothold) where there is a difficult step can help
      reduce fall potential and increase speed of the group. An etrier is a short ladder that can be made from any
      piece of rope or cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The
      etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.)

Caving Ladders
      11-54. Manufactured ladders can be useful for large steps and crevasse negotiation. They also enable Soldiers
      to navigate challenging terrain in the dark, much easier than if they had to search for hand and foot
      placements. Some are constructed of materials that can be rolled up for transport. While they may make the
      ascent of a blank wall easier, they are cumbersome to carry.

Cables and Via-Ferrata
      11-55. If terrain is to be repetitively used for access to higher points for something semi-permanent such as
      an observation post, it may be in the unit’s best interest to build a via-ferrata style system for access. A
      via-ferrata works similarly to a fixed rope with intermediate anchors, except it uses cable instead of rope.
      Using cable reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more
      time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended
      period. Given the cable’s rigidity, the attachment method used by Soldiers needs to provide the stretch to
      lessen fall forces. This equipment can be found on the civilian market. Another component of a
      via-ferrata-style system is the addition of metal ladder style and foot and handholds. These are for areas and
      routes that will see traffic over a long time, making the use of soft materials impractical.

SECTION II – TYPES OF RAPPELLING
   11-56. Rappelling is a method of descending steep terrain using a rope and a means of creating friction to
   control the rate of descent. This provides Soldiers with a safe way to descend terrain that would otherwise
   expose them to very high fall risks.
   11-57. If the descent distance is greater than a rope length (for example, multipitch), multiple, simple fixed
   lines can be linked together with anchors at the top and bottom of each rope. Soldiers can then rappel from
   anchor to anchor and transition from rope to rope until they reach the ground. This method requires many
   resources and numerous personnel to establish and manage safely.
   11-58. Small teams with fewer resources must use the one or two ropes they can carry to rappel the whole
   group from one anchor to a lower one, then retrieve the rope, and repeat the process until the ground is
   reached.



26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               287
Chapter 11



RAPPELLING FUNDAMENTALS
      11-59. Rappelling is a quick method of descent, but it can be extremely dangerous. The dangers include
      anchor failure, equipment failure, and individual error. Carefully select anchors in a mountainous
      environment. In a mountain environment, take great care to load the anchor slowly and to ensure that no
      excessive stress is placed on the anchor. To ensure this, prohibit bounding while rappelling; Soldiers should
      slowly descend. Soldiers should avoid dragging their feet when moving backwards towards the edge as this
      causes rockfall.
      11-60. Soldiers rappelling with weapons should sling them on the back or to the side when wearing packs.
      Soldiers carrying particularly heavy weapons, such as machine guns, sniper rifles, or mortars may need to
      strap them to the top of their pack and use additional techniques described below to make rappelling less
      difficult.
RAPPEL SITE SELECTION
      11-61. Selecting the rappel point depends on factors, such as mission, cover, route, anchor availability, and
      edge composition (for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave
      no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose.
      11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier and
      reduce the likelihood of Soldiers stumbling or falling. Stumbles and falls are likely to increase the risk of
      rope damage on sharp rock as well as increase force exerted on anchors.
      11-63. Rappel sites with suitable loading and off-loading platforms should be selected. Ideally, they are flat
      and allow for anchoring far enough away from the edge that Soldiers do not need to be attached to an anchor
      to prevent accidentally falling off the edge. If this is impossible, use fixed-rope techniques described in
      section I when approaching the rappel point. A staging area large enough to hold the group in a safe place
      nearby is also desirable.
INSTALLATION CONSIDERATIONS
      11-64. The two major factors in deciding how to attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs
      to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both
      characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time.
      11-65. In an operational environment, or during advanced military mountaineering training, ropes must be
      retrievable. This is because there is presumably no other feasible way to negotiate the vertical obstacle, or
      the group would be using it. All people and equipment must rappel, and the rope must be recovered for future
      use. This means that the rope cannot be fixed to the top anchor when the last Soldier begins rappelling.
      11-66. When training basic rappelling, retrieving ropes is not necessary. Appropriate rappel sites for
      inexperienced rappellers should include access between the top and bottom by some other safe means for set
      up and breakdown. This allows for a greater safety margin by using two fixed independent strands for rappel
      ropes. Not only does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical
      rappelling in an operational environment.
      11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in
      chapter 9. All rigging should be inspected by a qualified advanced military mountaineer, at a minimum.
RETRIEVABLE RAPPELS
      11-68. Retrievable rappels can be established using appropriate single-point anchors (such as a tree, boulder,
      horn of rock) using only the rope, or they can be attached to cordelettes, or webbing tied around the anchor
      feature. If other materials are used, then they cannot be retrieved from the bottom.
      11-69. Multipoint anchors require additional materials to establish. This material cannot be retrieved from
      the bottom.
      11-70. The minimum necessary equipment should be used in building retrievable rappel anchors.




288                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Fixed Ropes



Half-Rope Length
   11-71. The simplest and most common method is to just run one end of the rope around anchor feature, and
   then double back stack it until the middle of the rope is around the anchor feature. This ensures both strands
   are the same length. Tie a stopper knot at the bottom end with both strands leaving 12- to 18-inch tails. This
   prevents accidentally rappelling off the end of the rope. The ropes are then thrown or back stacked over the
   edge.
   11-72. Sometimes the rope cannot be routed directly around the anchor. The rope can then be back stacked
   so that the middle of the rope passes through the attachment point for an anchor made from cordelette or
   webbing or clipped to it using a locking carabiner.
   11-73. If a rope could be cut, it is possible to make the system redundant for all but the last rappeller. This
   system is established in the same manner as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with
   both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last
   Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK, and the system is retrievable again.

Full-Length Rope
   11-74. Full-length rappels require two standard-length ropes. Route the end of one rope around or through
   the anchor point and tie a flat double overhand with the ends of both ropes joining them. Double back stack
   the ropes and tie a stopper knot as described above. Using a flat overhand to join the rappel ropes reduces the
   likelihood of the knot being stuck in vegetation of rock features during retrieval.
   11-75. Full-length rappels can be made redundant for all but the last rappeller in the same manner as is
   described above.

Rappel Rope Retrieval
   11-76. Once all Soldiers have reached the bottom and any stopper knots have been untied, the rope can be
   retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. If there are any knots in
   it, they can become jammed in the anchor and prevent rope retrieval. It is a good idea to get excess personnel
   away from the area prior to pulling in case any loose rocks are dislodged above.
   11-77. When pulling the rope on a multipitch rappel, it is a good idea to route the end being pulled through
   the next anchor, so the rope is less likely to be dropped.
RAPPELS WITH FIXED STRANDS
   11-78. Whenever a threat of the installation rope being cut is identified, two fixed independent strands should
   be used. Two strands add redundancy and reduce the likelihood that a fall may occur in a cut rope incident.
   Installations with two fixed independent strands are typically the standard for rappelling training whether a
   hazard has been identified.

Half-Rope Length
   11-79. If using a single anchor, anchor the middle of the rope to it with a bowline knot. If using a pre-
   equalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two
   opposing locking carabiners.

Full-Rope Length
   11-80. Anchor the rappel ropes by tying a bowline knot with the top ends of both ropes.
   11-81. Situations may arise where the distance of anchors from each other, or the distance of the anchors
   from the rappel point, requires using a second rope to construct an anchor, or extend the anchor master point
   closer to the loading platform, allowing for the maximum amount of rope to be utilized for the rappel. In this
   case, tie a fixed loop with the top ends of both ropes, and clip it to the anchor system master point using two
   opposing locking carabiners.

RAPPEL INSTALLATION SPECIAL TECHNIQUES
      11-82. There are a few problems that mountaineers should be prepared to solve related to rappelling. The
      common problems are damaged ropes, short ropes, and the threat of a rope being cut when retrievability is
      necessary.

Damaged Rope
      11-83. Ropes occasionally become damaged but may need to be used until they can be replaced following
      an operation. Mountaineers must be familiar with how to safely use damaged ropes for rappelling.
      11-84. First, tie an overhand knot, isolating the damaged spot in the rope. The rope can then continue to be
      used for many mountaineering tasks. However, the knot in the rope prevents Soldiers from rappelling past.
      11-85. If a retrievable rappel is necessary, the damaged rope can be used as follows. The rope is back stacked
      around the anchor as usual. A fixed bight is tied in the damaged strand near the anchor. That bight is then
      clipped to the nondamaged strand with a locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor
      like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff.
      11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the nondamaged strand and descend the obstacle.

            Note. Rappelling on a single strand creates less friction.

      11-87. Once all Soldiers have rappelled, the damaged strand, or tagline, can be pulled to retrieve the rope.
      The nondamaged strand travels up through the carabiner, around the anchor and back down. More care should
      be taken when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. This
      technique also works when a full-length rappel is necessary and one of the ropes is damaged near the middle.




                          Figure 11-9. Tagline retrievable rappel using a tagline




290                                                  TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                                     Fixed Ropes



Short Rope
   11-88. Sometimes a group may only have one rope that is not long enough to reach the bottom of a cliff, and
   the rope cannot be retrieved because the cliff is taller than a half-rope length.
   11-89. If the group has enough cordelettes or shorter sections of rope, it can solve the problem. To do so, one
   end of the rope is lowered until it is on the ground. Cordelettes are then joined by a single strand to the other
   end until they reach the ground.
   11-90. The installation is then rigged to be retrievable with a tagline (as described in paragraphs 11-83
   through 11-87, page 290). Soldiers can then rappel on the strand of static rope. When personnel are at the
   bottom, the end with the cordelettes can be pulled to retrieve the rope. Take more care when pulling the rope
   because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique.
   11-91. Small units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Rather than carry
   two full-sized ropes to rappel a full-rope length, they can carry one rope and a 6- or 7-mm tagline that is cut
   the same length from a spool, or plan to use joined cordelettes that are spread out amongst their members.

Threat of Cut Rope Using a Retrievable System
   11-92. Some situations may require a retrievable rappel, but a threat to the rope is identified (such as sharp
   rock or falling rock hazard) that cannot be mitigated by simply padding an edge. This problem can be resolved
   by one of two methods.
   11-93. The first involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then attaching a
   tube-style device and locking carabiner tight to the anchor. This effectively fixes both strands. All but the
   last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier uses the attached device and rappels
   carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be
   pulled from below as previously described.
   11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then tying a big
   knot close to the anchor with both strands fixing them. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed
   strands. The last Soldier unties the knot and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but
   one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described.

RAPPELLING TECHNIQUES
   11-95. Different situations call for different rappel attachment techniques. They vary in how much friction
   they produce, the security in which the rappeller is attached to the rope, and whether they allow the rappeller
   to go hands free. The consequence of falling determines the type of attachment to the rope. Terrain severity
   determines how much friction is required to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted
   mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake.
   11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs
   straight, and buttocks parallel to the ground. When carrying equipment or additional weight, a modified
   L-shape is used with the legs slightly lower than the buttocks to compensate for the additional weight. The
   rappeller’s back is straight. Rappellers never let go of the ropes with their brake hand until the rappel is
   complete. Rappellers should keep their feet flat against the surface they are rappelling down and their weight
   fully on the rope throughout the rappel.

Hasty Rappel
   11-97. The hasty rappel technique is only used on low-angle slopes. Its primary advantages are that it is
   simple to learn and execute and requires no specialized equipment. However, take care not to underestimate
   the terrain being negotiated. Application of this technique in terrain that is too steep can have deadly
   consequences. The level of rappeller surefootedness determines the severity of terrain for which this
   technique is appropriate. Gloves can be worn to prevent rope burns.
   11-98. Facing slightly sideways to the anchor, rappellers place the ropes horizontally across their back, under
   their armpits, and palm up. The hand nearest to the anchor is the guide hand, and the other is the brake hand.
   Bending the rope around the body increases friction. (See figure 11-10, page 292.)


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 291
Chapter 11



      11-99. While moving, Soldiers should keep their legs as perpendicular to the slope as possible, leaning into
      the rope. This increases the security of foot placements and reduces the likelihood of a slip and fall.
      11-100. To stop, rappellers rotate their body to face uphill and bring their brake hand across the front of their
      body to their opposite shoulder.




                                           Figure 11-10. Hasty rappel

Munter Hitch Rappel
      11-101. This method provides adequate friction and control and is the simplest and easiest method of
      rappelling to establish on steep terrain when without a standard rappel device. Most often, it is used as a
      backup for when a more efficient device is lost or forgotten.
      11-102. The drawback of using a Munter hitch is that it twists the rope, causing snarl at the bottom that makes
      future use difficult. An experienced Soldier can separate the strands with the brake hand and counter the twist
      of the rope as it feeds through the hitch to lessen this effect. It is not recommended to have multiple Soldiers
      rappel on the same rope using this method. Twisting is lessened if the rappel is on steep terrain and the strands



292                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Fixed Ropes



   do not touch the ground. This allows the twists to undo themselves. Twisting becomes more of a problem if
   the terrain is at a low angle, and the rope is mostly lying on the ground.
   11-103. To use this technique, attach a locking carabiner into a harness. Then tie a Munter hitch in both
   strands of the rappel rope and place it in the locking carabiner. (See figure 11-11.)
   11-104. Descent is controlled in the same way as with the devices described above.




                                   Figure 11-11. Munter hitch rappel

Figure-Eight Descender
   11-105. Using a figure-eight descender provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction
   for use in steep-to-vertical terrain.
   11-106. The advantage of these is that they work well with both larger diameter ropes and static or low-stretch
   ropes. The disadvantages are that they are less versatile, heavier, and bulkier than tube-style devices, which
   serve multiple mountaineering purposes.
   11-107. To rig the device for descent, pass a double bight through the large opening, and then around the
   smaller one. Then attach the figure eight to a harness using a locking carabiner through the small opening.
   (See figure 11-12, page 294.)



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               293
Chapter 11



      11-108. Soldiers assume a typical L-shaped position while rappelling and control their rate of descent with
      the brake strand by slowly feeding slack from below them toward the device. Two hands should be used on
      the brake strand, positioned in front of the body below the device.




                                    Figure 11-12. Figure-eight descender

Tube-Style Devices
      11-109. Using a tube-style device provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction for
      use in steep to vertical terrain.
      11-110. Most climbing teams use these. The advantages are that they can be used for both belaying and
      rappelling with one or two ropes. They are compact and lightweight. They do not twist the ropes as much as
      figure-eight descenders. The disadvantages are that they do not work as smoothly when used with static or
      low-stretch ropes due to the more tightly woven rope sheath and stiffer feel. They also do not typically work
      well on ropes larger than 11 mm in diameter.




294                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                                   Fixed Ropes



   11-111. To rig the device for descent, pinch the rappel rope into a double bight, and then pass one through
   each hole in the tube starting on the side without a wire hanger. Clip a locking carabiner through the wire
   hanger and both bights of rope. Then attach the device to a harness with a locking carabiner so that the brake
   strands are oriented down or toward the intended brake hand. (See figure 11-13.)
   11-112. Descent is controlled in the same way as with figure-eight descenders.




                          Figure 11-13. Rappelling with a tube-style device

Extending Rappel Devices
   11-113. Using an extension moves the rappel device away from the body. This makes it easier to keep two
   hands on the brake strands. It also reduces the chance of straps or clothing from being caught in the device
   and stopping rope from feeding through it. This results in the rappeller becoming stuck on the rope, unable
   to descend, and requires advanced skills to fix. Wearing bulky cold-weather clothing or tactical load-bearing
   harnesses increase the likelihood of this occurring. Extending the device allows for the use of a hands-free
   backup.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               295
Chapter 11



      11-114. To extend a device, create an extension by girth hitching a sling to the harness. Insert the rappel
      ropes into the device as described above and clip them into the extension with a locking carabiner. A basket
      hitch can also be used to create a shorter extension. Under most circumstances, it is recommended to use an
      extension when rappelling in mountainous terrain because it makes controlling descent easier and less
      fatiguing to the core when heavy loads are carried. Rappels using the Munter hitch technique cannot be
      extended.

Hands-Free Backup
      11-115. A hands-free backup is a rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that
      prevent a load from falling should control of a brake strand be lost. To establish a hands-free backup, tie an
      autoblock around the rappel ropes below the device, and attach it to the climber’s harness with a locking
      carabiner. (See figure 11-15, page 300.) Any time an autoblock is used, it must be tested to ensure it grabs
      before starting the rappel. If it does not, more wraps should be added until it does.
      11-116. This allows Soldiers to perform other tasks mid-rappel. The most common example is the first
      rappeller needing to untangle the rope on the way down. During rappelling, Soldiers must prevent the
      autoblock from engaging and stopping their downward progress with one hand while the other feeds rope to
      the device. To engage the autoblock, the Soldier ceases minding the autoblock and it will engage, forcing the
      rappel rope into the brake position. When Soldiers are ready to continue rappelling, they resume control of
      the brake strands with both hands and disengage the autoblock. Descent can then continue.
      11-117. Using an autoblock can provide a backup in case Soldier drops the brake strand. However, it is not
      the best back-up technique for large groups of rappellers to use given the additional time it takes to establish,
      manage, and untie from the rope.

Rucksack Support
      11-118. An extension can be used to make rappelling with heavy rucksacks easier. (See figure 11-14.) This
      is done by rigging for rappel with an extension. Then Soldiers can girth hitch a sling to the frame of the pack
      and attach it to the locking carabiner in their rappel device using any carabiner. This allows the device to
      support some of the weight of the pack and reduce core fatigue while the Soldier rappels.




296                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                       Fixed Ropes




                         Figure 11-14. Extended device and hands-free break

Belaying Rappellers
   11-119. The fireman’s belay can be used to prevent rappellers from falling should they lose control of the
   brake strand. This technique involves a Soldier loosely holding the rappel rope and watching the rappeller
   from the bottom. If the rappeller falls, the Soldier pulls on the rope hard. This forces the device to brake and
   stop the rappeller’s fall. When the rappeller regains footing and control of the brake strand, tension is released,
   allowing them to continue rappelling.
RAPPEL SITE OPERATION
   11-120. Because of the inherent dangers of rappelling, special care must be taken to ensure safe and
   successful descents.
   11-121. High-consequence rappel sites must be established and managed with the supervision of a qualified
   advanced military mountaineer or higher.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  297
Chapter 11



Duties and Responsibilities of the Rappel Site Supervisor
      11-122. An experienced mountaineer should be overall in charge of any movement on a rope system. This
      person ensures safety checks are completed and that there is a plan for the flow of personnel onto and off the
      system and is the one responsible for the entire event.
      11-123. Duties of rappel site supervisors are as follows:
          • Ensures that the anchors are sound, and the knots are properly tied.
          • Ensures that loose rock and debris are cleared from the loading platform.
          • Allows only one Soldier per rappel point on the loading platform at a time and ensures that the
              rappel point is run orderly.
          • Ensures that each Soldier is properly prepared for the rappel: helmet with chinstrap fastened and
              harness or rappel seat is correct (if required). They ensure that the rappeller is hooked up to the rope
              correctly and is aware of the proper braking position.
          • Ensures that the proper signals or commands are used.
          • Dispatches each Soldier down the rope.
          • Ensures the ropes will pull nicely when the rappel is retrieved; gets the joining knot past the edge,
              if necessary.
          • Ensures safety lines or personal safeties for rappel site personnel are established and Soldiers remain
              clipped to them when necessary.

Communication
      11-124. Radio communication from the top to the bottom should be used to ensure all ropes touch the ground
      and someone is providing a fireman’s belay before the rappeller commits to the rappel.
      11-125. Loud voice commands for anything other than warning of falling objects should be discouraged, as
      they are unnecessary and tactically inappropriate. However, if they are used in training, they should be clear,
      concise, and understood by all participants.
      11-126. Soldiers can determine if the rappeller ahead of them is clear of the rope by testing it for tension. If
      someone is still attached to the rope, then the rope will be tight. If it is slack, the next rappeller can hook up.

Increasing Speed and Efficiency
      11-127. All Soldiers should prepare themselves for rappelling at a staging area a short distance from the
      rappel site. Ideally, all harness and rigging other than attachment to the rope is conducted there, prior to
      arrival at the site. This will make rappelling groups more efficient.
      11-128. The simplest method of speeding up rappelling is to instruct all rappellers to introduce slack into the
      system when they reach the bottom. This can be done by pulling slack through their device, or rappelling a
      couple steps further than necessary, and then stepping back toward the cliff. This will allow the next Soldier
      to hook up while they are unhooking from the system.
      11-129. Rappel devices and locking carabiners may be collected and stacked on the ropes by the site
      supervisor prior to beginning rappelling. Soldiers then only need to attach their extension to the device before
      rappelling.
      11-130. Retrievable rappels during tactical operations or advanced military mountaineer training can be sped
      up by establishing the rappel as usual, then tying a BHK knot in the ropes near the anchor. This fixes both
      strands. Soldiers can now rappel on each strand, doubling the rate that Soldiers can descend. This technique
      may not be appropriate if sharp rocks are present on the rappel route.
MULTIPITCH RAPPELLING
      11-131. Descent routes during tactical operations and advanced military mountaineer training often involve
      a series of rappels to reach the bottom. This requires additional techniques to ensure safety and efficiency of
      descent. The distance between anchor points is called a pitch.
      11-132. When conducting multiple rappels, the standard technique of extending the device should be used
      and the first Soldier down should use an autoblock for backup. Additionally, a second locking carabiner


298                                                    TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                     Fixed Ropes



   should be placed in each rappeller’s extension sling. They will use this to attach themselves to the next anchor
   point prior to detaching from the rappel rope to allow the next rappeller to descend. In this way, they remain
   safely attached to the rappel rope or an anchor point. Once the first rappeller is safely anchored below,
   preferably out of the way of possible rock or ice fall, they fireman belay the remaining rappellers one at a
   time down to this point. Once the last Soldier is secured to the second anchor point, the rope is pulled, and
   the next pitch is rigged for rappel.
   11-133. Soldiers can stack devices rigged for the rappel prior to the first one leaving, or each can hook up
   independently in turn. Typically, the most experienced members rappel first so that they can establish the
   next rappel anchor down. Stacking devices allows the leader to inspect all other Soldiers’ hookups prior to
   leaving, reducing the chance of error.
   11-134. The most difficult aspect of multipitch rappelling is when descending into unknown or unfamiliar
   terrain. The first Soldier down must effectively manage the ropes during the descent and have the necessary
   equipment for establishing the next anchor point. If adequate anchor points are found before nearing the ends
   of the rope, the decision must be made whether to use it or continue lower in hopes of finding something
   further down. Although it is most efficient to gain the maximum distance from each rappel, if a safe anchor
   point cannot be found lower, it will become necessary to ascend the ropes, taking much more time.

SECTION III – ASCENDING AND DESCENDING TRANSITIONS
   11-135. Many situations exist during which advanced military mountaineers must be able to change direction
   of travel while hanging from a fixed rope. The direction change can be planned or unplanned and involve
   single-strand or double-strand systems. Whenever mountaineers’ duties or tasks may require them to make
   hanging transitions, they should use single-strand systems that allow them to use safer special equipment and
   techniques. However, they should also be prepared to transition from rappelling to ascending on two-rope
   systems using equipment routinely carried.
   11-136. Transitioning while hanging on a rope should only be done by level 2 or higher mountaineers who
   have received formal training in ascending and descending transition techniques.

TECHNIQUES
   11-137. Conducting transition techniques without special equipment is not recommended. Not using the
   appropriate equipment will require mountaineers to transition alone and uninspected, utilizing a complex
   series of rigging steps while at risk of catastrophic fall. This situation should be avoided whenever possible
   and only attempted by mountaineers who are experienced in ascending and descending and load-transfer techniques.

SPECIAL EQUIPMENT
   11-138. Mechanical ascender—see paragraphs 11-15 through 11-18, page 277 for more description. Whereas
   these devices are not necessary for other fixed-rope movement situations, they should always be used when
   hanging transitions are planned.
   11-139. Assisted braking device (ABD)—the ABD allows mountaineers to change direction without
   changing primary attachment to a fixed rope. It can be used with single-rope systems for belaying, rappelling,
   or capturing progress during ascending. The ABD uses a toothless cam to grip the rope when loaded. Rope
   can be pulled through it to capture progress or allowed to move in the opposite direction under the control of
   a release lever providing variable friction. ABDs are not recommended for use in a winter environment
   because they can get jammed up with snow and fail to work properly. (See figure 11-15, page 300.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                299
Chapter 11




                                   Figure 11-15. Assisted braking device

TRANSITIONS ON SINGLE-STRAND SYSTEMS
      11-140. The following situations require or are likely to require ascent or descent transitions while hanging:
          • Descent route finding or reconnaissance. Obstacles such as overhanging cliffs longer than a rope
              length can prevent continued descent. Mountaineers may need to descend numerous possible routes
              before finding the best way down. When dead ends are discovered, they must ascend back up before
              trying the next path down.
          • Top-down fixed rope establishment when a mountaineer realizes that their path is a dead end and
              must ascend to re-route the rope on a different descent path.
          • Confined space reconnaissance. This involves descending into wells, tunnels, or shafts to look for
              caches or evidence of enemy activity, and then ascending back to the surface after.
      11-141. Whenever an ascent or descent transition is considered likely, then a single strand of fixed rope
      should be used. This allows the use of an ABD and mechanical ascender to establish the safest and most
      efficient transition possible.

Rapid Ascent and Descent Method
      11-142. This fixed-rope attachment method allows mountaineers to either travel up a rope and then transition
      to descent, or descend a rope and transition to ascent, all while remaining safely attached to the rope.

Transitioning from Ascent to Descent
      11-143. Route the fixed rope through the ABD properly, then attach an ABD to the harness with a locking
      carabiner. Attach an ascender to the rope above it with a cordelette or other long material hanging from it.
      Use this material to create a fixed loop for a foot stirrup. (See figure 11-16.)
      11-144. Ascending—to use the system, place one hand on the ascender and one on the free strand of rope.
      Place one foot into the foot stirrup. The foot used should be on the same side as the hand on the ascender.
      Pull down on the ascender while simultaneously standing up in the foot stirrup and pulling rope slack up
      through the ABD. Once the rope is tight, sit down and the ABD will grip the rope and capture progress. Slide
      the ascender back up to full arm’s length away and repeat. It is helpful to push both down and back with the
      leg when using the foot stirrup to keep body weight forward.
      11-145. Ascending (variation)—the pull strand of rope can be redirected into a carabiner attached to the
      ascender to change to a downward pull as shown below; however, this can limit the amount of vertical gain
      with each movement. (See figure 11-17, page 302.)
      11-146. Stopping on the rope—back-up stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope close to the ABD
      whenever the mountaineer stops on the rope for a period. This is especially true if the rope is unweighted.



300                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Fixed Ropes



    11-147. Transitioning—to transition to descent, the mountaineer only needs to disconnect the ascender and
    stow it.
    11-148. Descending—descent by rappel can then be conducted using the already attached ABD. Follow the
    manufacturer’s instructions for use. (See figure 11-16.)




                           Figure 11-16. Rapid ascent and descent method

Transitioning from Descent to Ascent
    11-149. Route the fixed rope through the ABD properly, then attach it to the harness with a locking carabiner.
    11-150. Descending—rappel using the ABD.
    11-151. Stopping on the rope—back-up stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope close to the ABD
    whenever the mountaineer stops on the rope for a period. This is especially true if the rope is unweighted.
    11-152. Transitioning—to transition to ascent, the mountaineer only needs to attach an ascender with a
    hanging foot stirrup to the fixed rope.
    11-153. Ascending—ascending can be conducted using the methods described in paragraph 11-154 or 11-155.

Improvised Rapid Ascent and Descent Method
    11-154. The same process for transitioning from ascending to descending, or descending to ascending, can
    be used if either piece of specialized equipment is not available (the ascender or ABD) using other commonly
    carried equipment. The ascender can be replaced with a prusik, and a carabiner attached to a fixed loop tied
    close with the tails. The tails are then used to create the foot stirrup. The ABD can be replaced with a belay
    or rappel device that can be used in autolocking mode. The device is attached to the Soldier’s harness in
    autolocking mode (see figure 10-20, page 266, for rigging techniques); then the brake strand is routed through
    a carabiner attached to an ascender (or prusik, as described above in this paragraph).




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               301
Chapter 11



      11-155. These improvised techniques require extensive practice before use, as they are somewhat more
      complex to rig and more difficult to operate during ascending. Soldiers employing them should use back-up
      attachments to the rope throughout the transition process to prevent a fall should a rigging mistake be made.
TRANSITIONS ON TWO-STRAND SYSTEMS
      11-156. The following situations require an unplanned transition from rappelling to ascending while hanging
      on a double-strand system:
          • The rappel ropes do not reach the ground, and there are no anchors available from which to establish
              another rappel pitch. Often, it is not possible to see if the ropes reach the ground due to overhanging
              terrain until it is too late. The rappeller must then ascend back to the top.
          • Occasionally during multipitch rappelling, the lead mountaineer misjudges anchor possibilities
              below and rappels past the last viable anchor on the pitch. This requires ascending back up to that
              anchor before the rest of the group can rappel down and the next pitch can be rigged.

Prusik Ascent Method
      11-157. Mountaineers can transition to ascending from rappelling using the prusik ascent technique described
      in this chapter.
      11-158. Descending—ensure stopper knots are tied in the rappel ropes. Use a basket hitch to extend the
      device and an autoblock for a hands-free backup. A shorter extension will make transitioning easier.
      11-159. Stopping on the rope—when mountaineers realize they cannot reach the ground, they should engage
      their autoblock and look for anchors that can be used to establish another rappel pitch. If none are available,
      or they must ascend to reach one, they will need to transition to ascent.
      11-160. Transitioning—to transition to ascent, mountaineers should tie a fixed loop a few feet below their
      autoblock with both rappel ropes and clip it to their harness using a locking carabiner. This serves as a backup
      for the whole transition process. The progress capture can then be tied around both ropes above the rappel
      device and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner. Once double-checked, mountaineers then release
      the autoblock and rappel until the progress captures prusik entirely supports their weight. The rappel device
      and autoblock can now be disconnected from the rappel ropes and stowed. The mountaineer then attaches
      the progress prusik to the rappel ropes below the progress capture and establishes a foot stirrup.
      11-161. Ascending—ascending is conducted as with prusik ascent. Back-up knots should be tied every 10 to
      15 feet and attached to the harness prior to untying the previous ones.

Other Methods
      11-162. Additional techniques for transitioning from rappelling to ascending exist. Some are more efficient
      but heavily dependent on specific circumstances and available special equipment. It is not feasible to cover
      them all in this training circular. Seek additional formal mountaineering training to expand upon the
      techniques covered above.
OTHER TRANSITION SITUATIONS AND TECHNIQUES
      11-163. Other more complex situations requiring ascent and descent transitions, such as climber rescue, are
      more involved and beyond the scope of this chapter. To obtain formal training or other specific
      transition-related problems that advanced military mountaineers may expect to encounter in the performance
      of their duties, consult with qualified mountaineering instructors.
      11-164. Opportunities for formal training are available from one of the Army’s three mountain training
      organizations by unit request (see chapter 2).
      11-165. An experienced level 3 mountaineer should supervise all sustainment and improvement training on
      these transition techniques.
