                                                Chapter 12
                       Hauling and Lowering Techniques
   Mountain warfare requires moving Soldiers, weapons, and equipment up, over, and down
   steep, rugged terrain. It is vital that Soldiers understand the principles and fundamental
   concepts of hauling and lowering heavy loads both efficiently and safely.

SECTION I – HAULING TECHNIQUES
   12-1. Mountain operations involve many situations that require hauling systems. A hauling system is a
   technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates
   increased mechanical advantage (MA) and captures progress. Properly using hauling systems allows Soldiers
   to move heavy loads through terrain obstacles that would have been impossible to overcome otherwise.
   Common situations requiring these systems are equipment recovery, resupply, and rescue operations.
   Choosing the right system for a given situation requires understanding the principles of MA, categories of
   systems, and solid judgement.

MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE
   12-2. A mechanical advantage is a reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the
   cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical
   advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques.
   The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary to move a load vertically. This makes
   hauling heavy loads easier. When choosing and constructing a hauling system, the goal is to use the lowest
   level of MA to move the load. As MA increases, efficiency and load sensitivity decrease. Efficiency is lost
   throughout the system anytime the rope touches a surface (including the edge of the cliff), moves through
   carabiners or pulleys, and rubs on itself in the system. Load sensitivity is the ability of the Soldier pulling on
   the rope to feel what is happening to the load on the end of the rope. For example, a Soldier pulling a heavy
   load up a slope by hand will know immediately if the load becomes stuck on an obstacle. However, a Soldier
   moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the
   system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time,
   materials, and personnel to construct and operate. The intent is not to make easy work of moving the load.
   The lowest level of MA is desired to maximize load sensitivity, efficiency, and time.
   12-3. The more MA a rope system produces, the less efficient it will be. For example, a Soldier operating a
   5:1 system only needs to exert 1/5 of the pulling force to move the load. However, that Soldier will need to
   pull 5 feet of rope through the system for the load to move 1 foot. A balance between work and efficiency
   must be achieved when selecting an appropriate MA for a given situation.

HAULING SYSTEM COMPONENTS
   12-4. The hauling system has five basic components. Understanding how they work to move the load together
   (see the list below) allows Soldiers to achieve greater efficiency during hauling:
        • Anchors—the anchors required for hauling a heavy load must be unquestionable (see chapter 9).
             Anchors should be located away from the edge of the slope or cliff to maximize the platform and
             working space.
        • Load—the equipment, weapons, or casualty to be hauled up the terrain.
        • Load strand—rope that serves as the connection to the load.
        • Pull strand—rope to which pulling force is applied.
        • Progress capture (ratchet)—hauling systems require a method of maintaining lift distance gained. A
             progress capture will only allow one-way rope movement and will maintain tension on the mainline.
             This may be because the hauler needs to move to the edge for communication or simply because the
             system has collapsed completely, and pulleys need to be reset. Progress captures can be created




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                 303
Chapter 12



               using friction hitches, such as a prusik, or mechanical devices, such as a rope grab or pulley with a
               built-in ratchet. Some plaquette and ABDs may be used, but they may cause an increase in friction.
          •    Moveable friction hitch or rope grab device (tractor)—these friction hitches or devices allow the
               system to collapse toward the anchor, and then are reset outward toward the load to allow continual
               hauling. Take care with respect to rope-grab devices with teeth. Over tensioning a stuck load with
               these devices can tear the sheath of the rope.
          •    Force—hauling systems are multipliers of force. They are expressed in terms of output versus input
               (for example, 2:1 and 3:1). This means that when Soldiers pull on the haul strand, the unit of force
               they exert is multiplied throughout the system until it reaches the load. When appropriate, multiple
               Soldiers may be used on the haul strand to increase the initial force put into the system.
      12-5. Static or low-stretch ropes should be used for hauling operations whenever possible. Dynamic ropes
      are less efficient due to increased rope stretch.

MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE CALCULATION
      12-6. It is vital that Soldiers constructing and operating hauling systems understand how to calculate MA.
      This ensures systems are constructed correctly and that Soldiers understand the forces they are applying.
      Memorizing rope systems does not constitute deliberate decision making or guarantee the correct solution to
      a problem. It is difficult to calculate all the factors that take away from MA. However, we can easily calculate
      the ideal MA to make decisions.
      12-7. To calculate the ideal MA of a constructed system, the tension method—or T-Method—is used. This
      method assigns one unit of tension, identified as T, to the pull strand of the system. That unit is then followed
      through the system to the load. To calculate the theoretical MA, compare the amount of tension the load
      receives to the initial input of tension. (See figure 12-1 and figure 12-2, page 306.)
      12-8. Static or low-stretch ropes should be used for lowering operations whenever possible. When dynamic
      ropes are used, care should be taken to preload the system prior to edge transfer due to increased rope stretch.

CATEGORIES OF HAULING SYSTEMS
      12-9. The three categories of hauling systems are simple, compound, and complex.
SIMPLE HAULING SYSTEM CHARACTERISTICS
      12-10. Simple hauling systems can be identified by the following characteristics:
          • One rope moving continuously and alternately between fixed and traveling pulleys.
          • Any traveling pulleys move toward the anchor at the same speed.
          • Examples are simple 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, and 5:1 systems. (See figures 12-3 and 12-4, and figure 12-5,
               page 308.)

                   Figure 12-3. Simple 2:1 hauling system




                   Figure 12-4. Simple 3:1 hauling system



26 November 2025               TC 3-97.61                                     307
Chapter 12




                                  Figure 12-5. Simple 5:1 hauling system

COMPOUND HAULING SYSTEM CHARACTERISTICS
      12-11. Compound hauling systems can be identified by the following characteristics:
          • One simple system acting on another simple system.
          • Any traveling pulleys move toward the anchor at different speeds.
          • Examples are compound 6:1 and 9:1 systems. (See figures 12-6 and 12-7.)




                               Figure 12-6. Compound 6:1 hauling system

                              Figure 12-7. Compound 9:1 hauling system

COMPLEX HAULING SYSTEM CHARACTERISTICS
   12-12. Complex hauling systems can be identified by the following characteristics:
       • Systems that do not fit into either category.
       • Examples are complex 5:1 and 7:1 systems.
       • These systems have limited practical application for military operations and, therefore, are beyond
           the scope of this training circular.

TECHNIQUES TO REDUCE FRICTION
   12-13. Friction reduces efficiency of rope movement and can drastically reduce MA. It is important to
   identify points of friction within the system and strive to reduce them. Efficiency is lost throughout the system
   anytime the rope touches hardware. Friction can be minimized by using pulleys. Pulleys are used to change
   direction in rope systems. Pulleys should be small, lightweight, and rated for mountaineering applications.
   They should accommodate the largest diameter of rope being used. Pulleys are made with several bearings,
   different-sized sheaves (wheels), and metal alloy side plates. (See figure 12-8, page 310.) Always avoid
   plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point
   along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than the rope’s diameter
   to maintain high rope strength. Pulleys with side plates designed to accommodate prusik knots are referred
   to as prusik minding pulleys. These pulleys are designed with tolerances that allow the ropes to run through
   them but block the passage of a prusik hitch, preventing it from being caught in the pulley.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 309
Chapter 12




                                         Figure 12-8. Types of pulleys

      12-14. Pulleys are estimated to be approximately 90-percent efficient, while carabiners are considered only
      60-percent efficient. The difference between a system that uses pulleys at direction changes and the same
      system that only uses carabiners is significant. If the team only has a few pulleys, they should be used at the
      direction changes closest to the system’s haul strand. Pulleys in these locations will maximize the force put
      into the system initially and carry 90-percent efficiency farther through the system.
      12-15. Friction also occurs where the mainline contacts the edge of the slope or cliff. If a suitable anchor can
      be found near the edge, this friction point can be minimized. The mainline can be lifted and routed through
      a high directional at the top of the slope or cliff to reduce rope contact and friction at the edge. (See
      figure 12-9.)

                                       Figure 12-9. High directional

VERTICAL HAULING AND A-FRAME
   12-16. The vertical hauling line is an installation used to move heavy equipment and supplies up vertical or
   near-vertical terrain. The vertical haul line is constructed to eliminate the friction caused by the loads
   contacting the terrain, rope friction at the cliff edge, and to increase the efficiency of moving loads. Although
   no real theoretical MA is gained, the function of the system is to reduce the friction against terrain. This
   system is more of a permanent installation and is most often used on a main supply line. The description
   below is generalized and based on concepts. Soldiers should seek further instruction and training prior to
   system use.
   12-17. The first and most important task is to determine where to construct the vertical hauling line. (See
   figure 12-10, page 312.) The site must have a top anchor that is secure enough to hold the system and load.
   Loading and unloading platforms should be easily accessible, natural platforms that provide a safe working
   area. Most sites will require the construction of an A-frame at the cliff edge to suspend the load away from



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 311
Chapter 12



      the cliff face. The site should also have sufficient clearance to allow for space between the slope and pulley
      rope for easy hauling of equipment.
      12-18. A-frames should be secured to an anchor behind the edge. (See figure 12-11.) A master point is created
      in the apex of the A-frame, the leg bottoms joined with cord and dug into the ground. (See chapter 13 for
      A-frame construction.) A rope is joined into a continuous loop and placed into a pulley in the master point
      so that the loop reaches the base of the cliff. The A-frame is positioned so that it is leaning out over the edge.
      This allows loads to hang freely during hauling. Loads are attached to the rope and hauled upward to the cliff
      top. This specific system requires time and experience to construct and operate. It should only be used if
      other options are unavailable.




                                         Figure 12-10. Vertical haul line

                                Figure 12-11. A-frame or master point

REDIRECTED HAULING SYSTEMS
   12-19. Some situations may require redirecting the hauling system away from the pathway of the load. This
   is done when the characteristics of the terrain allow for more work or pull space in an alternate or
   perpendicular direction. It can be achieved by first routing the load strand through an anchor to change
   direction. From this point, the hauling system can be constructed as before but using the more optimal
   workspace. This workspace makes pulling easier. When sufficient rope is available, longer systems can be
   constructed, reducing the number of resets needed during operation. A second technique involves
   constructing the hauling system in line with the load strand, but then redirecting just the hauling strand
   through a change in direction at the anchor. This can also be built upon with the use of piggybacked systems.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                              313
Chapter 12



OFFSET COMPOUND HAULING SYSTEMS
      12-20. Offset compound hauling systems involve attaching a second, separate hauling system to the haul
      strand of the first system. This technique allows for creating systems that collapse at relatively the same time,
      which minimizes resets. It also allows the haul team to operate further back from the edge increasing
      workspace. This technique requires sufficient rope length to construct. (See figure 12-12.)




                     Figure 12-12. Redirected and offset compound hauling system

      12-21. Operating and constructing hauling systems require training, experience, and judgement. Soldiers
      must understand both the advantages and disadvantages of using MA to apply these skills correctly.
      Efficiency can be improved by making practical and simple changes during operation when conditions change.

SECTION II – LOWERING TECHNIQUES
   12-22. A lowering system is a technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain
   in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. These sorts of systems are used to
   control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both high-
   and low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Lowering a victim or a load is always preferred over hauling if the
   terrain and situation allows. No two situations are identical. Each new situation will dictate which lowering
   techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe
   and efficient solution to the problem.

LOWERING CONCEPTS
   12-23. There are many devices and techniques available depending on the weight of the load. The bottom
   line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load.
   Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken,
   selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred.
   12-24. All lowering systems should be closed by securing the free end of the rope (the end not attached to
   the load). This prevents lowering the load off the end of the rope if the distance of the lower versus the length
   of rope is misjudged.
   12-25. When lowering Soldiers, a hands-free backup for the system should be used. (See figure 11-15,
   page 300.) This can be achieved in multiple ways. Hands-free backups provide additional measures of
   protection against human error and allow the Soldier or team operating the lowering system flexibility while
   controlling the brake strand.

TECHNIQUES AND DEVICES FOR CREATING FRICTION
   12-26. There are numerous ways to create friction for lowering. The least technical solution to safely lower
   the load is the goal. Three basic methods are the terrain feature, Munter hitch, and redirected belay device.
TERRAIN FEATURE
   12-27. This method involves simply wrapping the rope attached to the load around a natural object, such as
   a tree or boulder. (See figure 12-13, page 316.) The number of wraps depends on the amount of friction
   desired. This technique is used for gentle, low-angle terrain, when speed is needed, or when equipment is in
   short supply. It also provides variable friction but may often require more than one Soldier on the brake strand
   to operate safely.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 315
Chapter 12




                                          Figure 12-13. Terrain lower

MUNTER HITCH
      12-28. The Munter hitch provides enough friction for a one-person load. The Munter hitch can be easily
      converted to a super Munter if more friction is desired. (See figure 12-14.)

            Note. Take care not to open the gate of a fully loaded carabiner. This could cause potential failure
            of the carabiner.

      12-29. The super Munter provides an enormous amount of friction; it is used for lowering only. In most
      circumstances, the super Munter provides more friction than needed. Therefore, its use is limited to when a
      single Soldier is lowering a heavy load.

REDIRECTED BELAY DEVICE
   12-30. A redirected belay device provides enough friction for up to two people and causes fewer twists in the

TECHNIQUES FOR CREATING HANDS-FREE BACKUP
      12-31. Hands-free backups are an important component of lowering systems. They provide a critical element
      of safety when Soldiers are being lowered. There are two main options for creating hands-free backups: a
      friction hitch on the load strand or friction hitch on the brake strand.
      12-32. Friction hitches on the load strand are used when the Soldier operating the lowering system does not
      have a harness on. (See figure 12-16.) This can be achieved by tying a prusik with the middle of a cordelette
      to the lowering rope, then clipping a fixed loop tied with the tails to the master point of the anchor. If the
      backup must be releasable, a releasable knot such as a Munter mule can be used instead of a fixed loop.
      Deciding which technique to use is based off the terrain and the situation. Soldiers must be careful to keep
      the prusik close to the Munter hitch during the lower so that it does not grab the lowering rope and stop the
      operation unintentionally. They must also ensure that the wraps of the prusik do not become loose. This could
      prevent the prusik from automatically gripping the rope if control of the lower is lost. This requires careful
      operation from a single rescuer or the assistance of a second Soldier to mind the prusik.

                       Figure 12-16. Friction hitch on load strand (releasable)

   12-33. Friction hitches on the brake strand require the Soldier operating the lowering system to be wearing a
   harness. (See figure 12-17, page 320, and figure 12-18, page 321.) The preferred technique is an autoblock
   in a carabiner attached to the belay loop of the harness. This technique allows for Soldier flexibility in knot

CONCEPTS FOR PASSING A KNOT

                                    Knot Pass Special Note

       • A wide array of situations require a knot pass. It is not feasible to cover them in-depth
         in this training circular.
       • The conduct of a safe knot pass with a lowering system under tension can be
         complicated and technical. It should be conducted or overseen by a level 2
         mountaineer.
       • Seek qualified instruction to gain proficiency in the skills mentioned below.




26 November 2025                            TC 3-97.61                                               321
Chapter 12



      12-34. Situations arise when a knot must be passed through the lowering system. This can occur when there
      is a damaged section of the rope that has been isolated with a knot or when ropes have been joined to lower
      longer distances. If passing a knot is necessary, it is usually conducted or overseen by a level 2 mountaineer.
      It is preferable to construct the lowering system to facilitate passing the knot prior to beginning the lower.
      (See figure 12-19.)




                             Figure 12-19. Isolating a damaged section of rope

      12-35. The simplest way to pass the knot occurs when the terrain and situation facilitate safely unweighting
      the lowering system temporarily. This is generally in low-angle terrain where most of the load is resting on
      the ground. This unweighting enables creates enough slack to place a new friction hitch or device behind the
      knot, and then remove original friction hitch or device from in front of the knot, so that lowering can continue.
      12-36. If the terrain and weight of the load do not allow the lowering system to be safely unweighted, a
      weighted load transfer is required to pass the knot. These techniques are best learned with formal hands-on
      training and should only be conducted by level 2 and 3 mountaineers.
      12-37. The construction and operation of lowering systems requires training, experience, and judgement.
      Soldiers and leaders must understand what they are doing and why they are doing it. Strive to use the right
      amount of friction for the terrain, situation, and load.

                                                     Chapter 13
                                 Mountain Stream Crossing
   In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter
   across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of
   either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint
   potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct
   route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle
   involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach
   their objective.

SECTION I – MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
   13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold
   waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation
   of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous.
   13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an
   end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to
   protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum.
   13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or
   streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate
   route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable.
   Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing
   mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level.
   13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and
   is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as
   danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many
   techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed
   of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment.

RECONNAISSANCE
   13-5. Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal
   that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they
   may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation.
   13-6. Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated
   positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes
   better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and
   examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted.
   13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure
   to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize
   drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls,
   or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation
   team’s descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are
   preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place
   landmines and improvised explosive devices.
   13-8. The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause
   water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred,
   as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows
   clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on



26 November 2025                                     TC 3-97.61                                                      323
Chapter 13



      the need for concealment, proficiency of troops, nature of the terrain, characteristics of the water obstacle,
      enemy disposition and capabilities (such as minefields on far banks), and the need for speed.
      13-9. A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally
      yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since
      the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves.
      13-10. Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous
      braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of
      cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand
      depending on the riverbed composition.
      13-11. Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water. Banks that
      are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or
      simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278).
      13-12. Logjams and other large obstructions present their own hazards. Floating debris, while often hung up
      in shallow spots, can potentially hit personnel in the water. Water flowing around logjams creates riverbed
      erosion and swift waters. If crossing upstream of logjams, ensure that Soldiers are far enough away to react
      and do not become entangled in branches beneath the water surface.
      13-13. When possible, cross with ample overwatch in place for support and with an approach that offers
      minimal detection by enemy forces.

PREPARATION OF TROOPS AND EQUIPMENT
      13-14. Special considerations should be taken for personnel and the items they carry for the mission. Water
      can weigh personnel down, as can the uniform posture when dealing with submerged equipment. Most of the
      preparation should happen long before entering the water, with only special considerations executed in a
      short halt prior. Preparation should include—
          • Water-sensitive items. Wrap radios, binoculars, documents, maps, and any extra clothing in
               waterproof bags (trash bags also work well), if available. These bags also provide additional
               flotation, should Soldiers find themselves in deeper water than expected. Pack these dry clothing
               items on top, along with other necessary items (such as munitions, sensitive items, and machine gun
               tripods) quickly before getting into the water.
          • Uniform. If the tactical situation permits, a crossing can be made with minimal clothing. Once on
               the far side, Soldiers can change into dry clothing. Normally, a complete uniform is worn. Unblouse
               boots and untuck shirts. Ensure all pockets are buttoned or closed. If water has a point of entry,
               ensure that it has an easy way to exit. Trapped water can weigh down personnel who may need to
               swim at a moment’s notice. Socks and boot insoles can be removed and stowed. Once on the far
               bank, boots can be drained, and wet socks replaced.
          • Load-carrying equipment and body armor. Unbuckle fighting load carrier or other modular
               equipment and be prepared to remove, if necessary. It is difficult to remove a buckled harness in the
               water during an emergency.
          • Helmets can be removed and stowed, but if Soldiers fall in water with debris, the helmet protects
               their head from impacts.
          • The rucksack should be worn well up on the shoulders and snug, so it does not flop around and
               cause imbalance. The waist and chest straps must be unbuckled so Soldiers can rid themselves of
               the rucksack if they are swept off their feet and must resort to swimming. Securing everything inside
               the pack will help if it needs to be discarded. It is easier to find one large pack than several smaller
               items.
          • Weapons should be secured to the pack or slung over the shoulder.

SECTION II – CROSSING TECHNIQUES
      13-15. Several techniques and methods exist to successfully negotiate water obstacles. Variables that can
      influence the most optimal crossing style are water depth and speed, confidence around water and swimming




324                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                     Mountain Stream Crossing



   proficiency, riverbed surface, daylight or night crossing, and resources available. When available, a dry
   crossing is always preferred.
   13-16. In this section, we will discuss three different variations that work well for mountain stream crossings:
   the individual crossing, team crossing, and belayed crossing.

INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
   13-17. Whenever possible, and when the degree of experience permits, streams should be forded individually
   for a speedier crossing. (See figure 13-1.) The average Soldier should be able to cross most streams with mild
   to moderate currents and water depths of not much more than knee-deep using proper techniques. An
   advantage to the individual crossing is that there is nothing to recover once Soldiers have performed the
   crossing. A disadvantage is the time of exposure for the individual and time invested for the element to
   negotiate the water obstacle.
   13-18. The water depth at a suitable crossing site should be about knee height or below, and the water’s speed
   should be mild to moderate. The velocity of the water and the presence of debris are used to determine the
   effect, if any, on the ford’s condition. Currents are categorized as—ν Swift (more than 1.5 meters [5 feet] per
   second). ν Moderate (1 to 1.5 meters [3 to 5 feet] per second). ν Slow (less than 1 meter [3 feet] per second).
   13-19. Individuals should look upstream for obstacles, and pick up a good athletic stance, angling their body
   slightly perpendicular to the current. Adjust to a more parallel stance and lean upstream if the current is
   stronger.
   13-20. Pick a location slightly downstream to the Soldier’s position. Traveling at 90° causes Soldiers to fight
   the current rather than work with the flow of water as much as possible. Always lead off with the downstream
   foot and take small steps while keeping the feet close to the ground. Avoid moving one foot before securing
   the other foot, and do not cross legs. This will decrease the likelihood of moving water throwing the Soldier
   off balance. Additionally, it will allow the Soldier to explore the riverbed for obstacles such as holes, rocks,
   shoals, or debris for optimal management. If a sizeable rock is found, Soldiers should always step on the
   upstream side of it. Water cresting the top and sides of rocks picks up speed, digging around and on the
   downstream side. The integrity of these rocks is unknown and could roll downstream at any time.
   13-21. For added stability, using a third contact point is encouraged. A long stick or staff, ice axe, or tree
   limb could be used. By placing the end of the third point as upstream as possible, Soldiers can create a tripod,
   while exercising a body position described above to create a streamlined signature. The third point can be
   useful as a probe, searching for obstacles and depth.




                                     Figure 13-1. Individual crossing




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                325
Chapter 13



TEAM CROSSINGS
      13-22. When the water level begins to reach thigh deep, or anytime the current is too swift for personnel to
      safely perform an individual crossing, a team crossing may be used. With each of these methods, have a
      leader call each step. One advantage to the team crossing is reduced exposure time for higher concentration
      of personnel, and there is no equipment to recover once Soldiers have performed the crossing. Disadvantages
      for all team crossings include a lack of interval for free movement and negotiation of riverbed makeup.
      Additionally, the close concentration of personnel makes them an easy target for direct or indirect enemy
      fires. The speed at which Soldiers can move fire teams and squads is that of a singular unit.
CHAIN CROSSING
      13-23. Two or more individuals cross arms with each other and lock their hands in front of themselves. (See
      figure 13-2.) The line formed faces the far bank. The largest individual should be on the upstream side of the
      line to break the current for the group, leaning upstream, into the current. The line formed will then move
      across the stream using the same principles as for individual crossings but with the added support of each
      other. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead.
      If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. In
      that scenario, the alternative of swimming is the safest.




                              Figure 13-2. Chain method for stream crossing

CHAIN CROSSING (CONGA VARIATION)
      13-24. All personnel in the team face into the current, with their hands grasping clothing or gear just behind
      the shoulders of the person on their upstream side. The largest individual should be on the upstream side of
      the line to break the current for the group, leaning upstream, into the current. The line formed will then move
      across the stream using the same principles as for individual crossings but with the added support of each
      other. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead.
      If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. In
      that scenario, the alternative of swimming is the safest. (See figure 13-3.)

                                                                                      Mountain Stream Crossing




                        Figure 13-3. Insert side view, top view, and traveling

WEDGE OR DIAMOND TEAM CROSSING
   13-25. Three or more individuals form a wedge, with the largest individual upstream to break the current for
   the group. Cross arms behind the back or rucksack and grasp the upstream individual, developing structured
   support. Subsequent personnel widen the wedge with smaller personnel or casualties filling the middle
   portion. Maintain an interval that supports free movement without tripping on other personnel. The wedge
   formed has the added support of each other. Move across the stream using most of the same principles as for
   individual crossings but all facing upstream. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off
   with the downstream foot in the lead stepping together as one unit. If the formation begins to degrade, avoid
   trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. The alternative of swimming is the safest in
   that scenario.

BELAYED CROSSINGS
   13-26. Certain conditions may require using a rope system to aid in crossing or even keep Soldiers from
   being exposed to water. When the depth begins to approach knee to waist level and the current is strong
   enough to potentially knock a Soldier off balance, then using a handline (one rope bridge with belay line)
   could be appropriate. This is the safest form of crossing simply because Soldiers have direct influence from
   either riverbank.
   13-27. Crossing on a handline will still require everyone to enter the water. In a case where water and air
   temperature significantly increase the risk of hypothermia, artificial height or other considerations may need
   to be implemented. Joining two or more ropes will only be possible for a handline. The maximum distance a
   one-rope bridge is capable of spanning is about one-half to two-thirds the length of the rope in use.
   13-28. An advantage of using a belayed crossing is the safety aspect. If individual control is lost, personnel
   can be pulled to the unloading bank by those belaying. Disadvantages of this technique are the time required
   for preparation, the number of available anchors, and the time dedicated to recovering the crossing site.
ESTABLISHING THE FAR ANCHOR
   13-29. Whether a handline or rope bridge (see chapter 16) is to be installed, someone must cross the stream
   with one end of the rope and anchor it on the far side. The most capable and strongest swimmer in the party
   should perform this duty. Swimmers should be belayed across for their own safety. The belay position should
   be placed as far above the crossing as possible. If the current is too strong for individuals, they will pendulum
   back to the near bank. Rescuers should be poised on the near bank at points where individuals will pendulum
   back, should they fail to reach the far bank. The initial crossing site should be free of obstacles that would
   snag the rope and prevent the pendulum from going back to the bank for an easy recovery.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 327
Chapter 13



      13-30. Individuals may attach the belay rope to their seat harness or a swami belt with a carabiner. They
      should never tie directly into the rope when being belayed for a stream crossing. If swimmers are swept away
      and become tangled, they must be able to release themselves quickly from the rope and swim to shore as best
      they can. Individuals may also choose to tie a fixed loop into the end of the belay rope and hang on to it,
      where they can immediately release it in an emergency.
      13-31. Anytime a crossing site must be used where swimmers may encounter problems getting to the far
      bank, they should wear a life vest or other personal flotation device (PFD). If swimmers must release the
      rope at any time, they will have to rely on their own water survival skills and swimming ability to get to
      shore. A PFD greatly increases personal safety. A PFD may also be used by the last individuals across, as
      they will release the rope from the anchor and be belayed across as the first individual.
INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
      13-32. If it is possible to use a rope high enough above the water to enable Soldiers to perform a dry crossing,
      then a rope bridge should be installed as such. If this is impossible, and the rope must be installed to assist in
      a wet crossing, then it should be installed as a handline. (See figure 13-4.)
      13-33. The far anchor should be downstream from the near anchor so that the rope will run at an angle
      downstream from the near anchor, about 30° to 45°, rather than straight across the stream. Here again, it is
      easier to move with the current as opposed to directly across or against it.
      13-34. The rope may be anchored immediately on the far bank, pulled tight, and anchored on the near bank.
      If a tighter rope is required, the handline may be installed with a transport tightening system. (See chapter 16.)
      13-35. A second climbing rope is used as a belay. (See figure 13-5, page 330.) One end of the belay rope will
      be on the near bank and the other end on the far bank. It should be sent across with the strong swimmer. An
      appropriate knot is tied into the middle of the belay rope to form two fixed loops. Each loop is approximately
      6-inches long. One loop is connected to the handline with a carabiner and individuals crossing connect one
      loop to themselves. The loops are short enough so individuals are always within arm’s reach of the handline
      should they slip and let go. Individuals are belayed from both the near and far banks. If a mishap should
      occur, the individual can be retrieved from either shore, whichever appears easiest. The belay on the opposite
      shore can be released, allowing the individual to pendulum to the bank. It is important not to anchor or tie
      the belay rope to the belayer so that it may be released quickly if necessary.
MOVEMENT
      13-36. Crossing will always be performed on the downstream side of the handline, shuffling the feet with the
      downstream foot in the lead. Under most circumstances, the handline should be crossed by one person at a
      time. This keeps rope stretch and load on the anchors to a minimum. Hands should remain on the handline,
      on either side of the belay line tie-in point. Individuals should look upstream for obstacles, and pick up a
      good athletic stance, keeping their body slightly perpendicular to the current. Take small steps while keeping
      the feet close to the ground to avoid any unwanted influence forced onto the body by rushing water. Either
      rucksacks can be carried on the back the same way as for individual crossings, or they can be attached to the
      handline and pulled along behind the individual. If a large amount of equipment must be moved across the
      stream, especially heavier weapons, such as mortars, recoilless rifles, and so on, then a site should be selected
      to install a rope bridge. (See chapter 16.)
      13-37. Disadvantages to the belayed crossing include the large amount of time dedicated to site preparation,
      individual crossings, positioning of security teams, and lack of natural anchors on the riverbanks.
      Additionally, only one person is belayed at a single time, with personnel on each bank dedicated to the belay,
      leaving fewer personnel for security at any given time.

SWIMMING
      13-38. Soldiers may find themselves alone and have no choice but to swim across, or they may find
      themselves suddenly plunged into a swift river or rapids. Soldiers should consider the following actions if
      Soldiers are in a situation that forces them to swim during a crossing:
          • Immediately strip away gear or clothing that restricts free movement and increases their signature.
          • Instead of fighting the current, work with the flow of water to get to a dry location downstream. It
               is often easier to negotiate hazards and see where Soldiers are going if they face downstream and
               fan the hands alongside the body to add buoyancy. They should use their hands to also fend off
               submerged rocks and position their feet as a shock absorber to shove off unseen or hidden obstacles.
          • Keep the head above water to identify obstacles or debris that Soldiers may impact. Take the
               opportunity to breathe between breaks if waves begin to rise over Soldiers’ heads.
          • Avoid backwater eddies, bubbly water, water churning upwards, and converging currents. All these
               hazards have the potential to create unpredictable buoyancy and possibly undertow.




330                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                        Mountain Stream Crossing



       •    If the shore is too difficult to reach, seek out the closest and safest spot, such as a sandbar, to get out
            of the water as quickly as possible. Hypothermia will set in quickly in colder waters.

SECTION III – ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS AND HAZARDS
   13-39. River and stream crossings present one of the most hazardous situations faced by military
   mountaineers. Substantial experience is necessary to properly evaluate and mitigate swift water hazards.

SAFETY GUIDELINES FOR RIVER AND STREAM CROSSINGS
   13-40. The following safety procedures are minimum guidelines that should be followed when conducting a
   river or stream crossing:
        • All weak swimmers should be identified before a crossing so that stronger swimmers may assist in
             crossing.
        • Not every river or stream can be crossed safely. If it is possible, cross at a different time or place,
             use a different technique, or choose another route.
        • The technique used is directly dependent upon water depth, speed of the current, stream bottom
             configuration, width of the stream, and individual experience.
        • The safest methods of crossing in the water are always with the use of a handline or rope bridge.
        • If the installation of a handline or rope bridge becomes too difficult at a given crossing site, then
             that site should be considered too hazardous and another site selected.
        • A lookout should be posted 50 to 100 meters upstream to watch for any obstacles that may be carried
             downstream and interfere with the crossing.
        • When conducting individual crossings (those without a handline or rope bridge), spotters or security
             should be posted downstream with poles or ropes prepared to throw, for assistance or rescue.
             Medical personnel should be prepared for cases of hypothermia.
        • When the unit knows a rope installation is required for crossing, at least two life vests or other PFDs
             should be on hand. These PFDs provide additional safety for the strong swimmer who must establish
             the far anchor and the last individual across who retrieves the system.

WATER SURFACE CLUES
   13-41. Observing and analyzing the top of the water can give military mountaineers an indication of what to
   expect beneath the surface. Water is not often clear enough to see all the hazards that could make the crossing
   difficult or have adverse effects on personnel attempting to cross. The following are common clues that can
   provide ideas of what lies beneath the surface.
        • Riffles or ripples—if they are lined up, there are likely one or several rocks that form a line. In
             shallower water, it could mean a stable, rocky riverbed.
        • Holes, souse holes, or keepers—depressions that can form from water moving around an obstacle.
             The rise and drop on the surface can be visibly seen. Avoid stepping here as these rises and drops
             could suction Soldiers’ feet and debris can fall.
        • Convergences and their depth—can increase the force the water has on someone attempting to cross.
        • Eddy or back eddy—swirling of water and the reverse current created when water flows over or
             around an object or terrain. The consistency of a current is very unpredictable.

                    Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue
   Ten percent of the Earth’s land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing
   under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often
   provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other
   hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit’s mission. Soldiers operating in
   glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier
   travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques.

SECTION I – GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS
   14-1. Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of
   feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is
   important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they
   form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the
   easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces.

GLACIERS
   14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into
   ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of
   pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide.
   14-3. The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the
   accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the
   ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line.
CLASSIFICATION
   14-4. There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high
   mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and
   Antarctica.
TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS
   14-5. The following are four types of glaciers:
       • Valley glacier—resides and flows in a valley.
       • Cirque glacier—forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl.
       • Hanging glacier—these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. As the
           movement continues, portions separate and are sometimes left hanging on mountains, ridgelines, or
           cliffs.
       • Piedmont glacier—formed by one or more valley glaciers, spreads out into a large area.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                333
Chapter 14



GLACIER OBSTACLES
      14-6. Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics
      to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come
      in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can
      result in significant injury or loss of life.
      14-7. Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are—
          • Bergschrund—the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It
               is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The
               bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving
               from the valley floor onto the mountainsides.
          • Crevasses—crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the
               glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly,
               causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier
               makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the
               direction of the glacier’s movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet
               deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible
               major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Snow
               bridges that form over them can give way without warning. During the summer, the ice is less
               covered with snow and most crevasses are exposed. They can still be hazardous at night or in
               reduced visibility.
          • Moat—the moat is a gap formed where the snow and ice are melted by the warmer rock along the
               edge of a glacier. The edge of a moat is often undercut. Depending on its size, the moat may be an
               obstacle to moving on or off the glacier.
          • Icefalls—icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up
               into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable obstacles and
               should be avoided.
          • Serac—seracs are ice walls and towers that form in icefalls or on the lower edge of hanging glaciers.
               They are unstable and can fall unexpectedly. Travel below seracs or hanging glaciers should be
               avoided when possible.
          • Nunatak—a nunatak is an island of bedrock that protrudes up through the glacier, creating an
               obstacle to glacial movement. It creates pressure in the ice that can form crevasses, seracs, and
               icefalls.
          • Water hazards—streams that run on the surface and then disappear into a hole are called moulins.
               Moulins form when meltwater from the glacier finds a crevasse and moves to the ground below the
               ice. A fall into a moulin can carry a Soldier into the glacier and result in almost certain drowning.
               The glacial streams above this point must also be treated with respect. They are cold, can be deep,
               and the slick walls of their channels make them difficult to escape. In the summer, glacial thaw
               water can form troughs. This water can freeze at night, forming glacial swamps.
          • Steep slopes—glaciers often include steep slopes that can create falling hazards, especially in firm
               snow conditions.
          • Moraines—moraines are piles of rock and other debris that have either fallen onto the glacier or
               been pried loose by it as it moves along. There are four basic types:
                Lateral moraine—this is the rock debris along the valley wall.
                Medial moraine—formed when two glaciers come together, and the lateral moraines are forced
                    out into the middle of the glacier.
                Terminal moraine—the rock debris at the toe of the glacier, which is being dredged up and
                    pushed down the valley. A glacial stream often flows out from under the terminal moraine.
                Ground moraine—the rocks and debris under the glacier that can be exposed if the glacier stops
                    and then begins to move again.
                Generally, the outside of a moraine wall is stable, but the side facing the glacier can be steep
                    and loose and should be avoided. A moraine may be the only path, but it can be awkward and
                    tiring due to the unstable rocks.

                                     Figure 14-1. Glacier features


SECTION II – FUNDAMENTALS OF GLACIAL TRAVEL
   14-8. Glaciers are often good avenues of approach to the interior of a mountain range. Travel can be slow,
   and dangerous but easier than traveling on steep, loose, or exposed ridgelines. Glaciers are typically large
   open danger areas and should be treated as such during tactical operations. Units traveling on glaciers are
   subject to observation from all the surrounding high ground. A capable detachment may be required to
   provide an overwatch for the force traveling below.

EQUIPMENT
   14-9. A variety of specialized mountain equipment may be necessary for Soldiers traveling on glaciers. The
   following items are not a comprehensive list.
ROPES
   14-10. The use of ropes allows Soldiers to move in small rope teams and have some protection from crevasse
   falls. The type, length, and diameter of ropes selected for this purpose may vary depending upon how steep
   and heavily crevassed the glacier is. It is also determined by the number of Soldiers per rope team, and
   whether there are mutually supporting teams. Smaller diameter, lighter weight ropes are generally preferred.
HARNESSES
   14-11. Harnesses enable the individual connection to the rope team.



26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                              335
Chapter 14



ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS
      14-12. Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide
      the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice
      axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue.
SKIS AND SNOWSHOES
      14-13. In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute
      weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a
      hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members
      of a rope team are skilled skiers.
PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES
      14-14. Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They
      are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in
      crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the
      rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik.
SNOW ANCHORS
      14-15. Snow or ice anchors, such as pickets and ice screws, are often carried for use in crevasse rescue. In
      some snow conditions, ice axes, skis, and other items may be used to create an anchor.
WANDS
      14-16. Wands are sticks used as markers and can be utilized in many ways. They can be used to mark the
      location of known crevasses on frequently used routes or used in pairs forming an X to indicate danger. They
      can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful
      for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes
      with tape or flagging.
OTHER GLACIAL GEAR
      14-17. The following items are typically carried and necessary for connecting to rope, connecting to prusiks,
      securing rucksacks or sleds, and facilitating crevasse rescue.
          • 2 to 3 locking carabiners.
          • 2 or more nonlocking carabiners.
          • Belay or rappel device.
          • Rescue pulley (optional).

USE OF THE ROPE
      14-18. A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection.
      The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable
      to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a
      team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself.
      14-19. Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can
      be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for
      roped travel. It also allows for movement in tactical formations and a better security posture.
      14-20. During the summer season, with clear skies and good visibility, crevasse risk on a glacier below the
      ablation zone is often negligible because crevasses can easily be seen as avoided due to lack of snow cover.
      In early season, or in low visibility, this same glacier could be quite dangerous. The decision of whether to
      rope up should not be taken lightly and should be made by only experienced mountaineers. Below is an
      example of various risk levels and guidance:
           • Zero risk—bare glacier ice, free of snow and with few crevasses. There is no concern for hidden
               crevasses because all crevasses are visible. In periods of limited visibility, rope up. In good visibility,




336                                                    TC 3-97.61                                   26 November 2025
                                                                            Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



            travel unroped. If there is a danger of a sliding fall that could lead to a crevasse fall, use the belayed
            climbing techniques covered in chapter 10.
       •    Low risk—hard, dense snow conditions in summer, or early morning frozen conditions after a cold
            night. Concern for hidden crevasses is low and snow bridges are strong. In limited visibility, rope
            up. In good visibility, travel unroped with caution and be alert for changing conditions. Have
            harnesses on and equipment available to make the transition to roped travel easier.
       •    Moderate risk—soft summer snow conditions. Breaking through a snow bridge or into a hidden
            crevasse is possible. Rope up.
       •    High risk—soft or weak snow on a glacier with many crevasses. Crevasses are hidden and snow
            bridges are weak. Breaking through snow bridges and falling into hidden crevasses is likely. Avoid
            travel, if possible. If travel is required, rope up and use cautious route finding.
DETERMINING FALL HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD
   14-21. In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into
   crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route
   finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Rope teams can usually stop crevasse falls
   because these occur on low-angled terrain without falling hazard. On flat terrain or soft snow, the arresting
   Soldiers are not typically at risk of sliding into the crevasse and are often able to stop the fall by slumping in
   the snow, rather than a full team self-arrest.
   14-22. Falls on steep firm snow or an icy slope have almost no chance of being stopped by a rope team. Steep
   fall hazard is better managed by belaying Soldiers individually as described in chapter 10 or simul-climbing
   with protection placed for the team. It can be tempting to travel on steep slopes using crevasse fall protection
   techniques, but this is an illusion of safety. A fall can pull the entire rope team from the slope, often with
   fatal consequences.
   14-23. Since these risks can change often from crevasse hazard to falling hazard and vice versa, changing
   strategies is important. The following paragraphs discuss using the rope for crevasse fall protection only.
DETERMINING ROPE TEAM SIZE
   14-24. When using the rope, team size can be a difficult decision, and several factors must be considered.
   Smaller rope teams are faster and can move more efficiently than larger teams. Larger teams can easily arrest
   a fall and have more immediate resources to haul someone out of a crevasse. Training levels and overall unit
   size are also factors in determining team size. The following list describes advantages and disadvantages of
   various rope teams:
        • Two-person teams—travel is faster and more efficient. However, in the event of crevasse fall, one
             Soldier must hold the fall. When not traveling with other rope teams nearby, that Soldier must also
             construct an anchor while holding the fallen Soldier, transfer the weight, and then conduct a rescue.
             For this reason, only use two-person teams when both team members are highly experienced.
             Requires approximately 60 meters of rope.
        • Three-person teams—generally preferred for most glacier travel. Maintains a relatively low team
             size, while having two Soldiers to hold a fall and potentially haul the Soldier out. It is possible to
             have one untrained or minimally trained Soldier on this team when placed in the middle. End
             climbers must both have good route finding and crevasse detections skills and must be proficient
             with all crevasse rescue strategies. Requires 45 to 50 meters of rope.
        • Four-person teams—travel is slower and less efficient, but the large team is more likely to hold a
             fall. May be preferred versus multiple two-person teams when there is more than one untrained or
             inexperienced Soldier. Requires 30 to 40 meters of rope.
        • Teams of five or more—travel is slow and cumbersome. Obstacles slow the group even more with
             each additional Soldier. The entire team must slow down or wait as each member negotiates it. Rope
             management and communication between members become more difficult. Teams of five or more
             are not recommended but may be necessary in situations where there are many Soldiers without
             sufficient experience. Multiple ropes or sections of ropes may be necessary to ensure adequate
             spacing between Soldiers on rope teams of more than five.
        • Mutually supporting teams—mutually supporting teams, such as two teams of three, (rather than
             one team of six), or a team of two and a team of three, (rather than one team of five), should be used



26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                  337
Chapter 14



               when experience levels make it possible. Multiple teams allow one team to simply hold the fall and
               supporting teams to use their own rope and resources to conduct a crevasse rescue. This strategy
               can also decrease the amount of excess rescue rope that individual teams must carry.
DETERMINING SPACING BETWEEN SOLDIERS
      14-25. It is best to have no more rope between Soldiers than necessary. Longer rope distance slows progress
      and makes it more difficult to communicate and coordinate movements. Smaller teams need slightly more
      spacing than larger teams. This distance needs to span crevasses so that only one Soldier is at risk at a time
      when crossing. Some general guidelines are given but spacing may need to be increased for exceptionally
      large crevasses.
           • Two-person teams—10 to 12 meters.
           • Three-person teams—8 to 10 meters.
           • Four-person teams—7 to 9 meters.

Two-Person Teams
      14-26. In the event of a crevasse fall, each member of a two-person rope team must have enough spare rope
      available to reach fallen Soldiers and back to haul them out. (See figure 14-2.) This usually involves
      60 meters or more of rope to have adequate spacing between Soldiers. With Soldiers spaced approximately
      12-meters apart, they would each have 24 meters of spare rope to be used for rescue. A figure eight on a bight
      can be tied at 6 meters on each side of the rope’s middle mark. These can be used as attachment points for
      team members and are each clipped into the harness with a locking carabiner and a nonlocking carabiner
      opposite and opposed. The remaining rope can be coiled and worn over the shoulder or placed into the
      rucksack. Soldiers must also tie several stopper knots on the rope connecting them. These additional knots
      aid in arresting a fall by catching in the lip of the crevasse and can often greatly reduce tension on the arresting
      climber, making it easier to construct an anchor. These are mandatory for two-person teams and can be either
      alpine butterfly knots or overhands on a bight. Since each knot takes up about 1 meter of rope, this length
      must be factored in as well.




                                       Figure 14-2. Two-person rope team

Three-Person Teams
      14-27. For three-person teams, the rope is broken up into quarters. (See figure 14-3.) Each end Soldier carries
      enough extra rope to reach the middle Soldier. So, with 10 meters of spacing between people, each end
      Soldier will be carrying an additional 10 meters or more of rope each. Stopper knots are unnecessary in three-
      person teams because there is generally sufficient holding power. A figure eight on a bight is tied and attached
      to the middle person’s harness with a locking carabiner and nonlocking carabiner opposite and opposed. Each




338                                                    TC 3-97.61                                   26 November 2025
                                                                            Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



   end Soldier measures approximately 10 meters out from the middle and attaches the same way with a figure
   eight on a bight. Remaining rope can be coiled and worn over the shoulder or stuffed in the rucksack.




                                  Figure 14-3. Three-person rope team

Four-Person Teams
   14-28. Four-person teams can simply divide the rope into thirds and use the entire length. The end Soldiers
   tie into the ends of the rope and the middle Soldiers clip in as described for two- and three-person teams. If
   a longer rope is used and shorter spacing between Soldiers is desired, end climbers can coil and stow rope as
   described above.
OTHER PREPARATIONS
   14-29. Mountaineers often pre-place one or more prusiks on the rope. (See figure 14-4, page 340.) These can
   be used as part of a system to ascend a rope for self-rescue in a crevasse fall or for load transfer when rescuing
   another Soldier. Having at least one is useful for keeping slack out of the rope when grouping in one location
   to communicate or conduct other tasks. The prusik can be attached to the harness with a separate locking
   carabiner or the same locking carabiner used for the attachment to the rope.
   14-30. A 120-cm sling (48 inches), or two 60-cm slings (24 inches) attached together, can be improvised
   quickly to construct a chest harness. To do this, pass the loop through both arms and behind the back, forming
   an X in the back, then connect the two bights in the front with a carabiner. This is only to be used after a
   crevasse fall to remain upright and make self-rescue easier. Chest harnesses are worn when a crevasse fall is
   likely.
   14-31. Mountaineers can prepare the rucksack with a sling and carabiner so that in the event of a crevasse
   fall the Soldier can remove the rucksack immediately and clip to the rope to dangle below.
   14-32. Snow anchors, wands, or other equipment should be distributed among the team.

                    Figure 14-4. Preparation chest harness, rucksack removal sling
                                       for use with prusik ascent

ROPE MANAGEMENT
      14-33. The rope should be kept extended on a glacier. It should not have unnecessary slack or be taut. Excess
      slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team
      and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become
      stuck or wedged.
      14-34. A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the
      feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling
      uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and
      starts. The Soldier in the lead should set a pace that others can easily follow.




340                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



   14-35. During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of
   travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. During turns, team members should
   adjust pace and keep appropriate tension. New tracks may need to be made outside the leader’s footprints to
   do this.
   14-36. As a rope team reaches a rest area or bivouac location, the rope must remain extended until the area
   has been probed for crevasses. Once it has been deemed safe, the lead member may belay team members into
   the area by pulling rope through the prusik, with ice axe in hand, ready to self-arrest. Soldiers in the rear may
   also belay themselves into the location in the same manner. When leaving the location, the same process
   happens in reverse. (See figure 14-5.)




                           Figure 14-5. Using prusik to belay other Soldiers
