ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS
      14-37. Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers.
      Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result.
      Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary
      skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use
      an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of
      wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can
      reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body.
INFORMATION GATHERING
      14-38. Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily
      from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage
      point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even
      old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that
      contain satellite imagery can provide overhead views. These may contain imagery taken during the summer
      or late season and show the general trends and locations of dense crevasses that may be only partially filled
      in or have suspect snow bridges when traveling during winter and early season.
TIMING
      14-39. On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the
      morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can
      soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer
      alternative route.
      14-40. Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable
      crevasses.
      14-41. Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of
      year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface
      conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes:
          • Autumn—in late season conditions, most crevasses are clearly visible and snow bridges have melted
               out to their maximum extent. Travel is generally safest, as there is little risk of unexpected crevasse
               fall, but route finding can be difficult and require long detours and lengthy movement times around
               crevasse fields. In steeper terrain, firm conditions can make falling hazard a higher concern.
          • Winter—early winter is especially hazardous. Unconsolidated snow hides crevasses but often does
               not effectively bridge them. Crevasses are more difficult to detect, and unexpected falls are more
               likely. In late winter, deeper snow conditions may provide more effective snow bridges. Increased
               snow loads may cause bridges to sag, making detection easier. Skis or snowshoes are often required.
          • Spring—snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are
               at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often
               required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct.
          • Summer—early morning travel on firm snow surfaces makes travel easier, but snow bridges are
               beginning to weaken. As crevasses open, finding direct routes becomes challenging again. Seracs
               and icefalls also become more hazardous.
      14-42. In some geographical regions further from the poles, these trends can be nearly opposite with surface
      conditions revolving strictly around dry and rainy seasons.




342                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                           Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION
   14-43. Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain
   and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to
   the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their
   likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the
   terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where
   additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster.
   These “marginal” crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers
   of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes.
   14-44. Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down
   or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls
   and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively
   crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding.
SURFACE CLUES
   14-45. Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but
   it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize
   similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours.
         • Sagging—snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early
             in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more
             defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change
             in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should
             be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip,
             groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible
             to recognize.
         • Nearby crevasses—since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one
             another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation.
         • Parallel cracks—in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges
             of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can
             be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge.
PROBING
   14-46. Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses,
   determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the
   axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in
   resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow
   layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult.
   Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also
   required for determining safe bivouac locations.
CROSSING TECHNIQUES
   14-47. There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and
   be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel
   perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time.
   (See figure 14-6, page 344.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 343
Chapter 14




                             Figure 14-6. Crossing perpendicular to crevasses

End Running
      14-48. There is no guarantee as to the dependability of snow bridges. Sometimes it is preferable to cross at
      one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.)
      With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward
      progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like
      the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Make a
      wide swing, probe carefully, and cross at a right angle to the crevasse.




344                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                             Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue




                                   Figure 14-7. End running crevasses

Using a Snow Bridge
   14-49. When end running is not practical, use snow bridges to cross. (See figure 14-8.) Always attempt to
   get a look at the crevasse from the side before committing to it, and probe when approaching the lip. The
   remaining Soldier in the team provides a moving belay by controlling the slack and remaining ready to
   self-arrest. Once the leader is across, the rest of the team must follow exactly in the leader’s footsteps. At this
   point, the leader controls slack and remains prepared for self-arrest. Prusiks can be used here to manage slack
   in the rope during this process as well. If there is doubt as to one’s ability to stop a fall, a fixed belay must be
   constructed with a snow or ice anchor.




                                     Figure 14-8. Using a snow bridge




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                  345
Chapter 14



Jumping
      14-50. Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect
      crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other
      options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of
      catching a crampon and use common sense.

Climbing into the Crevasse
      14-51. Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other
      side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear
      solid but are not.

Echelon Formation
      14-52. When it is impractical to travel perpendicular to existing crevasses and Soldiers must travel parallel,
      the echelon formation can be used. (See figure 14-9.) This keeps team members still to the rear but offset
      slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader’s tracks in a single-file line. This
      should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk
      of falling into a hidden one.




                                        Figure 14-9. Echelon formation

SECTION III – CREVASSE RESCUE TECHNIQUES
      14-53. Solid crevasse rescue skills are essential for elements traveling in glaciated terrain. While this may be
      impractical in circumstances involving large numbers of personnel, the ability to react appropriately to
      crevasse fall cannot be overlooked.




346                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                          Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS
   14-54. Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in
   crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more
   experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope
   teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams.
   14-55. Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in
   someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge
   but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this,
   Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of
   circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the
   breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment
   carried. A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of
   this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used for a three-person rope team are
   described below.

STEPS TO TAKE FOR CREVASSE FALL
   14-56. The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team.
STOP THE FALL
   14-57. Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping
   into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult
   than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish
   a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made
   with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the
   snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. If a Soldier is not able to quickly self-recover, then
   the following steps must be taken. (See figure 14-10, page 348.)




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               347
Chapter 14




                                    Figure 14-10. Stopping a crevasse fall

CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD
      14-58. When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the
      load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the
      one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can
      still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the
      middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor
      with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the
      anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. In this case, the slack rope itself, between the middle
      and end climber can be used to attach directly to the anchor.




348                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                          Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



   14-59. Next, the end Soldiers get back into the self-arrest position to back up middle Soldiers as they transfer
   the weight of fallen Soldiers onto this prusik. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common
   for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional
   components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik
   should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor.




                      Figure 14-11. Construct the anchor and transfer the load

COMMUNICATE WITH THE FALLEN CLIMBER AND MAKE A PLAN
   14-60. To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where
   the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik
   attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what
   to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any
   injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become
   entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad
   underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid
   underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for
   padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described
   below.

Self-Rescue
   14-61. Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see
   paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is
   also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik
   ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack
   off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members
   may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained
   significant injuries.

Belay
   14-62. Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole,
   especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of
   the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above
   creates a belay at the anchor. Again, if the fallen Soldier is injured, this method may not be possible.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                349
Chapter 14



Haul
      14-63. If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will
      be needed.
HAULING
      14-64. Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are
      circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered.

Direct Haul
      14-65. This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber’s weighted strand of rope. A common
      example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup
      knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct
      haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if
      there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.)




                           Figure 14-12. Direct haul using a 3:1 hauling system


350                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                          Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue



Drop Loop
   14-66. Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber’s
   harness, independent of the climber’s weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling
   system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded
   prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand.
   Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious
   victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can
   be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether.
   Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the
   prusik on the original tensioned rope.




                             Figure 14-13. Drop-loop rescue system (2:1)

SECTION IV – TRAINING
      14-67. Even when mutually supporting rope teams are used, good route finding, and crevasse detection skills
      are critical. Every rope team must have at least one Soldier with solid crevasse rescue skills. Commanders
      cannot just hope for seasonally low-risk conditions, nor can they rely solely on advanced parties or recon
      teams to consistently find routes that are passable without the need for ropes. A lack of expertise can leave
      units with a large capability gap.
      14-68. Training and experience in glacier travel are most productive when conducted on glaciers. Most
      glaciated terrain in the lower 48 states is in the Pacific Northwest. The high cost of travel and time
      commitments to access them make training plans difficult for units to execute. Most of those glaciers involve
      acquiring climbing permits. It can take the better part of a training day for the approach on foot to these
      higher elevations; any training would typically involve a bivouac. This makes it inconvenient even for units
      located at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. Ambitious commanders, however, might utilize these or
      other glaciated terrain in Alaska, Europe, or elsewhere, to create training events that combine glacier
      experience with other aspects of mountain warfare.
      14-69. In the absence of glaciated terrain, units can still conduct simulated training exercises focusing on the
      basic strategies for roping up and preparing individual and team equipment. Crevasse rescue skills can be
      rehearsed using short sections of steep terrain. This should be conducted in locations without serious falling
      hazard, and back-up ropes or belays should be considered while techniques are being learned. Having a few
      unit members with advanced level training will improve the quality and outcomes of this training.




352                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                               Chapter 15
                       Mountain Rescue and Evacuation
   A unit’s capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain
   operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of
   a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor
   injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level
   of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation
   is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may
   make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain
   evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation.
   The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician’s
   assistant, or medic).

SECTION I – RESCUE OPERATIONS
   15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should
   have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single
   evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or
   inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes
   and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore,
   relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning.
   15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are
   deliberate and improvised.

DELIBERATE
   15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for
   focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment.

IMPROVISED
   15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations
   and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be
   practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a
   CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure
   that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who
   may be involved in a potential rescue.

PLANNING
   15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information:
       • Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience).
       • Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries.
       • Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties.
       • Tactical situation.
       • Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation.
       • If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location.
       • Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation.
       • Any circumstances that may require specialized skills.
       • Weather conditions.
       • Difficulty of the terrain.
       • Time available.


26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               353
Chapter 15



      15-6. Route selection when planning mountain CASEVAC often depends upon technical capabilities. In
      some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer,
      less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer
      distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers.

CONSIDERATIONS
      15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid).
      Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The
      key elements are the casualty’s condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance
      between these conditions and the resources and personnel available.
      15-8. There are many additional considerations for the rescue team during deliberate rescue:
          • Typically, team members must distribute and carry all equipment, including hot food and drinks,
              stoves, sleeping bags, bivouac equipment, warm clothes, ropes, and stretchers.
          • Evacuation routes often require extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points,
              belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises.
          • Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure,
              reliable trails or roads is essential.
          • Protection from the elements, such as blankets, tarps, warming layers and rain gear, can be vital.
              Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or
              strong winds can greatly increase the rescue’s time and complexity.

GENERAL STEPS
      15-9. Regardless of whether a rescue is deliberate or improvised, the following steps must be taken upon
      arrival at the rescue site to accomplish a safe and efficient rescue operation:
           • Assume command—one person and one person only is in charge.
           • Scene safety—prevent further injuries to the casualty and to others. Explore all options for casualty
                access prior to committing to one. Use reasonable care in reaching the casualty. Rescuers must not
                become casualties.
           • Immediately ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the
                casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious,
                continually monitor for a pulse.
           • Do not move the casualty until determining the extent of injuries unless necessary to prevent further
                injury or if the casualty is in a dangerous or exposed location.
           • Do nothing more until the situation has been thoroughly considered. Resist the urge for action. Speed
                is less important than correct actions and decision making. The decisions made on scene drive the
                rest of the rescue (for example, casualty rigging, packaging, route selection, anchors, and rope
                systems).
           • Decide whether to evacuate with available resources or to send or call for help. Speed in getting to
                the next level of care must be balanced against the probability of further injury. This is especially
                crucial if working with inexperienced personnel, insufficient equipment, or terrain or weather
                hazards.
           • When the evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be
                established, if possible. These help to manage the welfare of both the casualty and the rescue team.
                These stations should be staffed with the medical personnel and equipment necessary to provide
                proper treatment.
           • Helicopters or heated vehicles, if available, should be used for evacuation. While the use of aircraft
                or vehicles is preferred and can expedite a rescue operation, evacuation of a seriously wounded
                Soldier should never be delayed awaiting aircraft, vehicle, or a change in weather.

SPECIALIZED TRAINING
      15-10. Rescue team members must receive basic instruction in military mountaineering and first aid, prior to
      any training and rehearsals for mountain rescue and evacuation. Individual mobility skills, knowledge of
      knots and basic rope systems, and the ability to sustain and protect themselves from the environment are



354                                                  TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                 Mountain Rescue and Evacuation



   essential. Once formal evacuation training has been received, proficiency can be maintained by periodic
   integration with other concurrent training exercises. Scenarios that require simple casualty movement
   techniques, with and without litters, as well as low-angle slope evacuations (see section II) can easily be
   created. Scenarios are added when time becomes available during or following other training exercises. These
   opportunities allow commanders to quickly evaluate a unit’s preparedness to carry out basic rescues if
   needed, refresh level 1 skills, and help to reinforce unit teamwork and problem solving. Basic military
   mountaineers, at a minimum, should oversee this training. Medical personnel should be present. Rescues in
   complex 4th- and 5th-class terrain, whether real or simulated, require advanced-level training and skills, and
   they must be led by level 2 and level 3 mountaineers.

PROLONGED FIELD CARE
   15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined
   with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many
   hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement
   beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02).
   15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific
   training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations.
   Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of
   treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and
   immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure,
   respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles
   of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously
   be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to
   prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time.
   15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care
   unit, and advanced imaging. A combination of rescue skills training and prolonged field care skills are
   necessary to make this possible.

SECTION II – CASUALTY MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
   15-14. Casualties in the mountains can be moved and transported in a variety of ways, from simple manual
   field carries to high-angle evacuations using litters and complex rope systems. The type of injury, distance
   to be moved, time available, and resources will determine the best technique for a given situation.

MOVING CASUALTIES WITHOUT LITTERS
   15-15. There are varieties of circumstances where casualties may move, be moved, or be carried without the
   use of litters. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not
   having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in
   technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or
   more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult
   terrain. Have team members ahead to select the easiest route and remove loose branches and other obstacles.
   Ski poles may be helpful if they are available. In situations where the casualty cannot walk, simple techniques
   described in the Soldier’s Manual of Common Tasks (fireman’s carry, two-hand, four-hand, saddleback,
   piggyback, pistol belt, and poncho litter) may be useful. However, rugged mountainous terrain often demands
   other techniques. The most basic one-man carries include the webbing or rope carry, the rope coil carry, and
   the rucksack carry.
NYLON WEBBING OR ROPE CARRY
   15-16. A 4.5-meter piece of webbing or rope can be used to improvise a buddy carry system. (See figure 15-1,
   page 356.) Place the middle of the webbing around the casualty’s back and under the shoulders, crossing in
   front of the chest. Place the ends over the carrier’s shoulders (from back to front). Bring the ends alongside
   the carrier’s ribs, through the casualty’s crotch, and around the outside of the casualty’s thighs. The carrier
   then ties the ends of the webbing together around the waste with a square knot.



26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                   355
Chapter 15




                                      Figure 15-1. Webbing or rope carry

ROPE COIL CARRY
      15-17. A dynamic or static rope can also be used as an improvised buddy carry system. (See figure 15-2.)
      Coil the length of rope using the mountain coil technique, sizing the loops to fit from the casualty’s armpits
      to crotch, and then separate the coil in half to form a pair of loops. Place the casualty’s legs through the loops
      and slip the upper part of the loops over the carrier’s shoulders. A short piece of webbing can be used to tie
      these loops together.




356                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                              Mountain Rescue and Evacuation




                                       Figure 15-2. Rope coil carry

RUCKSACK CARRY
   15-18. The rucksack carry is another method of back carry. Make slits in the sides of a large rucksack so the
   casualty can step into it as though it were a pair of shorts. Then the carrier wears the backpack as usual. This
   requires the contents of the carrier’s pack to be carried by another Soldier.
TANDEM RAPPEL
   15-19. Rappelling with a casualty is not often the first choice in rescue. It is typically preferable to lower a
   casualty with a rescuer during descents because it allows the rescuer to focus on controlling the casualty
   rather than having to control both the casualty and a rappel. However, in the case of a sturdy, conscious
   patient with nonlife-threatening injuries, it is possible to rappel together with a rescuer. To do this, a rappel
   extension can be created using a 48-inch sling or cordelette as shown below to allow both the casualty and
   rescuer to rappel from the same device but slightly offset from one another. (See figure 15-3, page 358.) The
   rescuer must add an autoblock back up behind the device.

                                    Figure 15-3. Tandem rappel rigging

ROPED MOVEMENTS
      15-20. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep
      terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. This may be done with ambulatory patients or may be
      necessary in situations where an injured Soldier must be moved from a cliff to an alternate location where
      packaging in a litter is more easily accomplished. This may require considerable assistance from rescuers or
      other Soldiers. It should only be attempted when necessary and after any immediate life-threatening injuries
      have been treated. Remember the more complex the technical rope systems become, the more time
      consuming they tend to be, increasing exposure and vulnerability to enemy attack.

MOVING CASUALTIES IN LITTERS
      15-21. Usually, casualties with significant injuries in the mountains need to be evacuated with the use of a
      litter. Several types of litters are available for transporting casualties in rough terrain.




358                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                              Mountain Rescue and Evacuation



MANUFACTURED LITTERS
   15-22. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units:
       • The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does
           little to protect the patient’s injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system.
       • The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over
           rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its
           bulk and weight.
       • A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for
           moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient
           protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of
           technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed
           to slide over surfaces. A single-wheel attachment is available, which vastly increases the efficiency
           of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried.
       • The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic
           litter that can also be rigged to meet rating requirements for hoist operations. The most commonly
           issued and used version in mountaineering is the rescue litter, which provides excellent patient
           support and protection. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and
           relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. A backboard must be used
           with this system for patients who have injuries to the shoulder area. This system will accommodate
           long and short backboards, scoop stretchers, and most other immobilization equipment.
IMPROVISED LITTERS
   15-23. Litters can be improvised in the field using several techniques, but all of them require construction
   materials and time, generally offer less patient protection, and are more prone to breakage.
   15-24. Litters can be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags.
   Poles can be improvised from strong branches, tent supports, skis, and other similar items.
   15-25. If poles cannot be found, a large item, such as a blanket, can be rolled from both sides toward the
   center. Then the rolls can be used to obtain a firm grip to carry the casualty. If a poncho is used, the hood
   must be up and under the victim, not dragging on the ground.
PATIENT PACKAGING
   15-26. Casualties must be packaged and secured to litters before movement in rough terrain. Proper
   packaging should achieve stabilization, immobilization, protection from hypothermia, and preparation for
   transport. Physically strapping a person into a litter is relatively easy but making it comfortable and effective
   can be a challenge. The needs of litter bound casualties are great and should not be overlooked or
   underestimated. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes
   for the casualty in the end.
   15-27. The rescuer’s goals are as follows:
       • Package the casualty to avoid causing additional injury.
       • Ensure the casualty’s comfort and warmth with focus on preventing hypothermia.
       • Immobilize the casualty’s entire body in such a way as to allow continued assessment during transport.
       • Package the casualty neatly so that the litter can be moved easily and safely.
       • Ensure that casualties are safe during transport by securing them within the litter and belaying the
           litter as necessary.
   15-28. Rescuers follow the same basic principles of the cold-weather clothing system to create a hypothermia
   wrap (hypo-wrap). The fundamental goal is to reduce heat loss. The outermost layer should be a VB to protect
   the casualty and the insulating layers from the environment. Use a ground pad to protect against conductive
   heat loss using a closed cell or inflatable foam pad. A closed-cell foam sleep pad is preferable because it will
   not rupture, and it can be cut into pieces for additional medical treatments (such as splints and neck braces).
   Begin layering with available insulating materials. The casualty’s equipment should be used first before
   sacrificing clothing or sleep systems from non-injured Soldiers. Rescuers put the casualty into the wrap and
   place additional layers of insulation on top of the casualty.



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 359
Chapter 15



      15-29. Consider protecting the insulating layers from casualties themselves if there is a possibility they could
      become incontinent. A trash bag or waterproof bag with leg holes cut in it can be filled with socks or T-shirts
      to form a diaper. Wrap the casualty as completely as possible, leaving only necessary areas exposed. When
      available, hot water bottles should be added and placed by the casualty’s axillary areas (armpits, groin) and
      the neck to provide active rewarming.
MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
      15-30. ATP 4-02.13 covers general principles of handling and moving with litters—principles that apply in
      all terrain. However, in rugged mountainous terrain, teams must often move considerably slower. Extensive
      personnel may be required to ensure adequate rest and safety. Advanced teams may be useful for route
      selection and clearing.
      15-31. For longer movements, it can be useful to add slings or cordelettes to the litter rim or handles for each
      litter bearer. These slings can be passed over the shoulders to the opposite hand, allowing each bearer to push
      down with the hand opposite the litter. This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter,
      as well as providing some height adjustment.
      15-32. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make
      movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the
      pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the
      litter and as close to one another as possible. The litter is then passed forward into the hands of the extra litter
      bearers. As soon as litter bearers in the rear become obsolete, they move around and take up a new position
      further ahead in the direction of travel. They then wait until the litter reaches them and repeat the technique.
      This allows rescuers to remain still as the litter is transported, taking advantage of secure footing and stable
      positions. In this way, the litter is less likely to be dropped and litter bearers are less likely to sustain an injury
      attempting to move and carry the heavy load at the same time.
      15-33. If a litter can be dragged, attaching ropes may make doing so easier and more controllable. Ropes can
      be attached to the front of the litter for dragging purposes as well as to the rear of the litter for use with a
      brakeman to slow the speed of the litter on gentle descents. This technique can speed up evacuation in
      conditions that allow for it, such as snow-covered terrain. (See figure 15-4.)
      15-34. On flat or low-angle snow-covered terrain, two ropes can be attached to the corners of the litter with
      girth hitches to allow up to four Soldiers to pull, brake, and steer the litter. This enables moving up, down,
      and traversing slopes with better control to prevent the litter from tipping over.




                                            Figure 15-4. Rope litter drag

LOW-ANGLE RESCUE
   15-35. Low-angle rescue can generally be categorized by roped litter evacuations on low to moderately steep
   slopes where much of the weight of the casualty and rescuer is still supported by the ground. In this terrain,
   the litter slides along the slope, either up or down, depending on the direction of travel. The rope pathway
   should be cleared prior to casualty movement. All precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall
   line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. In all situations, the rescue team should strive to solve the
   terrain problem safely with the least technical solution.
ROPE ATTACHMENT
   15-36. Rescue litters are generally oriented vertically during low-angle slope evacuations. (See figure 15-5.)
   The rescue rope is attached to a vertical attachment point at the head of the litter with a locking carabiner or
   carabiners. The rope is connected at the head of the litter for comfort and for ensuring that blood does not
   pool at the casualty’s head during transport.
   15-37. Many techniques can be used to create a vertical attachment point at the head of the litter. (See
   figure 15-6, page 362.) Techniques may be improvised, based on the type of litter and available equipment.
   Ensure that this fixed loop attachment point connects multiple components of the litter for redundancy. In
   the case of the patient rescue and recovery system, use the short length of rope that comes with the system
   and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for creating this.
   15-38. The end of the rescue rope can then be attached to this point with a figure eight on a bight and
   connected with a locking carabiner. Ropes used for rescues should be static (low stretch) and should have a
   minimum breaking strength of 30 kilonewtons (kNs).




                           Figure 15-5. Litter rigged for vertical orientation

                          Figure 15-6. Basket litter rigged for vertical orientation

BELAYS
      15-39. In some situations, the rescue rope can be used to simply provide a tight belay for the casualty while
      litter teams carry a litter up or down slopes. Many of the various belay techniques described in chapter 10 are
      appropriate for this; however, the terrain must be gentle enough that there is no falling hazard to members of
      the litter team.
ATTENDANTS
      15-40. In steeper terrain where lowering or raising the litter from above is necessary, there is often a falling
      hazard for the litter team. If rescuers cannot safely walk beside the litter, it is typically advisable to use a
      single rescuer attached to the system as an attendant. This attendant’s primary responsibility is to ensure the
      litter and casualty do not roll over, become hung up on terrain obstacles, or create slack in the system.
      15-41. One technique is to attach the rescue rope to the litter head using a bowline with a tail that is long
      enough to reach the bottom of the litter when stretched out. The long tail is then be used by a litter attendant
      as an attachment point to the system in situations where it is necessary. (See figure 15-7.) This can also be
      achieved using a figure eight on a bight with enough rope behind the knot to extend this distance.
      15-42. The attendant can attach directly into the end of this rope with another figure eight on a bight attached
      to a locking carabiner in the harness or by tying directly in with a rerouted figure eight. An autoblock or
      prusik can also be attached to this strand of rope to allow the attendant to adjust position in relation to the
      litter and hang completely from the system. Occasionally but less often, two attendants may be required to
      manage the litter.
      15-43. These methods use some of the rope that is available for the rescue. In cases where the length of
      available rope is limited, it may be prudent to improvise the attendant’s attachment using other materials,
      such as a cordelette.

    Figure 15-7. Litter rigged for lowering with long-tailed bowline and attendant attached

LOWERING
   15-44. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12.
   Select or construct extremely solid anchors, tie off the end of the rope to close the system, and apply
   appropriate hands-free backups. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all
   precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A
   Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of
   the lower. Avoid rope pathways with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential.
   15-45. If it is necessary to lower the litter and attendant multiple rope lengths, multiple anchor stations and
   lowering teams may be required to achieve this. Complex situations such as this require excellent leadership,
   terrain assessment, and communication.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               363
Chapter 15



RAISING
      15-46. The litter and attendant can be raised through steep terrain using the various hauling techniques
      described in chapter 12. This could be done by a hauling team from above using main force or by creating
      MA using one of the systems previously described. If using main force, a prusik or other friction hitch should
      be attached to the rope and anchored as a progress capture. An additional member on the haul team must be
      dedicated to managing the prusik during this method. If using MA, the hauling team must pull slow and
      steady and should be extremely aware of the loss of feel for the load. In either case, the rope pathway should
      be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line
      of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay
      commands and help control the speed of the haul. Avoid hauling in terrain with sharp rock edges or loose
      terrain with rockfall potential.

HIGH-ANGLE RESCUE
      15-47. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain.
      High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical
      problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military
      mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables
      involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that
      can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including
      climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a
      comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some
      of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques.
LITTER RIGGING
      15-48. Whether a rescue litter or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is
      similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be
      rigged for a vertical orientation the same as described for lower-angle evacuations. In many cases, it is ideal
      to package the casualty in a manufactured or improvised harness. This allows the harness to connect to the
      rope system independently of the attachment to the litter itself. This can also be achieved with webbing using
      a variety of techniques.

Horizontal Orientation
      15-49. Horizontal orientation of the litter is often used in cases where the nature of the injury makes vertical
      orientation unsuitable, such as spinal, pelvic, and lower leg injuries. (See figure 15-8.) Severely hypothermic
      and cardiac patients should also be kept as horizontal as possible during transport. The rescue litter comes
      with two hoist straps that can be used for this. In the case of a similar metal basket litter, cordage or webbing
      can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the
      head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when unloaded. Use locking
      carabiners and ensure that all carabiners used in the rigging are oriented correctly. It is easy to create a
      dangerous situation by cross-loading carabiners.

                                                                               Mountain Rescue and Evacuation




                 Figure 15-8. Litter rigged horizontal orientation with hoist straps




                     Figure 15-9. Basket litter rigged for horizontal orientation

Vertical Orientation
   15-50. Vertical litter orientation is often preferred as it can make for a simpler and more fluid edge transition.
   It is also lower profile, protects the patient better from rockfall and other hazards, and does not require a
   change in rope attachment point when transitioning to or from low-angle terrain. However, this method can
   be unsuitable for casualties with spinal, pelvic, and some lower leg injuries and requires securing the patient
   in such a way to minimize movement in the litter once evacuation begins.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                                 365
Chapter 15



ROPE SELECTION
      15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF).
      Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the
      system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load.
      For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the
      10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to
      account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11
      mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more
      practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and
      function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less
      than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More
      important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These
      ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking
      strength of 26 kN.
      15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems.

Single Rope
      15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to
      construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include
      redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results.
      Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the
      pitch, and time and resources are limited.

Tandem Rope
      15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct.
      However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in
      rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions
      due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited
      team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems.
      15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each
      rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is
      there in case of main line failure.
      15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See
      figure 15-10.) The tail or free end of each bowline is used as a secondary attachment point for the patient and
      the litter attendant.

                                                                           Mountain Rescue and Evacuation




                            Figure 15-10. Interlocking long tail bowlines

   15-57. The main line is often routed through a high directional or A-frame near the top edge of the cliff to
   reduce friction at the edge, and to make the transition over the edge easier. (See figure 15-11, page 368.)




26 November 2025                              TC 3-97.61                                              367

                                      Figure 15-11. Tandem prusik belay

LOWERING
      15-58. Sites suitable for lowering should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms,
      and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with
      rockfall potential should be avoided when lowering is necessary. The litter and attendant can be lowered
      using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12, but techniques that generally provide greater
      friction are preferred. The end of the rope should be tied off to close the system.
RAISING
      15-59. Sites suitable for hauling should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and
      good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall
      potential should be avoided when hauling is necessary. The litter and attendant may be hauled using
      techniques described in chapter 12. Systems with higher ratios may be necessary, as well as redirection and
      piggyback techniques.
BELAY LINE
      15-60. While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for
      a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load
      will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all
      the system components. The separate belay line is also here for this purpose. If a high directional is used, the
      belay line should not be routed through it. This would cause a greater fall distance before the belay line could
      catch the load in the event of failure or breakage of the high directional.
      15-61. While there are manufactured devices available that meet the criteria for a technical rescue belay, the
      simplest and most field expedient method is called the tandem prusik belay. Two prusiks, preferably made
      from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. The length
      of the prusik closer to the anchor should be a few inches shorter than the other prusik. These prusiks are then
      attached to the belay anchor with a locking carabiner. To use the belay, keep an uphill hand on the two prusiks



368                                                  TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                             Mountain Rescue and Evacuation



   together and the downhill hand on the downhill side of the rope. Feed rope through the prusiks with a
   “hitchhikers grip” (thumbs out) and keep a bow of rope approximately 8 to 12 inches of slack between the
   hands. There should be only a few inches of slack between the downhill hand and the litter. In the event of a
   blown edge transition or of main line failure, the prusiks will be ripped out of the belayer’s hands and catch
   the load. Tandem prusiks and belay line are also helpful when transitioning from a lower to a raise or when
   passing a knot through the lowering system.
POSITIONS AND RESPONSIBILITIES
   15-62. A high-angle rescue requires a skilled team to be conducted. The following positions are a bare
   minimum and mandatory for a safe evacuation.

Team Leader
   15-63. The team leader has overall responsibility for the operation. The team leader considers all available
   options and selects the most appropriate technique for the situation. The team leader makes judgments based
   on the nature or urgency of the injury, the tactical situation, the nature of the terrain, and the personnel and
   resources available. The team leader briefs the plan, provides the necessary guidance to the team members,
   and oversees the operation until complete. The team leader should not handle the main line or the belay, but
   in short workforce situations, should be found near the edge to assist in communication. The team leader
   establishes and supervises a formal rigging inspection process, as well as the command and control protocol
   for all technical operations.

Belayer
   15-64. The belayer manages the belay ensuring the prusiks do not lock out. Typically, the belayer is
   responsible for construction and rigging of the belay.

Main line
   15-65. The main line will consist of either a one- or two-person lowering team or a haul team for raises. In
   the case of teams, only one person should be the spokesperson to keep communications clear. Typically, the
   main line team is responsible for anchor construction and hauling system rigging.

Edge Safety
   15-66. The edge safety keeps the edge area clean of debris, places edge protection if necessary, and assists
   the load over the edge during the transition. The edge safety also relays commands between the attendant and
   the personnel above. During difficult edge transitions, two edge safeties may be used.

Attendant
   15-67. This litter attendant manages the handling of the patient and litter during the technical portion of the
   rescue. Often the primary focus of the attendant is making sure that the litter is protected and keeping slack
   out of the system. These often require pulling the litter out away from the terrain for smooth lowers or raises.
   This is considerably taxing and may require having an adjustable length attachment to the rope system. The
   litter attendant should have both primary and secondary attachment points for redundancy. The litter attendant
   determines and adjusts the rate of litter movement up or down as necessary.

Inspections
   15-68. Units should develop their own deliberate inspection protocols for rescue rope system rigging. At a
   minimum, rigging for each system component (for example, main, belay, litter) should be inspected
   systematically as a deliberate step by advanced mountaineers who did not participate in building it.

Control
   15-69. In some cases, to free up the team leader, a separate control person is used for actual commands. This
   allows the team leader to maintain a broader perspective and continue to think about the next phase or stage



26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                369
Chapter 15



      of the operation. The control gives commands to lower or raise the load, especially during the critical edge
      transition phase.
COMMAND AND CONTROL
      15-70. Precise commands and singular control are necessary for safe operations. All commands should
      originate either with the team leader, control, or, in some cases, the edge safety. A variety of commands can
      be used but must be short, simple, and clear. Always include the name of the position in the command, such
      as SLACK ON MAIN or TENSION ON BELAY. Before any lowering or raising operations take place, a
      roll call is necessary to ensure all personnel are ready. The roll call should start with personnel near or at the
      edge and work backwards to the main. Once all personnel are ready and checked and the litter and attendant
      are in position, begin the operation by calling UP ON MAIN or DOWN ON MAIN. Once the litter is moving,
      the speed can be adjusted, as necessary. To halt all movement, call STOP. All teams continue to act as if the
      load is on belay until the command OFF BELAY is given.
      15-71. Radios are usually necessary to maintain contact with the attendant on the litter. Once the attendant is
      over the edge, in high winds, yelling is not reliable and produces a sound signature that can travel
      unpredictable distances in mountainous terrain.

                                          Rope Bridges
   Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water,
   ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope
   bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope
   suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms
   are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for
   the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting
   personnel for river crossings and the term “high lines” to denote rope installations used to span
   longer or higher gaps in terrain.

SECTION I – TECHNIQUES
   16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units
   with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very
   cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important.
   16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a
   tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed
   and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical
   disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.)

CONSTRUCTION
   16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle
   in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then
   tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending
   upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles
   for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still
   facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be
   used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation.
METHODS OF TENSIONING
   16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the
   bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle
   remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain.


                                                WARNING
               Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its
               weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during
               use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes.




26 November 2025                               TC 3-97.61                                               371
Chapter 16



HAND TIGHT
      16-5. The simplest and least equipment-intensive method is hand tightening the rope. Once Soldiers anchor
      one side of the rope, they pull the rope as tight as they can. Next, they tie off the rope using one of three
      methods: mule knot secured with an overhand knot (see figure 16-1), round turn around anchor and two half
      hitches on a bight, or a high strength tie off (tensionless hitch). (See figure 16-4, page 374.)

            Note. Figure 16-2, and figures 16-3 and 16-4, page 374, illustrate the transport tightening system.

      16-6. The benefit of hand tensioning the rope is that it is the fastest way to get the rope tight. The limitation
      is that if the rope bridge span is long, it may not be possible to apply adequate tension to the rope using this
      method. Adequate tension may require more personnel than units have available.
TRANSPORT TIGHTENING SYSTEM
      16-7. The transport tightening system can be used to tighten a rope bridge when additional tension is
      necessary. One Soldier on the near side ties a knot that is easily untied after being placed under tension (for
      example, an alpine butterfly or figure-eight slip knot with a half hitch to stabilize the adjustable bight [see
      figure 16-1]) approximately 1 to 2 meters from the near side anchor. They place a locking carabiner into the
      loop of the knot. At that time, Soldiers route the remainder of the rope around the near side anchor point and
      clip the rope into the carabiner.




                                  Figure 16-1. Transport tightening system

      16-8. The pull team on the near side pulls the slack out of the installation rope. The knot should be close
      enough to the near side anchor to allow personnel to easily load the installation.
      16-9. The rope then can be secured using one of the same three methods described above.

                   Figure 16-2. Mule knot secured with an overhand knot
