               Figure 16-3. Round turn around anchor and two half hitches on a bight




                           Figure 16-4. High strength tie off (tensionless hitch)

      16-10. The benefit of using the transport tightening system is that the MA allows more tension to be applied
      to the rope with limited personnel and minimal equipment. The limitations are the increased system platform
      size required, reduced MA due to friction generated by rope redirects, and time of construction.
SIMPLE 3:1 TIGHTENING SYSTEM
      16-11. The simple 3:1 tightening system is another method for gaining MA (see chapter 12).




374                                                 TC 3-97.61                               26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Rope Bridges



   16-12. The benefits of the simple 3:1 system are increased efficiency in tensioning, the capability to tension
   on a smaller platform, and the ability to re-tension due to rope stretch. The drawbacks are increased
   complexity, time, equipment, and the possibility of overtensioning the rope. The limitations are that the
   system requires more equipment, is more complex to construct, is easier to overtension and the increased
   time required to construct.


                                                 WARNING
               No more than four personnel should be used to tighten the rope
               when a simple 3:1 or a transport tightening system is used to
               apply tension. Using more personnel can overtighten the rope
               and bring the rope critically close to failure.


REDUNDANCY
   16-13. A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks
   redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of
   any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional
   level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical
   loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where
   a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single
   carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having
   a backup in case of failure. Redundancy is not always necessary or practical but is typically used in training
   as a risk management tool.

METHODS OF CROSSING
   16-14. All wet crossing techniques using handlines are covered in chapter 13. Methods of dry crossings using
   rope bridges is determined by several factors:
       • The load being transported on the rope bridge (such as personnel, equipment, and litter).
       • The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls).
       • The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending).
       • Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment).
   16-15. Leaders must evaluate the situation and determine the most efficient means of crossing. For example,
   the method chosen for moving a light element with no sustainment gear across a 10-foot stream is different
   from the method chosen for moving crew-served weapons across a 50-foot-wide, fast-moving river.
   16-16. If Soldiers can transport themselves across, they can choose either the commando crawl or the
   Tyrolean traverse.
COMMANDO CRAWL
   16-17. Soldiers lie on top of the rope with a foot hooked on the rope and a knee bent, o positioned nearly in
   line with the buttocks; the other leg hangs straight to maintain balance. They progress by pulling with their
   arms. To recover if they fall over, Soldiers hook one leg and the opposite arm over the rope, and then push
   down with the other hand to regain position.
TYROLEAN TRAVERSE
   16-18. Soldiers don a harness or tie a field expedient harness and attach a locking carabiner into it, with the
   nose of the carabiner facing up and away from their body. They then face the rope and clip into the rope
   bridge. Soldiers rotate under the rope and pull with their hands and arms to make progress. The Tyrolean
   traverse is the preferred method. If crossing with rucksacks, a carabiner is inserted into the frame and attached
   to the rope bridge. Soldiers then place one or both legs through the shoulder carrying straps and pull the
   rucksack across.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 375
Chapter 16



TAGLINES
      16-19. Heavy equipment will require the use of a tagline. A tagline is used to pull objects from the near side
      to the far side. An additional rope is brought across the rope bridge and anchored to the far side. The other
      end is anchored on the near side. All the slack is pulled to the near side, and a figure eight on a bight knot is
      tied at the loading platform. A carabiner is inserted into the loop and clipped onto the rope bridge.
      16-20. If the rope bridge is longer than half a rope length, two separate ropes are required to create a tagline.
      One end of the far-side tagline is brought across the obstacle and anchored to the far side. The other end is
      secured to a carabiner. One end of the near side tagline is secured at the near side, and the other end is secured
      into the same carabiner as the far-side tagline. That carabiner is then placed onto the rope bridge.
      16-21. If the rope bridge is descending (the far-side anchor is significantly lower than the near side), a belay
      may need to be added to the tagline system. The tagline attached to the near side will be converted into a
      belay (see chapter 10) to allow for a controlled movement across and down the rope bridge.
EQUIPMENT RIGGING
      16-22. Any special equipment, such as crew-served weapons, ammunition, or supplies, must be rigged for
      movement across the rope bridge. A unit SOP may dictate the rigging of these items, but many expedient
      methods exist. The rigging should use various items that would be readily available to a deployed unit. Some
      of these items include tubular nylon webbing, cordage (various sizes), and carabiners.
      16-23. Equipment that can be bundled together, such as rucksacks, should be Bundles can be created with a
      cordelette. If there are insufficient personnel on the far side to lift the bundle for unloading, a releasable
      Munter mule can be utilized at the point of attachment to the tagline.
      16-24. Litters can be transported across a rope bridge if there is a secure means of attaching the litter to the
      rope, such as the rescue litter with its horizontal lift straps. The carabiner of the tagline will remain on the
      rope bridge. On each side of this carabiner, using the hauling line tie a middle-of-the-rope clove hitch around
      the carabiners of both horizontal lift straps of the litter. Remove the slack between the carabiners. Then place
      the carabiners in each of the lift straps onto the rope bridge. (See figure 16-5.) The same technique used for
      the rucksacks is used to pull the litter across.




376                                                   TC 3-97.61                                  26 November 2025
                                                                                                    Rope Bridges




                                         Figure 16-5. Litter rigging

ARTIFICIAL HEIGHT
   16-25. Artificial height is often useful or even necessary to raise the height of rope bridges. (See figure 16-6,
   page 378.) This may be needed when desiring dry river crossings or to better facilitate the loading and
   unloading of personnel or equipment. Artificial height may be needed on one or both sides of a rope bridge.
   16-26. Occasionally, bridge sites may be selected where a tree with a high sturdy limb may be slung with
   rope or cord. On rock faces, artificial anchors may be constructed in convenient locations. Otherwise,
   A-frames may need to be constructed.
   16-27. A-frames are structures constructed with poles to create artificial height for use with rope bridges.
   Two sturdy poles are needed. The exact size of the poles depends on the type of load and location of the
   installation. The average size A-frame pole should be at least 3 inches in diameter and 9 to 12 feet long.
   Three to five 13-foot cordelettes are needed depending on the size of the poles used for the A-frame.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                                 377
Chapter 16




                        Figure 16-6. Artificial height (A-frame) used with high line

A-FRAME CONSTRUCTION
      16-28. There are many acceptable techniques and variations for the construction of A-frames. The general
      process is described as follows: (See figure 16-7.)
          • Place two suitable poles with the butt ends flush and mark the desired apex on both poles.
          • With a section of rope or cordelette, tie a clove hitch around one of the poles a few inches above the
               apex marking, leaving about 12 inches of tail to the outside of the poles. (See figure 16-7[A].)
          • With the poles side by side, wrap the remaining length of rope horizontally around both poles six to
               eight times, wrapping downward from the clove hitch. (See figure 16-7[B].) It may be necessary to
               join another section of rope to the first with an appropriate joining knot. Position this knot on the
               outside of one of the poles so as not to interfere with the vertical wraps. (See figure 16-7[C].)
          • On the last horizontal wrap, continue around the pole that does not contain the clove hitch, pass the
               rope between the poles below the wraps, and make four to six tight vertical wraps around the
               horizontal wraps. (See figure 16-7[D].) Make the wraps as tight as possible. The vertical wraps must
               be as flat as possible next to each other. Insert a carabiner into the last two vertical wraps. (See
               figure 16-7[E].)
          • On the last vertical wrap, pass the rope between the poles above the horizontal wraps. Tie it off with
               a square knot in the section of rope coming from the clove hitch. Secure with overhand knots tied
               in the tails. (See figure 16-7[F].)




378                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                  Rope Bridges




                         Figure 16-7. A-frame horizontal and vertical wraps

   16-29. Use a spreader rope to prevent the A-frame from collapsing from pressure applied at the apex. (See
   figure 16-8, page 380.) Secure the legs of the A-frame together with a cordelette to fix the maximum spread.
   If the ground is soft, dig the legs in about 6 inches. If the ground is a hard surface, anchor the bases of the
   poles at a 45°-angle to secondary anchor points. The spreader rope should be no more than 6 inches above
   ground level.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               379
Chapter 16




                                        Figure 16-8. A-frame spreader

ANCHORING THE A-FRAME TO THE INSTALLATION ROPE
      16-30. If used, an A-frame must be anchored to the installation rope. Tie a clove hitch at the center of a
      cordelette. Place it over one of the poles above the apex and move down to the apex so that the locking bar
      of the clove hitch is to the inside of the A-frame. Secure each end of the cordelette to one of the tightened
      static lines with two prusik knots—one forward and one to the rear of the A-frame on the same static line
      rope. (See figure 16-9.)




                       Figure 16-9. Anchoring the A-frame to the installation rope



380                                                 TC 3-97.61                                26 November 2025
                                                                                                  Rope Bridges



   16-31. Position the A-frame so that the angles created by the A-frame bisecting the installation rope are
   approximately equal on both sides. This creates downward pressure holding the A-frame in position, not
   forcing it in a lateral direction. It must also be placed in a straight line between the upper and lower anchor
   points.

RETRIEVAL
   16-32. If the element is crossing the obstacle as part of a longer movement, and there are no follow-on troops,
   the system must be installed to be retrievable:
        • Nearside personnel untie the high-line system maintaining the near side ends of both the installation
            rope and belay or tagline rope.
        • Far-side personnel pull all slack across the obstacle.
        • Nearside personnel secure the end of the installation line to the anchor.
        • Tie a fixed loop in the near side end of the installation rope.
        • Secure the fixed loop to the installation rope around the nearside anchor with a locked carabiner.
        • Far-side personnel pull the installation rope tight with several personnel, and then wrap it around an
            anchor tree with a minimum of two full wraps. Those personnel maintain control of the end of the
            rope keeping it tight with the tree by hand or can close out the rope by means of two half hitches
            like the close out on the transport tightening system. Another method is for far-side personnel to
            build a new tightening system on their side to tighten the rope.
        • Nearside personnel attach the tagline to installation line figure eight on a bight using a locked
            carabiner and a fixed loop. The tagline remains slack.
        • Nearside personnel attach themselves to the installation line in the same way as the main body and
            cross the high line.
        • Once all personnel are on the far side, the installation rope is unwrapped from the far-side anchor
            and allowed to go slack. If a new tightening system was used, it is broken down.
        • The tagline is then pulled across the obstacle dragging the installation line with it until both ropes
            are on the far side. Ensure all knots are removed from both ropes before pulling.

HIGH LINES
   16-33. A high line is a type of suspended rope bridge used to transport equipment or casualties high above
   difficult terrain that might otherwise be impassable. These can be used for personnel movement as well,
   although this is less common. The high line is used over large rivers, ravines, chasms, or diagonally from the
   top of a cliff to the ground below. The system may be established on different planes, varying from horizontal
   to near vertical. High lines keep the load suspended above the terrain as it travels directly between the near-
   and far-side anchors.
   16-34. High lines come with a high level of risk due to the height of the load above the ground. High lines
   used for personnel movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in
   catastrophic fall injury. They should only be constructed by advanced or master military mountaineers who
   have been formally trained in high-line construction for this purpose.
SITE SELECTION
   16-35. The crossing site must have appropriate anchors at the near side and the far side and suitable loading
   and off-loading platforms. If the anchors do not provide enough height to allow clearance, additional height,
   such as an A-frame, may be used.
INSTALLATION
   16-36. The same options and tightening techniques used for rope bridges can also be used for high lines;
   however, due to the higher consequences of rope or equipment failure, a second rope as described earlier
   must always be used for redundancy. Construction of high lines can be time-consuming and equipment
   intensive. Installation teams are likely to require additional skills and techniques to get the far end of the
   installation ropes to the far side of the obstacle.
   16-37. Artificial height is used the same way as described for rope bridges.




26 November 2025                                TC 3-97.61                                               381
Chapter 16



EQUIPMENT RIGGING, BELAYS, AND TAGLINES
      16-38. Slings and cordelettes can be used to attach loads to the installation ropes and can be modified as
      necessary. (See figure 16-10.) Two examples are using two ends of a piece of webbing with a water knot or
      using a sewn sling. Place a locking carabiner on the high line and place the webbing or sling into it. Bring
      the bight at the bottom end of the sling up (double it) and clip it into the locking carabiner. A second locking
      carabiner can now be placed into the two bights. Attach the load by running the long loop of the carrying
      sling through the load and attaching the bottom loop to the traverse rope carabiner.




                                            Figure 16-10. Carrying sling

      16-39. Attach a lowering rope to the second locking carabiner in the carrying sling when speed of the load
      must be controlled. (See figure 16-10.) Standard lowering techniques discussed in chapter 12 can be used.
      This rope can be attached to the A-frame using an additional carabiner attached to the carabiner that is in the
      apex. If Soldiers are crossing, they should hold onto the carrying sling and keep their hands off the installation
      rope.
      16-40. Taglines can also be used as described for rope bridges and are nearly always necessary when the high
      line does not contain a relatively constant downgrade.
RETRIEVAL
      16-41. The high line can be retrieved in a manner like the one rope bridge. However, as it is often used to
      move equipment and casualties, it can be dismantled after it is no longer needed without being retrievable.

SECTION II – GUIDING LINES
      16-42. A guiding line (see figure 16-11) is an effective means of transporting a litter over uneven, broken
      terrain (talus) commonly found at the base of cliffs. A guiding line is established and tightened in the same
      manner as a descending high line using MA but is not tied off once tensioned. The tensioning team retains
      control of the haul strand and adjusts tension in the installation line as the litter is lowered down it. The litter’s



382                                                     TC 3-97.61                                    26 November 2025
                                                                                                        Rope Bridges



   descent is controlled by a separate team operating the lowering system using a second rope. (See chapter 12
   for hauling and lowering systems.) These two teams work together to ensure the litter travels just high enough
   above the broken terrain to keep movement smooth. Additionally, attendants may move on foot through the
   terrain to help guide the litter around obstacles.
   16-43. The main benefit gained from using a guiding line over a high line is the reduction in risk. Because
   the guiding line is only tensioned enough to lift the litter in the air, the rope is at a very low risk of being over
   tensioned and the litter is never high above the ground. Using a high line in the same piece of terrain would
   usually involve suspending the litter high above the ground on a highly tensioned rope. Additionally,
   movement down a guiding line is much easier on the casualty than being hand carried through large talus.
   16-44. While guiding lines can be a lower risk solution, they can be more complex and are usually more
   time-consuming. Leaders must ensure that their element is formally trained on guiding lines and has the
   equipment necessary to accomplish the task safely.




                                         Figure 16-11. Guiding lines

                                                  Appendix A
                            Climbing Route Classification
   The most important tools for risk management in the mountains are route selection and
   evaluation. Accurately evaluating and selecting routes in high consequence terrain requires a
   well-developed understanding of technical route classification systems and experience
   climbing the terrain they describe. Route classifications allow military mountaineers to identify
   appropriate routes for their Soldiers’ skill levels and the technical rope systems required to
   move on them safely. Misunderstanding or miscommunicating route difficulty can place the
   life of the mountaineer or the lives of the Soldiers they lead in danger. The U.S. military does
   not have its own technical route classification systems. Therefore, military mountaineers must
   use those developed for civilian mountaineering. The classifications discussed in this chapter
   breakdown and describe the difficulty associated with routes in various types of terrain.
   Understanding them provides military mountaineers with the base from which to build route
   identification and selection experience.

ROCK CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS
   A-1. There are several systems for classifying different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types
   of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty.
   The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than what the
   hardest move on it is. Depending on the type of route being planned, one or all these route difficulty systems
   should be considered.
YOSEMITE DECIMAL SYSTEM
   A-2. In North America, the YDS is used to rate the difficulty of rock-climbing routes. It categorizes terrain
   according to the techniques and physical difficulties encountered when rock climbing. The YDS classes are—
       • Class 1—hiking.
       • Class 2—off-trail scramble with the occasional use of hands.
       • Class 3—moderate scrambling, with short steps of easy climbing. Ropes may be used for beginners,
           but a guide can often manage the terrain with good coaching and modeling.
       • Class 4—simple climbing, with exposure. A rope is often used. A fall could be fatal.
       • Class 5—rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect
           the leader from a long fall.
   A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest
   move on a pitch and does not account for strenuousness, difficulty of placing protection, or quality of the
   protection:
       • Class 5.0 to 5.4—easy. This is the simplest form of free climbing. Hands are necessary to support
            balance. Easy for experienced climbers.
       • Class 5.5 to 5.6—intermediate. Often no more physically difficult than easier climbing but requires
            trusting friction and smaller holds. The climber can experience vertical position or overhangs where
            there are positive holds that require moderate levels of energy expenditure.
       • Class 5.7 to 5.8—moderate. Considerable climbing experience is necessary. Longer stretches of
            climbing requiring several points of intermediate protection. Climbing often requires specific
            techniques, such as jamming, liebacks, or mantles.
       • Class 5.9 to 5.10—hard. Requires well above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed
            positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be
            accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing.
       • Class 5.11 to 5.15—very difficult. Requires more climbing ability, experience, and energy
            expenditure. Only talented and dedicated climbers reach this level.




26 November 2025                                  TC 3-97.61                                                   385
Appendix A



      A-4. The original YDS was designed as a closed scale ending at 5.9. When climbing standards surpassed
      the original scale, 5.10 was added, and broken down further into a, b, c, and d categories (for example, 5.10d).
      Each increase in letter grade is comparably to an increase in grade in the original system.
      A-5. A plus sign (+) or minus sign (-) are sometimes added, denoting that a pitch is more strenuous at the
      grade.
      A-6. The YDS only rates the difficulty of the climbing and does not denote the quality and quantity of
      protection and consequence of a fall; therefore, guidebooks often use a second protection rating.
          • G—good protection options in quality rock that are closely spaced.
          • PG—good protection, but runout sections on easier parts of pitches may exist.
          • PG-13—route requires climbing sections where protection cannot be placed. A lead climber should
               be confident climbing at the grade. Protection is adequate, and if it is placed correctly, it should
               protect the leader.
          • R—protection is inadequate and there is potential for a long fall, which may cause serious injuries.
               A lead climber should be extremely confident at the grade.
          • X—little to no protection on the pitch. Ground fall, serious injury, or death possible from a fall.
AID CLIMBING RATINGS
      A-7. Aid climbing is done using gear and protection to create upward progress on the rock, instead of hands
      and feet. It is rated not by the physical difficulty of the climbing but the quality and spacing of the placements
      for gear:
           • A0—French-free. No aiders are required. This technique involves using a piece of gear to make
                progress, such as clipping a sling into a bolt or piece of protection, and then pulling up on it or
                stepping up in the sling. Usually this is only needed to get past one or two moves that are more
                difficult on free climbs.
           • A1—Easy aid. The placement of protection is straightforward and reliable. Every placement can
                hold a fall. This technique requires aiders (etriers) and is fast and simple.
           • A2—Moderate aid. Placements are good but may be difficult to place. Usually, A2 involves one or
                two moves that are difficult with good protection placement below and above the difficult moves,
                with no serious fall danger.
           • A3—Hard aid. Each pitch may require several hours to lead. There will only be a few pieces of gear
                in the pitch capable of holding a fall, with potential falls of 15 to 20 meters. These falls, however,
                are usually clean and might not cause serious bodily harm.
           • A4––Serious aid. Most placements will hold only body weight. There may only be a few solid pieces
                in a pitch. Falls can be 25 to 30 meters, with bad landings and risk of serious injury.
           • A5—Extreme aid. All placements can hold only body weight. Usually, no protection placed on the
                entire route can be trusted to stop a fall.
CLIMBING COMMITMENT GRADE
      A-8. Commitment grades (National Climbing Classification System) inform the climber of the approximate
      time a climber trained to the level of the climb will take to complete the route:
          • I—several hours.
          • II—half of a day for the technical portion of the route.
          • III—most of the day for the technical climbing, any difficulty.
          • IV—long, full day of climbing. Hardest pitch rated 5.7 YDS or harder.
          • V—requires at least a day and a half to complete the technical portion of the route, with the hardest
                pitch rated at 5.8 or harder. Requires a planned bivouac on the route for most teams.
          • VI—longer than 2 days. Big wall-style climbing, often with extensive aid climbing, hauling of
                equipment, and supplies for many days on the wall.
INTERNATIONAL RATINGS
      A-9. Climbing difficulties are rated by different systems in other parts of the world. There are countless
      systems in use, and even within these systems, there are regional variations in the ratings. All ratings are
      highly subjective. When traveling and climbing, local guidebooks include charts that compare rating systems.

                                                                                  Climbing Route Classification



ICE CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS
   A-10. Ice formations change from year to year and throughout the season, causing their difficulty rating to
   fluctuate. However, they generally form in the same areas and with the same steepness as the underlying
   features that they build on. Ice climbing ratings have technical and commitment ratings. The numerical
   ratings are often prefaced with waterfall ice, alpine ice, or mixed rock and ice.
   A-11. Technical difficulty ratings are as follows:
      • 1—a frozen lake or streambed.
      • 2—a pitch with short sections of ice up to 80°; lots of opportunity for protection and good anchors.
      • 3—sustained ice up to 80°; the ice is usually good, with places to rest, but it requires skill at placing
           protection and setting anchors.
      • 4—a sustained pitch that is vertical or slightly less than vertical; may have special features, such as
           chandeliers and run-outs between protection.
      • 5—a long, strenuous pitch, possibly 50 meters of 85° to 90° ice, with few, if any, rests between
           anchors. The pitch may be shorter but on featureless ice. Good skills at placing protection are required.
      • 6—a full 50-meter pitch of dead vertical ice, possibly of poor quality; requires efficiency of
           movement and ability to place protection while in awkward stances.
      • 7—a full-rope length of thin vertical or overhanging ice of dubious adhesion. An extremely tough
           pitch, physically and mentally, requiring agility and creativity.
      • 8—simply the hardest ice climbing ever done; extremely bold and gymnastic.
   A-12. Commitment ratings are as follows:
      • I—a short, easy climb near the road, with no avalanche hazard and a straightforward descent.
      • II—a route of one or two pitches within a short distance of rescue assistance, with little objective hazard.
      • III—a multipitch route at low elevation or a one-pitch climb with an approach that takes about an
           hour. The route requires anywhere from a few hours to a long day to complete. The descent may
           require building rappel anchors, and the route might be prone to avalanche.
      • IV—a multipitch route at higher elevations; may require several hours of approach on skis or foot.
           This route is subject to objective hazards, possibly with a hazardous descent.
      • V—a long climb in a remote setting, requiring all day to complete the climb itself. Requires many
           rappels off anchors for the descent. This route has sustained exposure to avalanches or other
           objective hazards.
      • VI—a long ice climb in an alpine setting, with sustained technical climbing. Only elite climbers will
           complete it in a day. A difficult and involved approach and descent, with objective hazards
           ever-present, all in a remote area.

                                                Appendix B
                                   Route Planning Tools

 SECTION I – ONLINE RESOURCES
   B-1. There are many online resources available to assist with route planning in the mountains. It is important
   to note that these resources are not secure. Therefore, they should never be used for operational planning.
   They are an excellent resource for conducting mountaineering training off military installations.
   B-2. Online resources are an excellent tool to use while gaining experience training in mountainous
   environments to further develop as a military mountaineer. These resources will help develop solid
   information-gathering habits. This collection must go beyond standard map reconnaissance. It allows
   Soldiers to gather important information that would not otherwise be discovered from a map sheet.
   B-3. These resources when combined with solid map reconnaissance are vital to aid in safe navigation and
   information gathering. This will enable Soldiers to create the most accurate picture of the terrain and
   environment in which they are about to step foot in. They are also essential in mitigating the risk associated
   in the pursuit of the highly demanding training required to become a proficient military mountaineer.
   B-4. See TC 3-25.26 for more information on general route planning strategies.

NAVIGATIONAL RESOURCES
   B-5. Numerous free web-based mapping resources combine detailed maps and excellent route planning
   tools in a user-friendly format. Many allow users to create printable maps that also show the route, distance,
   and change in elevation. These programs have slope-shading functions, which help to easily identify steeper
   sections of terrain. This is particularly useful when identifying avalanche hazards. Soldiers should seek out
   digital mapping resources to aid in their planning, hazard assessment, and route creation.

CLIMBING ROUTE INFORMATION
   B-6. From a unit training perspective, the two resources listed in paragraphs B-7 and B-8 can aid leaders in
   the planning process by identifying specific areas that meet realistic training objectives. These resources
   provide leaders with information that helps prevent potentially dangerous situations or exposing Soldiers to
   training that is more aggressive than they can conduct safely.
   B-7. Mountain Project is the most popular free online climbing guidebook. The website has detailed
   information about rock-climbing routes all over the world. The mobile, app-based program allows
   mountaineers to view information on the go. It is a comprehensive collection of information, but it is user
   submitted. Using a current guidebook for a specific climbing area can still be the most reliable resource.
   B-8. Summit Post is an online-based mountaineering resource for information about hiking or climbing
   larger nontechnical and technical peaks. The nonprofit website has user-submitted trip reports and updated
   trail and route conditions. It is a great resource for planning expedition-style climbs for high-altitude
   mountaineering objectives. The website features a vast selection of mountains from around the world.

 SECTION II – OTHER RESOURCES
   B-9. Guidebooks, local climbing organizations, governmental and private land management organizations,
   and national alpine associations are all great additional resources for route planning and information gathering.
   B-10. There are many other additional resources available; it would be difficult to name them all. It is best
   to research the specific area in which Soldiers intend to travel and gather as much relevant and current
   information as possible. It is also important to use any resources available to research seasonal weather
   patterns, prevailing winds, and areas of potential flooding.

Appendix B



GUIDEBOOKS
      B-11. A guidebook is a publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information.
      Current local guidebooks are still the most comprehensive and useful tool for gathering information on a
      specific climbing route or mountain. They contain detailed instructions for getting to these remote areas
      including the approach to the climb or trailhead. They contain invaluable route information and are readily
      available for most established mountaineering training areas.

LOCAL CLIMBING ORGANIZATIONS
      B-12. When information is not readily available in guidebooks (such as when training overseas), it may be
      beneficial to contact a local climbing organization in the area. These organizations exist all over the world
      even in the most remote and unlikely locations. The local community can provide some of the most accurate
      and current information that may not be available anywhere else.

U.S. GOVERNMENT LAND MANAGEMENT AGENCIES
      B-13. The U.S. government manages millions of acres of public lands that are excellent training venues for
      military mountaineering training. Generally, most training areas are managed by the Bureau of Land
      Management, National Park Service, or U.S. Forest Service. Other outstanding areas fall under the
      management of a state government, such as the Adirondack Park in New York. Training on public lands can
      be a complicated process that varies from organization to organization. Units planning to train on public lands
      must contact the land management organization early in the planning process to determine requirements and
      restrictions. Often, some agencies require up to 9 months of lead time.

NONGOVERNMENTAL LAND MANAGEMENT ORGANIZATIONS
      B-14. Some outstanding training areas such as the Shawangunk Mountain range in New York and New Jersey
      are under the management of private, nongovernmental land management, or conservation organizations. As
      with federal and state land management agencies, training planners should research regulations and
      restrictions on group and military use of the training area and contact the managing organization early in the
      planning process to ensure success in the training event.

 SECTION III – TIME-DISTANCE ESTIMATION
      B-15. The time-distance method covered in chapter 7, table 7-2, page 148 is useful but very general. The
      Munter method described below affords planners more options to enhance their time-to-distance estimate.

THE MUNTER METHOD
      B-16. The Munter method is an accurate method of calculating route times during planning. It is the most
      accepted time-distance formula used by mountain professionals and guides. The Munter method combines
      map distance (kilometers) and elevation change (meters) into a unit of time (hours), then it is divided by an
      estimated movement rate (kilometers per hour) using various terrain conditions. This method allows the user
      the ability to break the movement up into different legs and account for different modes of travel. This method
      is simple to calculate and allows the planner increased flexibility to account for the various paces, changes
      in elevation, increased loads, and environmental conditions that exist in mountainous terrain.
      B-17. When planning, create a route table like the one in the examples below. (See figure B-1 and figure B-3,
      page 392.) The Munter method form below is meant to be a baseline tool for route planners. It begins with
      basic data about the weather, situation, hazards, load, and group assessment to set the framework for decision
      making. These pieces of data paint a picture of the situation and enable the planner to properly account for
      terrain difficulties, rest breaks, and other additional time requirements. A sample calculation is provided as
      well as a baseline table to begin determining route legs. As planners become more experienced in the terrain,
      the table can be customized to their unit abilities.

      FORMULA                                UNITS                                     MODIFIERS
   # of units x 60 min    1 unit for every 1 km of travel                 Descending:         Ascending:
         Modifier         1 unit for every 100 meters change (gain        Walking 6           Walking 4

                     Figure B-2. Munter calculation formula and modifier guide

   B-20. For each route leg, add one unit for every kilometer of distance. A half kilometer would be 0.5 units.
   Then find the change in elevation between points and add 1 unit for every 100 meters change (gain or loss)
   in elevation during the leg. Add the number of units together for the specific leg.
   B-21. Next, multiply this number by 60 (minutes).
   B-22. Identify if it is an ascent or decent of the terrain. Then select the appropriate modifier to describe the
   type of movement through the terrain.
   B-23. If moving at a patrolling pace, use the bushwacking modifier. Walking should be considered movement
   on a trail or in open unrestrictive terrain.
   B-24. Scree or boulder fields should be considered bushwhacking. Movement in deep snow without flotation
   from skis or snowshoes should be considered bushwhacking.
   B-25. With the modifier identified, the formula can now be calculated. The result is time in minutes to move
   that leg.
   B-26. Complete the route table to estimate the total movement time. Keep in mind this method does not
   account for any halts in movement, recon, or other operational tasks associated with a patrol. (See figure B-3,
   page 392.)

      B-27. Calculate travel time from point X to point Y:
          • Determine units—there is a 500-meters elevation gain (5 units) and a travel distance of 3.5
              (3.5 units). Therefore, the total units for this leg are 8.5. Record in appropriate box in chart.
          • Determine raw travel time—8.5 units are then multiplied by 60 minutes, yielding 510 minutes.
          • Determine adjusted travel time—this movement involves significant ascent, and the method of
              travel is walking. Therefore, a modifier of 4 is used.

              Note. This example assumes the movement is in unrestrictive terrain.
          •     The raw travel time (510 minutes) is then divided by the modifier (4) to yield an actual projected
                leg time of 127.5 minutes (or 2 hours and 8 minutes). Record in appropriate box in chart.
          •     Determine approximate point arrival time—add the actual projected leg time (2 hours and 8 minutes)
                to the start time for the leg. Record in appropriate box in chart.
      B-28. Calculate travel time from point Y to point Z:
          • Determine units—there are 600 meters of elevation loss (6 units) and a travel distance of
              4 kilometers (4 units). Therefore, the total units for this leg are 10. Record in appropriate box in
              chart.
          • Determine raw travel time—10 units are then multiplied by 60 minutes, yielding 600 minutes.
          • Determine adjusted travel time—this movement involves a significant descent; the method of travel
              is walking. Therefore, a modifier of 6 is used.

              Note. This example assumes the movement is in unrestrictive terrain.
          •     The raw travel time (600 minutes) is then divided by the modifier (6) to yield an actual projected
                leg time of 100 minutes (or 1 hour and 40 minutes). Record in appropriate box in chart.
          •     Determine approximate point arrival time—add the actual projected leg time (1 hour and
                40 minutes) to the start time for the leg. Record in appropriate box in chart.

NORTHERN WARFARE TRAINING CENTER METHOD
      B-29. This technique was developed specifically for military mountaineers:
          • 4 kilometers per hour flat terrain. 2 to 3 for elevation.
          • 1 hour per 300 meters (1,000 feet) elevation gain.
          • 1 hour per 400 to 600 meters (1,600 feet) elevation loss.
          • + 10 minutes per kilometer for every 20 pounds over 50 pounds.

 SECTION I – SAFETY STANDARDS
   C-1. The UIAA Safety Commission develops and maintains safety standards for mountaineering
   equipment. They are an independent safety commission recognized by 60 manufacturers and certify over
   1,800 mountaineering products sold worldwide. Manufacturers must meet the standards set forth by the
   UIAA to be certified.

   definitions differ, (Army) precedes the definition. Terms for which TC 3-97.61 is the proponent
   are marked with an asterisk (*). The proponent publication for other terms is listed in
   parentheses after the definition. The majority of terms are defined IAW current common usage
   across the mountaineering community.

  SECTION II – TERMS
*advanced military mountaineer
       A Soldier who has graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer Course and at least one of the
       Advanced Military Mountaineer courses. An advanced military mountaineer has been trained in
       advanced mountaineering techniques and is also known as a level 2 mountaineer.
*aid climbing
         Climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed
         protection is used to make upward progress.
*assault climber
         A role assigned to a Soldier or team during tactical operations who is responsible for the location and
         establishment of technical routes in class 3 or higher terrain; ideally, a level 2 mountaineer.
*basic military mountaineer
        A Soldier who graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer Course. Basic military mountaineers
        have been trained in basic mountaineering techniques, such as fundamental mobility skills necessary to
        move safely and efficiently in mountainous terrain, and are also known as level 1 military
        mountaineers.
*belay
         A system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier’s fall should one occur.




400                                                   TC 3-97.61                              26 November 2025
                                                                                                       Glossary



*bolt
          A type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft
          attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached.
*brake strand
        The strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends.
carabiner
        A D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a
        connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope.
*cold-weather injury
        Any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions.
*coil
          A secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling.
couloir
          Narrow snow- or ice-filled gully.
dynamic rope
       Kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from
       fall injuries.
fall protection
         Any anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber
         falls, should a fall occur.
friction hitch
         A type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is
         applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned.
guidebook
       A publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information.
gully
          A channel caused by erosion, especially by water running down a slope; it is generally narrower and
          steeper than a draw.
hands-free backup
        A rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that prevent a load from falling
        should control of a brake strand be lost.
hauling system
        A technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that
        generates increased mechanical advantage and captures progress.
high-strength tie off
        A single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability,
        using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to
        itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners.
installation rope
          The primary load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system.
kernmantle rope
      A rope constructed with a load-bearing core of twisted synthetic fibers and a protective outer sheath of
      interwoven synthetic fibers.




26 November 2025                                 TC 3-97.61                                              401
Glossary



knot
         The fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the
         process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes referred to as a “hard knot” since its condition will
         remain intact until actively untied.
*lead climbing
         Climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall
         protection with a belayer located below.
*lead climber
         The first climber to negotiate a route, for whom a top belay is not possible, and who assumes the most
         risk of injury in a fall.
*load management
       The act or strategy of planning and packing loads to reduce negative impacts on Soldier physical
       performance.
*lowering system
        A technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion
        using friction hitches or mechanical devices.
*master military mountaineer
        A Soldier extensively trained and experienced with mountaineering techniques who the commander
        appoints to serve as a subject matter expert. Master military mountaineers are graduates of the Basic
        Military Mountaineer Course and Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. They possess all the skills
        of the advanced military mountaineer and have extensive practical experience in a variety of mountain
        environments in both winter and summer conditions.
*mechanical advantage
       Reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific
       rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage.
multipoint anchor
        More than one fixed object joined with technical rigging to form an anchor system capable of
        suspending the weight or arresting the fall of an attached load.
natural anchor
        A natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be
        secured, and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an
        attached load.
pitch
         A section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a
         standard rope length (60 meters).
prolonged field care
        The continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that
        role of care. (JP 4-02)
redundancy (in rigging)
       The condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system
       failing.
safety knot
         A backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose.
scrambling
        The act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques
        but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques.




402                                                 TC 3-97.61                                 26 November 2025
                                                                                                          Glossary



self-equalizing anchor
         A multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor component to a shared
         attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull changes
         during use.
*simul-climbing
        A belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope
        which runs through the fall protection.
snowpack
       The entire mass of snow covering a given area of terrain.
static rope
         Kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and
         anchor systems construction.
*technical route
        A route through steep or broken mountainous terrain that presents significant risk of fall injury and
        requires special movement techniques or ropes to ensure adequate safety for Soldiers moving
        through it.
*vertical danger area
         Steep terrain that significantly restricts a unit’s ability to maneuver, thereby putting the unit at
         significant tactical disadvantage should enemy contact be made while moving through the VDA.
